And it has been said: in the speech there is a fronting and deferring, and the estimate is: He sent down upon His servant the Book, upright, and did not make for Him crookedness. Then He, glory be to Him, wished to explain what He had summarised in His saying ﴿qayyiman﴾, so He said: ﴿to warn of severe punishment﴾. The one warned is omitted for knowledge of him together with the intention of generality; the meaning is: to warn the disbelievers.

The ﴿ba's (بَأْسًا)﴾ means punishment, and the meaning of ﴿min ladunhu﴾ is: proceeding from Him, descending from His presence.

Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim that he recited ﴿min ladunihi﴾ (مِن لَدُنِهِ) with a hint of the dammah on the dal, and with a kasra on the nun and the ha'. This is the dialect of the Kilab.

Abu Zayd narrated from all the readers the fatha on the lam, the damma on the dal, and sukun on the nun (مِن لَدُنْهُ). ﴿And gives good news to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾: it has been read ﴿yubashshiru﴾ with tashdid and with takhfif, and the relative clause was given the same relative clause mentioned earlier, because the basis of the acceptance of deeds is faith. ﴿That they will have a good reward﴾, which is Paradise, while they are ﴿remaining therein﴾, meaning: in that reward, ﴿forever﴾, meaning: a lasting stay with no cessation. The placing of the warning before the good news is to show complete concern for restraining the disbelievers.

Then He repeated the warning and mentioned the one warned specifically, and omitted what is warned of, which is the severe punishment, since it had already been mentioned. He said: ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ They are the Jews, the Christians, and some of the disbelievers of Quraysh, who say that the angels are the daughters of Allah. So He, glory be to Him, first mentioned a universal proposition, which is the warning of disbelievers in general, then He followed it with a specific proposition which is a part of the particulars of that universal, to draw attention to it being the greatest of the particulars of that universal. This indicates that attributing a son to Allah, glory be to Him, is the most hideous kind of disbelief.

﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾, meaning: of the son, or of Allah taking him. The ﴿min (مِن)﴾ is extra for emphasis of the negation, and the clause is in a place of accusative as a state, or it is a new sentence; the meaning is: they have no knowledge of that at all. ﴿Nor did their fathers﴾ have knowledge; rather, in this claim of theirs they were in error, and their children imitated them, so they all went astray. ﴿Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾: the accusative of ﴿kalimatan (كَلِمَةً)﴾ is as a specification (tamyiz), and it has been read in the nominative as the subject.

Al-Farra' said: That word was great as a word.

Al-Zajjaj said: Their statement was great as a word, and what is meant by this word is their saying: "Allah has taken a son."

Then He described the word with His saying ﴿that comes out of their mouths﴾, and the benefit of this description is to magnify their audacity in uttering it. What comes out of the mouth is only mere breath, but since letters and sounds are qualities subsisting in the breath, He attributed to the state what belongs to the place. Then He increased in disparaging what had occurred from them and said: ﴿they say nothing but a lie﴾, meaning: they say nothing but a lie with no room for truth in it in any way.

Then He consoled His Messenger (ﷺ) with His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their footsteps.﴾ Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: al-bakhʿ (البَخْعُ) is exertion.

Al-Kisa'i said: I exhausted the land by farming when you make it weak through continuous ploughing, and the man exhausted himself when he wore it out.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: its meaning is: destroying yourself, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah: "O you, the one whom grief has destroyed (al-bakhi' al-wajd) himself." So the meaning according to these statements is: perhaps you would exhaust yourself, or weaken it, or destroy it, over their footsteps, meaning after their departure and after their turning away and aversion, ﴿if they do not believe in this message﴾, meaning: the Qur'an. The answer of the condition is omitted, and what precedes it indicates it.

It has been read with fatha on the ﴿an (أنْ)﴾, meaning: because they did not believe, ﴿out of grief (asafan)﴾, meaning: anger and sorrow. It is either an object of purpose or a verbal noun in the place of a state. So said al-Zajjaj.

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾: this sentence is a new beginning.

The meaning is: Indeed, We have made what is on the earth, of what is fit to be an adornment for it, of animals, plants, and inanimate things, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He it is who created for you all that is on the earth﴾. The accusative of ﴿zinatan (زِينَةً)﴾ is that it is the second object of ﴿ja'ala (جَعَلَ)﴾. The lam in ﴿that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ is connected to ﴿ja'alna (جَعَلْنا)﴾, and it is either for purpose or for consequence. What is meant by the trial is that He, glory be to Him, treats them with a treatment which, if it came from other than Him, would be of the kind of trial and examination.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Ayyuhum (أيُّهم)﴾ is raised as the subject, except that its form is the form of a question, and the meaning is: that We may examine: is this one better in deed, or that one? Al-Hasan said: ﴿ayyuhum (أيُّهم)﴾ means: which of them is more ascetic. Muqatil said: which of them is most righteous in what he has been given of knowledge.

Then He, glory be to Him, informed that He will annihilate and destroy all of that, so He said: ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it into barren dust (sa'idan juruzan)﴾, meaning: indeed, We will make what is upon it of this adornment, at the end of the life of this world, into dust.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-sa'id (الصَّعِيدُ) is the level of the earth.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is the road which has no vegetation in it.

Al-Farra' said: al-juruz (الجُرُزُ) is the land in which there is no vegetation. From their saying: a woman who is jurraz (جُرازٌ) when she is a great eater; a sword which is jurraz when it is cutting off completely; and the locust, the sheep and the camels "jarazat" the land when they have eaten what is on it.

Dhu al-Rummah said: "The pressing and the grazing (al-ijraz) have emptied what is in their bellies."

The meaning of the structure is: Do not grieve, O Muhammad, over what has happened from these people of denial. Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for the testing of their deeds, and indeed, We will remove that at the completion of the life of this world, and We will recompense them: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

Al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on Surah 18, verses 1–8 (part 2 of 2):

It has been related by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh, through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who sent down to His servant the Book﴾ (the verse), that he said: He sent down the Book as "upright" (ʿadlan qayyiman), ﴿and has not made in it any deviance﴾ meaning, ambiguity (multabisan).

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Dahhak regarding (qayyiman) that he said: "Straight" (mustaqiman).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding (min ladunhu) that it means: from Him (min ʿindihi).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding (hasanan), meaning Paradise, ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾. He said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Ibn Mardawayh also related, "from Ibn Abbas, who said: ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabiʿah, Abu Jahl, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib and Abu al-Bukhturi gathered with a group of the Quraysh, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been deeply grieved by what he saw of his people's opposition to him and their rejection of the counsel he brought, which saddened him greatly. Thereupon Allah, glorified is He, sent down: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him regarding (bakhiʿun nafsaka) that it means: "Killing yourself" (qatilun nafsaka).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid the like of this, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi the like of this.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding (asafan) that he said: "Distress" (jazʿan).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding (asafan) that he said: "Sorrow" (huznan).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related, through the chain of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is upon the earth an adornment for it﴾, that he said: "The men."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from his own statement, the like of this.

Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in al-Ibanah related, through the chain of Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, that he said: "The scholars are the adornment of the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan who said: They are the men who worship and labor for Allah through obedience.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Tarikh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Umar who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿That He may test you [as to] which of you is best in deed﴾. I said: 'What is the meaning of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'That He may test you as to which of you is best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah who said: "to test them" (liyakhtabirahum), ﴿which of them is best in deed﴾: "which of them is most complete in intellect."

He related from al-Hasan, ﴿which of them is best in deed﴾, who said: "The one most abstaining from this world," and he also related from al-Thawri who said: "The most ascetic of them in this world."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed, We will make what is upon it a barren wasteland (saʿidan juruzan)﴾, that he said: "He destroys everything and annihilates it."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah who said: "The saʿid is the dust, and the mountains in which there is no crop."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan who said: "By juruz he means the ruined."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 18, verses 9–16:

﴿Or did you think...﴾ Here "am" (أم) is the disconnected particle (al-muntaqi'a, the particle that begins a new topic), estimated to be equivalent to "bal" (بل, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza according to the majority of grammarians, and to "bal" alone according to some. The implied sense is "Rather, did you think..." or "Rather, you thought...". Its meaning is the transition from one topic to another, not the cancellation of the first and turning away from it, which is the basic meaning of "bal."

The meaning is this: when the people were astonished by the story of the Companions of the Cave and asked the Messenger about it as a test, the Exalted said: "Rather, did you suppose, O Muhammad, that they were only a wonder among Our signs? Do not think that, for all of Our signs are a wonder. Whoever is able to make what is on the earth an adornment for it, to test people, and then to reduce what is on it to barren dust as though it had not flourished yesterday, is not to be thought incapable of His power, protection and mercy toward a particular group, even if their story is extraordinary and beyond custom, for the signs of God the Exalted are like that and greater than that."

"Wonder" (عجبا) is in the accusative as the predicate of "kana" (كان), meaning "possessing wonder," or it is described as wonder for emphasis. "Among Our signs" (من آياتنا) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (حال).

﴿When the youths took refuge...﴾ This is a temporal clause governed by "hasibta" (you thought), or by an estimated verb, namely "remember" (اذكر). That is, they went to it and made it their refuge. "Al-fityah" (the youths) are the Companions of the Cave. "Al-kahf" is a wide cave in a mountain; if it is small it is called a ghar (غار).

As for "al-Raqim": Ka'b and al-Suddi said it is the name of the town from which the Companions of the Cave came out. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said it is a tablet of stone or lead on which their names were inscribed, placed at the entrance of the cave. Al-Farra' said: "It is reported that it was only called 'raqim' because their names were written (marqumah) on it." "Al-raqm" means writing. Something similar is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. From this is the saying of al-'Ajjaj in one of his rajaz poems: "And my resting place is the Mushaf, the Raqim." It is also said that al-Raqim is the name of their dog, or the name of the valley in which they were, or the name of the mountain in which the cave was.

Al-Zajjaj said: God the Exalted informed us that the story of the Companions of the Cave is not the most wondrous of His signs, because the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is more wondrous than the story of the Companions of the Cave.

﴿They said: "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself..."﴾ That is, from Your presence. "Min" (من) here indicates origin and is connected to "ayatina" (Our signs), or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause. The nunation in "rahmah" (mercy) is either for magnification or for variety. The fronting of "min ladunka" (from Yourself) indicates exclusivity: a mercy specifically from the treasuries of Your mercy, which is forgiveness in the Hereafter, safety from enemies and provision in this world. ﴿And prepare for us from our affair a right course...﴾ That is, set right for us, from your saying "hayya'tu al-amr fa-tahayya'a" (I prepared the matter and it became prepared). "Our affair" is the matter they were in, namely their separation from the disbelievers. "Rashad" (right course) is the opposite of misguidance. "Min" here indicates beginning, and it may also be a partitive or a "tajrid" (abstraction) as in your saying "I saw from you a right course." The fronting of the two prepositional phrases is for emphasis.

﴿So We struck upon their ears...﴾ The commentators said: "We put them to sleep." The meaning is: We closed their ears with a deep sleep that prevents hearing sounds. The object is omitted, that is, We struck upon their ears a veil, comparing the heavy slumber that prevents sounds from reaching the ears to the drawing of a veil over them. "In the cave" (في الكهف) is an adverbial phrase governing "We struck." "Years" (سنين) is accusative as a time adverb, and "a number" (عددا) is an adjective of "years," meaning years of a counted number, either as a verbal noun or with the sense of "counted." From describing the years with "a number" one derives the sense of abundance. Al-Zajjaj said: when a thing is small its quantity is understood, so it does not need counting; if it is large, it needs to be counted. It is also said that the sense derived is that of few, because much is little with God: ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

﴿Then We raised them up...﴾ That is, We awoke them from that sleep, "so that We may know," that is, so that what We know may become manifest. It is also read in the form with the verb in the third person, in the active voice, following the technique of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). "Which of the two parties" (أي الحزبين) is a subject whose verb of knowing is suspended because of the interrogative sense in "ayy". Its predicate is "ahsa" (he has counted), which is a past-tense verb. It is said that the knowledge which is made the cause of the awakening is, by metaphor, testing, so the meaning is: We awakened them to treat them as one who tests them. But the better view is what we have mentioned, that the meaning is the manifestation of God's known to His servants. The "two parties" are the two groups, believers and disbelievers, among the Companions of the Cave, who differed about the length of their stay.

The meaning of "ahsa" is "most precise in reckoning." It seems there was a dispute among them about the length of their stay in the cave, so God awakened them to make clear to them this matter and to show who had reckoned accurately among those who had not. "Ma" in "for what they stayed" is a verbal-noun particle, that is, "in counting their stay." It is also said that the lam is superfluous and "ma" means "what." "Amadan" (period) is a specification (tamyiz). "Amad" means the limit. It is also said that "ahsa" is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), a superlative form.

This was refuted on the ground that it contradicts what is established in the science of grammar (i'rab), and that what occurs as irregular cannot be used as a model, as in the expressions "more bankrupt than Ibn al-Mudhallaq" and "more hostile than mange." It was answered that the elative formed from a derived verb (al-mazid) is a regular, consistent form according to Sibawayh and Ibn 'Usfur.

It is also said that the two parties are the Companions of the Cave themselves, who differed after they awoke about how long they had stayed. It is also said that the Companions of the Cave are one party and their companions are another party. Al-Farra' said: two groups of Muslims at the time of the Companions of the Cave differed about the length of their stay.

﴿We relate to you their story with truth...﴾ This is the beginning of the detailed account of what was summarized in His saying "When the youths took refuge." That is, We inform you of their news "with truth," meaning We have narrated it truthfully, or as one clothed in truth. ﴿Indeed they were youths...﴾ That is, young men. The clause "who believed in their Lord" is an attribute of "youths." The sentence is independent, presupposing a question. "Al-fityah" is the plural of paucity. "We increased them in guidance" by firmness and success. Within this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

﴿And We strengthened their hearts...﴾ That is, We fortified them with patience in forsaking family and homeland and parting from friends and companions. ﴿When they stood up...﴾ The temporal clause is governed by "We strengthened."

The exegetes differed about this standing in several statements. It is said: they gathered outside the city without prior appointment, and a man among them, the oldest of the group, said: "I find something in myself: indeed my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." They said: "We too find this in ourselves," and they all stood up and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." This was reported by Mujahid.

Most exegetes said: there was a tyrannical king called Decius (Diqyanus), who used to call people to worship idols. God strengthened these youths, preserved them, and they stood before him and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." 'Ata' and Muqatil said: they said this when they arose from sleep. ﴿We shall never call upon any god besides Him...﴾ That is, we shall never worship any other deity besides God, neither as a partner nor independently. ﴿For then we would have uttered an enormity...﴾ That is, a saying of excess, or a saying which is itself excess, for emphasis in describing it by the verbal noun. The "lam" is the lam of oath preparation (al-muwattiʾah lil-qasam). "Shatat" means exaggeration and transgression of the limit.

Al-A'sha ibn Qays said:
"Will you desist, when he who forbids those of excess (is not heeded)? Like the spear-thrust in which oil and wick go." [Translation of the verse's sense.]

﴿These our people have taken gods besides Him...﴾ "These" is the subject, and its predicate is "have taken." "Our people" is an explanatory apposition. In this statement is a sense of denunciation, and in pointing to them is a belittling of them. ﴿Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?﴾ That is, why do they not bring a manifest proof suitable for being relied upon? ﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents against God a lie?﴾ Who claims that He has a partner in worship. That is, no one is more unjust than him.

﴿And when you have separated from them...﴾ That is, you have parted from them and withdrawn from them to one side, that is, from those who worship idols. The statement ﴿and what they worship other than God﴾ is conjoined to the accusative pronoun (الضمير المنصوب). "Ma" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal-noun particle, meaning: "and when you have separated from them and from what they worship, or from what they worship." "Illa Allah" (except God) is an exceptive clause, either disconnected (muntaqi') on the assumption that they worshipped only idols, or connected (muttasil) on the assumption that they associated these with God in worship. It is also said that it is a parenthetical statement, a report from God the Exalted about the youths that they did not worship other than God, in which case "ma" here is negative.

﴿So retreat to the cave...﴾ That is, go to it and make it your refuge. Al-Farra' said: it is the answer (جواب) of "idh" (when), meaning: go to it and make it your refuge. It is also said: it is an indication of its answer, meaning: when you have separated from them in belief, then separate from them physically, and when you wish to separate from them, do so by taking refuge in the cave. ﴿Your Lord will spread for you of His mercy...﴾ That is, He will extend and widen it. ﴿And will prepare for you of your affair a means of support (mirfaq)...﴾ That is, He will make easy and facilitate for you, out of your affair which you are about, a means of support. "Mirfaq" may be read with a fatha or a kasra on the mim; both are dialects, and both have been recited. It is derived from "irtifaq," which means benefit. It is said that the fatha is more analogical, and the kasra more common.

Al-Farra' said: most Arabs use the kasra in the mim both for "the matter" (al-amr) and for "the elbow of a person" (mirfaq al-insan), though Arabs may also use the fatha in both, so they are two dialects. It seems that those who used the fatha wanted to distinguish between the mirfaq of a matter and the mirfaq of a person.

Al-Kisa'i said: the kasra is used for the elbow of the arm. It is also said: the mirfaq with a kasra is that by which you are assisted, and the marfaq with a fatha is the advantageous matter. The meaning here is what they are supported by and benefit from upon its attainment. The fronting in both places indicates exclusivity.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-Raqim" is the book.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-'Awfi from him, who said: "al-Raqim" is a valley below Palestine near Ayla. The two narrators from Ibn 'Abbas are weak.

Ibn Jarir reported through Ibn Juraij from him, also, who said: it is the mountain in which the cave is.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: "By God, I do not know what al-Raqim is, a book or a building?" In another report from him through another chain, he said: "I asked Ka'b, and he said: it is the name of the town from which they came out."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Anas, who said: "al-Raqim" is the dog.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿they were among Our signs a wonder﴾: he said: what I have given you of knowledge, the Sunnah and the Book, is better than the matter of the Companions of the Cave and al-Raqim.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying ﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾: he said: We put them to sleep.

﴿Then We raised them up that We might know which of the two parties﴾ from among the people of the youths, the people of guidance and the people of misguidance, ﴿was most precise in counting what they remained﴾. That is because they recorded the day on which they went out, the month and the year.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning His saying ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾: he said: sincerity.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada concerning His saying ﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾: he said: with faith. And concerning His saying ﴿For then we would have uttered an enormity﴾: he said: a lie.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, who said: injustice.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani concerning His saying ﴿And when you have separated from them and what they worship other than God﴾: he said: the people of the youths used to worship God and worship with Him various gods; the youths separated from the worship of those gods but did not separate from the worship of God.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada concerning the verse, who said: it is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "and what they worship apart from God," and this is its explanation.

Al-Zajjaj said: God the Exalted informed us that the story of the Companions of the Cave is not the most wondrous of His signs, because the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them is more wondrous than the story of the Companions of the Cave.

﴿They said: "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself..."﴾ That is, from Your presence. "Min" (من) here indicates origin and is connected to "ayatina" (Our signs), or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause. The nunation in "rahmah" (mercy) is either for magnification or for variety. The fronting of "min ladunka" (from Yourself) indicates exclusivity: a mercy specifically from the treasuries of Your mercy, which is forgiveness in the Hereafter, safety from enemies and provision in this world. ﴿And prepare for us from our affair a right course...﴾ That is, set right for us, from your saying "hayya'tu al-amr fa-tahayya'a" (I prepared the matter and it became prepared). "Our affair" is the matter they were in, namely their separation from the disbelievers. "Rashad" (right course) is the opposite of misguidance. "Min" here indicates beginning, and it may also be a partitive or a "tajrid" (abstraction) as in your saying "I saw from you a right course." The fronting of the two prepositional phrases is for emphasis.

﴿So We struck upon their ears...﴾ The commentators said: "We put them to sleep." The meaning is: We closed their ears with a deep sleep that prevents hearing sounds. The object is omitted, that is, We struck upon their ears a veil, comparing the heavy slumber that prevents sounds from reaching the ears to the drawing of a veil over them. "In the cave" (في الكهف) is an adverbial phrase governing "We struck." "Years" (سنين) is accusative as a time adverb, and "a number" (عددا) is an adjective of "years," meaning years of a counted number, either as a verbal noun or with the sense of "counted." From describing the years with "a number" one derives the sense of abundance. Al-Zajjaj said: when a thing is small its quantity is understood, so it does not need counting; if it is large, it needs to be counted. It is also said that the sense derived is that of few, because much is little with God: ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ [al-Hajj: 47].

﴿Then We raised them up...﴾ That is, We awoke them from that sleep, "so that We may know," that is, so that what We know may become manifest. It is also read in the form with the verb in the third person, in the active voice, following the technique of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). "Which of the two parties" (أي الحزبين) is a subject whose verb of knowing is suspended because of the interrogative sense in "ayy". Its predicate is "ahsa" (he has counted), which is a past-tense verb. It is said that the knowledge which is made the cause of the awakening is, by metaphor, testing, so the meaning is: We awakened them to treat them as one who tests them. But the better view is what we have mentioned, that the meaning is the manifestation of God's known to His servants. The "two parties" are the two groups, believers and disbelievers, among the Companions of the Cave, who differed about the length of their stay.

The meaning of "ahsa" is "most precise in reckoning." It seems there was a dispute among them about the length of their stay in the cave, so God awakened them to make clear to them this matter and to show who had reckoned accurately among those who had not. "Ma" in "for what they stayed" is a verbal-noun particle, that is, "in counting their stay." It is also said that the lam is superfluous and "ma" means "what." "Amadan" (period) is a specification (tamyiz). "Amad" means the limit. It is also said that "ahsa" is an elative (af'al al-tafdil), a superlative form.

This was refuted on the ground that it contradicts what is established in the science of grammar (i'rab), and that what occurs as irregular cannot be used as a model, as in the expressions "more bankrupt than Ibn al-Mudhallaq" and "more hostile than mange." It was answered that the elative formed from a derived verb (al-mazid) is a regular, consistent form according to Sibawayh and Ibn 'Usfur.

It is also said that the two parties are the Companions of the Cave themselves, who differed after they awoke about how long they had stayed. It is also said that the Companions of the Cave are one party and their companions are another party. Al-Farra' said: two groups of Muslims at the time of the Companions of the Cave differed about the length of their stay.

﴿We relate to you their story with truth...﴾ This is the beginning of the detailed account of what was summarized in His saying "When the youths took refuge." That is, We inform you of their news "with truth," meaning We have narrated it truthfully, or as one clothed in truth. ﴿Indeed they were youths...﴾ That is, young men. The clause "who believed in their Lord" is an attribute of "youths." The sentence is independent, presupposing a question. "Al-fityah" is the plural of paucity. "We increased them in guidance" by firmness and success. Within this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

﴿And We strengthened their hearts...﴾ That is, We fortified them with patience in forsaking family and homeland and parting from friends and companions. ﴿When they stood up...﴾ The temporal clause is governed by "We strengthened."

The exegetes differed about this standing in several statements. It is said: they gathered outside the city without prior appointment, and a man among them, the oldest of the group, said: "I find something in myself: indeed my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." They said: "We too find this in ourselves," and they all stood up and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." This was reported by Mujahid.

Most exegetes said: there was a tyrannical king called Decius (Diqyanus), who used to call people to worship idols. God strengthened these youths, preserved them, and they stood before him and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." 'Ata' and Muqatil said: they said this when they arose from sleep. ﴿We shall never call upon any god besides Him...﴾ That is, we shall never worship any other deity besides God, neither as a partner nor independently. ﴿For then we would have uttered an enormity...﴾ That is, a saying of excess, or a saying which is itself excess, for emphasis in describing it by the verbal noun. The "lam" is the lam of oath preparation (al-muwattiʾah lil-qasam). "Shatat" means exaggeration and transgression of the limit.

Al-A'sha ibn Qays said:
"Will you desist, when he who forbids those of excess (is not heeded)? Like the spear-thrust in which oil and wick go." [Translation of the verse's sense.]

﴿These our people have taken gods besides Him...﴾ "These" is the subject, and its predicate is "have taken." "Our people" is an explanatory apposition. In this statement is a sense of denunciation, and in pointing to them is a belittling of them. ﴿Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?﴾ That is, why do they not bring a manifest proof suitable for being relied upon? ﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents against God a lie?﴾ Who claims that He has a partner in worship. That is, no one is more unjust than him.

﴿And when you have separated from them...﴾ That is, you have parted from them and withdrawn from them to one side, that is, from those who worship idols. The statement ﴿and what they worship other than God﴾ is conjoined to the accusative pronoun (الضمير المنصوب). "Ma" is either a relative pronoun or a verbal-noun particle, meaning: "and when you have separated from them and from what they worship, or from what they worship." "Illa Allah" (except God) is an exceptive clause, either disconnected (muntaqi') on the assumption that they worshipped only idols, or connected (muttasil) on the assumption that they associated these with God in worship. It is also said that it is a parenthetical statement, a report from God the Exalted about the youths that they did not worship other than God, in which case "ma" here is negative.

﴿So retreat to the cave...﴾ That is, go to it and make it your refuge. Al-Farra' said: it is the answer (جواب) of "idh" (when), meaning: go to it and make it your refuge. It is also said: it is an indication of its answer, meaning: when you have separated from them in belief, then separate from them physically, and when you wish to separate from them, do so by taking refuge in the cave. ﴿Your Lord will spread for you of His mercy...﴾ That is, He will extend and widen it. ﴿And will prepare for you of your affair a means of support (mirfaq)...﴾ That is, He will make easy and facilitate for you, out of your affair which you are about, a means of support. "Mirfaq" may be read with a fatha or a kasra on the mim; both are dialects, and both have been recited. It is derived from "irtifaq," which means benefit. It is said that the fatha is more analogical, and the kasra more common.

Al-Farra' said: most Arabs use the kasra in the mim both for "the matter" (al-amr) and for "the elbow of a person" (mirfaq al-insan), though Arabs may also use the fatha in both, so they are two dialects. It seems that those who used the fatha wanted to distinguish between the mirfaq of a matter and the mirfaq of a person.

Al-Kisa'i said: the kasra is used for the elbow of the arm. It is also said: the mirfaq with a kasra is that by which you are assisted, and the marfaq with a fatha is the advantageous matter. The meaning here is what they are supported by and benefit from upon its attainment. The fronting in both places indicates exclusivity.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "al-Raqim" is the book.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through al-'Awfi from him, who said: "al-Raqim" is a valley below Palestine near Ayla. The two narrators from Ibn 'Abbas are weak.

Ibn Jarir reported through Ibn Juraij from him, also, who said: it is the mountain in which the cave is.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: "By God, I do not know what al-Raqim is, a book or a building?" In another report from him through another chain, he said: "I asked Ka'b, and he said: it is the name of the town from which they came out."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Anas, who said: "al-Raqim" is the dog.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿they were among Our signs a wonder﴾: he said: what I have given you of knowledge, the Sunnah and the Book, is better than the matter of the Companions of the Cave and al-Raqim.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij concerning His saying ﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾: he said: We put them to sleep.

﴿Then We raised them up that We might know which of the two parties﴾ from among the people of the youths, the people of guidance and the people of misguidance, ﴿was most precise in counting what they remained﴾. That is because they recorded the day on which they went out, the month and the year.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning His saying ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾: he said: sincerity.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada concerning His saying ﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾: he said: with faith. And concerning His saying ﴿For then we would have uttered an enormity﴾: he said: a lie.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, who said: injustice.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani concerning His saying ﴿And when you have separated from them and what they worship other than God﴾: he said: the people of the youths used to worship God and worship with Him various gods; the youths separated from the worship of those gods but did not separate from the worship of God.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada concerning the verse, who said: it is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "and what they worship apart from God," and this is its explanation.

The Shaykh (al-Shawkani) said regarding His saying, ﴿And you see the sun when it rises﴾, that Allah, glorified is He, began to explain their condition after they had sought refuge in the cave. ﴿Declines away﴾ (*tazawaru*): the people of Kufa read it by omitting the second *ta* of the reciprocal form. Ibn 'Amir read *tazawarru* (with the *ta* assimilated into the *za* and the form written with doubled *ra*). Al-Akhfash said: "The verb *izwirar* is not used in this meaning. One says only: *huwa muzawarrun 'anni*, meaning he is withdrawn (*munqabid*) from me."

The rest read it with a shadda on the *zay* and the assimilation of the *ta* of the reciprocal form after it has been made quiescent (*sukun*). *Tazawara* is derived from *al-zawar* with a *fatha* on the *waw*, which means inclining, and from it comes *zarahu*, meaning he inclined toward him. *Al-zawar* means inclining. So the meaning of the verse is that when the sun rises, it inclines and turns away ﴿from their cave﴾. The rajaz poet al-Kalbi said:

*Jaba al-mundā 'an hawānā azwar*

That is: leaning to the right, i.e., toward the right side, which is the direction called "right." The accusative of *dhāta* is adverbial (*zarf*).

﴿And when it sets, it passes them by on the left﴾. *Al-qard* means cutting off.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ubayda said: it turns away from them and leaves them. One says *qaradtu al-makān* meaning I turned away from the place. You say to your companion: "Did you pass by such-and-such a place?" and he replies: "I only *qaradtu* it," when he passed by it and went beyond it. The meaning is that when the sun rises, it inclines away from their cave to the right, i.e., the right side of the cave, and when it sets, it passes ﴿on the left﴾, i.e., the left side of the cave, without touching it.

Rather, it turns away from its direction to both sides. *Al-fajwa* is a wide open space. The clause ﴿and they were in an open space from it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The exegetes have two views on this clause. The first: that although they were in a place wide open and spacious throughout their day, the sun did not strike them at its rising or its setting, because Allah, glorified is He, had screened it from them.

The second: that the door of that cave was open toward the north side, so when the sun rose it was on the right of the cave, and when it set it was on its left. The first view is supported by His saying ﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾, for turning the sun away from them while the open space faces a place the sun normally reaches is more fitting to the meaning of its being a sign. It is also supported by the unrestricted wording of *al-fajwa* and its not being limited by specifying a direction. Something that shows *al-fajwa* means a wide place is the poet's saying:

*Albasta qawmaka makhzāh wa manqasa*
*Hattā ubīḥū wa khallaw fajwat al-dār*

Then He, glorified is He, praised them by His saying: ﴿Whom Allah guides, he is the guided one﴾, i.e., to the truth, the one who attains guidance, reaches right direction and success. ﴿And whom He leaves astray, you will never find for him a protecting friend who guides him﴾, i.e., a helper who guides him to the truth, such as Daqyanus and his companions.

Then He, glorified is He, related another aspect of their wondrous conditions, saying: ﴿And you would think them awake﴾. *Ayqāẓ* is the plural of *yaqiẓ*, with either a kasra or fatha on the *qaf*. ﴿While they were asleep﴾, i.e., sleeping; it is the plural of *rāqid*, like *quʿūd* for *qāʿid*.

It has been said: the cause of this supposition is that their eyes were open while they were sleeping. Al-Zajjaj said: because of how much they turned over. ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left﴾, i.e., We turn them in their sleep to both sides, so that the earth does not consume their bodies. ﴿And their dog stretched out its forelegs at the entrance﴾: this is a description of a past state, because the active participle does not govern when it has the meaning of the past, as established in the science of grammar (*ʿilm al-naḥw*).

Most of the exegetes said: they fled from their king by night, passing by a shepherd who had a dog, and the dog followed them.

Regarding *al-waṣīd* (the threshold/entrance), Abu 'Ubayd and Abu 'Ubayda said it is the courtyard of the door, and the exegetes said likewise. It was also said: the threshold. This was rejected on the grounds that a cave does not have a threshold or a door; rather, what is meant is that the dog was located at the threshold of the dwelling.

﴿If you had looked at them, you would have turned away from them in flight﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *firāran* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) with the sense of turning away, and *al-firār* means fleeing. ﴿And you would have been filled with dread﴾: it has been read with the doubling of the *lam* and with its lightening. ﴿From them﴾: *ruʿban* has been read with the *ʿayn* quiescent and with a *damma*, i.e., fear that fills the chest. The accusative of *ruʿban* is either as a specification (*tamyīz*) or as a second object. The cause of the dread is the awe that Allah clothed them with. It was also said: the length of their nails and hair, the largeness of their bodies, and the desolation of their place. This is refuted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day﴾, for that indicates that they did not find anything strange in their condition, nor did they perceive from their nails and hair anything indicating a long period.

﴿And thus We raised them up that they might question one another among themselves﴾. The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned before: that is, just as We did for them what We did of marvels, We raised them from their sleep. In this is a reminder of His power to cause death and resurrection together. Then He mentioned the matter for which He raised them, saying: ﴿that they might question one another among themselves﴾, i.e., that questioning, disagreement and dispute about the duration of their stay should occur among them, because of what follows from that: the revealing of the condition and the manifestation of the overwhelming power. Restricting it to the reason of questioning does not negate other reasons; He mentioned it singly because it entails all the other effects.

The clause ﴿A speaker among them said: How long have you remained?﴾ explains what came before it about the questioning, i.e., how long was the duration of your stay in sleep? They said this because they saw in themselves something other than what they were accustomed to. ﴿They said: We have remained a day or part of a day﴾: some of them answered the question of whoever asked among them. The exegetes said: they had entered the cave in the morning, and Allah, glorified is He, raised them at the end of the day, so they said "a day." Then when they saw the sun, they said "or part of a day," and some remnant of the day remained. A similar answer has passed in the story of 'Uzayr in al-Baqara.

﴿They said: Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾: the others said this statement, either as a method of inference, or it was an inspiration to them from Allah, glorified is He, meaning: you do not know the duration of your stay, and only Allah, glorified is He, knows it.

﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾: they turned away from discussing the duration of their stay and began on something else, as if the speaker among them had said: leave what you are discussing and turn to something else that concerns you. The *fa'* is for causation. *Al-wariq* is silver, whether minted or unminted.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read it with a kasra on the *ra'*. Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it with the *ra'* quiescent. It has also been read with a kasra on the *ra'* and the *qaf* assimilated into the *kaf*. Ibn Muhaysin read it with a kasra on the *waw* and the *ra'* quiescent.

In their carrying this silver with them is evidence that holding some of what a person needs does not contradict trust in Allah (*tawakkul*). *Al-madīna* is Daqsus, which was their city in which they lived, and it is said that today it is called Tarsus; so said al-Wahidi. ﴿Let him look to see which of them has the purest food﴾, i.e., let him see which of its people has the best food and the most lawful earnings, or the cheapest price. It was said: the pronoun may refer to the foods implied by the context, as one says: "Zayd, you are good as a father," though the father is Zayd; but this is far-fetched.

The verse was used as evidence for the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book, because most of the people of the city were disbelievers, and among them were people who concealed their faith. The reasoning is that food includes meat as it includes other things that are called food. ﴿And let him be gentle﴾: i.e., let him scrutinize carefully so that he is not recognized or defrauded, and the first meaning is the better. This is supported by ﴿and let him not make anyone aware of you﴾, i.e., let him not do anything that leads to awareness or causes it. This prohibition therefore emphasizes the command to gentleness.

Then He gave the reason for the preceding command and prohibition, saying: ﴿Indeed, if they gain power over you﴾, i.e., they find out about you and learn your location, meaning the people of the city, ﴿they will stone you﴾, i.e., kill you by stoning. This is the most vile of killings, for that was their custom, and for this reason it was singled out from among the kinds of killing. ﴿Or they will return you to their religion﴾, i.e., they will send you back to their creed in which you were before Allah guided you. Or the meaning of "return" here is "become," on the assumption that they had not been in their creed. The choice of the word *fī* (in) rather than *ilā* (to) indicates permanence. ﴿And you will never succeed then, ever﴾: *idhan* contains the sense of a condition, as if He said: if you return to their religion, then you will never succeed, ever, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿declines away﴾ that he said: it inclines. And regarding His saying ﴿passes them by﴾ he said: it leaves them.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿passes them by﴾ that he said: it leaves them. ﴿And they were in an open space from it﴾: he said: the inner place.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: *al-fajwa* is the empty space of the earth, and by the empty space he means the area of the earth.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and We turn them﴾ to the end of the verse that he said: six months on the right side, and six months on the left side.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding the verse that he said: so that the earth does not consume their flesh. (p-854)

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that the name of their dog was Qitmir.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan who said: its name was Qitmir.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿at the threshold﴾ that he said: at the courtyard.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: at the door.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His saying ﴿the purest food﴾ that he said: the most lawful slaughtered animal, and they used to slaughter for the idols (*al-ṭawāghīt*).

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿the purest food﴾: he meant the cleanest, because they used to slaughter for the idols.

The Shaykh (al-Shawkani) said regarding His saying, ﴿And you see the sun when it rises﴾, that Allah, glorified is He, began to explain their condition after they had sought refuge in the cave. ﴿Declines away﴾ (*tazawaru*): the people of Kufa read it by omitting the second *ta* of the reciprocal form. Ibn 'Amir read *tazawarru* (with the *ta* assimilated into the *za* and the form written with doubled *ra*). Al-Akhfash said: "The verb *izwirar* is not used in this meaning. One says only: *huwa muzawarrun 'anni*, meaning he is withdrawn (*munqabid*) from me."

The rest read it with a shadda on the *zay* and the assimilation of the *ta* of the reciprocal form after it has been made quiescent (*sukun*). *Tazawara* is derived from *al-zawar* with a *fatha* on the *waw*, which means inclining, and from it comes *zarahu*, meaning he inclined toward him. *Al-zawar* means inclining. So the meaning of the verse is that when the sun rises, it inclines and turns away ﴿from their cave﴾. The rajaz poet al-Kalbi said:

*Jaba al-mundā 'an hawānā azwar*

That is: leaning to the right, i.e., toward the right side, which is the direction called "right." The accusative of *dhāta* is adverbial (*zarf*).

﴿And when it sets, it passes them by on the left﴾. *Al-qard* means cutting off.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ubayda said: it turns away from them and leaves them. One says *qaradtu al-makān* meaning I turned away from the place. You say to your companion: "Did you pass by such-and-such a place?" and he replies: "I only *qaradtu* it," when he passed by it and went beyond it. The meaning is that when the sun rises, it inclines away from their cave to the right, i.e., the right side of the cave, and when it sets, it passes ﴿on the left﴾, i.e., the left side of the cave, without touching it.

Rather, it turns away from its direction to both sides. *Al-fajwa* is a wide open space. The clause ﴿and they were in an open space from it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The exegetes have two views on this clause. The first: that although they were in a place wide open and spacious throughout their day, the sun did not strike them at its rising or its setting, because Allah, glorified is He, had screened it from them.

The second: that the door of that cave was open toward the north side, so when the sun rose it was on the right of the cave, and when it set it was on its left. The first view is supported by His saying ﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾, for turning the sun away from them while the open space faces a place the sun normally reaches is more fitting to the meaning of its being a sign. It is also supported by the unrestricted wording of *al-fajwa* and its not being limited by specifying a direction. Something that shows *al-fajwa* means a wide place is the poet's saying:

*Albasta qawmaka makhzāh wa manqasa*
*Hattā ubīḥū wa khallaw fajwat al-dār*

Then He, glorified is He, praised them by His saying: ﴿Whom Allah guides, he is the guided one﴾, i.e., to the truth, the one who attains guidance, reaches right direction and success. ﴿And whom He leaves astray, you will never find for him a protecting friend who guides him﴾, i.e., a helper who guides him to the truth, such as Daqyanus and his companions.

Then He, glorified is He, related another aspect of their wondrous conditions, saying: ﴿And you would think them awake﴾. *Ayqāẓ* is the plural of *yaqiẓ*, with either a kasra or fatha on the *qaf*. ﴿While they were asleep﴾, i.e., sleeping; it is the plural of *rāqid*, like *quʿūd* for *qāʿid*.

It has been said: the cause of this supposition is that their eyes were open while they were sleeping. Al-Zajjaj said: because of how much they turned over. ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left﴾, i.e., We turn them in their sleep to both sides, so that the earth does not consume their bodies. ﴿And their dog stretched out its forelegs at the entrance﴾: this is a description of a past state, because the active participle does not govern when it has the meaning of the past, as established in the science of grammar (*ʿilm al-naḥw*).

Most of the exegetes said: they fled from their king by night, passing by a shepherd who had a dog, and the dog followed them.
