In their carrying this silver with them is evidence that holding some of what a person needs does not contradict trust in Allah (*tawakkul*). *Al-madīna* is Daqsus, which was their city in which they lived, and it is said that today it is called Tarsus; so said al-Wahidi. ﴿Let him look to see which of them has the purest food﴾, i.e., let him see which of its people has the best food and the most lawful earnings, or the cheapest price. It was said: the pronoun may refer to the foods implied by the context, as one says: "Zayd, you are good as a father," though the father is Zayd; but this is far-fetched.

The verse was used as evidence for the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book, because most of the people of the city were disbelievers, and among them were people who concealed their faith. The reasoning is that food includes meat as it includes other things that are called food. ﴿And let him be gentle﴾: i.e., let him scrutinize carefully so that he is not recognized or defrauded, and the first meaning is the better. This is supported by ﴿and let him not make anyone aware of you﴾, i.e., let him not do anything that leads to awareness or causes it. This prohibition therefore emphasizes the command to gentleness.

Then He gave the reason for the preceding command and prohibition, saying: ﴿Indeed, if they gain power over you﴾, i.e., they find out about you and learn your location, meaning the people of the city, ﴿they will stone you﴾, i.e., kill you by stoning. This is the most vile of killings, for that was their custom, and for this reason it was singled out from among the kinds of killing. ﴿Or they will return you to their religion﴾, i.e., they will send you back to their creed in which you were before Allah guided you. Or the meaning of "return" here is "become," on the assumption that they had not been in their creed. The choice of the word *fī* (in) rather than *ilā* (to) indicates permanence. ﴿And you will never succeed then, ever﴾: *idhan* contains the sense of a condition, as if He said: if you return to their religion, then you will never succeed, ever, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿declines away﴾ that he said: it inclines. And regarding His saying ﴿passes them by﴾ he said: it leaves them.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿passes them by﴾ that he said: it leaves them. ﴿And they were in an open space from it﴾: he said: the inner place.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: *al-fajwa* is the empty space of the earth, and by the empty space he means the area of the earth.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿and We turn them﴾ to the end of the verse that he said: six months on the right side, and six months on the left side.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding the verse that he said: so that the earth does not consume their flesh. (p-854)

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that the name of their dog was Qitmir.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan who said: its name was Qitmir.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿at the threshold﴾ that he said: at the courtyard.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: at the door.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His saying ﴿the purest food﴾ that he said: the most lawful slaughtered animal, and they used to slaughter for the idols (*al-ṭawāghīt*).

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿the purest food﴾: he meant the cleanest, because they used to slaughter for the idols.

And thus We made [people] come upon them: that is, just as We put them to sleep and raised them, We made [people] come upon them, meaning We informed people about them. He called the informing "i'thar" (coming upon) because whoever is heedless of something and stumbles upon it looks at it and recognizes it, so the coming upon became a cause for knowledge. ﴿So that they might know that the promise of God is true﴾: that is, so that those whom God caused to come upon them would know that God's promise of resurrection is true.

It was said: The king of that era was among those who denied resurrection, so God showed him this sign.

It was said: The cause of their being discovered was that the man they had sent with the silver, which was from the minting of Dihyanus, went to the market. When the people of the market saw the coins, they accused him of having found a treasure, and they took him to the king. The king said to him: "From where did you get these dirhams?" He said: "I sold some dates with them yesterday." The king recognized his truthfulness, then he related the story to him. The king rode out, and his companions rode with him, until they reached the cave. ﴿And that the Hour is not in doubt﴾: that is, so that they would know that the Resurrection will certainly take place, for whoever witnesses the condition of the People of the Cave knows the truth of what God promised concerning resurrection. ﴿When they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾: the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to "a'thar-na" (We made [them] come upon them), meaning: We made them come upon them at the time of the dispute and disagreement among those whom God had made to come upon them concerning the matter of resurrection. It was also said that the dispute was over the matter of the People of the Cave: their length of stay, their number, and what they should do after people had discovered them.

﴿So they said: "Build over them a structure"﴾: so that people would not reach them. That is because when the king and his companions stood over them while they were still alive, God caused the youths to die. Some of them said: "Build over them a structure that will shield them from people's eyes." Then He, glorified is He, said, relating the words of those who disputed about them, concerning their number, the length of their stay, and similar matters related to them: ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾, that is, better than these disputants. They said this by entrusting knowledge to God, glorified is He. It was also said that it is part of God's speech, glorified is He, as a rebuttal to the words of those disputing about them, meaning: leave what you are disputing, for I know them better than you do.

It was also said that the adverbial clause in ﴿when they disputed﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "udhkur" (remember). This is supported by the fact that the discovery did not take place at the time of the dispute but before it. It may be said that those people continued to dispute among themselves generation after generation, from the time they took refuge in the cave until the time of the discovery. This is supported by the fact that their story was written at the entrance of the cave by one of their contemporaries among the believers who were concealing their faith, as the commentators have said.

﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said: "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ Mentioning the taking of a place of worship suggests that these who prevailed in their affair were the Muslims. It was also said that they were the people of authority and rule among the aforementioned people, for they are the ones who prevail over the affairs of others. The first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: This indicates that when their matter became manifest, those who believed in resurrection prevailed, because mosques belong to believers.

﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth being their dog."﴾ Those who say they were three, or five, or seven, are the ones who disputed about their number at the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the Muslims. It was also said that they are the People of the Book specifically. In either case, it does not mean that they all said all of this together; rather, some of them said one thing, some another, and some another. ﴿Three, the fourth being their dog﴾: that is, they are three persons, and the clause ﴿the fourth being their dog﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning that their dog, by joining them, makes them four. ﴿And they say: "Five, the sixth being their dog."﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of what came before. The accusative of ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾ is either a circumstantial clause, meaning "as conjecturers," or a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "they conjecture a conjecture." Conjecturing about the unseen is saying something on the basis of assumption and guesswork without certainty. Those described as conjecturing about the unseen are both groups: those who say they were three and those who say they were five. ﴿And they say: "Seven, and the eighth being their dog."﴾ It seems that the statement of this group is closer to the truth, as indicated by their not being included among those who conjecture about the unseen.

It was said: The appearance of the wāw (and) in this sentence indicates that it is intended in the two previous sentences as well.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: ﴿Their fourth being their dog﴾ and ﴿their sixth being their dog﴾ are two sentences that dispense with the conjunction because they include the mention of the first sentence, which is "three." The meaning is: "They are three." This is what al-Wahidi related from Abu Ali, then he said: This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement about the entry of the wāw in "wa-thāminuhum" (and the eighth of them) and its exclusion from the first. It was also said: it is an extra wāw for emphasis. It was also said: it is the "wāw of eight," and mentioning it is common in the speech of the Arabs when they reach eight, as in God's words: ﴿And its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and His words: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

Then God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to inform those who differed about their number with what would end the dispute among them, so He said: ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number"﴾, meaning better than you, you who differ. Then He affirmed the knowledge of this to a few people, saying: ﴿None knows them except a few of the people﴾, that is, knows their essence, let alone their number; or it means "none knows their number," with an omitted noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf). Then God, glorified is He, forbade His Messenger (ﷺ) from disputing with the People of the Book concerning the matter of the People of the Cave, so He said: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾. Al-mirā' in the language means argument; it is said: "māra yumārī mumārāh and mirā'," meaning he argued. Then God, glorified is He, excepted from arguing that which was apparent and clear, so He said: ﴿except with an apparent argument﴾, that is, not going deeply into it, which is merely to relate to them what God revealed to him.

Al-Razi said: It is that he should not deny them regarding the specification of that number, but say: "This specification has no evidence, so suspension of judgment is required." Then He, glorified is He, forbade him from seeking a ruling concerning them, so He said: ﴿and do not seek a ruling concerning them from any of them﴾, that is, do not seek a ruling concerning their matter from any of the disputants about them, from any of them, because the one giving a ruling must be more knowledgeable than the one seeking it, and here the situation is reversed, especially in the case of the People of the Cave. What God related to you about that suffices you from asking one who has no knowledge.

﴿And never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow,"﴾: that is, concerning something you resolve upon in the future time, He expressed it with "tomorrow," not meaning tomorrow itself, so that tomorrow would enter into it primarily.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators said: "When the Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the story of the youths, he said: 'I will inform you tomorrow,' and he did not say: 'If God wills.' So revelation was withheld from him until it grieved him, then God revealed this verse commanding him to make the exception by God's will. It says: If you say concerning something: 'Indeed I will do that tomorrow,' then say: 'If God wills.'"

Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: ﴿Never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow," unless you say: "If God wills."﴾ So the verb "say" is implied, and when the verb "taqulu" was omitted, the verb "shā'a" (wills) was shifted to the form of the future. It was said: This exception is "mufarragh" (an exception with no stated subject), meaning: do not say that in any state except the state of being connected to God's will, which is saying: "If God wills," or at any time except the time when God wills that you say it unconditionally. It was also said: The exception is intended as a perpetual prohibition, as if it were said: "Never say it ever," like His words: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], because their return to their religion is something God does not will.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: the exception by God's will, that is, say "If God wills," whether the interval is short or long.

The scholars have differed about the length of time within which it is permissible to attach the exception after the thing excepted from, according to well-known opinions set out in their places.

It was also said: The meaning is "remember your Lord by seeking forgiveness when you forget." ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right guidance than this."﴾ The referent of "than this" (min hādhā) is the story of the People of the Cave, meaning: say, O Muhammad, perhaps my Lord will grant me success in something closer than this story, from among the signs and proofs that indicate my prophethood.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Perhaps my Lord will give me, from among the signs of prophethood, what will be closer to right guidance and more indicative than the story of the People of the Cave." God did that for him, as He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their stories, which was clearer in proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave.

It was also said: The reference is to His words: ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾, meaning: perhaps my Lord will guide me, at this forgetting, to something else in place of this forgotten thing, something closer to right guidance and nearer to good and benefit than it. The first view is preferable.

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and gained nine more.﴾ The majority recited "mi'atin" with tanwīn and "sinīna" in the accusative, so "sinīn" in this reading is either an apposition (badal) or a clarifying appositive (ʿaṭf bayān).

Al-Farra', Abu Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and al-Kisa'i said: There is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it, and the implied meaning is: "sinīn thalātha mi'atin" (years, three hundred).

Abu Ali al-Farisi preferred the first reading.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited with the idiomatic construction of "mi'a" as a genitive of "sinīn"; in this reading, "sinīn" is a specification (tamyīz), with the plural placed in the position of the singular in specification, as in God's words: ﴿the greatest losers in deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 103]. Al-Farra' said: Some Arabs place "sinīn" in the position of "sana" (year).

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: These numbers which, in the well-known usage, are attached to singular nouns, such as "thalātha mi'ati rajul" (three hundred men) and "thawb" (a garment), may also be attached to a plural noun. In the Mushaf of Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] it reads "thalātha mi'ati sana" (three hundred years).

Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs hardly ever say "mi'at sinīn" (a hundred years).

Al-Dahhak recited "thalātha mi'atin sunūn" with a waw. The majority recited "tis'an" with a kasra on the tā'; Abu 'Amr recited it with a fatḥa. This is a report from God, glorified is He, about the length of their stay.

Ibn Jarir said: The Children of Israel differed about the period of time that passed for them after they were discovered. Some of them said: "They remained three hundred and nine years." So God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that this period was the period of their sleeping, and that what came after that is unknown to humans, so God commanded him to refer the knowledge of that to Him, and He said: ﴿Say: "God knows best how long they remained."﴾

Ibn 'Atiyya said: According to this, the first "labithū" (they remained) refers to the day of the cave, and the second "labithū" refers to the period after their discovery until the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), or until they died.

Some of them said: When He said: ﴿and gained nine more,﴾ people did not know whether these were hours, days, weeks, months, or years, and the Children of Israel differed accordingly. So God commanded that knowledge of the nine be referred to Him, and according to this, they are unspecified.

The first view is preferable, because the apparent meaning of Arabic speech, as understood according to their language, is that the nine are years, as evidenced by the fact that the number in this statement is for "years" and not for months, days, or hours.

It is related from al-Zajjaj that the intended meaning is three hundred solar years, and three hundred and nine lunar years. This, from al-Zajjaj, is only given as an approximation.

Then He, glorified is He, emphasized His exclusive knowledge of how long they stayed by His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: whatever is hidden within them and concealed of their conditions, none other than Him has any share in that. Then He increased the emphasis and intensification by bringing what indicates wonder at His perception of visible and audible things, saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾. This wonder conveys that His knowledge of visible and audible things, glorified is He, is beyond what the perceptions of perceivers are capable of, and that in His knowledge the absent and the present, the hidden and the manifest, the small and the great, the subtle and the dense are alike. It seems its original form was: "How much He sees and how much He hears!", then it was transferred to the imperative form for the sake of expression (inshā'). The bā' (ب) is superfluous according to Sibawayh, and al-Akhfash disagreed with him; the discussion is established in the science of grammar (naḥw). ﴿They have no protector besides Him, from among them﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of the heavens and the earth. It is said it refers to the People of the Cave, and it is said it refers to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) among the disbelievers, meaning: they have no ally who befriends them, or who takes charge of their affairs, or who helps them. In this there is an explanation of the extent of His power and that all things are under His dominion. ﴿And He does not make anyone share in His judgment﴾: Al-Jumhur read it with a raised kāf (ُ), as a predicate about Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Qatada read it with a initial tā' (ت) and a sukun on the kāf, as a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should not make a partner for Allah in His judgment. This reading is also narrated from Ibn 'Amir.

Mujahid read it with a yā' (ي) and a jazm. Ya'qub said: "I do not know its basis." The meaning of "Allah's judgment" is what He decrees, or the knowledge of the unseen; the first is preferable.

The knowledge of the unseen enters into this in a primary way, since His knowledge, glorified is He, is part of His decree.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾ that he said: "We let them be made known."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾ that he said: "The rulers," or he said: "The sultans."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ that he said: "The Jews," ﴿and they will say, "Five"﴾ he said: "The Christians."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾ that he said: "Casting by assumption."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among the few; they were seven."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suyuti said with a sahih chain, regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among those few; they were seven," then he mentioned their names.

Ibn Kathir related it from Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Qatada, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah, then said: "These are sound chains to Ibn 'Abbas that they were seven."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾ that he said: "It means: what I have related to you is sufficient for you."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through various routes from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And do not consult any of them about them﴾ that he said: "The Jews."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And never say of anything﴾ (the verse), that he said: "If you forget to say, 'I will do such-and-such,' and forget to say, 'if Allah wills,' then when you remember, say: 'if Allah wills.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he used to hold that the exception (istithna') is valid even after a year, then he recited: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also regarding the verse that he said: "It is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one may make an exception except in the context of an oath."

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Every exception that is connected, there is no breaking of the oath for its one who makes it; and if it is not connected, then he has broken it."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sulayman ibn Dawud said: 'Tonight I will go around to seventy women' — and in another narration: 'ninety' — each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah. The angel said to him: 'Say, if Allah wills.' But he did not say it. So he went around, and none of them gave birth except one woman, half a human." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said, 'if Allah wills,' he would not have broken his oath, and it would have been a fulfilment of his need."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Ikrimah regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you become angry."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you do not say, 'if Allah wills.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A man may interpret the verse, thinking it is so, and then he falls farther than the distance between the heaven and the earth." Then he recited: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ (the verse), then said: "How long did the people stay?" They said: "Three hundred and nine years." He said: "If they had stayed like that, Allah would not have said, ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾; rather He related the statement of the people, saying: ﴿They will say, 'They were three'﴾ up to His saying: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾, so He informed that they do not know. Then He said: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and they said: "(﴿And they remained in their cave﴾) the verse," meaning: it is only what the people said. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾?

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾, it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, days or months or years?' So Allah revealed: ﴿years, and they added nine﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from al-Dahhak without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾ that he said: "Allah Himself says it."

And thus We made [people] come upon them: that is, just as We put them to sleep and raised them, We made [people] come upon them, meaning We informed people about them. He called the informing "i'thar" (coming upon) because whoever is heedless of something and stumbles upon it looks at it and recognizes it, so the coming upon became a cause for knowledge. ﴿So that they might know that the promise of God is true﴾: that is, so that those whom God caused to come upon them would know that God's promise of resurrection is true.

It was said: The king of that era was among those who denied resurrection, so God showed him this sign.

It was said: The cause of their being discovered was that the man they had sent with the silver, which was from the minting of Dihyanus, went to the market. When the people of the market saw the coins, they accused him of having found a treasure, and they took him to the king. The king said to him: "From where did you get these dirhams?" He said: "I sold some dates with them yesterday." The king recognized his truthfulness, then he related the story to him. The king rode out, and his companions rode with him, until they reached the cave. ﴿And that the Hour is not in doubt﴾: that is, so that they would know that the Resurrection will certainly take place, for whoever witnesses the condition of the People of the Cave knows the truth of what God promised concerning resurrection. ﴿When they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾: the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to "a'thar-na" (We made [them] come upon them), meaning: We made them come upon them at the time of the dispute and disagreement among those whom God had made to come upon them concerning the matter of resurrection. It was also said that the dispute was over the matter of the People of the Cave: their length of stay, their number, and what they should do after people had discovered them.

﴿So they said: "Build over them a structure"﴾: so that people would not reach them. That is because when the king and his companions stood over them while they were still alive, God caused the youths to die. Some of them said: "Build over them a structure that will shield them from people's eyes." Then He, glorified is He, said, relating the words of those who disputed about them, concerning their number, the length of their stay, and similar matters related to them: ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾, that is, better than these disputants. They said this by entrusting knowledge to God, glorified is He. It was also said that it is part of God's speech, glorified is He, as a rebuttal to the words of those disputing about them, meaning: leave what you are disputing, for I know them better than you do.

It was also said that the adverbial clause in ﴿when they disputed﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "udhkur" (remember). This is supported by the fact that the discovery did not take place at the time of the dispute but before it. It may be said that those people continued to dispute among themselves generation after generation, from the time they took refuge in the cave until the time of the discovery. This is supported by the fact that their story was written at the entrance of the cave by one of their contemporaries among the believers who were concealing their faith, as the commentators have said.

﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said: "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ Mentioning the taking of a place of worship suggests that these who prevailed in their affair were the Muslims. It was also said that they were the people of authority and rule among the aforementioned people, for they are the ones who prevail over the affairs of others. The first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: This indicates that when their matter became manifest, those who believed in resurrection prevailed, because mosques belong to believers.

﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth being their dog."﴾ Those who say they were three, or five, or seven, are the ones who disputed about their number at the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the Muslims. It was also said that they are the People of the Book specifically. In either case, it does not mean that they all said all of this together; rather, some of them said one thing, some another, and some another. ﴿Three, the fourth being their dog﴾: that is, they are three persons, and the clause ﴿the fourth being their dog﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning that their dog, by joining them, makes them four. ﴿And they say: "Five, the sixth being their dog."﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of what came before. The accusative of ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾ is either a circumstantial clause, meaning "as conjecturers," or a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "they conjecture a conjecture." Conjecturing about the unseen is saying something on the basis of assumption and guesswork without certainty. Those described as conjecturing about the unseen are both groups: those who say they were three and those who say they were five. ﴿And they say: "Seven, and the eighth being their dog."﴾ It seems that the statement of this group is closer to the truth, as indicated by their not being included among those who conjecture about the unseen.

It was said: The appearance of the wāw (and) in this sentence indicates that it is intended in the two previous sentences as well.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: ﴿Their fourth being their dog﴾ and ﴿their sixth being their dog﴾ are two sentences that dispense with the conjunction because they include the mention of the first sentence, which is "three." The meaning is: "They are three." This is what al-Wahidi related from Abu Ali, then he said: This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement about the entry of the wāw in "wa-thāminuhum" (and the eighth of them) and its exclusion from the first. It was also said: it is an extra wāw for emphasis. It was also said: it is the "wāw of eight," and mentioning it is common in the speech of the Arabs when they reach eight, as in God's words: ﴿And its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and His words: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

Then God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to inform those who differed about their number with what would end the dispute among them, so He said: ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number"﴾, meaning better than you, you who differ. Then He affirmed the knowledge of this to a few people, saying: ﴿None knows them except a few of the people﴾, that is, knows their essence, let alone their number; or it means "none knows their number," with an omitted noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf). Then God, glorified is He, forbade His Messenger (ﷺ) from disputing with the People of the Book concerning the matter of the People of the Cave, so He said: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾. Al-mirā' in the language means argument; it is said: "māra yumārī mumārāh and mirā'," meaning he argued. Then God, glorified is He, excepted from arguing that which was apparent and clear, so He said: ﴿except with an apparent argument﴾, that is, not going deeply into it, which is merely to relate to them what God revealed to him.

Al-Razi said: It is that he should not deny them regarding the specification of that number, but say: "This specification has no evidence, so suspension of judgment is required." Then He, glorified is He, forbade him from seeking a ruling concerning them, so He said: ﴿and do not seek a ruling concerning them from any of them﴾, that is, do not seek a ruling concerning their matter from any of the disputants about them, from any of them, because the one giving a ruling must be more knowledgeable than the one seeking it, and here the situation is reversed, especially in the case of the People of the Cave. What God related to you about that suffices you from asking one who has no knowledge.

﴿And never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow,"﴾: that is, concerning something you resolve upon in the future time, He expressed it with "tomorrow," not meaning tomorrow itself, so that tomorrow would enter into it primarily.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators said: "When the Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the story of the youths, he said: 'I will inform you tomorrow,' and he did not say: 'If God wills.' So revelation was withheld from him until it grieved him, then God revealed this verse commanding him to make the exception by God's will. It says: If you say concerning something: 'Indeed I will do that tomorrow,' then say: 'If God wills.'"

Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: ﴿Never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow," unless you say: "If God wills."﴾ So the verb "say" is implied, and when the verb "taqulu" was omitted, the verb "shā'a" (wills) was shifted to the form of the future. It was said: This exception is "mufarragh" (an exception with no stated subject), meaning: do not say that in any state except the state of being connected to God's will, which is saying: "If God wills," or at any time except the time when God wills that you say it unconditionally. It was also said: The exception is intended as a perpetual prohibition, as if it were said: "Never say it ever," like His words: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], because their return to their religion is something God does not will.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: the exception by God's will, that is, say "If God wills," whether the interval is short or long.

The scholars have differed about the length of time within which it is permissible to attach the exception after the thing excepted from, according to well-known opinions set out in their places.

It was also said: The meaning is "remember your Lord by seeking forgiveness when you forget." ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right guidance than this."﴾ The referent of "than this" (min hādhā) is the story of the People of the Cave, meaning: say, O Muhammad, perhaps my Lord will grant me success in something closer than this story, from among the signs and proofs that indicate my prophethood.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Perhaps my Lord will give me, from among the signs of prophethood, what will be closer to right guidance and more indicative than the story of the People of the Cave." God did that for him, as He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their stories, which was clearer in proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave.

It was also said: The reference is to His words: ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾, meaning: perhaps my Lord will guide me, at this forgetting, to something else in place of this forgotten thing, something closer to right guidance and nearer to good and benefit than it. The first view is preferable.

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and gained nine more.﴾ The majority recited "mi'atin" with tanwīn and "sinīna" in the accusative, so "sinīn" in this reading is either an apposition (badal) or a clarifying appositive (ʿaṭf bayān).

Al-Farra', Abu Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and al-Kisa'i said: There is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it, and the implied meaning is: "sinīn thalātha mi'atin" (years, three hundred).

Abu Ali al-Farisi preferred the first reading.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited with the idiomatic construction of "mi'a" as a genitive of "sinīn"; in this reading, "sinīn" is a specification (tamyīz), with the plural placed in the position of the singular in specification, as in God's words: ﴿the greatest losers in deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 103]. Al-Farra' said: Some Arabs place "sinīn" in the position of "sana" (year).

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: These numbers which, in the well-known usage, are attached to singular nouns, such as "thalātha mi'ati rajul" (three hundred men) and "thawb" (a garment), may also be attached to a plural noun. In the Mushaf of Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] it reads "thalātha mi'ati sana" (three hundred years).

Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs hardly ever say "mi'at sinīn" (a hundred years).

Al-Dahhak recited "thalātha mi'atin sunūn" with a waw. The majority recited "tis'an" with a kasra on the tā'; Abu 'Amr recited it with a fatḥa. This is a report from God, glorified is He, about the length of their stay.

Ibn Jarir said: The Children of Israel differed about the period of time that passed for them after they were discovered. Some of them said: "They remained three hundred and nine years." So God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that this period was the period of their sleeping, and that what came after that is unknown to humans, so God commanded him to refer the knowledge of that to Him, and He said: ﴿Say: "God knows best how long they remained."﴾

Ibn 'Atiyya said: According to this, the first "labithū" (they remained) refers to the day of the cave, and the second "labithū" refers to the period after their discovery until the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), or until they died.

Some of them said: When He said: ﴿and gained nine more,﴾ people did not know whether these were hours, days, weeks, months, or years, and the Children of Israel differed accordingly. So God commanded that knowledge of the nine be referred to Him, and according to this, they are unspecified.

The first view is preferable, because the apparent meaning of Arabic speech, as understood according to their language, is that the nine are years, as evidenced by the fact that the number in this statement is for "years" and not for months, days, or hours.

It is related from al-Zajjaj that the intended meaning is three hundred solar years, and three hundred and nine lunar years. This, from al-Zajjaj, is only given as an approximation.

Then He, glorified is He, emphasized His exclusive knowledge of how long they stayed by His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: whatever is hidden within them and concealed of their conditions, none other than Him has any share in that. Then He increased the emphasis and intensification by bringing what indicates wonder at His perception of visible and audible things, saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾. This wonder conveys that His knowledge of visible and audible things, glorified is He, is beyond what the perceptions of perceivers are capable of, and that in His knowledge the absent and the present, the hidden and the manifest, the small and the great, the subtle and the dense are alike. It seems its original form was: "How much He sees and how much He hears!", then it was transferred to the imperative form for the sake of expression (inshā'). The bā' (ب) is superfluous according to Sibawayh, and al-Akhfash disagreed with him; the discussion is established in the science of grammar (naḥw). ﴿They have no protector besides Him, from among them﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of the heavens and the earth. It is said it refers to the People of the Cave, and it is said it refers to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) among the disbelievers, meaning: they have no ally who befriends them, or who takes charge of their affairs, or who helps them. In this there is an explanation of the extent of His power and that all things are under His dominion. ﴿And He does not make anyone share in His judgment﴾: Al-Jumhur read it with a raised kāf (ُ), as a predicate about Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Qatada read it with a initial tā' (ت) and a sukun on the kāf, as a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should not make a partner for Allah in His judgment. This reading is also narrated from Ibn 'Amir.

Mujahid read it with a yā' (ي) and a jazm. Ya'qub said: "I do not know its basis." The meaning of "Allah's judgment" is what He decrees, or the knowledge of the unseen; the first is preferable.

The knowledge of the unseen enters into this in a primary way, since His knowledge, glorified is He, is part of His decree.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾ that he said: "We let them be made known."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾ that he said: "The rulers," or he said: "The sultans."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ that he said: "The Jews," ﴿and they will say, "Five"﴾ he said: "The Christians."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾ that he said: "Casting by assumption."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among the few; they were seven."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suyuti said with a sahih chain, regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among those few; they were seven," then he mentioned their names.

Ibn Kathir related it from Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Qatada, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah, then said: "These are sound chains to Ibn 'Abbas that they were seven."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾ that he said: "It means: what I have related to you is sufficient for you."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through various routes from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And do not consult any of them about them﴾ that he said: "The Jews."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And never say of anything﴾ (the verse), that he said: "If you forget to say, 'I will do such-and-such,' and forget to say, 'if Allah wills,' then when you remember, say: 'if Allah wills.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he used to hold that the exception (istithna') is valid even after a year, then he recited: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also regarding the verse that he said: "It is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one may make an exception except in the context of an oath."

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Every exception that is connected, there is no breaking of the oath for its one who makes it; and if it is not connected, then he has broken it."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sulayman ibn Dawud said: 'Tonight I will go around to seventy women' — and in another narration: 'ninety' — each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah. The angel said to him: 'Say, if Allah wills.' But he did not say it. So he went around, and none of them gave birth except one woman, half a human." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said, 'if Allah wills,' he would not have broken his oath, and it would have been a fulfilment of his need."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Ikrimah regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you become angry."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you do not say, 'if Allah wills.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A man may interpret the verse, thinking it is so, and then he falls farther than the distance between the heaven and the earth." Then he recited: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ (the verse), then said: "How long did the people stay?" They said: "Three hundred and nine years." He said: "If they had stayed like that, Allah would not have said, ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾; rather He related the statement of the people, saying: ﴿They will say, 'They were three'﴾ up to His saying: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾, so He informed that they do not know. Then He said: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and they said: "(﴿And they remained in their cave﴾) the verse," meaning: it is only what the people said. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾?

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾, it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, days or months or years?' So Allah revealed: ﴿years, and they added nine﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from al-Dahhak without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾ that he said: "Allah Himself says it."

And thus We made [people] come upon them: that is, just as We put them to sleep and raised them, We made [people] come upon them, meaning We informed people about them. He called the informing "i'thar" (coming upon) because whoever is heedless of something and stumbles upon it looks at it and recognizes it, so the coming upon became a cause for knowledge. ﴿So that they might know that the promise of God is true﴾: that is, so that those whom God caused to come upon them would know that God's promise of resurrection is true.

It was said: The king of that era was among those who denied resurrection, so God showed him this sign.

It was said: The cause of their being discovered was that the man they had sent with the silver, which was from the minting of Dihyanus, went to the market. When the people of the market saw the coins, they accused him of having found a treasure, and they took him to the king. The king said to him: "From where did you get these dirhams?" He said: "I sold some dates with them yesterday." The king recognized his truthfulness, then he related the story to him. The king rode out, and his companions rode with him, until they reached the cave. ﴿And that the Hour is not in doubt﴾: that is, so that they would know that the Resurrection will certainly take place, for whoever witnesses the condition of the People of the Cave knows the truth of what God promised concerning resurrection. ﴿When they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾: the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to "a'thar-na" (We made [them] come upon them), meaning: We made them come upon them at the time of the dispute and disagreement among those whom God had made to come upon them concerning the matter of resurrection. It was also said that the dispute was over the matter of the People of the Cave: their length of stay, their number, and what they should do after people had discovered them.

﴿So they said: "Build over them a structure"﴾: so that people would not reach them. That is because when the king and his companions stood over them while they were still alive, God caused the youths to die. Some of them said: "Build over them a structure that will shield them from people's eyes." Then He, glorified is He, said, relating the words of those who disputed about them, concerning their number, the length of their stay, and similar matters related to them: ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾, that is, better than these disputants. They said this by entrusting knowledge to God, glorified is He. It was also said that it is part of God's speech, glorified is He, as a rebuttal to the words of those disputing about them, meaning: leave what you are disputing, for I know them better than you do.

It was also said that the adverbial clause in ﴿when they disputed﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "udhkur" (remember). This is supported by the fact that the discovery did not take place at the time of the dispute but before it. It may be said that those people continued to dispute among themselves generation after generation, from the time they took refuge in the cave until the time of the discovery. This is supported by the fact that their story was written at the entrance of the cave by one of their contemporaries among the believers who were concealing their faith, as the commentators have said.

﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said: "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ Mentioning the taking of a place of worship suggests that these who prevailed in their affair were the Muslims. It was also said that they were the people of authority and rule among the aforementioned people, for they are the ones who prevail over the affairs of others. The first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: This indicates that when their matter became manifest, those who believed in resurrection prevailed, because mosques belong to believers.

﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth being their dog."﴾ Those who say they were three, or five, or seven, are the ones who disputed about their number at the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the Muslims. It was also said that they are the People of the Book specifically. In either case, it does not mean that they all said all of this together; rather, some of them said one thing, some another, and some another. ﴿Three, the fourth being their dog﴾: that is, they are three persons, and the clause ﴿the fourth being their dog﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning that their dog, by joining them, makes them four. ﴿And they say: "Five, the sixth being their dog."﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of what came before. Conjecturing about the unseen is saying something on the basis of assumption and guesswork without certainty. Those described as conjecturing about the unseen are both groups: those who say they were three and those who say they were five. ﴿And they say: "Seven, and the eighth being their dog."﴾ It seems that the statement of this group is closer to the truth, as indicated by their not being included among those who conjecture about the unseen.

It was said: The appearance of the wāw (and) in this sentence indicates that it is intended in the two previous sentences as well.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: ﴿Their fourth being their dog﴾ and ﴿their sixth being their dog﴾ are two sentences that dispense with the conjunction because they include the mention of the first sentence, which is "three." The meaning is: "They are three." This is what al-Wahidi related from Abu Ali, then he said: This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement about the entry of the wāw in "wa-thāminuhum" (and the eighth of them) and its exclusion from the first. It was also said: it is an extra wāw for emphasis. It was also said: it is the "wāw of eight," and mentioning it is common in the speech of the Arabs when they reach eight, as in God's words: ﴿And its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and His words: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

Then God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to inform those who differed about their number with what would end the dispute among them, so He said: ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number"﴾, meaning better than you, you who differ. Then He affirmed the knowledge of this to a few people, saying: ﴿None knows them except a few of the people﴾, that is, knows their essence, let alone their number; or it means "none knows their number," with an omitted noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf). So revelation was withheld from him until it grieved him, then God revealed this verse commanding him to make the exception by God's will. It was also said: The exception is intended as a perpetual prohibition, as if it were said: "Never say it ever," like His words: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], because their return to their religion is something God does not will.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: the exception by God's will, that is, say "If God wills," whether the interval is short or long.

God did that for him, as He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their stories, which was clearer in proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave.

It was also said: The reference is to His words: ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾, meaning: perhaps my Lord will guide me, at this forgetting, to something else in place of this forgotten thing, something closer to right guidance and nearer to good and benefit than it. The first view is preferable.

Al-Dahhak recited "thalātha mi'atin sunūn" with a waw. The majority recited "tis'an" with a kasra on the tā'; Abu 'Amr recited it with a fatḥa. This is a report from God, glorified is He, about the length of their stay.

Ibn Jarir said: The Children of Israel differed about the period of time that passed for them after they were discovered. Some of them said: "They remained three hundred and nine years." So God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that this period was the period of their sleeping, and that what came after that is unknown to humans, so God commanded him to refer the knowledge of that to Him, and He said: ﴿Say: "God knows best how long they remained."﴾

Ibn 'Atiyya said: According to this, the first "labithū" (they remained) refers to the day of the cave, and the second "labithū" refers to the period after their discovery until the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), or until they died.

Some of them said: When He said: ﴿and gained nine more,﴾ people did not know whether these were hours, days, weeks, months, or years, and the Children of Israel differed accordingly. So God commanded that knowledge of the nine be referred to Him, and according to this, they are unspecified.

The first view is preferable, because the apparent meaning of Arabic speech, as understood according to their language, is that the nine are years, as evidenced by the fact that the number in this statement is for "years" and not for months, days, or hours.

It is related from al-Zajjaj that the intended meaning is three hundred solar years, and three hundred and nine lunar years. This, from al-Zajjaj, is only given as an approximation.

Then He, glorified is He, emphasized His exclusive knowledge of how long they stayed by His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: whatever is hidden within them and concealed of their conditions, none other than Him has any share in that. Then He increased the emphasis and intensification by bringing what indicates wonder at His perception of visible and audible things, saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾. This wonder conveys that His knowledge of visible and audible things, glorified is He, is beyond what the perceptions of perceivers are capable of, and that in His knowledge the absent and the present, the hidden and the manifest, the small and the great, the subtle and the dense are alike. It seems its original form was: "How much He sees and how much He hears!", then it was transferred to the imperative form for the sake of expression (inshā'). The bā' (ب) is superfluous according to Sibawayh, and al-Akhfash disagreed with him; the discussion is established in the science of grammar (naḥw). ﴿They have no protector besides Him, from among them﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of the heavens and the earth. It is said it refers to the People of the Cave, and it is said it refers to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) among the disbelievers, meaning: they have no ally who befriends them, or who takes charge of their affairs, or who helps them. In this there is an explanation of the extent of His power and that all things are under His dominion. ﴿And He does not make anyone share in His judgment﴾: Al-Jumhur read it with a raised kāf (ُ), as a predicate about Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Qatada read it with a initial tā' (ت) and a sukun on the kāf, as a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should not make a partner for Allah in His judgment. This reading is also narrated from Ibn 'Amir.

Mujahid read it with a yā' (ي) and a jazm. Ya'qub said: "I do not know its basis." The meaning of "Allah's judgment" is what He decrees, or the knowledge of the unseen; the first is preferable.

The knowledge of the unseen enters into this in a primary way, since His knowledge, glorified is He, is part of His decree.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾ that he said: "We let them be made known."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾ that he said: "The rulers," or he said: "The sultans."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ that he said: "The Jews," ﴿and they will say, "Five"﴾ he said: "The Christians."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾ that he said: "Casting by assumption."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among the few; they were seven."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suyuti said with a sahih chain, regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among those few; they were seven," then he mentioned their names.

Ibn Kathir related it from Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Qatada, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah, then said: "These are sound chains to Ibn 'Abbas that they were seven."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾ that he said: "It means: what I have related to you is sufficient for you."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through various routes from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And do not consult any of them about them﴾ that he said: "The Jews."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And never say of anything﴾ (the verse), that he said: "If you forget to say, 'I will do such-and-such,' and forget to say, 'if Allah wills,' then when you remember, say: 'if Allah wills.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he used to hold that the exception (istithna') is valid even after a year, then he recited: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also regarding the verse that he said: "It is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one may make an exception except in the context of an oath."

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Every exception that is connected, there is no breaking of the oath for its one who makes it; and if it is not connected, then he has broken it."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sulayman ibn Dawud said: 'Tonight I will go around to seventy women' — and in another narration: 'ninety' — each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah. The angel said to him: 'Say, if Allah wills.' But he did not say it. So he went around, and none of them gave birth except one woman, half a human." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said, 'if Allah wills,' he would not have broken his oath, and it would have been a fulfilment of his need."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Ikrimah regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you become angry."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you do not say, 'if Allah wills.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A man may interpret the verse, thinking it is so, and then he falls farther than the distance between the heaven and the earth." Then he recited: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ (the verse), then said: "How long did the people stay?" They said: "Three hundred and nine years." He said: "If they had stayed like that, Allah would not have said, ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾; rather He related the statement of the people, saying: ﴿They will say, 'They were three'﴾ up to His saying: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾, so He informed that they do not know. Then He said: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and they said: "(﴿And they remained in their cave﴾) the verse," meaning: it is only what the people said. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾?

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾, it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, days or months or years?' So Allah revealed: ﴿years, and they added nine﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from al-Dahhak without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾ that he said: "Allah Himself says it."

And thus We made [people] come upon them: that is, just as We put them to sleep and raised them, We made [people] come upon them, meaning We informed people about them. He called the informing "i'thar" (coming upon) because whoever is heedless of something and stumbles upon it looks at it and recognizes it, so the coming upon became a cause for knowledge. ﴿So that they might know that the promise of God is true﴾: that is, so that those whom God caused to come upon them would know that God's promise of resurrection is true.

It was said: The king of that era was among those who denied resurrection, so God showed him this sign.

It was said: The cause of their being discovered was that the man they had sent with the silver, which was from the minting of Dihyanus, went to the market. When the people of the market saw the coins, they accused him of having found a treasure, and they took him to the king. The king said to him: "From where did you get these dirhams?" He said: "I sold some dates with them yesterday." The king recognized his truthfulness, then he related the story to him. The king rode out, and his companions rode with him, until they reached the cave. ﴿And that the Hour is not in doubt﴾: that is, so that they would know that the Resurrection will certainly take place, for whoever witnesses the condition of the People of the Cave knows the truth of what God promised concerning resurrection. ﴿When they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾: the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to "a'thar-na" (We made [them] come upon them), meaning: We made them come upon them at the time of the dispute and disagreement among those whom God had made to come upon them concerning the matter of resurrection. It was also said that the dispute was over the matter of the People of the Cave: their length of stay, their number, and what they should do after people had discovered them.

﴿So they said: "Build over them a structure"﴾: so that people would not reach them. That is because when the king and his companions stood over them while they were still alive, God caused the youths to die. Some of them said: "Build over them a structure that will shield them from people's eyes." Then He, glorified is He, said, relating the words of those who disputed about them, concerning their number, the length of their stay, and similar matters related to them: ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾, that is, better than these disputants. They said this by entrusting knowledge to God, glorified is He. It was also said that it is part of God's speech, glorified is He, as a rebuttal to the words of those disputing about them, meaning: leave what you are disputing, for I know them better than you do.

It was also said that the adverbial clause in ﴿when they disputed﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "udhkur" (remember). This is supported by the fact that the discovery did not take place at the time of the dispute but before it. It may be said that those people continued to dispute among themselves generation after generation, from the time they took refuge in the cave until the time of the discovery. This is supported by the fact that their story was written at the entrance of the cave by one of their contemporaries among the believers who were concealing their faith, as the commentators have said.

﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said: "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ Mentioning the taking of a place of worship suggests that these who prevailed in their affair were the Muslims. It was also said that they were the people of authority and rule among the aforementioned people, for they are the ones who prevail over the affairs of others. The first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: This indicates that when their matter became manifest, those who believed in resurrection prevailed, because mosques belong to believers.

﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth being their dog."﴾ Those who say they were three, or five, or seven, are the ones who disputed about their number at the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the Muslims. It was also said that they are the People of the Book specifically. In either case, it does not mean that they all said all of this together; rather, some of them said one thing, some another, and some another. ﴿Three, the fourth being their dog﴾: that is, they are three persons, and the clause ﴿the fourth being their dog﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning that their dog, by joining them, makes them four. ﴿And they say: "Five, the sixth being their dog."﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of what came before. The accusative of ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾ is either a circumstantial clause, meaning "as conjecturers," or a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "they conjecture a conjecture." Conjecturing about the unseen is saying something on the basis of assumption and guesswork without certainty. Those described as conjecturing about the unseen are both groups: those who say they were three and those who say they were five. ﴿And they say: "Seven, and the eighth being their dog."﴾ It seems that the statement of this group is closer to the truth, as indicated by their not being included among those who conjecture about the unseen.

It was said: The appearance of the wāw (and) in this sentence indicates that it is intended in the two previous sentences as well.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: ﴿Their fourth being their dog﴾ and ﴿their sixth being their dog﴾ are two sentences that dispense with the conjunction because they include the mention of the first sentence, which is "three." The meaning is: "They are three." This is what al-Wahidi related from Abu Ali, then he said: This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement about the entry of the wāw in "wa-thāminuhum" (and the eighth of them) and its exclusion from the first. It was also said: it is an extra wāw for emphasis. It was also said: it is the "wāw of eight," and mentioning it is common in the speech of the Arabs when they reach eight, as in God's words: ﴿And its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and His words: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

Then God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to inform those who differed about their number with what would end the dispute among them, so He said: ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number"﴾, meaning better than you, you who differ. Then He affirmed the knowledge of this to a few people, saying: ﴿None knows them except a few of the people﴾, that is, knows their essence, let alone their number; or it means "none knows their number," with an omitted noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf). Then God, glorified is He, forbade His Messenger (ﷺ) from disputing with the People of the Book concerning the matter of the People of the Cave, so He said: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾. Al-mirā' in the language means argument; it is said: "māra yumārī mumārāh and mirā'," meaning he argued. Then God, glorified is He, excepted from arguing that which was apparent and clear, so He said: ﴿except with an apparent argument﴾, that is, not going deeply into it, which is merely to relate to them what God revealed to him.

Al-Razi said: It is that he should not deny them regarding the specification of that number, but say: "This specification has no evidence, so suspension of judgment is required." Then He, glorified is He, forbade him from seeking a ruling concerning them, so He said: ﴿and do not seek a ruling concerning them from any of them﴾, that is, do not seek a ruling concerning their matter from any of the disputants about them, from any of them, because the one giving a ruling must be more knowledgeable than the one seeking it, and here the situation is reversed, especially in the case of the People of the Cave. What God related to you about that suffices you from asking one who has no knowledge.

﴿And never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow,"﴾: that is, concerning something you resolve upon in the future time, He expressed it with "tomorrow," not meaning tomorrow itself, so that tomorrow would enter into it primarily.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators said: "When the Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the story of the youths, he said: 'I will inform you tomorrow,' and he did not say: 'If God wills.' So revelation was withheld from him until it grieved him, then God revealed this verse commanding him to make the exception by God's will. It says: If you say concerning something: 'Indeed I will do that tomorrow,' then say: 'If God wills.'"

Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: ﴿Never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow," unless you say: "If God wills."﴾ So the verb "say" is implied, and when the verb "taqulu" was omitted, the verb "shā'a" (wills) was shifted to the form of the future. It was said: This exception is "mufarragh" (an exception with no stated subject), meaning: do not say that in any state except the state of being connected to God's will, which is saying: "If God wills," or at any time except the time when God wills that you say it unconditionally. It was also said: The exception is intended as a perpetual prohibition, as if it were said: "Never say it ever," like His words: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], because their return to their religion is something God does not will.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: the exception by God's will, that is, say "If God wills," whether the interval is short or long.

The scholars have differed about the length of time within which it is permissible to attach the exception after the thing excepted from, according to well-known opinions set out in their places.

It was also said: The meaning is "remember your Lord by seeking forgiveness when you forget." ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right guidance than this."﴾ The referent of "than this" (min hādhā) is the story of the People of the Cave, meaning: say, O Muhammad, perhaps my Lord will grant me success in something closer than this story, from among the signs and proofs that indicate my prophethood.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Perhaps my Lord will give me, from among the signs of prophethood, what will be closer to right guidance and more indicative than the story of the People of the Cave." God did that for him, as He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their stories, which was clearer in proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave.

It was also said: The reference is to His words: ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾, meaning: perhaps my Lord will guide me, at this forgetting, to something else in place of this forgotten thing, something closer to right guidance and nearer to good and benefit than it. The first view is preferable.

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and gained nine more.﴾ The majority recited "mi'atin" with tanwīn and "sinīna" in the accusative, so "sinīn" in this reading is either an apposition (badal) or a clarifying appositive (ʿaṭf bayān).

Al-Farra', Abu Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and al-Kisa'i said: There is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it, and the implied meaning is: "sinīn thalātha mi'atin" (years, three hundred).

Abu Ali al-Farisi preferred the first reading.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited with the idiomatic construction of "mi'a" as a genitive of "sinīn"; in this reading, "sinīn" is a specification (tamyīz), with the plural placed in the position of the singular in specification, as in God's words: ﴿the greatest losers in deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 103]. Al-Farra' said: Some Arabs place "sinīn" in the position of "sana" (year).

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: These numbers which, in the well-known usage, are attached to singular nouns, such as "thalātha mi'ati rajul" (three hundred men) and "thawb" (a garment), may also be attached to a plural noun. In the Mushaf of Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] it reads "thalātha mi'ati sana" (three hundred years).

Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs hardly ever say "mi'at sinīn" (a hundred years).

Al-Dahhak recited "thalātha mi'atin sunūn" with a waw. The majority recited "tis'an" with a kasra on the tā'; Abu 'Amr recited it with a fatḥa. This is a report from God, glorified is He, about the length of their stay.

So God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that this period was the period of their sleeping, and that what came after that is unknown to humans, so God commanded him to refer the knowledge of that to Him, and He said: ﴿Say: "God knows best how long they remained."﴾

Some of them said: When He said: ﴿and gained nine more,﴾ people did not know whether these were hours, days, weeks, months, or years, and the Children of Israel differed accordingly. So God commanded that knowledge of the nine be referred to Him, and according to this, they are unspecified.
