The knowledge of the unseen enters into this in a primary way, since His knowledge, glorified is He, is part of His decree.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾ that he said: "We let them be made known."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾ that he said: "The rulers," or he said: "The sultans."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ that he said: "The Jews," ﴿and they will say, "Five"﴾ he said: "The Christians."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾ that he said: "Casting by assumption."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among the few; they were seven."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suyuti said with a sahih chain, regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among those few; they were seven," then he mentioned their names.

Ibn Kathir related it from Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Qatada, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah, then said: "These are sound chains to Ibn 'Abbas that they were seven."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾ that he said: "It means: what I have related to you is sufficient for you."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through various routes from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And do not consult any of them about them﴾ that he said: "The Jews."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And never say of anything﴾ (the verse), that he said: "If you forget to say, 'I will do such-and-such,' and forget to say, 'if Allah wills,' then when you remember, say: 'if Allah wills.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he used to hold that the exception (istithna') is valid even after a year, then he recited: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also regarding the verse that he said: "It is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one may make an exception except in the context of an oath."

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Every exception that is connected, there is no breaking of the oath for its one who makes it; and if it is not connected, then he has broken it."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sulayman ibn Dawud said: 'Tonight I will go around to seventy women' — and in another narration: 'ninety' — each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah. The angel said to him: 'Say, if Allah wills.' But he did not say it. So he went around, and none of them gave birth except one woman, half a human." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said, 'if Allah wills,' he would not have broken his oath, and it would have been a fulfilment of his need."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Ikrimah regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you become angry."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you do not say, 'if Allah wills.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A man may interpret the verse, thinking it is so, and then he falls farther than the distance between the heaven and the earth." Then he recited: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ (the verse), then said: "How long did the people stay?" They said: "Three hundred and nine years." He said: "If they had stayed like that, Allah would not have said, ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾; rather He related the statement of the people, saying: ﴿They will say, 'They were three'﴾ up to His saying: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾, so He informed that they do not know. Then He said: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and they said: "(﴿And they remained in their cave﴾) the verse," meaning: it is only what the people said. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾?

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾, it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, days or months or years?' So Allah revealed: ﴿years, and they added nine﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from al-Dahhak without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾ that he said: "Allah Himself says it."

And thus We made [people] come upon them: that is, just as We put them to sleep and raised them, We made [people] come upon them, meaning We informed people about them. He called the informing "i'thar" (coming upon) because whoever is heedless of something and stumbles upon it looks at it and recognizes it, so the coming upon became a cause for knowledge. ﴿So that they might know that the promise of God is true﴾: that is, so that those whom God caused to come upon them would know that God's promise of resurrection is true.

It was said: The king of that era was among those who denied resurrection, so God showed him this sign.

It was said: The cause of their being discovered was that the man they had sent with the silver, which was from the minting of Dihyanus, went to the market. When the people of the market saw the coins, they accused him of having found a treasure, and they took him to the king. The king said to him: "From where did you get these dirhams?" He said: "I sold some dates with them yesterday." The king recognized his truthfulness, then he related the story to him. The king rode out, and his companions rode with him, until they reached the cave. ﴿And that the Hour is not in doubt﴾: that is, so that they would know that the Resurrection will certainly take place, for whoever witnesses the condition of the People of the Cave knows the truth of what God promised concerning resurrection. ﴿When they disputed among themselves over their affair﴾: the adverbial clause (al-zarf) is connected to "a'thar-na" (We made [them] come upon them), meaning: We made them come upon them at the time of the dispute and disagreement among those whom God had made to come upon them concerning the matter of resurrection. It was also said that the dispute was over the matter of the People of the Cave: their length of stay, their number, and what they should do after people had discovered them.

﴿So they said: "Build over them a structure"﴾: so that people would not reach them. That is because when the king and his companions stood over them while they were still alive, God caused the youths to die. Some of them said: "Build over them a structure that will shield them from people's eyes." Then He, glorified is He, said, relating the words of those who disputed about them, concerning their number, the length of their stay, and similar matters related to them: ﴿Their Lord knows best about them﴾, that is, better than these disputants. They said this by entrusting knowledge to God, glorified is He. It was also said that it is part of God's speech, glorified is He, as a rebuttal to the words of those disputing about them, meaning: leave what you are disputing, for I know them better than you do.

It was also said that the adverbial clause in ﴿when they disputed﴾ is connected to an omitted verb, which is "udhkur" (remember). This is supported by the fact that the discovery did not take place at the time of the dispute but before it. It may be said that those people continued to dispute among themselves generation after generation, from the time they took refuge in the cave until the time of the discovery. This is supported by the fact that their story was written at the entrance of the cave by one of their contemporaries among the believers who were concealing their faith, as the commentators have said.

﴿Those who prevailed in their affair said: "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ Mentioning the taking of a place of worship suggests that these who prevailed in their affair were the Muslims. It was also said that they were the people of authority and rule among the aforementioned people, for they are the ones who prevail over the affairs of others. The first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: This indicates that when their matter became manifest, those who believed in resurrection prevailed, because mosques belong to believers.

﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth being their dog."﴾ Those who say they were three, or five, or seven, are the ones who disputed about their number at the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the Muslims. It was also said that they are the People of the Book specifically. In either case, it does not mean that they all said all of this together; rather, some of them said one thing, some another, and some another. ﴿Three, the fourth being their dog﴾: that is, they are three persons, and the clause ﴿the fourth being their dog﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning that their dog, by joining them, makes them four. ﴿And they say: "Five, the sixth being their dog."﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of what came before. The accusative of ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾ is either a circumstantial clause, meaning "as conjecturers," or a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "they conjecture a conjecture." Conjecturing about the unseen is saying something on the basis of assumption and guesswork without certainty. Those described as conjecturing about the unseen are both groups: those who say they were three and those who say they were five. ﴿And they say: "Seven, and the eighth being their dog."﴾ It seems that the statement of this group is closer to the truth, as indicated by their not being included among those who conjecture about the unseen.

It was said: The appearance of the wāw (and) in this sentence indicates that it is intended in the two previous sentences as well.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: ﴿Their fourth being their dog﴾ and ﴿their sixth being their dog﴾ are two sentences that dispense with the conjunction because they include the mention of the first sentence, which is "three." The meaning is: "They are three." This is what al-Wahidi related from Abu Ali, then he said: This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's statement about the entry of the wāw in "wa-thāminuhum" (and the eighth of them) and its exclusion from the first. It was also said: it is an extra wāw for emphasis. It was also said: it is the "wāw of eight," and mentioning it is common in the speech of the Arabs when they reach eight, as in God's words: ﴿And its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and His words: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

Then God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to inform those who differed about their number with what would end the dispute among them, so He said: ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number"﴾, meaning better than you, you who differ. Then He affirmed the knowledge of this to a few people, saying: ﴿None knows them except a few of the people﴾, that is, knows their essence, let alone their number; or it means "none knows their number," with an omitted noun (ḥadhf al-muḍāf). Then God, glorified is He, forbade His Messenger (ﷺ) from disputing with the People of the Book concerning the matter of the People of the Cave, so He said: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾. Al-mirā' in the language means argument; it is said: "māra yumārī mumārāh and mirā'," meaning he argued. Then God, glorified is He, excepted from arguing that which was apparent and clear, so He said: ﴿except with an apparent argument﴾, that is, not going deeply into it, which is merely to relate to them what God revealed to him.

Al-Razi said: It is that he should not deny them regarding the specification of that number, but say: "This specification has no evidence, so suspension of judgment is required." Then He, glorified is He, forbade him from seeking a ruling concerning them, so He said: ﴿and do not seek a ruling concerning them from any of them﴾, that is, do not seek a ruling concerning their matter from any of the disputants about them, from any of them, because the one giving a ruling must be more knowledgeable than the one seeking it, and here the situation is reversed, especially in the case of the People of the Cave. What God related to you about that suffices you from asking one who has no knowledge.

﴿And never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow,"﴾: that is, concerning something you resolve upon in the future time, He expressed it with "tomorrow," not meaning tomorrow itself, so that tomorrow would enter into it primarily.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators said: "When the Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the story of the youths, he said: 'I will inform you tomorrow,' and he did not say: 'If God wills.' So revelation was withheld from him until it grieved him, then God revealed this verse commanding him to make the exception by God's will. It says: If you say concerning something: 'Indeed I will do that tomorrow,' then say: 'If God wills.'"

Al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: ﴿Never say of anything: "Indeed I will do that tomorrow," unless you say: "If God wills."﴾ So the verb "say" is implied, and when the verb "taqulu" was omitted, the verb "shā'a" (wills) was shifted to the form of the future. It was said: This exception is "mufarragh" (an exception with no stated subject), meaning: do not say that in any state except the state of being connected to God's will, which is saying: "If God wills," or at any time except the time when God wills that you say it unconditionally. It was also said: The exception is intended as a perpetual prohibition, as if it were said: "Never say it ever," like His words: ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], because their return to their religion is something God does not will.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾: the exception by God's will, that is, say "If God wills," whether the interval is short or long.

The scholars have differed about the length of time within which it is permissible to attach the exception after the thing excepted from, according to well-known opinions set out in their places.

It was also said: The meaning is "remember your Lord by seeking forgiveness when you forget." ﴿And say: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is closer to right guidance than this."﴾ The referent of "than this" (min hādhā) is the story of the People of the Cave, meaning: say, O Muhammad, perhaps my Lord will grant me success in something closer than this story, from among the signs and proofs that indicate my prophethood.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Perhaps my Lord will give me, from among the signs of prophethood, what will be closer to right guidance and more indicative than the story of the People of the Cave." God did that for him, as He gave him knowledge of the unseen matters of the messengers and their stories, which was clearer in proof and closer to right guidance than the story of the People of the Cave.

It was also said: The reference is to His words: ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾, meaning: perhaps my Lord will guide me, at this forgetting, to something else in place of this forgotten thing, something closer to right guidance and nearer to good and benefit than it. The first view is preferable.

﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and gained nine more.﴾ The majority recited "mi'atin" with tanwīn and "sinīna" in the accusative, so "sinīn" in this reading is either an apposition (badal) or a clarifying appositive (ʿaṭf bayān).

Al-Farra', Abu Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and al-Kisa'i said: There is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it, and the implied meaning is: "sinīn thalātha mi'atin" (years, three hundred).

Abu Ali al-Farisi preferred the first reading.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited with the idiomatic construction of "mi'a" as a genitive of "sinīn"; in this reading, "sinīn" is a specification (tamyīz), with the plural placed in the position of the singular in specification, as in God's words: ﴿the greatest losers in deeds﴾ [al-Kahf: 103]. Al-Farra' said: Some Arabs place "sinīn" in the position of "sana" (year).

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: These numbers which, in the well-known usage, are attached to singular nouns, such as "thalātha mi'ati rajul" (three hundred men) and "thawb" (a garment), may also be attached to a plural noun. In the Mushaf of Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] it reads "thalātha mi'ati sana" (three hundred years).

Al-Akhfash said: The Arabs hardly ever say "mi'at sinīn" (a hundred years).

Al-Dahhak recited "thalātha mi'atin sunūn" with a waw. The majority recited "tis'an" with a kasra on the tā'; Abu 'Amr recited it with a fatḥa. This is a report from God, glorified is He, about the length of their stay.

Ibn Jarir said: The Children of Israel differed about the period of time that passed for them after they were discovered. Some of them said: "They remained three hundred and nine years." So God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that this period was the period of their sleeping, and that what came after that is unknown to humans, so God commanded him to refer the knowledge of that to Him, and He said: ﴿Say: "God knows best how long they remained."﴾

Ibn 'Atiyya said: According to this, the first "labithū" (they remained) refers to the day of the cave, and the second "labithū" refers to the period after their discovery until the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), or until they died.

Some of them said: When He said: ﴿and gained nine more,﴾ people did not know whether these were hours, days, weeks, months, or years, and the Children of Israel differed accordingly. So God commanded that knowledge of the nine be referred to Him, and according to this, they are unspecified.

The first view is preferable, because the apparent meaning of Arabic speech, as understood according to their language, is that the nine are years, as evidenced by the fact that the number in this statement is for "years" and not for months, days, or hours.

It is related from al-Zajjaj that the intended meaning is three hundred solar years, and three hundred and nine lunar years. This, from al-Zajjaj, is only given as an approximation.

Then He, glorified is He, emphasized His exclusive knowledge of how long they stayed by His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: whatever is hidden within them and concealed of their conditions, none other than Him has any share in that. Then He increased the emphasis and intensification by bringing what indicates wonder at His perception of visible and audible things, saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾. This wonder conveys that His knowledge of visible and audible things, glorified is He, is beyond what the perceptions of perceivers are capable of, and that in His knowledge the absent and the present, the hidden and the manifest, the small and the great, the subtle and the dense are alike. It seems its original form was: "How much He sees and how much He hears!", then it was transferred to the imperative form for the sake of expression (inshā'). The bā' (ب) is superfluous according to Sibawayh, and al-Akhfash disagreed with him; the discussion is established in the science of grammar (naḥw). ﴿They have no protector besides Him, from among them﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of the heavens and the earth. It is said it refers to the People of the Cave, and it is said it refers to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) among the disbelievers, meaning: they have no ally who befriends them, or who takes charge of their affairs, or who helps them. In this there is an explanation of the extent of His power and that all things are under His dominion. ﴿And He does not make anyone share in His judgment﴾: Al-Jumhur read it with a raised kāf (ُ), as a predicate about Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Qatada read it with a initial tā' (ت) and a sukun on the kāf, as a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should not make a partner for Allah in His judgment. This reading is also narrated from Ibn 'Amir.

Mujahid read it with a yā' (ي) and a jazm. Ya'qub said: "I do not know its basis." The meaning of "Allah's judgment" is what He decrees, or the knowledge of the unseen; the first is preferable.

The knowledge of the unseen enters into this in a primary way, since His knowledge, glorified is He, is part of His decree.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾ that he said: "We let them be made known."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾ that he said: "The rulers," or he said: "The sultans."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿They will say, "They were three"﴾ that he said: "The Jews," ﴿and they will say, "Five"﴾ he said: "The Christians."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾ that he said: "Casting by assumption."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among the few; they were seven."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suyuti said with a sahih chain, regarding His saying: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾ that he said: "I am among those few; they were seven," then he mentioned their names.

Ibn Kathir related it from Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Qatada, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah, then said: "These are sound chains to Ibn 'Abbas that they were seven."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿So do not argue concerning them﴾ that he said: "It means: what I have related to you is sufficient for you."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through various routes from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And do not consult any of them about them﴾ that he said: "The Jews."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And never say of anything﴾ (the verse), that he said: "If you forget to say, 'I will do such-and-such,' and forget to say, 'if Allah wills,' then when you remember, say: 'if Allah wills.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he used to hold that the exception (istithna') is valid even after a year, then he recited: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him also regarding the verse that he said: "It is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one may make an exception except in the context of an oath."

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "Every exception that is connected, there is no breaking of the oath for its one who makes it; and if it is not connected, then he has broken it."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sulayman ibn Dawud said: 'Tonight I will go around to seventy women' — and in another narration: 'ninety' — each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of Allah. The angel said to him: 'Say, if Allah wills.' But he did not say it. So he went around, and none of them gave birth except one woman, half a human." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had he said, 'if Allah wills,' he would not have broken his oath, and it would have been a fulfilment of his need."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Ikrimah regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you become angry."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from al-Hasan regarding ﴿if you forget﴾ that he said: "If you do not say, 'if Allah wills.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A man may interpret the verse, thinking it is so, and then he falls farther than the distance between the heaven and the earth." Then he recited: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ (the verse), then said: "How long did the people stay?" They said: "Three hundred and nine years." He said: "If they had stayed like that, Allah would not have said, ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾; rather He related the statement of the people, saying: ﴿They will say, 'They were three'﴾ up to His saying: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾, so He informed that they do not know. Then He said: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and they said: "(﴿And they remained in their cave﴾) the verse," meaning: it is only what the people said. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾?

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred﴾, it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, days or months or years?' So Allah revealed: ﴿years, and they added nine﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from al-Dahhak without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿How clearly He sees, and how keenly He hears﴾ that he said: "Allah Himself says it."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 29–31 (part 1 of 2):

.
His words: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you﴾. Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to be constant in reciting the Book that was revealed to him. It has been said: it is possible that the meaning of His words "wa-tlu" is "and follow," an imperative from talw (following), not from tilawa (recitation). And "from the Book of your Lord" explains what was revealed. ﴿There is none who can alter His words﴾: that is, none is able to change or alter them, and only He has that power.
Al-Zajjaj said: that is, what Allah has informed of and what He has commanded, so there is no one who can alter it. On this reading the sense is: there is no one who can alter the judgment of His words.
﴿And you will not find, other than Him, any refuge﴾. Multahad means refuge, a place one seeks shelter in. The root laHd means inclination.
Al-Zajjaj said: you will not find an escape from His command and His prohibition. (p-857) The meaning is: if you do not follow the Qur'an, recite it, and act by its rulings, you will not find any alternative to turn to or any place to incline toward. This verse is the end of the story of the People of the Cave.
Then, as is the custom of the Noble Book, He began another theme, saying: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾. His prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) from driving away the poor believers was already mentioned in al-An'am, in His words: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-An'am 6:52]. Here He commanded him to restrain himself in their company. So the patience of the self is its restraint. The mention of the morning and the evening is a metaphor for continuity in supplication at all times.
It has been said: at the two ends of the day. It has also been said: what is meant is the Asr and Fajr prayers.
Nasr ibn 'Asim, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿bil-ghadwa﴾ with a waw, and they argued that it is written that way with a waw in the Mushaf.
Al-Nahhas said: this does not follow, since they write "al-hayat" and "al-salat" with a waw, and the Arabs hardly say "al-ghadwa." The meaning of ﴿seeking His face﴾ is that they intend by their supplication the good pleasure of Allah, glorified is He. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). Then He commanded him to watch over their conditions, saying: ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, that is, do not let your eyes go beyond them to others.
Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: do not turn your eyes away from them. Al-Zajjaj said: do not turn your gaze to others from among the people of rank and adornment. Its use with "'an" is because it contains the sense of turning away, from 'adawtuhu 'an al-amr, meaning I diverted him from it. It has also been said: its meaning is: do not let your eyes look down on them.
﴿Desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾: that is, sitting with the people of nobility and wealth. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning while you are desiring that. This applies if the subject of "turid" (desire) is the Prophet (ﷺ). If the subject is a pronoun referring to "the two eyes," then the sense is: desiring the adornment of the worldly life. Attributing desire to the eyes is a metaphor, and the singular pronoun is used because of mutual association, as in the words of the poet:
"How many a glance (zuhluqa) have the two eyes stumbled upon, and they pour forth tears."
﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾: that is, We made it heedless by sealing it. He forbade the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from obeying one whom Allah had made heedless of His remembrance, like those who asked him to remove the poor from his assembly. They demanded the removal of those who call upon their Lord in the morning and evening, seeking His face, while they themselves were heedless of the remembrance of Allah. Yet despite this, they were among those who followed their desires and preferred them over the truth, choosing shirk over tawhid. ﴿And his affair has become excessive﴾: that is, going beyond the limit of moderation. From their saying: "a fras (horse) furuṭ" when it is ahead of the other horses. On this reading it is from excess (ifrat). It has also been said that it is from neglect (tafrit), which means shortcoming and waste.
Al-Zajjaj said: whoever puts weakness first in his affair destroys and ruins it.
Then He, glorified is He, made clear to His Prophet (ﷺ) what he should say to those heedless ones. He said: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord"﴾: that is, say to them: what has been revealed to you and what you were commanded to recite is the truth, which comes from Allah, not from anyone else, such that alteration and change could be possible in it. It has been said that the truth here means patience with the poor.
Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the truth that I have brought you. ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ means: I did not bring it to you from my own self; I brought it to you from Allah. ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. It has been said that this is part of the statement which He commanded His Messenger to say. The "fa" indicates the sequence of what precedes it from what follows it. It is also possible that it is from the speech of Allah, glorified is He, and not from the statement which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say, and in it is a severe threat. The meaning would be: say to them, O Muhammad, "The truth is from your Lord." After you have said this to them, whoever wills to believe in Allah and affirm you, let him believe; and whoever wills to disbelieve in Him and deny you, let him disbelieve.
Then He reinforced and intensified the warning, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾: that is, We have readied and prepared for the wrongdoers, who chose disbelief in Allah, denial of Him, and rejection of His prophets, a great fire. ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾: that is, it encompasses them.
Al-Suradiq is the singular of al-sarādiqāt. Al-Jawhari said: it is what is stretched over the courtyard of a house, and every tent made of cotton is a surādiq. From this is the saying of Ru'ba:
"O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn Jarud, the canopy of glory is stretched over you."
And the poet said:
"He is the one who admitted al-Nu'man into a house whose roof was the chests of elephants, after a covered tent."
Salam ibn Jandal said this when the king of Persia killed the king of the Arabs, al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, beneath the feet of the elephants.
Ibn al-A'rabi said: its surādiq is its wall. Al-Qutaybi said: al-surādiq is the enclosure that surrounds the tent.
The meaning is: the enclosure of the fire has surrounded the disbelievers, likening what surrounds them of fire to the enclosure that surrounds whoever is within it. ﴿And if they call for help﴾ from the heat of the fire, ﴿they will be given relief with water like molten metal﴾. Al-Muhl is molten iron.
Al-Zajjaj said: they will be given relief with water like molten lead or copper. It has been said that it is the dregs of oil.
Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: it is everything that is melted from the substances of the earth, of iron, lead and copper. It has also been said that it is a kind of tar.
Then He described this water with which they are given relief as ﴿scalding the faces﴾: when it is brought to them, their faces become roasted from its heat. ﴿Evil is the drink﴾: their drink is this. ﴿And evil is the resting place﴾ (murtafaqan): a place of reclining. It is said: irtafaqtu, meaning I reclined. The root of irtifaq is placing the elbow, and it is said: "irtafaqa al-rajul" when a man sleeps on his elbow. Al-Qutaybi said: it is a sitting place. It has also been said: a gathering place.
﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: this begins the promise to the believers after finishing the warning to the disbelievers.
The meaning: indeed, those who believed in the truth that was revealed to you and did righteous deeds among the actions, ﴿indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾. This is the predicate of "inna alladhina amanu," and the returning pronoun is omitted, that is, "whoever among them does good work."
The clause ﴿Those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is a resumptive sentence explaining the reward. The demonstrative refers to those previously mentioned. It has been said that "ulā'ika" may be the predicate of "inna alladhina amanu," and the clause "indeed We do not waste" is then a parenthetical statement. It is also possible that "ulā'ika" is a second predicate. The discussion of the Gardens of Eden and of how the rivers flow beneath them has already been mentioned.
﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: asawir is the plural of uswira, and uswira is the plural of siwar, which is an ornament worn on the wrist of the hand, and is among the adornments of kings. It has been said: each one of them will be adorned with three bracelets: one of silver, one of pearls, and one of gold. The apparent meaning of the verse is that all of them are of gold. It is possible that the speaker's statement here is a combination of verses, in light of His words in another verse: ﴿bracelets of silver﴾ [al-Insan 76:21], and His words in another verse: "and pearls" [al-Hajj 22:23]. The "min" in "min asawir" is for beginning, and in "min dhahab" it is for specification.
Al-Farra' transmitted "yuhallawna" with a fatha on the ya, a sukun on the ha, and a fatha on the lam. It is said: "halat al-mar'ah tuhla," so she is "haliyah" when she wears jewelry.
﴿And they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: sundus is the thin silk, its singular being sundusa, and istabraq is the thick. The commentators also said the same. It has been said that istabraq is brocade, as the poet said:
"And brocade at times is their clothing."
It has also been said that it is what is woven with gold. Al-Qutaybi said: it is a loanword from Persian (mu'arrab). Al-Jawhari said: its diminutive is ubayriq. Green is specified because it is pleasing to the eye and because it is the most beautiful of colors.
﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ara'ik is the plural of arika, which are beds inside canopies. It has been said: they are thrones of gold adorned with pearls and rubies. The original form of ittaka' is iwtaka', and the original form of muttaki'in is mu'tatakin. Al-Ittika' is leaning heavily upon something.
﴿How excellent is the reward﴾: that with which Allah rewarded them. ﴿And how good is the resting place﴾ (murtafaqan), that is, the reclining place. This has been mentioned shortly before.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, regarding His words "multahadan," that he said: a refuge.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Salman, who said: "The ones whose hearts were to be won over came: 'Uyayna ibn Badr and al-Aqra' ibn Habis. They said: O Messenger of Allah, if you were to sit at the head of the assembly and keep away from these people, and the odor of their coarse woolen garments (wa-arwah jibabihim, that is, Salman, Abu Dharr and the poor Muslims, who wore woolen robes), we would sit with you, converse with you, and learn from you." So Allah revealed: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you﴾ up to His words: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a fire﴾. Abu al-Shaykh added, from Salman, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got up searching for them until he found them at the back of the mosque remembering Allah, the Exalted. He said: "All praise is due to Allah, who did not take my life until He commanded me to keep myself patient with men of my community; with you is my life and my death."

Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf, who said: "This verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in some of his dwellings: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening﴾. So he went out seeking them and found a group remembering Allah, among them one with disheveled hair, one with a roughened skin, and one wearing a worn garment. When he saw them, he sat with them and said: 'All praise is due to Allah, who has placed in my community one whom He commanded me to keep myself patient with.'"

Al-Bazzar transmitted from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah, who both said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came while a man was reciting Surat al-Hijr or Surat al-Kahf, and he fell silent. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'This is the gathering with which I was commanded to keep myself patient.'"

There are other narrations on this topic.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Nafi', who said: "'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar informed me concerning this verse, ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾, that they are those who attend the five prayers."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted, through 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, concerning His words: "And keep yourself patient" (the verse), that he said: it was revealed concerning the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted, through Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾, that he said: it was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf. This is because he invited the Prophet (ﷺ) to a matter that Allah disliked, namely driving away the poor from him and bringing near the chieftains of the people of Makkah. So Allah revealed this verse, meaning "whose heart We have sealed," meaning from tawhid, "and who followed his desire," meaning shirk, ﴿and his affair has become excessive﴾, meaning excess in the matter of Allah and ignorance of Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 29–31 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, from Ibn Buraydah, who said: "Uyayna ibn Hisn entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) on a hot day, and with him was Salman, who wore a woollen cloak, and the smell of sweat from the wool became noticeable. Uyayna said: 'O Muhammad, when we come to you, remove this man and his like from your presence, so that they do not trouble us. When we have left, you may sit with them as you wish.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless...﴾ the verse."

It is also established in Sahih Muslim concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse that contains the meaning of this verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-An'am: 52]. From Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), six men. The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Drive these away, so that they will not dare against us.' He said: I was there, and Ibn Mas'ud, a man from Hudhayl, Bilal, and two men whose names I have forgotten. Then something came into the soul of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of what Allah willed to occur, so he spoke to himself, and Allah revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ the verse."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And his affair was [ever] fruT﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], that he said: "Loss (ḍayā')."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding (﴿And say, "The truth..."﴾): he said: "It is the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. He said: "Whomever Allah wills to have faith, believes; and whomever He wills to have disbelief, disbelieves. This is His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [at-Takwir: 29]."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, concerning the verse, that he said: "This is a threat and a warning."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him, regarding His saying: ﴿Its enclosure will surround them﴾, that he said: "A wall of fire."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The enclosure of the Fire has four walls, the thickness of each wall being a journey of forty years."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying (﴿with water like molten brass﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]) (p-859) (﴿like molten brass﴾)": He said: "Like the dregs of oil. When it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: (﴿like molten brass﴾), that he said: "Black, like the dregs of oil."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Atiyyah, who said: "Ibn Abbas was asked about al-Muhl (molten brass), and he said: 'It is a thick water like the sediment of oil.'"

Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about al-Muhl, so he called for gold and silver and melted them. When they had melted, he said: "This is the most similar thing to al-Muhl, which is the drink of the people of the Fire, and its colour is the colour of the sky, except that the drink of the people of the Fire is far hotter than this."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "Do you know what al-Muhl is? Al-Muhl is the dregs of oil, meaning its last part."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And evil is it as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], that he said: "A gathering place."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The adornment (ḥilyah) of the believer will reach as far as his ablution reaches."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Khayr Martad ibn Abd Allah, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree that grows sundus, from which are the garments of the people of Paradise."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "Istabraq is thick brocade (dibaj)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid the like of this.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Haytham ibn Malik al-Ta'i, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed a man will recline on a couch for a period of forty years, not turning from it and not growing weary of it; there comes to him what his soul desires and what his eye delights in."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The arara'ik (couches) are the beds inside the canopies (hijal), upon which is the spread, piled up, in the sky, a farsakh (a league) high."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from him, who said: "A couch is not an arika until the bed is within a canopy (hajalah)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah that he was asked about the arara'ik, and he said: "They are the canopies over the beds."

﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ara'ik is the plural of arika, which are beds inside canopies. It has been said: they are thrones of gold adorned with pearls and rubies. The original form of ittaka' is iwtaka', and the original form of muttaki'in is mu'tatakin. Al-Ittika' is leaning heavily upon something.
﴿How excellent is the reward﴾: that with which Allah rewarded them. ﴿And how good is the resting place﴾ (murtafaqan), that is, the reclining place. This has been mentioned shortly before.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, regarding His words "multahadan," that he said: a refuge.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Salman, who said: "The ones whose hearts were to be won over came: 'Uyayna ibn Badr and al-Aqra' ibn Habis. They said: O Messenger of Allah, if you were to sit at the head of the assembly and keep away from these people, and the odor of their coarse woolen garments (wa-arwah jibabihim, that is, Salman, Abu Dharr and the poor Muslims, who wore woolen robes), we would sit with you, converse with you, and learn from you." So Allah revealed: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you﴾ up to His words: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a fire﴾. Abu al-Shaykh added, from Salman, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got up searching for them until he found them at the back of the mosque remembering Allah, the Exalted. He said: "All praise is due to Allah, who did not take my life until He commanded me to keep myself patient with men of my community; with you is my life and my death."

Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf, who said: "This verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in some of his dwellings: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening﴾. So he went out seeking them and found a group remembering Allah, among them one with disheveled hair, one with a roughened skin, and one wearing a worn garment. When he saw them, he sat with them and said: 'All praise is due to Allah, who has placed in my community one whom He commanded me to keep myself patient with.'"

Al-Bazzar transmitted from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah, who both said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came while a man was reciting Surat al-Hijr or Surat al-Kahf, and he fell silent. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'This is the gathering with which I was commanded to keep myself patient.'"

There are other narrations on this topic.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Nafi', who said: "'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar informed me concerning this verse, ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾, that they are those who attend the five prayers."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted, through 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, concerning His words: "And keep yourself patient" (the verse), that he said: it was revealed concerning the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted, through Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾, that he said: it was revealed concerning Umayya ibn Khalaf. This is because he invited the Prophet (ﷺ) to a matter that Allah disliked, namely driving away the poor from him and bringing near the chieftains of the people of Makkah. So Allah revealed this verse, meaning "whose heart We have sealed," meaning from tawhid, "and who followed his desire," meaning shirk, ﴿and his affair has become excessive﴾, meaning excess in the matter of Allah and ignorance of Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 29–31 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, from Ibn Buraydah, who said: "Uyayna ibn Hisn entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) on a hot day, and with him was Salman, who wore a woollen cloak, and the smell of sweat from the wool became noticeable. Uyayna said: 'O Muhammad, when we come to you, remove this man and his like from your presence, so that they do not trouble us. When we have left, you may sit with them as you wish.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless...﴾ the verse."

It is also established in Sahih Muslim concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse that contains the meaning of this verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-An'am: 52]. From Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), six men. The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Drive these away, so that they will not dare against us.' He said: I was there, and Ibn Mas'ud, a man from Hudhayl, Bilal, and two men whose names I have forgotten. Then something came into the soul of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of what Allah willed to occur, so he spoke to himself, and Allah revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ the verse."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And his affair was [ever] fruT﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], that he said: "Loss (ḍayā')."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding (﴿And say, "The truth..."﴾): he said: "It is the Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. He said: "Whomever Allah wills to have faith, believes; and whomever He wills to have disbelief, disbelieves. This is His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [at-Takwir: 29]."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, concerning the verse, that he said: "This is a threat and a warning."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him, regarding His saying: ﴿Its enclosure will surround them﴾, that he said: "A wall of fire."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The enclosure of the Fire has four walls, the thickness of each wall being a journey of forty years."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying (﴿with water like molten brass﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]) (p-859) (﴿like molten brass﴾)": He said: "Like the dregs of oil. When it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: (﴿like molten brass﴾), that he said: "Black, like the dregs of oil."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Atiyyah, who said: "Ibn Abbas was asked about al-Muhl (molten brass), and he said: 'It is a thick water like the sediment of oil.'"

Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about al-Muhl, so he called for gold and silver and melted them. When they had melted, he said: "This is the most similar thing to al-Muhl, which is the drink of the people of the Fire, and its colour is the colour of the sky, except that the drink of the people of the Fire is far hotter than this."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "Do you know what al-Muhl is? Al-Muhl is the dregs of oil, meaning its last part."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And evil is it as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], that he said: "A gathering place."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The adornment (ḥilyah) of the believer will reach as far as his ablution reaches."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Khayr Martad ibn Abd Allah, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree that grows sundus, from which are the garments of the people of Paradise."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "Istabraq is thick brocade (dibaj)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid the like of this.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Haytham ibn Malik al-Ta'i, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed a man will recline on a couch for a period of forty years, not turning from it and not growing weary of it; there comes to him what his soul desires and what his eye delights in."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The arara'ik (couches) are the beds inside the canopies (hijal), upon which is the spread, piled up, in the sky, a farsakh (a league) high."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from him, who said: "A couch is not an arika until the bed is within a canopy (hajalah)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah that he was asked about the arara'ik, and he said: "They are the canopies over the beds."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 29–31 (part 1 of 2):

.
His words: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you﴾. Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to be constant in reciting the Book that was revealed to him. It has been said: it is possible that the meaning of His words "wa-tlu" is "and follow," an imperative from talw (following), not from tilawa (recitation). And "from the Book of your Lord" explains what was revealed. ﴿There is none who can alter His words﴾: that is, none is able to change or alter them, and only He has that power.
Al-Zajjaj said: that is, what Allah has informed of and what He has commanded, so there is no one who can alter it. On this reading the sense is: there is no one who can alter the judgment of His words.
﴿And you will not find, other than Him, any refuge﴾. Multahad means refuge, a place one seeks shelter in. The root laHd means inclination.
Al-Zajjaj said: you will not find an escape from His command and His prohibition. (p-857) The meaning is: if you do not follow the Qur'an, recite it, and act by its rulings, you will not find any alternative to turn to or any place to incline toward. This verse is the end of the story of the People of the Cave.
Then, as is the custom of the Noble Book, He began another theme, saying: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾. His prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) from driving away the poor believers was already mentioned in al-An'am, in His words: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ [al-An'am 6:52]. Here He commanded him to restrain himself in their company. So the patience of the self is its restraint. The mention of the morning and the evening is a metaphor for continuity in supplication at all times.
It has been said: at the two ends of the day. It has also been said: what is meant is the Asr and Fajr prayers.
Nasr ibn 'Asim, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿bil-ghadwa﴾ with a waw, and they argued that it is written that way with a waw in the Mushaf.
Al-Nahhas said: this does not follow, since they write "al-hayat" and "al-salat" with a waw, and the Arabs hardly say "al-ghadwa." The meaning of ﴿seeking His face﴾ is that they intend by their supplication the good pleasure of Allah, glorified is He. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). Then He commanded him to watch over their conditions, saying: ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾, that is, do not let your eyes go beyond them to others.
Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: do not turn your eyes away from them. Al-Zajjaj said: do not turn your gaze to others from among the people of rank and adornment. Its use with "'an" is because it contains the sense of turning away, from 'adawtuhu 'an al-amr, meaning I diverted him from it. It has also been said: its meaning is: do not let your eyes look down on them.
﴿Desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾: that is, sitting with the people of nobility and wealth. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning while you are desiring that. This applies if the subject of "turid" (desire) is the Prophet (ﷺ). If the subject is a pronoun referring to "the two eyes," then the sense is: desiring the adornment of the worldly life. Attributing desire to the eyes is a metaphor, and the singular pronoun is used because of mutual association, as in the words of the poet:
"How many a glance (zuhluqa) have the two eyes stumbled upon, and they pour forth tears."
﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾: that is, We made it heedless by sealing it. He forbade the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from obeying one whom Allah had made heedless of His remembrance, like those who asked him to remove the poor from his assembly. They demanded the removal of those who call upon their Lord in the morning and evening, seeking His face, while they themselves were heedless of the remembrance of Allah. Yet despite this, they were among those who followed their desires and preferred them over the truth, choosing shirk over tawhid. ﴿And his affair has become excessive﴾: that is, going beyond the limit of moderation. From their saying: "a fras (horse) furuṭ" when it is ahead of the other horses. On this reading it is from excess (ifrat). It has also been said that it is from neglect (tafrit), which means shortcoming and waste.
Al-Zajjaj said: whoever puts weakness first in his affair destroys and ruins it.
Then He, glorified is He, made clear to His Prophet (ﷺ) what he should say to those heedless ones. He said: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord"﴾: that is, say to them: what has been revealed to you and what you were commanded to recite is the truth, which comes from Allah, not from anyone else, such that alteration and change could be possible in it. It has been said that the truth here means patience with the poor.
Al-Zajjaj said: that is, the truth that I have brought you. ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ means: I did not bring it to you from my own self; I brought it to you from Allah. ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. It has been said that this is part of the statement which He commanded His Messenger to say. The "fa" indicates the sequence of what precedes it from what follows it. It is also possible that it is from the speech of Allah, glorified is He, and not from the statement which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say, and in it is a severe threat. The meaning would be: say to them, O Muhammad, "The truth is from your Lord." After you have said this to them, whoever wills to believe in Allah and affirm you, let him believe; and whoever wills to disbelieve in Him and deny you, let him disbelieve.
Then He reinforced and intensified the warning, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers﴾: that is, We have readied and prepared for the wrongdoers, who chose disbelief in Allah, denial of Him, and rejection of His prophets, a great fire. ﴿Its enclosure surrounds them﴾: that is, it encompasses them.
Al-Suradiq is the singular of al-sarādiqāt. Al-Jawhari said: it is what is stretched over the courtyard of a house, and every tent made of cotton is a surādiq. From this is the saying of Ru'ba:
"O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn Jarud, the canopy of glory is stretched over you."
And the poet said:
"He is the one who admitted al-Nu'man into a house whose roof was the chests of elephants, after a covered tent."
Salam ibn Jandal said this when the king of Persia killed the king of the Arabs, al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, beneath the feet of the elephants.
Ibn al-A'rabi said: its surādiq is its wall. Al-Qutaybi said: al-surādiq is the enclosure that surrounds the tent.
The meaning is: the enclosure of the fire has surrounded the disbelievers, likening what surrounds them of fire to the enclosure that surrounds whoever is within it. ﴿And if they call for help﴾ from the heat of the fire, ﴿they will be given relief with water like molten metal﴾. Al-Muhl is molten iron.
Al-Zajjaj said: they will be given relief with water like molten lead or copper. It has been said that it is the dregs of oil.
Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: it is everything that is melted from the substances of the earth, of iron, lead and copper. It has also been said that it is a kind of tar.
Then He described this water with which they are given relief as ﴿scalding the faces﴾: when it is brought to them, their faces become roasted from its heat. ﴿Evil is the drink﴾: their drink is this. ﴿And evil is the resting place﴾ (murtafaqan): a place of reclining. It is said: irtafaqtu, meaning I reclined. The root of irtifaq is placing the elbow, and it is said: "irtafaqa al-rajul" when a man sleeps on his elbow. Al-Qutaybi said: it is a sitting place. It has also been said: a gathering place.
﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: this begins the promise to the believers after finishing the warning to the disbelievers.
The meaning: indeed, those who believed in the truth that was revealed to you and did righteous deeds among the actions, ﴿indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work﴾. This is the predicate of "inna alladhina amanu," and the returning pronoun is omitted, that is, "whoever among them does good work."
The clause ﴿Those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is a resumptive sentence explaining the reward. The demonstrative refers to those previously mentioned. It has been said that "ulā'ika" may be the predicate of "inna alladhina amanu," and the clause "indeed We do not waste" is then a parenthetical statement. It is also possible that "ulā'ika" is a second predicate. The discussion of the Gardens of Eden and of how the rivers flow beneath them has already been mentioned.
﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: asawir is the plural of uswira, and uswira is the plural of siwar, which is an ornament worn on the wrist of the hand, and is among the adornments of kings. It has been said: each one of them will be adorned with three bracelets: one of silver, one of pearls, and one of gold. The apparent meaning of the verse is that all of them are of gold. It is possible that the speaker's statement here is a combination of verses, in light of His words in another verse: ﴿bracelets of silver﴾ [al-Insan 76:21], and His words in another verse: "and pearls" [al-Hajj 22:23]. The "min" in "min asawir" is for beginning, and in "min dhahab" it is for specification.
Al-Farra' transmitted "yuhallawna" with a fatha on the ya, a sukun on the ha, and a fatha on the lam. It is said: "halat al-mar'ah tuhla," so she is "haliyah" when she wears jewelry.
﴿And they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: sundus is the thin silk, its singular being sundusa, and istabraq is the thick. The commentators also said the same. It has been said that istabraq is brocade, as the poet said:
"And brocade at times is their clothing."
It has also been said that it is what is woven with gold. Al-Qutaybi said: it is a loanword from Persian (mu'arrab). Al-Jawhari said: its diminutive is ubayriq. Green is specified because it is pleasing to the eye and because it is the most beautiful of colors.

When it is brought near to him, the skin of his face falls off into it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: (﴿like molten brass﴾), that he said: "Black, like the dregs of oil."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Atiyyah, who said: "Ibn Abbas was asked about al-Muhl (molten brass), and he said: 'It is a thick water like the sediment of oil.'"

Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about al-Muhl, so he called for gold and silver and melted them. When they had melted, he said: "This is the most similar thing to al-Muhl, which is the drink of the people of the Fire, and its colour is the colour of the sky, except that the drink of the people of the Fire is far hotter than this."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "Do you know what al-Muhl is? Al-Muhl is the dregs of oil, meaning its last part."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And evil is it as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], that he said: "A gathering place."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The adornment (ḥilyah) of the believer will reach as far as his ablution reaches."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu al-Khayr Martad ibn Abd Allah, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree that grows sundus, from which are the garments of the people of Paradise."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "Istabraq is thick brocade (dibaj)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid the like of this.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Haytham ibn Malik al-Ta'i, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed a man will recline on a couch for a period of forty years, not turning from it and not growing weary of it; there comes to him what his soul desires and what his eye delights in."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The arara'ik (couches) are the beds inside the canopies (hijal), upon which is the spread, piled up, in the sky, a farsakh (a league) high."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from him, who said: "A couch is not an arika until the bed is within a canopy (hajalah)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah that he was asked about the arara'ik, and he said: "They are the canopies over the beds."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

.

His saying: ﴿And set forth for them a parable: two men﴾. This parable was set forth by God, glorified is He, for the one who is proud of worldly things and disdains sitting with the poor. On this reading it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep yourself patient﴾.

Scholars differ over whether the two men are hypothetical (muqaddarān) or real (muḥaqqaqān). Some exegetes held the first view, and others held the second.

They also differed over their identity. It was said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel. It was said that they were two brothers from the Makhzum clan of Makkah, one a believer and the other an unbeliever. It was said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51].

The words ﴿a parable﴾ and ﴿two men﴾ are in the accusative because they are the two objects of the verb ﴿set forth﴾ (iḍrib). It was said: the first is the second and the second is the first.

﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾: this is the unbeliever. The phrase ﴿of grapevines﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of what the two gardens contained, meaning: of varied vines.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: al-ḥaff (ḥaff) means encircling. From it comes ﴿encircling (ḥāffīn) the Throne﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. It is said: ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān, yaḥiffūna ḥaffan, meaning they went around him. So the meaning of the verse is: We made the palm trees go around the two gardens on all their sides.

﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: meaning between the two gardens, at their middle, so that each of them would combine both sustenance and fruits.

Then God, glorified is He, informed about the two gardens that each one was yielding its produce and what was in it. He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾. He used the feminine singular verb (ātat) with kilā (both), because its wording is singular, so He observed the aspect of the wording.

The Basran grammarians held that kilā and kilā are singular nouns, not dual. Al-Farra' said that it is dual and derived from kull, with the lām lightened and an alif added to form the dual. Sibawayh said: the alif of kilā is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the third radical of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original is kulwā.

Abu 'Amr said: the tā' is an added (mulḥaqa) letter.

Ukulahā (its produce) means its fruit. This indicates that it had become fit for eating.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu" (each of the gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿And did not fall short of it in anything﴾: meaning it did not diminish its produce in any way. It is said: ẓalamahu ḥaqqahu, meaning he deprived him of his right. He described the two gardens with this quality to indicate that they were contrary to what is usual in other orchards, since those usually produce abundantly in one year and little in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: meaning We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens to water them constantly without interruption. It was recited as "fajjarnā" with doubled letters for emphasis, and with a single letter, which is the original form.

﴿And he had fruit﴾: meaning the owner of the two gardens had fruit. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read thamar with a fatḥa on the thā' and the mīm, and they read it likewise in His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm in both places. The rest read it with a ḍamma on both letters in both places.

Al-Jawhari said: thamarah is the singular of thamar, and the plural of thamar is thimār, like jabal and jibāl. Al-Farra' said: the plural of thimār is thumur, like kitāb and kutub, and the plural of thumur is athmār, like 'unuq and a'nāq.

It was said: thamar means all wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. It was also said that it means gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: meaning the unbeliever, the owner of the two gardens, said to his believing companion.

﴿While he was conversing with him﴾: meaning the unbeliever was conversing with the believer. The meaning is that he was answering back in speech. Al-muḥāwara means responding in discussion, and at-taḥāwur means mutual response.

﴿I have more wealth than you and mightier in manpower﴾ (nafar). Nafar means a group, which is fewer than ten people. Here it means followers, servants and children.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾: meaning the unbeliever entered the garden of his own self.

The exegetes said: he took his Muslim brother by the hand, brought him into his garden, walked him around it and showed him its wonders. The singular "garden" here may be explained in several ways: he only brought his brother into one of the two; or because the two were connected, they were like one; or because he brought him into one, then another; or because the purpose does not depend on mentioning both. How far from the truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that he used the singular "garden" to indicate that the unbeliever has no share in the garden promised to the believers.

The clause ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that unbeliever was wronging himself by his disbelief and self-admiration.

﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾: meaning the unbeliever said, out of extreme heedlessness and long hope: I do not think this garden that you see will ever be destroyed.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come to be﴾: he denied the Resurrection after denying the destruction of his garden.

Al-Zajjaj said: he informed his brother of his disbelief in the end of this world and the arrival of the Hour.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾: the lām is the one that prepares for an oath (al-lām al-mūṭi'a lil-qasam). The meaning is: if he were returned to his Lord, supposedly and hypothetically as his companion claimed, then the lām in la-ajidanna is the answer of the oath and the condition, meaning: I will surely find on that day something better than this garden.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā) in the singular.

Munqalaban is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), meaning: a return and an outcome. He said this by analogy of the absent to the present.

Since he was rich in this world, he thought he would be rich in the next, deceived by the wealth he had, which was in fact a means of luring him on by God.

﴿His companion said to him﴾: meaning his believing companion said to the unbeliever during their conversation, rejecting what he had said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾, by your saying: I do not think the Hour will come to be. He said ﴿created you from dust﴾: meaning He made the origin of your creation from dust, since He created your father Adam from it. That is your origin and the origin of mankind, so every individual has a share of that. It was also said: it is possible that he was an unbeliever in God, so he rejected what he was upon of disbelief, and did not intend that disbelief had arisen in him because of this statement.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: which is the immediate material cause. ﴿Then He fashioned you into a man﴾: meaning He made you a male human being, balanced your limbs and perfected you. In this there is an allusion to proof for the Resurrection, and that the One who is able to originate is able to repeat. The accusative of rajulan is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz).

﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾: thus the majority read it, with an alif after the doubled lākinna.

Its original form is lākinna anā. The hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent nūn, so it became lākinnanā. Then they disliked the meeting of two nūns, so the first was made quiescent and the second was assimilated. The pronoun huwa refers to the matter (al-shān), and the clause after it is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of anā, and the returning pronoun is the suffix of the first person. The sense of the sentence is: but as for me, the matter is that God is my Lord.

The grammarians of Arabic said: keeping the alif of anā when connected is weak.

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is lākinna anā, and he mentioned something similar to what we have stated.

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that the original is lākinna Allāh huwa rabbī anā.

Al-Zajjaj said: keeping the alif in lākinnā during connected speech is good, because the alif of anā was dropped, so they brought it back as a replacement. He said: in the recitation of Ubayy it is "lākinna anā huwa Allāhu rabbī." Ibn 'Amir, al-Muthanna from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub read "lākinnā" both in connected speech and in pause, with the alif kept. A similar usage is the poet's verse:

"I am the sword of the clan, so know me,
for I have indeed reached the summit."

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"How could I, when the melodies of verses (are my delight),
and after gray hair, that is a sufficient disgrace?"

There is no disagreement about keeping it in pause.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i, read "lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī." Then he (the believer) disowned associating anyone with God for himself, saying: ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. In this there is an indication that his brother was a polytheist.

Then he turned to him rebuking him, saying: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What God wills (ma shā'a Allāh)"?﴾ Lawlā here expresses reproach (taḥḍīḍ), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, these words?

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: mā is in the nominative position with the sense of a verbal phrase (ma'nā al-amr), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, "the matter is by the will of God (mā shā'a Allāh)"? What God wills comes to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a subject (mubtada') with an implied predicate, meaning: what God wills is coming to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a conditional particle with an omitted apodosis, meaning: whatever thing God wills, it comes to be.

﴿There is no power except in God﴾: meaning, why did you not say, "What God wills, there is no power except in God", urging him to acknowledge that it and everything in it is by the will of God, if He wills He keeps it and if He wills He destroys it, and to acknowledge his own helplessness, and that whatever he was able to do of maintaining it was only with God's help, not by his own power and strength.

Al-Zajjaj said: no one has power over what is in his hand of dominion and blessing except by God, and nothing happens except what God wills.

Then, when He had taught him faith and the entrusting of affairs to God, glorified is He, he answered him regarding his boasting in wealth and manpower, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. The first object is the pronoun ya' (me), anā is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and aqalla is the second object of the verb of seeing if it is knowledge-seeing; if it is sight-seeing, then aqalla is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is also permissible for anā to be an emphasis for the pronoun ya'. The accusative of māl and walad is a specification (tamyīz).

﴿Then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾: this is the answer of the condition, meaning: if you see me poorer than you, then I hope that God, glorified is He, will grant me a garden better than your garden, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

﴿And He will send upon it a ḥusbān﴾: meaning He will send upon your garden a ḥusbān. Ḥusbān is a verbal noun in the sense of reckoning, like ghufrān (forgiveness), meaning a measure that God determined for it and which fell within His reckoning, and that is the decree of its destruction.
