Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾ that he said: "like the scorched (juruz)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿a reckoning from the heaven﴾ that he said: "a punishment. ﴿So it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾, meaning its produce has been reaped so that nothing remains in it. ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾, meaning gone, having sunk into the earth. ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over﴾ — he said: he clapped (his hands), ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, lamenting what had escaped him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

.

His saying: ﴿And set forth for them a parable: two men﴾. This parable was set forth by God, glorified is He, for the one who is proud of worldly things and disdains sitting with the poor. On this reading it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep yourself patient﴾.

Scholars differ over whether the two men are hypothetical (muqaddarān) or real (muḥaqqaqān). Some exegetes held the first view, and others held the second.

They also differed over their identity. It was said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel. It was said that they were two brothers from the Makhzum clan of Makkah, one a believer and the other an unbeliever. It was said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51].

The words ﴿a parable﴾ and ﴿two men﴾ are in the accusative because they are the two objects of the verb ﴿set forth﴾ (iḍrib). It was said: the first is the second and the second is the first.

﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾: this is the unbeliever. The phrase ﴿of grapevines﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of what the two gardens contained, meaning: of varied vines.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: al-ḥaff (ḥaff) means encircling. From it comes ﴿encircling (ḥāffīn) the Throne﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. It is said: ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān, yaḥiffūna ḥaffan, meaning they went around him. So the meaning of the verse is: We made the palm trees go around the two gardens on all their sides.

﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: meaning between the two gardens, at their middle, so that each of them would combine both sustenance and fruits.

Then God, glorified is He, informed about the two gardens that each one was yielding its produce and what was in it. He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾. He used the feminine singular verb (ātat) with kilā (both), because its wording is singular, so He observed the aspect of the wording.

The Basran grammarians held that kilā and kilā are singular nouns, not dual. Al-Farra' said that it is dual and derived from kull, with the lām lightened and an alif added to form the dual. Sibawayh said: the alif of kilā is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the third radical of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original is kulwā.

Abu 'Amr said: the tā' is an added (mulḥaqa) letter.

Ukulahā (its produce) means its fruit. This indicates that it had become fit for eating.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu" (each of the gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿And did not fall short of it in anything﴾: meaning it did not diminish its produce in any way. It is said: ẓalamahu ḥaqqahu, meaning he deprived him of his right. He described the two gardens with this quality to indicate that they were contrary to what is usual in other orchards, since those usually produce abundantly in one year and little in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: meaning We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens to water them constantly without interruption. It was recited as "fajjarnā" with doubled letters for emphasis, and with a single letter, which is the original form.

﴿And he had fruit﴾: meaning the owner of the two gardens had fruit. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read thamar with a fatḥa on the thā' and the mīm, and they read it likewise in His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm in both places. The rest read it with a ḍamma on both letters in both places.

Al-Jawhari said: thamarah is the singular of thamar, and the plural of thamar is thimār, like jabal and jibāl. Al-Farra' said: the plural of thimār is thumur, like kitāb and kutub, and the plural of thumur is athmār, like 'unuq and a'nāq.

It was said: thamar means all wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. It was also said that it means gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: meaning the unbeliever, the owner of the two gardens, said to his believing companion.

﴿While he was conversing with him﴾: meaning the unbeliever was conversing with the believer. The meaning is that he was answering back in speech. Al-muḥāwara means responding in discussion, and at-taḥāwur means mutual response.

﴿I have more wealth than you and mightier in manpower﴾ (nafar). Nafar means a group, which is fewer than ten people. Here it means followers, servants and children.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾: meaning the unbeliever entered the garden of his own self.

The exegetes said: he took his Muslim brother by the hand, brought him into his garden, walked him around it and showed him its wonders. The singular "garden" here may be explained in several ways: he only brought his brother into one of the two; or because the two were connected, they were like one; or because he brought him into one, then another; or because the purpose does not depend on mentioning both. How far from the truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that he used the singular "garden" to indicate that the unbeliever has no share in the garden promised to the believers.

The clause ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that unbeliever was wronging himself by his disbelief and self-admiration.

﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾: meaning the unbeliever said, out of extreme heedlessness and long hope: I do not think this garden that you see will ever be destroyed.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come to be﴾: he denied the Resurrection after denying the destruction of his garden.

Al-Zajjaj said: he informed his brother of his disbelief in the end of this world and the arrival of the Hour.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾: the lām is the one that prepares for an oath (al-lām al-mūṭi'a lil-qasam). The meaning is: if he were returned to his Lord, supposedly and hypothetically as his companion claimed, then the lām in la-ajidanna is the answer of the oath and the condition, meaning: I will surely find on that day something better than this garden.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā) in the singular.

Munqalaban is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), meaning: a return and an outcome. He said this by analogy of the absent to the present.

Since he was rich in this world, he thought he would be rich in the next, deceived by the wealth he had, which was in fact a means of luring him on by God.

﴿His companion said to him﴾: meaning his believing companion said to the unbeliever during their conversation, rejecting what he had said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾, by your saying: I do not think the Hour will come to be. He said ﴿created you from dust﴾: meaning He made the origin of your creation from dust, since He created your father Adam from it. That is your origin and the origin of mankind, so every individual has a share of that. It was also said: it is possible that he was an unbeliever in God, so he rejected what he was upon of disbelief, and did not intend that disbelief had arisen in him because of this statement.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: which is the immediate material cause. ﴿Then He fashioned you into a man﴾: meaning He made you a male human being, balanced your limbs and perfected you. In this there is an allusion to proof for the Resurrection, and that the One who is able to originate is able to repeat. The accusative of rajulan is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz).

﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾: thus the majority read it, with an alif after the doubled lākinna.

Its original form is lākinna anā. The hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent nūn, so it became lākinnanā. Then they disliked the meeting of two nūns, so the first was made quiescent and the second was assimilated. The pronoun huwa refers to the matter (al-shān), and the clause after it is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of anā, and the returning pronoun is the suffix of the first person. The sense of the sentence is: but as for me, the matter is that God is my Lord.

The grammarians of Arabic said: keeping the alif of anā when connected is weak.

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is lākinna anā, and he mentioned something similar to what we have stated.

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that the original is lākinna Allāh huwa rabbī anā.

Al-Zajjaj said: keeping the alif in lākinnā during connected speech is good, because the alif of anā was dropped, so they brought it back as a replacement. He said: in the recitation of Ubayy it is "lākinna anā huwa Allāhu rabbī." Ibn 'Amir, al-Muthanna from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub read "lākinnā" both in connected speech and in pause, with the alif kept. A similar usage is the poet's verse:

"I am the sword of the clan, so know me,
for I have indeed reached the summit."

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"How could I, when the melodies of verses (are my delight),
and after gray hair, that is a sufficient disgrace?"

There is no disagreement about keeping it in pause.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i, read "lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī." Then he (the believer) disowned associating anyone with God for himself, saying: ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. In this there is an indication that his brother was a polytheist.

Then he turned to him rebuking him, saying: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What God wills (ma shā'a Allāh)"?﴾ Lawlā here expresses reproach (taḥḍīḍ), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, these words?

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: mā is in the nominative position with the sense of a verbal phrase (ma'nā al-amr), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, "the matter is by the will of God (mā shā'a Allāh)"? What God wills comes to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a subject (mubtada') with an implied predicate, meaning: what God wills is coming to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a conditional particle with an omitted apodosis, meaning: whatever thing God wills, it comes to be.

﴿There is no power except in God﴾: meaning, why did you not say, "What God wills, there is no power except in God", urging him to acknowledge that it and everything in it is by the will of God, if He wills He keeps it and if He wills He destroys it, and to acknowledge his own helplessness, and that whatever he was able to do of maintaining it was only with God's help, not by his own power and strength.

Al-Zajjaj said: no one has power over what is in his hand of dominion and blessing except by God, and nothing happens except what God wills.

Then, when He had taught him faith and the entrusting of affairs to God, glorified is He, he answered him regarding his boasting in wealth and manpower, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. The first object is the pronoun ya' (me), anā is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and aqalla is the second object of the verb of seeing if it is knowledge-seeing; if it is sight-seeing, then aqalla is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is also permissible for anā to be an emphasis for the pronoun ya'. The accusative of māl and walad is a specification (tamyīz).

﴿Then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾: this is the answer of the condition, meaning: if you see me poorer than you, then I hope that God, glorified is He, will grant me a garden better than your garden, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

﴿And He will send upon it a ḥusbān﴾: meaning He will send upon your garden a ḥusbān. Ḥusbān is a verbal noun in the sense of reckoning, like ghufrān (forgiveness), meaning a measure that God determined for it and which fell within His reckoning, and that is the decree of its destruction.

Al-Zajjaj said: ḥusbān is from ḥisāb (reckoning), meaning He sends upon it a punishment of reckoning, which is the reckoning of what your hands have earned.

Al-Akhfash said: ḥusbān means targets (marāmī) "from the sky." Its singular is ḥusbāna. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said the same.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-ḥusbāna is a cloud, al-ḥusbāna is a cushion, and al-ḥusbāna is a thunderbolt. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-ḥusbān is arrows which a man shoots from inside a reed, drawn in a bow, and then he shoots twenty of them at once. The meaning is: He sends upon it targets of His punishment, either hail, or stones, or other things, from kinds of punishment which He wills.

From it is the saying of Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi:

"A ḥusbān has struck the earth,"

meaning locusts.

﴿So it will become a bare surface (ṣa'īdan), slippery﴾: meaning, your garden will become, after God sends upon it a ḥusbān, a bare surface (ṣa'īd), that is, land with no vegetation in it, and its verification has already been discussed. Zalaqan means that feet slip on it because of its smoothness. It is said: makān zalaq (with a fatḥa on the lām) meaning slippery ground. It is originally the verbal noun of your saying zalaqat rijluhu, tazlaqu zalaqan, and "azlaqahā" means someone else made it slip. Al-mazlaqa is a place where no foot can stand, and likewise al-zallāqa. He described the ṣa'īd with a verbal noun for emphasis, or it is intended to mean the object.

The clause ﴿or its water will become sunken﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūfa) with the clause before it. Ghawr means sunken, that which has sunk into the ground.

He described the water with a verbal noun for emphasis. The meaning is that it becomes devoid of water, after it had been full of it, and that stream had been constantly watering it through the middle of it. Ghawr may also mean setting (ghurūb), and from it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Is time anything but a night and its day,
and the rising of the sun, then its setting?"

﴿So you will not be able to seek it (lahu ṭalaban)﴾: meaning you will not be able to seek the sunken water, let alone find it, bring it back, or have power over it by any trick. It was also said: the meaning is: you will not be able to seek something else to replace it.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of the occurrence of what that believer had hoped for and anticipated concerning the destruction of the disbeliever's garden. He said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾. The variant readings of this word and its interpretation have already been mentioned. The root meaning of ihatah (encompassing) is from the encompassing of an enemy around a person, as has passed in His words: ﴿unless you are surrounded (by enemies)﴾ [Yusuf: 66], and it is an expression for its destruction and annihilation. It is conjoined to an implied clause, as if it were said: so what the believer had anticipated came to pass, and his fruit was encompassed (by ruin). ﴿So he began to turn his palms over﴾, meaning he struck one of his hands upon the other, and this is a metaphor for regret, as if it were said: so he began to regret. ﴿Over what he had spent upon it﴾, meaning on its cultivation and improvement from wealth. It was also said: the meaning is that he turns over his property and sees no return for what he spent, because possession is sometimes expressed by "hand," from their saying: "he has wealth in his hand." This is very far-fetched. The clause ﴿while it was fallen over its trellises﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause, meaning: and the state was that this garden had collapsed upon its supports on which it had propped up the vines; or some of that garden had fallen upon another part, derived from "the stars fell (khawat al-nujum takhwa)," meaning when they fell and did not rain in their season. From it is His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 52]. It was said: the specific mention of what had trellises rather than the palm trees and crops is because it is the principal part; and also its destruction suffices as an indication of the destruction of the remainder. The clause ﴿and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ is conjoined to ﴿turning his palms over﴾, or is a circumstantial clause from his pronoun, meaning: while he was saying, wishing upon witnessing the destruction of his garden, that he had not associated (anyone) with Allah, so that his garden would have been spared from destruction; or this statement of his was in its true sense, not for what had escaped him of worldly purpose, but for the intention of repenting from shirk and regretting what had passed from him.

﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah﴾. (Fi'ah) is the subject of kana and (lahu) is its predicate, and (yansurunahu) is an attribute of (fi'ah), meaning a helping company. It is permissible for (yansurunahu) to be the predicate. Sibawayh preferred the first, and al-Mubarrad preferred the second, citing His words: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]. The meaning is: there was no group or company for him to take refuge with and be victorious through, nor did the men he boasted of before benefit him, and he was not one who defended himself by his own strength against Allah's destruction of his garden and His retribution against him.

﴿There, the guardianship is for Allah, the True﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read (al-haqq) with a raised vowel as an attribute of (al-walayah). Ahl al-Madinah, Ahl Makkah, 'Asim and Hamzah read (al-haqqi) with a lowered vowel as an attribute of Allah, glory be to Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a verbal noun and for emphasis, as you say: "this is yours, truly." Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (al-wilayah) with a kasrah on the waw, and the rest read it with a fatha; they are two dialects with the same meaning. The meaning is: there, in that situation, the support belongs to Allah alone, and none other is able to provide it. It was also said that it is by inversion: the guardianship is for Allah, the True, there. ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, meaning: He, glory be to Him, is best in reward for His friends in this world and the Hereafter. (﴿And best in outcome﴾), meaning: in consequence. Al-A'mash, 'Asim and Hamzah read (uqban) with a sukun on the qaf, and the rest read it with a damma; both have the same meaning, meaning: He is best in outcome for whoever hopes in Him and believes in Him. It is said: "This is the outcome of so-and-so's affair, and its 'uqba," meaning its end.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, concerning His words ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, that he said: "The jannah is the orchard. He had one orchard and one wall, and between them was a river, and for this reason they were two gardens; and for this reason he called it a garden because of the wall that surrounded it."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr al-Shaybani who said: "The River of Abu Qartas is the River of the Two Gardens." Ibn Abi Hatim said: it is a well-known river in al-Ramlah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and did not wrong anything from it﴾ that he said: "It did not diminish; every tree of the garden bore fruit."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that it means wealth.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah who said: "Ibn 'Abbas read (wa kana lahu thumurun) with a damma, and said: they are kinds of wealth."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that he said: "gold and silver."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ that he said: "ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Asma' bint 'Umays who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, taught me words to say at times of distress: Allah is my Lord, I do not associate anything with Him."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad transmitted in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi from one he named, who said: "Musa asked his Lord for a need, and it was delayed for him, so he said: 'What Allah wills.' Then his need was before him, and he said: 'O Lord, I have been asking for my need for such-and-such a time, and now it has been given to me.' So Allah revealed to him: 'O Musa, do you not know that your saying "What Allah wills" is the most successful thing with which needs are sought?'"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant in family, wealth or child, and he says: 'What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah,' except that Allah repels from him every calamity until his death comes to him." Then he recited: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"﴾. Its isnad contains 'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas.

Abu al-Fath al-Azdi said: (p-862) "'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas: his hadith is not sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from another route from Anas something similar, as a mawquf report.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from him something similar, as a marfu' report.

Ahmad transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to me: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise beneath the Throne? I said: Yes. He said: Saying: there is no power and no strength except through Allah."

It is firmly established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to him: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise? There is no power and no strength except through Allah." Hadiths and reports from the Salaf have come concerning the virtue of this phrase.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾ that he said: "like the scorched (juruz)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿a reckoning from the heaven﴾ that he said: "a punishment. ﴿So it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾, meaning its produce has been reaped so that nothing remains in it. ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾, meaning gone, having sunk into the earth. ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over﴾ — he said: he clapped (his hands), ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, lamenting what had escaped him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

.

His saying: ﴿And set forth for them a parable: two men﴾. This parable was set forth by God, glorified is He, for the one who is proud of worldly things and disdains sitting with the poor. On this reading it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep yourself patient﴾.

Scholars differ over whether the two men are hypothetical (muqaddarān) or real (muḥaqqaqān). Some exegetes held the first view, and others held the second.

They also differed over their identity. It was said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel. It was said that they were two brothers from the Makhzum clan of Makkah, one a believer and the other an unbeliever. It was said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51].

The words ﴿a parable﴾ and ﴿two men﴾ are in the accusative because they are the two objects of the verb ﴿set forth﴾ (iḍrib). It was said: the first is the second and the second is the first.

﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾: this is the unbeliever. The phrase ﴿of grapevines﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of what the two gardens contained, meaning: of varied vines.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: al-ḥaff (ḥaff) means encircling. From it comes ﴿encircling (ḥāffīn) the Throne﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. It is said: ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān, yaḥiffūna ḥaffan, meaning they went around him. So the meaning of the verse is: We made the palm trees go around the two gardens on all their sides.

﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: meaning between the two gardens, at their middle, so that each of them would combine both sustenance and fruits.

Then God, glorified is He, informed about the two gardens that each one was yielding its produce and what was in it. He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾. He used the feminine singular verb (ātat) with kilā (both), because its wording is singular, so He observed the aspect of the wording.

The Basran grammarians held that kilā and kilā are singular nouns, not dual. Al-Farra' said that it is dual and derived from kull, with the lām lightened and an alif added to form the dual. Sibawayh said: the alif of kilā is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the third radical of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original is kulwā.

Abu 'Amr said: the tā' is an added (mulḥaqa) letter.

Ukulahā (its produce) means its fruit. This indicates that it had become fit for eating.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu" (each of the gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿And did not fall short of it in anything﴾: meaning it did not diminish its produce in any way. It is said: ẓalamahu ḥaqqahu, meaning he deprived him of his right. He described the two gardens with this quality to indicate that they were contrary to what is usual in other orchards, since those usually produce abundantly in one year and little in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: meaning We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens to water them constantly without interruption. It was recited as "fajjarnā" with doubled letters for emphasis, and with a single letter, which is the original form.

﴿And he had fruit﴾: meaning the owner of the two gardens had fruit. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read thamar with a fatḥa on the thā' and the mīm, and they read it likewise in His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm in both places. The rest read it with a ḍamma on both letters in both places.

Al-Jawhari said: thamarah is the singular of thamar, and the plural of thamar is thimār, like jabal and jibāl. Al-Farra' said: the plural of thimār is thumur, like kitāb and kutub, and the plural of thumur is athmār, like 'unuq and a'nāq.

It was said: thamar means all wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. It was also said that it means gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: meaning the unbeliever, the owner of the two gardens, said to his believing companion.

﴿While he was conversing with him﴾: meaning the unbeliever was conversing with the believer. The meaning is that he was answering back in speech. Al-muḥāwara means responding in discussion, and at-taḥāwur means mutual response.

﴿I have more wealth than you and mightier in manpower﴾ (nafar). Nafar means a group, which is fewer than ten people. Here it means followers, servants and children.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾: meaning the unbeliever entered the garden of his own self.

The exegetes said: he took his Muslim brother by the hand, brought him into his garden, walked him around it and showed him its wonders. The singular "garden" here may be explained in several ways: he only brought his brother into one of the two; or because the two were connected, they were like one; or because he brought him into one, then another; or because the purpose does not depend on mentioning both. How far from the truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that he used the singular "garden" to indicate that the unbeliever has no share in the garden promised to the believers.

The clause ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that unbeliever was wronging himself by his disbelief and self-admiration.

﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾: meaning the unbeliever said, out of extreme heedlessness and long hope: I do not think this garden that you see will ever be destroyed.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come to be﴾: he denied the Resurrection after denying the destruction of his garden.

Al-Zajjaj said: he informed his brother of his disbelief in the end of this world and the arrival of the Hour.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾: the lām is the one that prepares for an oath (al-lām al-mūṭi'a lil-qasam). The meaning is: if he were returned to his Lord, supposedly and hypothetically as his companion claimed, then the lām in la-ajidanna is the answer of the oath and the condition, meaning: I will surely find on that day something better than this garden.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā) in the singular.

Munqalaban is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), meaning: a return and an outcome. He said this by analogy of the absent to the present.

Since he was rich in this world, he thought he would be rich in the next, deceived by the wealth he had, which was in fact a means of luring him on by God.

﴿His companion said to him﴾: meaning his believing companion said to the unbeliever during their conversation, rejecting what he had said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾, by your saying: I do not think the Hour will come to be. He said ﴿created you from dust﴾: meaning He made the origin of your creation from dust, since He created your father Adam from it. That is your origin and the origin of mankind, so every individual has a share of that. It was also said: it is possible that he was an unbeliever in God, so he rejected what he was upon of disbelief, and did not intend that disbelief had arisen in him because of this statement.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: which is the immediate material cause. ﴿Then He fashioned you into a man﴾: meaning He made you a male human being, balanced your limbs and perfected you. In this there is an allusion to proof for the Resurrection, and that the One who is able to originate is able to repeat. The accusative of rajulan is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz).

﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾: thus the majority read it, with an alif after the doubled lākinna.

Its original form is lākinna anā. The hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent nūn, so it became lākinnanā. Then they disliked the meeting of two nūns, so the first was made quiescent and the second was assimilated. The pronoun huwa refers to the matter (al-shān), and the clause after it is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of anā, and the returning pronoun is the suffix of the first person. The sense of the sentence is: but as for me, the matter is that God is my Lord.

The grammarians of Arabic said: keeping the alif of anā when connected is weak.

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is lākinna anā, and he mentioned something similar to what we have stated.

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that the original is lākinna Allāh huwa rabbī anā.

Al-Zajjaj said: keeping the alif in lākinnā during connected speech is good, because the alif of anā was dropped, so they brought it back as a replacement. He said: in the recitation of Ubayy it is "lākinna anā huwa Allāhu rabbī." Ibn 'Amir, al-Muthanna from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub read "lākinnā" both in connected speech and in pause, with the alif kept. A similar usage is the poet's verse:

"I am the sword of the clan, so know me,
for I have indeed reached the summit."

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"How could I, when the melodies of verses (are my delight),
and after gray hair, that is a sufficient disgrace?"

There is no disagreement about keeping it in pause.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i, read "lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī." Then he (the believer) disowned associating anyone with God for himself, saying: ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. In this there is an indication that his brother was a polytheist.

Then he turned to him rebuking him, saying: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What God wills (ma shā'a Allāh)"?﴾ Lawlā here expresses reproach (taḥḍīḍ), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, these words?

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: mā is in the nominative position with the sense of a verbal phrase (ma'nā al-amr), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, "the matter is by the will of God (mā shā'a Allāh)"? What God wills comes to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a subject (mubtada') with an implied predicate, meaning: what God wills is coming to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a conditional particle with an omitted apodosis, meaning: whatever thing God wills, it comes to be.

﴿There is no power except in God﴾: meaning, why did you not say, "What God wills, there is no power except in God", urging him to acknowledge that it and everything in it is by the will of God, if He wills He keeps it and if He wills He destroys it, and to acknowledge his own helplessness, and that whatever he was able to do of maintaining it was only with God's help, not by his own power and strength.

Al-Zajjaj said: no one has power over what is in his hand of dominion and blessing except by God, and nothing happens except what God wills.

Then, when He had taught him faith and the entrusting of affairs to God, glorified is He, he answered him regarding his boasting in wealth and manpower, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. The first object is the pronoun ya' (me), anā is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and aqalla is the second object of the verb of seeing if it is knowledge-seeing; if it is sight-seeing, then aqalla is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is also permissible for anā to be an emphasis for the pronoun ya'. The accusative of māl and walad is a specification (tamyīz).

﴿Then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾: this is the answer of the condition, meaning: if you see me poorer than you, then I hope that God, glorified is He, will grant me a garden better than your garden, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

﴿And He will send upon it a ḥusbān﴾: meaning He will send upon your garden a ḥusbān. Ḥusbān is a verbal noun in the sense of reckoning, like ghufrān (forgiveness), meaning a measure that God determined for it and which fell within His reckoning, and that is the decree of its destruction.

Al-Zajjaj said: ḥusbān is from ḥisāb (reckoning), meaning He sends upon it a punishment of reckoning, which is the reckoning of what your hands have earned.

Al-Akhfash said: ḥusbān means targets (marāmī) "from the sky." Its singular is ḥusbāna. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said the same.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-ḥusbāna is a cloud, al-ḥusbāna is a cushion, and al-ḥusbāna is a thunderbolt. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-ḥusbān is arrows which a man shoots from inside a reed, drawn in a bow, and then he shoots twenty of them at once. The meaning is: He sends upon it targets of His punishment, either hail, or stones, or other things, from kinds of punishment which He wills.

From it is the saying of Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi:

"A ḥusbān has struck the earth,"

meaning locusts.

﴿So it will become a bare surface (ṣa'īdan), slippery﴾: meaning, your garden will become, after God sends upon it a ḥusbān, a bare surface (ṣa'īd), that is, land with no vegetation in it, and its verification has already been discussed. Zalaqan means that feet slip on it because of its smoothness. It is said: makān zalaq (with a fatḥa on the lām) meaning slippery ground. It is originally the verbal noun of your saying zalaqat rijluhu, tazlaqu zalaqan, and "azlaqahā" means someone else made it slip. Al-mazlaqa is a place where no foot can stand, and likewise al-zallāqa. He described the ṣa'īd with a verbal noun for emphasis, or it is intended to mean the object.

The clause ﴿or its water will become sunken﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūfa) with the clause before it. Ghawr means sunken, that which has sunk into the ground.

He described the water with a verbal noun for emphasis. The meaning is that it becomes devoid of water, after it had been full of it, and that stream had been constantly watering it through the middle of it. Ghawr may also mean setting (ghurūb), and from it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Is time anything but a night and its day,
and the rising of the sun, then its setting?"

﴿So you will not be able to seek it (lahu ṭalaban)﴾: meaning you will not be able to seek the sunken water, let alone find it, bring it back, or have power over it by any trick. It was also said: the meaning is: you will not be able to seek something else to replace it.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of the occurrence of what that believer had hoped for and anticipated concerning the destruction of the disbeliever's garden. He said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾. The variant readings of this word and its interpretation have already been mentioned. The root meaning of ihatah (encompassing) is from the encompassing of an enemy around a person, as has passed in His words: ﴿unless you are surrounded (by enemies)﴾ [Yusuf: 66], and it is an expression for its destruction and annihilation. It is conjoined to an implied clause, as if it were said: so what the believer had anticipated came to pass, and his fruit was encompassed (by ruin). ﴿So he began to turn his palms over﴾, meaning he struck one of his hands upon the other, and this is a metaphor for regret, as if it were said: so he began to regret. ﴿Over what he had spent upon it﴾, meaning on its cultivation and improvement from wealth. It was also said: the meaning is that he turns over his property and sees no return for what he spent, because possession is sometimes expressed by "hand," from their saying: "he has wealth in his hand." This is very far-fetched. The clause ﴿while it was fallen over its trellises﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause, meaning: and the state was that this garden had collapsed upon its supports on which it had propped up the vines; or some of that garden had fallen upon another part, derived from "the stars fell (khawat al-nujum takhwa)," meaning when they fell and did not rain in their season. From it is His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 52]. It was said: the specific mention of what had trellises rather than the palm trees and crops is because it is the principal part; and also its destruction suffices as an indication of the destruction of the remainder. The clause ﴿and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ is conjoined to ﴿turning his palms over﴾, or is a circumstantial clause from his pronoun, meaning: while he was saying, wishing upon witnessing the destruction of his garden, that he had not associated (anyone) with Allah, so that his garden would have been spared from destruction; or this statement of his was in its true sense, not for what had escaped him of worldly purpose, but for the intention of repenting from shirk and regretting what had passed from him.

﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah﴾. (Fi'ah) is the subject of kana and (lahu) is its predicate, and (yansurunahu) is an attribute of (fi'ah), meaning a helping company. It is permissible for (yansurunahu) to be the predicate. Sibawayh preferred the first, and al-Mubarrad preferred the second, citing His words: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]. The meaning is: there was no group or company for him to take refuge with and be victorious through, nor did the men he boasted of before benefit him, and he was not one who defended himself by his own strength against Allah's destruction of his garden and His retribution against him.

﴿There, the guardianship is for Allah, the True﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read (al-haqq) with a raised vowel as an attribute of (al-walayah). Ahl al-Madinah, Ahl Makkah, 'Asim and Hamzah read (al-haqqi) with a lowered vowel as an attribute of Allah, glory be to Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a verbal noun and for emphasis, as you say: "this is yours, truly." Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (al-wilayah) with a kasrah on the waw, and the rest read it with a fatha; they are two dialects with the same meaning. The meaning is: there, in that situation, the support belongs to Allah alone, and none other is able to provide it. It was also said that it is by inversion: the guardianship is for Allah, the True, there. ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, meaning: He, glory be to Him, is best in reward for His friends in this world and the Hereafter. (﴿And best in outcome﴾), meaning: in consequence. Al-A'mash, 'Asim and Hamzah read (uqban) with a sukun on the qaf, and the rest read it with a damma; both have the same meaning, meaning: He is best in outcome for whoever hopes in Him and believes in Him. It is said: "This is the outcome of so-and-so's affair, and its 'uqba," meaning its end.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, concerning His words ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, that he said: "The jannah is the orchard. He had one orchard and one wall, and between them was a river, and for this reason they were two gardens; and for this reason he called it a garden because of the wall that surrounded it."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr al-Shaybani who said: "The River of Abu Qartas is the River of the Two Gardens." Ibn Abi Hatim said: it is a well-known river in al-Ramlah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and did not wrong anything from it﴾ that he said: "It did not diminish; every tree of the garden bore fruit."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that it means wealth.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah who said: "Ibn 'Abbas read (wa kana lahu thumurun) with a damma, and said: they are kinds of wealth."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that he said: "gold and silver."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ that he said: "ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Asma' bint 'Umays who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, taught me words to say at times of distress: Allah is my Lord, I do not associate anything with Him."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad transmitted in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi from one he named, who said: "Musa asked his Lord for a need, and it was delayed for him, so he said: 'What Allah wills.' Then his need was before him, and he said: 'O Lord, I have been asking for my need for such-and-such a time, and now it has been given to me.' So Allah revealed to him: 'O Musa, do you not know that your saying "What Allah wills" is the most successful thing with which needs are sought?'"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant in family, wealth or child, and he says: 'What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah,' except that Allah repels from him every calamity until his death comes to him." Then he recited: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"﴾. Its isnad contains 'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas.

Abu al-Fath al-Azdi said: (p-862) "'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas: his hadith is not sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from another route from Anas something similar, as a mawquf report.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from him something similar, as a marfu' report.

Ahmad transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to me: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise beneath the Throne? I said: Yes. He said: Saying: there is no power and no strength except through Allah."

It is firmly established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to him: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise? There is no power and no strength except through Allah." Hadiths and reports from the Salaf have come concerning the virtue of this phrase.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾ that he said: "like the scorched (juruz)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿a reckoning from the heaven﴾ that he said: "a punishment. ﴿So it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾, meaning its produce has been reaped so that nothing remains in it. ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾, meaning gone, having sunk into the earth. ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over﴾ — he said: he clapped (his hands), ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, lamenting what had escaped him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

.

His saying: ﴿And set forth for them a parable: two men﴾. This parable was set forth by God, glorified is He, for the one who is proud of worldly things and disdains sitting with the poor. On this reading it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep yourself patient﴾.

Scholars differ over whether the two men are hypothetical (muqaddarān) or real (muḥaqqaqān). Some exegetes held the first view, and others held the second.

They also differed over their identity. It was said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel. It was said that they were two brothers from the Makhzum clan of Makkah, one a believer and the other an unbeliever. It was said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51].

The words ﴿a parable﴾ and ﴿two men﴾ are in the accusative because they are the two objects of the verb ﴿set forth﴾ (iḍrib). It was said: the first is the second and the second is the first.

﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾: this is the unbeliever. The phrase ﴿of grapevines﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of what the two gardens contained, meaning: of varied vines.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: al-ḥaff (ḥaff) means encircling. From it comes ﴿encircling (ḥāffīn) the Throne﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. It is said: ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān, yaḥiffūna ḥaffan, meaning they went around him. So the meaning of the verse is: We made the palm trees go around the two gardens on all their sides.

﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: meaning between the two gardens, at their middle, so that each of them would combine both sustenance and fruits.

Then God, glorified is He, informed about the two gardens that each one was yielding its produce and what was in it. He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾. He used the feminine singular verb (ātat) with kilā (both), because its wording is singular, so He observed the aspect of the wording.

The Basran grammarians held that kilā and kilā are singular nouns, not dual. Al-Farra' said that it is dual and derived from kull, with the lām lightened and an alif added to form the dual. Sibawayh said: the alif of kilā is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the third radical of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original is kulwā.

Abu 'Amr said: the tā' is an added (mulḥaqa) letter.

Ukulahā (its produce) means its fruit. This indicates that it had become fit for eating.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu" (each of the gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿And did not fall short of it in anything﴾: meaning it did not diminish its produce in any way. It is said: ẓalamahu ḥaqqahu, meaning he deprived him of his right. He described the two gardens with this quality to indicate that they were contrary to what is usual in other orchards, since those usually produce abundantly in one year and little in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: meaning We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens to water them constantly without interruption. It was recited as "fajjarnā" with doubled letters for emphasis, and with a single letter, which is the original form.

﴿And he had fruit﴾: meaning the owner of the two gardens had fruit. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read thamar with a fatḥa on the thā' and the mīm, and they read it likewise in His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm in both places. The rest read it with a ḍamma on both letters in both places.

Al-Jawhari said: thamarah is the singular of thamar, and the plural of thamar is thimār, like jabal and jibāl. Al-Farra' said: the plural of thimār is thumur, like kitāb and kutub, and the plural of thumur is athmār, like 'unuq and a'nāq.

It was said: thamar means all wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. It was also said that it means gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: meaning the unbeliever, the owner of the two gardens, said to his believing companion.

﴿While he was conversing with him﴾: meaning the unbeliever was conversing with the believer. The meaning is that he was answering back in speech. Al-muḥāwara means responding in discussion, and at-taḥāwur means mutual response.

﴿I have more wealth than you and mightier in manpower﴾ (nafar). Nafar means a group, which is fewer than ten people. Here it means followers, servants and children.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾: meaning the unbeliever entered the garden of his own self.

The exegetes said: he took his Muslim brother by the hand, brought him into his garden, walked him around it and showed him its wonders. The singular "garden" here may be explained in several ways: he only brought his brother into one of the two; or because the two were connected, they were like one; or because he brought him into one, then another; or because the purpose does not depend on mentioning both. How far from the truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that he used the singular "garden" to indicate that the unbeliever has no share in the garden promised to the believers.

The clause ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that unbeliever was wronging himself by his disbelief and self-admiration.

﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾: meaning the unbeliever said, out of extreme heedlessness and long hope: I do not think this garden that you see will ever be destroyed.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come to be﴾: he denied the Resurrection after denying the destruction of his garden.

Al-Zajjaj said: he informed his brother of his disbelief in the end of this world and the arrival of the Hour.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾: the lām is the one that prepares for an oath (al-lām al-mūṭi'a lil-qasam). The meaning is: if he were returned to his Lord, supposedly and hypothetically as his companion claimed, then the lām in la-ajidanna is the answer of the oath and the condition, meaning: I will surely find on that day something better than this garden.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā) in the singular.

Munqalaban is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), meaning: a return and an outcome. He said this by analogy of the absent to the present.

Since he was rich in this world, he thought he would be rich in the next, deceived by the wealth he had, which was in fact a means of luring him on by God.

﴿His companion said to him﴾: meaning his believing companion said to the unbeliever during their conversation, rejecting what he had said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾, by your saying: I do not think the Hour will come to be. He said ﴿created you from dust﴾: meaning He made the origin of your creation from dust, since He created your father Adam from it. That is your origin and the origin of mankind, so every individual has a share of that. It was also said: it is possible that he was an unbeliever in God, so he rejected what he was upon of disbelief, and did not intend that disbelief had arisen in him because of this statement.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: which is the immediate material cause. ﴿Then He fashioned you into a man﴾: meaning He made you a male human being, balanced your limbs and perfected you. In this there is an allusion to proof for the Resurrection, and that the One who is able to originate is able to repeat. The accusative of rajulan is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz).

﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾: thus the majority read it, with an alif after the doubled lākinna.

Its original form is lākinna anā. The hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent nūn, so it became lākinnanā. Then they disliked the meeting of two nūns, so the first was made quiescent and the second was assimilated. The pronoun huwa refers to the matter (al-shān), and the clause after it is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of anā, and the returning pronoun is the suffix of the first person. The sense of the sentence is: but as for me, the matter is that God is my Lord.

The grammarians of Arabic said: keeping the alif of anā when connected is weak.

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is lākinna anā, and he mentioned something similar to what we have stated.

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that the original is lākinna Allāh huwa rabbī anā.

Al-Zajjaj said: keeping the alif in lākinnā during connected speech is good, because the alif of anā was dropped, so they brought it back as a replacement. He said: in the recitation of Ubayy it is "lākinna anā huwa Allāhu rabbī." Ibn 'Amir, al-Muthanna from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub read "lākinnā" both in connected speech and in pause, with the alif kept. A similar usage is the poet's verse:

"I am the sword of the clan, so know me,
for I have indeed reached the summit."

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"How could I, when the melodies of verses (are my delight),
and after gray hair, that is a sufficient disgrace?"

There is no disagreement about keeping it in pause.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i, read "lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī." Then he (the believer) disowned associating anyone with God for himself, saying: ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. In this there is an indication that his brother was a polytheist.

Then he turned to him rebuking him, saying: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What God wills (ma shā'a Allāh)"?﴾ Lawlā here expresses reproach (taḥḍīḍ), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, these words?

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: mā is in the nominative position with the sense of a verbal phrase (ma'nā al-amr), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, "the matter is by the will of God (mā shā'a Allāh)"? What God wills comes to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a subject (mubtada') with an implied predicate, meaning: what God wills is coming to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a conditional particle with an omitted apodosis, meaning: whatever thing God wills, it comes to be.

﴿There is no power except in God﴾: meaning, why did you not say, "What God wills, there is no power except in God", urging him to acknowledge that it and everything in it is by the will of God, if He wills He keeps it and if He wills He destroys it, and to acknowledge his own helplessness, and that whatever he was able to do of maintaining it was only with God's help, not by his own power and strength.

Al-Zajjaj said: no one has power over what is in his hand of dominion and blessing except by God, and nothing happens except what God wills.

Then, when He had taught him faith and the entrusting of affairs to God, glorified is He, he answered him regarding his boasting in wealth and manpower, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. The first object is the pronoun ya' (me), anā is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and aqalla is the second object of the verb of seeing if it is knowledge-seeing; if it is sight-seeing, then aqalla is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is also permissible for anā to be an emphasis for the pronoun ya'. The accusative of māl and walad is a specification (tamyīz).

﴿Then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾: this is the answer of the condition, meaning: if you see me poorer than you, then I hope that God, glorified is He, will grant me a garden better than your garden, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

﴿And He will send upon it a ḥusbān﴾: meaning He will send upon your garden a ḥusbān. Ḥusbān is a verbal noun in the sense of reckoning, like ghufrān (forgiveness), meaning a measure that God determined for it and which fell within His reckoning, and that is the decree of its destruction.

Al-Zajjaj said: ḥusbān is from ḥisāb (reckoning), meaning He sends upon it a punishment of reckoning, which is the reckoning of what your hands have earned.

Al-Akhfash said: ḥusbān means targets (marāmī) "from the sky." Its singular is ḥusbāna. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said the same.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-ḥusbāna is a cloud, al-ḥusbāna is a cushion, and al-ḥusbāna is a thunderbolt. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-ḥusbān is arrows which a man shoots from inside a reed, drawn in a bow, and then he shoots twenty of them at once. The meaning is: He sends upon it targets of His punishment, either hail, or stones, or other things, from kinds of punishment which He wills.

From it is the saying of Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi:

"A ḥusbān has struck the earth,"

meaning locusts.

﴿So it will become a bare surface (ṣa'īdan), slippery﴾: meaning, your garden will become, after God sends upon it a ḥusbān, a bare surface (ṣa'īd), that is, land with no vegetation in it, and its verification has already been discussed. Zalaqan means that feet slip on it because of its smoothness. It is said: makān zalaq (with a fatḥa on the lām) meaning slippery ground. It is originally the verbal noun of your saying zalaqat rijluhu, tazlaqu zalaqan, and "azlaqahā" means someone else made it slip. Al-mazlaqa is a place where no foot can stand, and likewise al-zallāqa. He described the ṣa'īd with a verbal noun for emphasis, or it is intended to mean the object.

The clause ﴿or its water will become sunken﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūfa) with the clause before it. Ghawr means sunken, that which has sunk into the ground.

He described the water with a verbal noun for emphasis. The meaning is that it becomes devoid of water, after it had been full of it, and that stream had been constantly watering it through the middle of it. Ghawr may also mean setting (ghurūb), and from it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Is time anything but a night and its day,
and the rising of the sun, then its setting?"

﴿So you will not be able to seek it (lahu ṭalaban)﴾: meaning you will not be able to seek the sunken water, let alone find it, bring it back, or have power over it by any trick. It was also said: the meaning is: you will not be able to seek something else to replace it.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of the occurrence of what that believer had hoped for and anticipated concerning the destruction of the disbeliever's garden. He said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾. The variant readings of this word and its interpretation have already been mentioned. The root meaning of ihatah (encompassing) is from the encompassing of an enemy around a person, as has passed in His words: ﴿unless you are surrounded (by enemies)﴾ [Yusuf: 66], and it is an expression for its destruction and annihilation. It is conjoined to an implied clause, as if it were said: so what the believer had anticipated came to pass, and his fruit was encompassed (by ruin). ﴿So he began to turn his palms over﴾, meaning he struck one of his hands upon the other, and this is a metaphor for regret, as if it were said: so he began to regret. ﴿Over what he had spent upon it﴾, meaning on its cultivation and improvement from wealth. It was also said: the meaning is that he turns over his property and sees no return for what he spent, because possession is sometimes expressed by "hand," from their saying: "he has wealth in his hand." This is very far-fetched. The clause ﴿while it was fallen over its trellises﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause, meaning: and the state was that this garden had collapsed upon its supports on which it had propped up the vines; or some of that garden had fallen upon another part, derived from "the stars fell (khawat al-nujum takhwa)," meaning when they fell and did not rain in their season. From it is His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 52]. It was said: the specific mention of what had trellises rather than the palm trees and crops is because it is the principal part; and also its destruction suffices as an indication of the destruction of the remainder. The clause ﴿and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ is conjoined to ﴿turning his palms over﴾, or is a circumstantial clause from his pronoun, meaning: while he was saying, wishing upon witnessing the destruction of his garden, that he had not associated (anyone) with Allah, so that his garden would have been spared from destruction; or this statement of his was in its true sense, not for what had escaped him of worldly purpose, but for the intention of repenting from shirk and regretting what had passed from him.

﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah﴾. (Fi'ah) is the subject of kana and (lahu) is its predicate, and (yansurunahu) is an attribute of (fi'ah), meaning a helping company. It is permissible for (yansurunahu) to be the predicate. Sibawayh preferred the first, and al-Mubarrad preferred the second, citing His words: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]. The meaning is: there was no group or company for him to take refuge with and be victorious through, nor did the men he boasted of before benefit him, and he was not one who defended himself by his own strength against Allah's destruction of his garden and His retribution against him.

﴿There, the guardianship is for Allah, the True﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read (al-haqq) with a raised vowel as an attribute of (al-walayah). Ahl al-Madinah, Ahl Makkah, 'Asim and Hamzah read (al-haqqi) with a lowered vowel as an attribute of Allah, glory be to Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a verbal noun and for emphasis, as you say: "this is yours, truly." Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (al-wilayah) with a kasrah on the waw, and the rest read it with a fatha; they are two dialects with the same meaning. The meaning is: there, in that situation, the support belongs to Allah alone, and none other is able to provide it. It was also said that it is by inversion: the guardianship is for Allah, the True, there. ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, meaning: He, glory be to Him, is best in reward for His friends in this world and the Hereafter. (﴿And best in outcome﴾), meaning: in consequence. Al-A'mash, 'Asim and Hamzah read (uqban) with a sukun on the qaf, and the rest read it with a damma; both have the same meaning, meaning: He is best in outcome for whoever hopes in Him and believes in Him. It is said: "This is the outcome of so-and-so's affair, and its 'uqba," meaning its end.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, concerning His words ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, that he said: "The jannah is the orchard. He had one orchard and one wall, and between them was a river, and for this reason they were two gardens; and for this reason he called it a garden because of the wall that surrounded it."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr al-Shaybani who said: "The River of Abu Qartas is the River of the Two Gardens." Ibn Abi Hatim said: it is a well-known river in al-Ramlah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and did not wrong anything from it﴾ that he said: "It did not diminish; every tree of the garden bore fruit."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that it means wealth.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah who said: "Ibn 'Abbas read (wa kana lahu thumurun) with a damma, and said: they are kinds of wealth."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that he said: "gold and silver."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ that he said: "ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Asma' bint 'Umays who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, taught me words to say at times of distress: Allah is my Lord, I do not associate anything with Him."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad transmitted in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi from one he named, who said: "Musa asked his Lord for a need, and it was delayed for him, so he said: 'What Allah wills.' Then his need was before him, and he said: 'O Lord, I have been asking for my need for such-and-such a time, and now it has been given to me.' So Allah revealed to him: 'O Musa, do you not know that your saying "What Allah wills" is the most successful thing with which needs are sought?'"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant in family, wealth or child, and he says: 'What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah,' except that Allah repels from him every calamity until his death comes to him." Then he recited: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"﴾. Its isnad contains 'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas.

Abu al-Fath al-Azdi said: (p-862) "'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas: his hadith is not sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from another route from Anas something similar, as a mawquf report.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from him something similar, as a marfu' report.

Ahmad transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to me: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise beneath the Throne? I said: Yes. He said: Saying: there is no power and no strength except through Allah."

It is firmly established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to him: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise? There is no power and no strength except through Allah." Hadiths and reports from the Salaf have come concerning the virtue of this phrase.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾ that he said: "like the scorched (juruz)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿a reckoning from the heaven﴾ that he said: "a punishment. ﴿So it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾, meaning its produce has been reaped so that nothing remains in it. ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾, meaning gone, having sunk into the earth. ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over﴾ — he said: he clapped (his hands), ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, lamenting what had escaped him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

.

His saying: ﴿And set forth for them a parable: two men﴾. This parable was set forth by God, glorified is He, for the one who is proud of worldly things and disdains sitting with the poor. On this reading it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep yourself patient﴾.

Scholars differ over whether the two men are hypothetical (muqaddarān) or real (muḥaqqaqān). Some exegetes held the first view, and others held the second.

They also differed over their identity. It was said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel. It was said that they were two brothers from the Makhzum clan of Makkah, one a believer and the other an unbeliever. It was said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51].

The words ﴿a parable﴾ and ﴿two men﴾ are in the accusative because they are the two objects of the verb ﴿set forth﴾ (iḍrib). It was said: the first is the second and the second is the first.

﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾: this is the unbeliever. The phrase ﴿of grapevines﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of what the two gardens contained, meaning: of varied vines.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: al-ḥaff (ḥaff) means encircling. From it comes ﴿encircling (ḥāffīn) the Throne﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. It is said: ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān, yaḥiffūna ḥaffan, meaning they went around him. So the meaning of the verse is: We made the palm trees go around the two gardens on all their sides.

﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: meaning between the two gardens, at their middle, so that each of them would combine both sustenance and fruits.

Then God, glorified is He, informed about the two gardens that each one was yielding its produce and what was in it. He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾. He used the feminine singular verb (ātat) with kilā (both), because its wording is singular, so He observed the aspect of the wording.

The Basran grammarians held that kilā and kilā are singular nouns, not dual. Al-Farra' said that it is dual and derived from kull, with the lām lightened and an alif added to form the dual. Sibawayh said: the alif of kilā is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the third radical of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original is kulwā.

Abu 'Amr said: the tā' is an added (mulḥaqa) letter.

Ukulahā (its produce) means its fruit. This indicates that it had become fit for eating.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu" (each of the gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿And did not fall short of it in anything﴾: meaning it did not diminish its produce in any way. It is said: ẓalamahu ḥaqqahu, meaning he deprived him of his right. He described the two gardens with this quality to indicate that they were contrary to what is usual in other orchards, since those usually produce abundantly in one year and little in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: meaning We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens to water them constantly without interruption. It was recited as "fajjarnā" with doubled letters for emphasis, and with a single letter, which is the original form.

﴿And he had fruit﴾: meaning the owner of the two gardens had fruit. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read thamar with a fatḥa on the thā' and the mīm, and they read it likewise in His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm in both places. The rest read it with a ḍamma on both letters in both places.

Al-Jawhari said: thamarah is the singular of thamar, and the plural of thamar is thimār, like jabal and jibāl. Al-Farra' said: the plural of thimār is thumur, like kitāb and kutub, and the plural of thumur is athmār, like 'unuq and a'nāq.

It was said: thamar means all wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. It was also said that it means gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: meaning the unbeliever, the owner of the two gardens, said to his believing companion.

﴿While he was conversing with him﴾: meaning the unbeliever was conversing with the believer. The meaning is that he was answering back in speech. Al-muḥāwara means responding in discussion, and at-taḥāwur means mutual response.

﴿I have more wealth than you and mightier in manpower﴾ (nafar). Nafar means a group, which is fewer than ten people. Here it means followers, servants and children.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾: meaning the unbeliever entered the garden of his own self.

The exegetes said: he took his Muslim brother by the hand, brought him into his garden, walked him around it and showed him its wonders. The singular "garden" here may be explained in several ways: he only brought his brother into one of the two; or because the two were connected, they were like one; or because he brought him into one, then another; or because the purpose does not depend on mentioning both. How far from the truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that he used the singular "garden" to indicate that the unbeliever has no share in the garden promised to the believers.

The clause ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that unbeliever was wronging himself by his disbelief and self-admiration.

﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾: meaning the unbeliever said, out of extreme heedlessness and long hope: I do not think this garden that you see will ever be destroyed.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come to be﴾: he denied the Resurrection after denying the destruction of his garden.

Al-Zajjaj said: he informed his brother of his disbelief in the end of this world and the arrival of the Hour.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾: the lām is the one that prepares for an oath (al-lām al-mūṭi'a lil-qasam). The meaning is: if he were returned to his Lord, supposedly and hypothetically as his companion claimed, then the lām in la-ajidanna is the answer of the oath and the condition, meaning: I will surely find on that day something better than this garden.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā) in the singular.

Munqalaban is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), meaning: a return and an outcome. He said this by analogy of the absent to the present.

Since he was rich in this world, he thought he would be rich in the next, deceived by the wealth he had, which was in fact a means of luring him on by God.

﴿His companion said to him﴾: meaning his believing companion said to the unbeliever during their conversation, rejecting what he had said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾, by your saying: I do not think the Hour will come to be. He said ﴿created you from dust﴾: meaning He made the origin of your creation from dust, since He created your father Adam from it. That is your origin and the origin of mankind, so every individual has a share of that. It was also said: it is possible that he was an unbeliever in God, so he rejected what he was upon of disbelief, and did not intend that disbelief had arisen in him because of this statement.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: which is the immediate material cause. ﴿Then He fashioned you into a man﴾: meaning He made you a male human being, balanced your limbs and perfected you. In this there is an allusion to proof for the Resurrection, and that the One who is able to originate is able to repeat. The accusative of rajulan is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz).

﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾: thus the majority read it, with an alif after the doubled lākinna.

Its original form is lākinna anā. The hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent nūn, so it became lākinnanā. Then they disliked the meeting of two nūns, so the first was made quiescent and the second was assimilated. The pronoun huwa refers to the matter (al-shān), and the clause after it is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of anā, and the returning pronoun is the suffix of the first person. The sense of the sentence is: but as for me, the matter is that God is my Lord.

The grammarians of Arabic said: keeping the alif of anā when connected is weak.

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is lākinna anā, and he mentioned something similar to what we have stated.

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that the original is lākinna Allāh huwa rabbī anā.

Al-Zajjaj said: keeping the alif in lākinnā during connected speech is good, because the alif of anā was dropped, so they brought it back as a replacement. He said: in the recitation of Ubayy it is "lākinna anā huwa Allāhu rabbī." Ibn 'Amir, al-Muthanna from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub read "lākinnā" both in connected speech and in pause, with the alif kept. A similar usage is the poet's verse:

"I am the sword of the clan, so know me,
for I have indeed reached the summit."

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"How could I, when the melodies of verses (are my delight),
and after gray hair, that is a sufficient disgrace?"

There is no disagreement about keeping it in pause.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i, read "lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī."
