Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that he said: "gold and silver."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ that he said: "ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Asma' bint 'Umays who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, taught me words to say at times of distress: Allah is my Lord, I do not associate anything with Him."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad transmitted in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi from one he named, who said: "Musa asked his Lord for a need, and it was delayed for him, so he said: 'What Allah wills.' Then his need was before him, and he said: 'O Lord, I have been asking for my need for such-and-such a time, and now it has been given to me.' So Allah revealed to him: 'O Musa, do you not know that your saying "What Allah wills" is the most successful thing with which needs are sought?'"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant in family, wealth or child, and he says: 'What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah,' except that Allah repels from him every calamity until his death comes to him." Then he recited: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"﴾. Its isnad contains 'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas.

Abu al-Fath al-Azdi said: (p-862) "'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas: his hadith is not sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from another route from Anas something similar, as a mawquf report.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from him something similar, as a marfu' report.

Ahmad transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to me: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise beneath the Throne? I said: Yes. He said: Saying: there is no power and no strength except through Allah."

It is firmly established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to him: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise? There is no power and no strength except through Allah." Hadiths and reports from the Salaf have come concerning the virtue of this phrase.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾ that he said: "like the scorched (juruz)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿a reckoning from the heaven﴾ that he said: "a punishment. ﴿So it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾, meaning its produce has been reaped so that nothing remains in it. ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾, meaning gone, having sunk into the earth. ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over﴾ — he said: he clapped (his hands), ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, lamenting what had escaped him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

.

His saying: ﴿And set forth for them a parable: two men﴾. This parable was set forth by God, glorified is He, for the one who is proud of worldly things and disdains sitting with the poor. On this reading it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep yourself patient﴾.

Scholars differ over whether the two men are hypothetical (muqaddarān) or real (muḥaqqaqān). Some exegetes held the first view, and others held the second.

They also differed over their identity. It was said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel. It was said that they were two brothers from the Makhzum clan of Makkah, one a believer and the other an unbeliever. It was said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51].

The words ﴿a parable﴾ and ﴿two men﴾ are in the accusative because they are the two objects of the verb ﴿set forth﴾ (iḍrib). It was said: the first is the second and the second is the first.

﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾: this is the unbeliever. The phrase ﴿of grapevines﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of what the two gardens contained, meaning: of varied vines.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: al-ḥaff (ḥaff) means encircling. From it comes ﴿encircling (ḥāffīn) the Throne﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. It is said: ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān, yaḥiffūna ḥaffan, meaning they went around him. So the meaning of the verse is: We made the palm trees go around the two gardens on all their sides.

﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: meaning between the two gardens, at their middle, so that each of them would combine both sustenance and fruits.

Then God, glorified is He, informed about the two gardens that each one was yielding its produce and what was in it. He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾. He used the feminine singular verb (ātat) with kilā (both), because its wording is singular, so He observed the aspect of the wording.

The Basran grammarians held that kilā and kilā are singular nouns, not dual. Al-Farra' said that it is dual and derived from kull, with the lām lightened and an alif added to form the dual. Sibawayh said: the alif of kilā is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the third radical of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original is kulwā.

Abu 'Amr said: the tā' is an added (mulḥaqa) letter.

Ukulahā (its produce) means its fruit. This indicates that it had become fit for eating.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu" (each of the gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿And did not fall short of it in anything﴾: meaning it did not diminish its produce in any way. It is said: ẓalamahu ḥaqqahu, meaning he deprived him of his right. He described the two gardens with this quality to indicate that they were contrary to what is usual in other orchards, since those usually produce abundantly in one year and little in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: meaning We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens to water them constantly without interruption. It was recited as "fajjarnā" with doubled letters for emphasis, and with a single letter, which is the original form.

﴿And he had fruit﴾: meaning the owner of the two gardens had fruit. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read thamar with a fatḥa on the thā' and the mīm, and they read it likewise in His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm in both places. The rest read it with a ḍamma on both letters in both places.

Al-Jawhari said: thamarah is the singular of thamar, and the plural of thamar is thimār, like jabal and jibāl. Al-Farra' said: the plural of thimār is thumur, like kitāb and kutub, and the plural of thumur is athmār, like 'unuq and a'nāq.

It was said: thamar means all wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. It was also said that it means gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: meaning the unbeliever, the owner of the two gardens, said to his believing companion.

﴿While he was conversing with him﴾: meaning the unbeliever was conversing with the believer. The meaning is that he was answering back in speech. Al-muḥāwara means responding in discussion, and at-taḥāwur means mutual response.

﴿I have more wealth than you and mightier in manpower﴾ (nafar). Nafar means a group, which is fewer than ten people. Here it means followers, servants and children.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾: meaning the unbeliever entered the garden of his own self.

The exegetes said: he took his Muslim brother by the hand, brought him into his garden, walked him around it and showed him its wonders. The singular "garden" here may be explained in several ways: he only brought his brother into one of the two; or because the two were connected, they were like one; or because he brought him into one, then another; or because the purpose does not depend on mentioning both. How far from the truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that he used the singular "garden" to indicate that the unbeliever has no share in the garden promised to the believers.

The clause ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that unbeliever was wronging himself by his disbelief and self-admiration.

﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾: meaning the unbeliever said, out of extreme heedlessness and long hope: I do not think this garden that you see will ever be destroyed.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come to be﴾: he denied the Resurrection after denying the destruction of his garden.

Al-Zajjaj said: he informed his brother of his disbelief in the end of this world and the arrival of the Hour.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾: the lām is the one that prepares for an oath (al-lām al-mūṭi'a lil-qasam). The meaning is: if he were returned to his Lord, supposedly and hypothetically as his companion claimed, then the lām in la-ajidanna is the answer of the oath and the condition, meaning: I will surely find on that day something better than this garden.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā) in the singular.

Munqalaban is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), meaning: a return and an outcome. He said this by analogy of the absent to the present.

Since he was rich in this world, he thought he would be rich in the next, deceived by the wealth he had, which was in fact a means of luring him on by God.

﴿His companion said to him﴾: meaning his believing companion said to the unbeliever during their conversation, rejecting what he had said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾, by your saying: I do not think the Hour will come to be. He said ﴿created you from dust﴾: meaning He made the origin of your creation from dust, since He created your father Adam from it. That is your origin and the origin of mankind, so every individual has a share of that. It was also said: it is possible that he was an unbeliever in God, so he rejected what he was upon of disbelief, and did not intend that disbelief had arisen in him because of this statement.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: which is the immediate material cause. ﴿Then He fashioned you into a man﴾: meaning He made you a male human being, balanced your limbs and perfected you. In this there is an allusion to proof for the Resurrection, and that the One who is able to originate is able to repeat. The accusative of rajulan is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz).

﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾: thus the majority read it, with an alif after the doubled lākinna.

Its original form is lākinna anā. The hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent nūn, so it became lākinnanā. Then they disliked the meeting of two nūns, so the first was made quiescent and the second was assimilated. The pronoun huwa refers to the matter (al-shān), and the clause after it is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of anā, and the returning pronoun is the suffix of the first person. The sense of the sentence is: but as for me, the matter is that God is my Lord.

The grammarians of Arabic said: keeping the alif of anā when connected is weak.

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is lākinna anā, and he mentioned something similar to what we have stated.

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that the original is lākinna Allāh huwa rabbī anā.

Al-Zajjaj said: keeping the alif in lākinnā during connected speech is good, because the alif of anā was dropped, so they brought it back as a replacement. He said: in the recitation of Ubayy it is "lākinna anā huwa Allāhu rabbī." Ibn 'Amir, al-Muthanna from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub read "lākinnā" both in connected speech and in pause, with the alif kept. A similar usage is the poet's verse:

"I am the sword of the clan, so know me,
for I have indeed reached the summit."

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"How could I, when the melodies of verses (are my delight),
and after gray hair, that is a sufficient disgrace?"

There is no disagreement about keeping it in pause.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i, read "lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī." Then he (the believer) disowned associating anyone with God for himself, saying: ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. In this there is an indication that his brother was a polytheist.

Then he turned to him rebuking him, saying: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What God wills (ma shā'a Allāh)"?﴾ Lawlā here expresses reproach (taḥḍīḍ), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, these words?

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: mā is in the nominative position with the sense of a verbal phrase (ma'nā al-amr), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, "the matter is by the will of God (mā shā'a Allāh)"? What God wills comes to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a subject (mubtada') with an implied predicate, meaning: what God wills is coming to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a conditional particle with an omitted apodosis, meaning: whatever thing God wills, it comes to be.

﴿There is no power except in God﴾: meaning, why did you not say, "What God wills, there is no power except in God", urging him to acknowledge that it and everything in it is by the will of God, if He wills He keeps it and if He wills He destroys it, and to acknowledge his own helplessness, and that whatever he was able to do of maintaining it was only with God's help, not by his own power and strength.

Al-Zajjaj said: no one has power over what is in his hand of dominion and blessing except by God, and nothing happens except what God wills.

Then, when He had taught him faith and the entrusting of affairs to God, glorified is He, he answered him regarding his boasting in wealth and manpower, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. The first object is the pronoun ya' (me), anā is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and aqalla is the second object of the verb of seeing if it is knowledge-seeing; if it is sight-seeing, then aqalla is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is also permissible for anā to be an emphasis for the pronoun ya'. The accusative of māl and walad is a specification (tamyīz).

﴿Then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾: this is the answer of the condition, meaning: if you see me poorer than you, then I hope that God, glorified is He, will grant me a garden better than your garden, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

﴿And He will send upon it a ḥusbān﴾: meaning He will send upon your garden a ḥusbān. Ḥusbān is a verbal noun in the sense of reckoning, like ghufrān (forgiveness), meaning a measure that God determined for it and which fell within His reckoning, and that is the decree of its destruction.

Al-Zajjaj said: ḥusbān is from ḥisāb (reckoning), meaning He sends upon it a punishment of reckoning, which is the reckoning of what your hands have earned.

Al-Akhfash said: ḥusbān means targets (marāmī) "from the sky." Its singular is ḥusbāna. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said the same.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-ḥusbāna is a cloud, al-ḥusbāna is a cushion, and al-ḥusbāna is a thunderbolt. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-ḥusbān is arrows which a man shoots from inside a reed, drawn in a bow, and then he shoots twenty of them at once. The meaning is: He sends upon it targets of His punishment, either hail, or stones, or other things, from kinds of punishment which He wills.

From it is the saying of Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi:

"A ḥusbān has struck the earth,"

meaning locusts.

﴿So it will become a bare surface (ṣa'īdan), slippery﴾: meaning, your garden will become, after God sends upon it a ḥusbān, a bare surface (ṣa'īd), that is, land with no vegetation in it, and its verification has already been discussed. Zalaqan means that feet slip on it because of its smoothness. It is said: makān zalaq (with a fatḥa on the lām) meaning slippery ground. It is originally the verbal noun of your saying zalaqat rijluhu, tazlaqu zalaqan, and "azlaqahā" means someone else made it slip. Al-mazlaqa is a place where no foot can stand, and likewise al-zallāqa. He described the ṣa'īd with a verbal noun for emphasis, or it is intended to mean the object.

The clause ﴿or its water will become sunken﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūfa) with the clause before it. Ghawr means sunken, that which has sunk into the ground.

He described the water with a verbal noun for emphasis. The meaning is that it becomes devoid of water, after it had been full of it, and that stream had been constantly watering it through the middle of it. Ghawr may also mean setting (ghurūb), and from it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Is time anything but a night and its day,
and the rising of the sun, then its setting?"

﴿So you will not be able to seek it (lahu ṭalaban)﴾: meaning you will not be able to seek the sunken water, let alone find it, bring it back, or have power over it by any trick. It was also said: the meaning is: you will not be able to seek something else to replace it.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of the occurrence of what that believer had hoped for and anticipated concerning the destruction of the disbeliever's garden. He said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾. The variant readings of this word and its interpretation have already been mentioned. The root meaning of ihatah (encompassing) is from the encompassing of an enemy around a person, as has passed in His words: ﴿unless you are surrounded (by enemies)﴾ [Yusuf: 66], and it is an expression for its destruction and annihilation. It is conjoined to an implied clause, as if it were said: so what the believer had anticipated came to pass, and his fruit was encompassed (by ruin). ﴿So he began to turn his palms over﴾, meaning he struck one of his hands upon the other, and this is a metaphor for regret, as if it were said: so he began to regret. ﴿Over what he had spent upon it﴾, meaning on its cultivation and improvement from wealth. It was also said: the meaning is that he turns over his property and sees no return for what he spent, because possession is sometimes expressed by "hand," from their saying: "he has wealth in his hand." This is very far-fetched. The clause ﴿while it was fallen over its trellises﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause, meaning: and the state was that this garden had collapsed upon its supports on which it had propped up the vines; or some of that garden had fallen upon another part, derived from "the stars fell (khawat al-nujum takhwa)," meaning when they fell and did not rain in their season. From it is His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 52]. It was said: the specific mention of what had trellises rather than the palm trees and crops is because it is the principal part; and also its destruction suffices as an indication of the destruction of the remainder. The clause ﴿and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ is conjoined to ﴿turning his palms over﴾, or is a circumstantial clause from his pronoun, meaning: while he was saying, wishing upon witnessing the destruction of his garden, that he had not associated (anyone) with Allah, so that his garden would have been spared from destruction; or this statement of his was in its true sense, not for what had escaped him of worldly purpose, but for the intention of repenting from shirk and regretting what had passed from him.

﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah﴾. (Fi'ah) is the subject of kana and (lahu) is its predicate, and (yansurunahu) is an attribute of (fi'ah), meaning a helping company. It is permissible for (yansurunahu) to be the predicate. Sibawayh preferred the first, and al-Mubarrad preferred the second, citing His words: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]. The meaning is: there was no group or company for him to take refuge with and be victorious through, nor did the men he boasted of before benefit him, and he was not one who defended himself by his own strength against Allah's destruction of his garden and His retribution against him.

﴿There, the guardianship is for Allah, the True﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read (al-haqq) with a raised vowel as an attribute of (al-walayah). Ahl al-Madinah, Ahl Makkah, 'Asim and Hamzah read (al-haqqi) with a lowered vowel as an attribute of Allah, glory be to Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a verbal noun and for emphasis, as you say: "this is yours, truly." Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (al-wilayah) with a kasrah on the waw, and the rest read it with a fatha; they are two dialects with the same meaning. The meaning is: there, in that situation, the support belongs to Allah alone, and none other is able to provide it. It was also said that it is by inversion: the guardianship is for Allah, the True, there. ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, meaning: He, glory be to Him, is best in reward for His friends in this world and the Hereafter. (﴿And best in outcome﴾), meaning: in consequence. Al-A'mash, 'Asim and Hamzah read (uqban) with a sukun on the qaf, and the rest read it with a damma; both have the same meaning, meaning: He is best in outcome for whoever hopes in Him and believes in Him. It is said: "This is the outcome of so-and-so's affair, and its 'uqba," meaning its end.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, concerning His words ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, that he said: "The jannah is the orchard. He had one orchard and one wall, and between them was a river, and for this reason they were two gardens; and for this reason he called it a garden because of the wall that surrounded it."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr al-Shaybani who said: "The River of Abu Qartas is the River of the Two Gardens." Ibn Abi Hatim said: it is a well-known river in al-Ramlah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and did not wrong anything from it﴾ that he said: "It did not diminish; every tree of the garden bore fruit."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that it means wealth.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah who said: "Ibn 'Abbas read (wa kana lahu thumurun) with a damma, and said: they are kinds of wealth."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that he said: "gold and silver."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ that he said: "ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Asma' bint 'Umays who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, taught me words to say at times of distress: Allah is my Lord, I do not associate anything with Him."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad transmitted in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi from one he named, who said: "Musa asked his Lord for a need, and it was delayed for him, so he said: 'What Allah wills.' Then his need was before him, and he said: 'O Lord, I have been asking for my need for such-and-such a time, and now it has been given to me.' So Allah revealed to him: 'O Musa, do you not know that your saying "What Allah wills" is the most successful thing with which needs are sought?'"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant in family, wealth or child, and he says: 'What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah,' except that Allah repels from him every calamity until his death comes to him." Then he recited: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"﴾. Its isnad contains 'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas.

Abu al-Fath al-Azdi said: (p-862) "'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas: his hadith is not sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from another route from Anas something similar, as a mawquf report.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from him something similar, as a marfu' report.

Ahmad transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to me: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise beneath the Throne? I said: Yes. He said: Saying: there is no power and no strength except through Allah."

It is firmly established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to him: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise? There is no power and no strength except through Allah." Hadiths and reports from the Salaf have come concerning the virtue of this phrase.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾ that he said: "like the scorched (juruz)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿a reckoning from the heaven﴾ that he said: "a punishment. ﴿So it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾, meaning its produce has been reaped so that nothing remains in it. ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾, meaning gone, having sunk into the earth. ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over﴾ — he said: he clapped (his hands), ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, lamenting what had escaped him."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

.

His saying: ﴿And set forth for them a parable: two men﴾. This parable was set forth by God, glorified is He, for the one who is proud of worldly things and disdains sitting with the poor. On this reading it is connected to His saying: ﴿and keep yourself patient﴾.

Scholars differ over whether the two men are hypothetical (muqaddarān) or real (muḥaqqaqān). Some exegetes held the first view, and others held the second.

They also differed over their identity. It was said that they were two brothers from the Children of Israel. It was said that they were two brothers from the Makhzum clan of Makkah, one a believer and the other an unbeliever. It was said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying: ﴿One of them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ [al-Saffat: 51].

The words ﴿a parable﴾ and ﴿two men﴾ are in the accusative because they are the two objects of the verb ﴿set forth﴾ (iḍrib). It was said: the first is the second and the second is the first.

﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾: this is the unbeliever. The phrase ﴿of grapevines﴾ is an explanation (bayān) of what the two gardens contained, meaning: of varied vines.

﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: al-ḥaff (ḥaff) means encircling. From it comes ﴿encircling (ḥāffīn) the Throne﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. It is said: ḥaffa al-qawm bi-fulān, yaḥiffūna ḥaffan, meaning they went around him. So the meaning of the verse is: We made the palm trees go around the two gardens on all their sides.

﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾: meaning between the two gardens, at their middle, so that each of them would combine both sustenance and fruits.

Then God, glorified is He, informed about the two gardens that each one was yielding its produce and what was in it. He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾. He used the feminine singular verb (ātat) with kilā (both), because its wording is singular, so He observed the aspect of the wording.

The Basran grammarians held that kilā and kilā are singular nouns, not dual. Al-Farra' said that it is dual and derived from kull, with the lām lightened and an alif added to form the dual. Sibawayh said: the alif of kilā is for the feminine, and the tā' is a replacement for the third radical of the verb, which is a wāw, and the original is kulwā.

Abu 'Amr said: the tā' is an added (mulḥaqa) letter.

Ukulahā (its produce) means its fruit. This indicates that it had become fit for eating.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Kull al-jannatayn ātā ukulahu" (each of the gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿And did not fall short of it in anything﴾: meaning it did not diminish its produce in any way. It is said: ẓalamahu ḥaqqahu, meaning he deprived him of his right. He described the two gardens with this quality to indicate that they were contrary to what is usual in other orchards, since those usually produce abundantly in one year and little in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾: meaning We made a river flow and split through the middle of the two gardens to water them constantly without interruption. It was recited as "fajjarnā" with doubled letters for emphasis, and with a single letter, which is the original form.

﴿And he had fruit﴾: meaning the owner of the two gardens had fruit. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Asim, Ya'qub and Ibn Abi Ishaq read thamar with a fatḥa on the thā' and the mīm, and they read it likewise in His saying ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm in both places. The rest read it with a ḍamma on both letters in both places.

Al-Jawhari said: thamarah is the singular of thamar, and the plural of thamar is thimār, like jabal and jibāl. Al-Farra' said: the plural of thimār is thumur, like kitāb and kutub, and the plural of thumur is athmār, like 'unuq and a'nāq.

It was said: thamar means all wealth, of gold, silver, livestock and other things. It was also said that it means gold and silver specifically.

﴿So he said to his companion﴾: meaning the unbeliever, the owner of the two gardens, said to his believing companion.

﴿While he was conversing with him﴾: meaning the unbeliever was conversing with the believer. The meaning is that he was answering back in speech. Al-muḥāwara means responding in discussion, and at-taḥāwur means mutual response.

﴿I have more wealth than you and mightier in manpower﴾ (nafar). Nafar means a group, which is fewer than ten people. Here it means followers, servants and children.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾: meaning the unbeliever entered the garden of his own self.

The exegetes said: he took his Muslim brother by the hand, brought him into his garden, walked him around it and showed him its wonders. The singular "garden" here may be explained in several ways: he only brought his brother into one of the two; or because the two were connected, they were like one; or because he brought him into one, then another; or because the purpose does not depend on mentioning both. How far from the truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf said: that he used the singular "garden" to indicate that the unbeliever has no share in the garden promised to the believers.

The clause ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that unbeliever was wronging himself by his disbelief and self-admiration.

﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾: meaning the unbeliever said, out of extreme heedlessness and long hope: I do not think this garden that you see will ever be destroyed.

﴿Nor do I think the Hour will come to be﴾: he denied the Resurrection after denying the destruction of his garden.

Al-Zajjaj said: he informed his brother of his disbelief in the end of this world and the arrival of the Hour.

﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾: the lām is the one that prepares for an oath (al-lām al-mūṭi'a lil-qasam). The meaning is: if he were returned to his Lord, supposedly and hypothetically as his companion claimed, then the lām in la-ajidanna is the answer of the oath and the condition, meaning: I will surely find on that day something better than this garden.

In the codices of Makkah, Madinah and Syria it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā). In the codices of the people of Basra and Kufa it is read ﴿better than it﴾ (khayran minhā) in the singular.

Munqalaban is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), meaning: a return and an outcome. He said this by analogy of the absent to the present.

Since he was rich in this world, he thought he would be rich in the next, deceived by the wealth he had, which was in fact a means of luring him on by God.

﴿His companion said to him﴾: meaning his believing companion said to the unbeliever during their conversation, rejecting what he had said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾, by your saying: I do not think the Hour will come to be. He said ﴿created you from dust﴾: meaning He made the origin of your creation from dust, since He created your father Adam from it. That is your origin and the origin of mankind, so every individual has a share of that. It was also said: it is possible that he was an unbeliever in God, so he rejected what he was upon of disbelief, and did not intend that disbelief had arisen in him because of this statement.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: which is the immediate material cause. ﴿Then He fashioned you into a man﴾: meaning He made you a male human being, balanced your limbs and perfected you. In this there is an allusion to proof for the Resurrection, and that the One who is able to originate is able to repeat. The accusative of rajulan is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or a specification (tamyīz).

﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾: thus the majority read it, with an alif after the doubled lākinna.

Its original form is lākinna anā. The hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent nūn, so it became lākinnanā. Then they disliked the meeting of two nūns, so the first was made quiescent and the second was assimilated. The pronoun huwa refers to the matter (al-shān), and the clause after it is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of anā, and the returning pronoun is the suffix of the first person. The sense of the sentence is: but as for me, the matter is that God is my Lord.

The grammarians of Arabic said: keeping the alif of anā when connected is weak.

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Mazini is that the original is lākinna anā, and he mentioned something similar to what we have stated.

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that the original is lākinna Allāh huwa rabbī anā.

Al-Zajjaj said: keeping the alif in lākinnā during connected speech is good, because the alif of anā was dropped, so they brought it back as a replacement. He said: in the recitation of Ubayy it is "lākinna anā huwa Allāhu rabbī." Ibn 'Amir, al-Muthanna from Nafi', and Ruways from Ya'qub read "lākinnā" both in connected speech and in pause, with the alif kept. A similar usage is the poet's verse:

"I am the sword of the clan, so know me,
for I have indeed reached the summit."

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"How could I, when the melodies of verses (are my delight),
and after gray hair, that is a sufficient disgrace?"

There is no disagreement about keeping it in pause.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i, read "lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī." Then he (the believer) disowned associating anyone with God for himself, saying: ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. In this there is an indication that his brother was a polytheist.

Then he turned to him rebuking him, saying: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "What God wills (ma shā'a Allāh)"?﴾ Lawlā here expresses reproach (taḥḍīḍ), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, these words?

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: mā is in the nominative position with the sense of a verbal phrase (ma'nā al-amr), meaning: why did you not say, when you entered it, "the matter is by the will of God (mā shā'a Allāh)"? What God wills comes to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a subject (mubtada') with an implied predicate, meaning: what God wills is coming to be. It is also permissible for mā to be a conditional particle with an omitted apodosis, meaning: whatever thing God wills, it comes to be.

﴿There is no power except in God﴾: meaning, why did you not say, "What God wills, there is no power except in God", urging him to acknowledge that it and everything in it is by the will of God, if He wills He keeps it and if He wills He destroys it, and to acknowledge his own helplessness, and that whatever he was able to do of maintaining it was only with God's help, not by his own power and strength.

Al-Zajjaj said: no one has power over what is in his hand of dominion and blessing except by God, and nothing happens except what God wills.

Then, when He had taught him faith and the entrusting of affairs to God, glorified is He, he answered him regarding his boasting in wealth and manpower, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾. The first object is the pronoun ya' (me), anā is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl), and aqalla is the second object of the verb of seeing if it is knowledge-seeing; if it is sight-seeing, then aqalla is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is also permissible for anā to be an emphasis for the pronoun ya'. The accusative of māl and walad is a specification (tamyīz).

﴿Then perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾: this is the answer of the condition, meaning: if you see me poorer than you, then I hope that God, glorified is He, will grant me a garden better than your garden, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both.

﴿And He will send upon it a ḥusbān﴾: meaning He will send upon your garden a ḥusbān. Ḥusbān is a verbal noun in the sense of reckoning, like ghufrān (forgiveness), meaning a measure that God determined for it and which fell within His reckoning, and that is the decree of its destruction.

Al-Zajjaj said: ḥusbān is from ḥisāb (reckoning), meaning He sends upon it a punishment of reckoning, which is the reckoning of what your hands have earned.

Al-Akhfash said: ḥusbān means targets (marāmī) "from the sky." Its singular is ḥusbāna. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said the same.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-ḥusbāna is a cloud, al-ḥusbāna is a cushion, and al-ḥusbāna is a thunderbolt. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-ḥusbān is arrows which a man shoots from inside a reed, drawn in a bow, and then he shoots twenty of them at once. The meaning is: He sends upon it targets of His punishment, either hail, or stones, or other things, from kinds of punishment which He wills.

From it is the saying of Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi:

"A ḥusbān has struck the earth,"

meaning locusts.

﴿So it will become a bare surface (ṣa'īdan), slippery﴾: meaning, your garden will become, after God sends upon it a ḥusbān, a bare surface (ṣa'īd), that is, land with no vegetation in it, and its verification has already been discussed. Zalaqan means that feet slip on it because of its smoothness. It is said: makān zalaq (with a fatḥa on the lām) meaning slippery ground. It is originally the verbal noun of your saying zalaqat rijluhu, tazlaqu zalaqan, and "azlaqahā" means someone else made it slip. Al-mazlaqa is a place where no foot can stand, and likewise al-zallāqa. He described the ṣa'īd with a verbal noun for emphasis, or it is intended to mean the object.

The clause ﴿or its water will become sunken﴾ is coordinated (ma'ṭūfa) with the clause before it. Ghawr means sunken, that which has sunk into the ground.

He described the water with a verbal noun for emphasis. The meaning is that it becomes devoid of water, after it had been full of it, and that stream had been constantly watering it through the middle of it. Ghawr may also mean setting (ghurūb), and from it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Is time anything but a night and its day,
and the rising of the sun, then its setting?"

﴿So you will not be able to seek it (lahu ṭalaban)﴾: meaning you will not be able to seek the sunken water, let alone find it, bring it back, or have power over it by any trick. It was also said: the meaning is: you will not be able to seek something else to replace it.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed of the occurrence of what that believer had hoped for and anticipated concerning the destruction of the disbeliever's garden. He said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾. The variant readings of this word and its interpretation have already been mentioned. The root meaning of ihatah (encompassing) is from the encompassing of an enemy around a person, as has passed in His words: ﴿unless you are surrounded (by enemies)﴾ [Yusuf: 66], and it is an expression for its destruction and annihilation. It is conjoined to an implied clause, as if it were said: so what the believer had anticipated came to pass, and his fruit was encompassed (by ruin). ﴿So he began to turn his palms over﴾, meaning he struck one of his hands upon the other, and this is a metaphor for regret, as if it were said: so he began to regret. ﴿Over what he had spent upon it﴾, meaning on its cultivation and improvement from wealth. It was also said: the meaning is that he turns over his property and sees no return for what he spent, because possession is sometimes expressed by "hand," from their saying: "he has wealth in his hand." This is very far-fetched. The clause ﴿while it was fallen over its trellises﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause, meaning: and the state was that this garden had collapsed upon its supports on which it had propped up the vines; or some of that garden had fallen upon another part, derived from "the stars fell (khawat al-nujum takhwa)," meaning when they fell and did not rain in their season. From it is His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah) because of what they wronged﴾ [al-Naml: 52]. It was said: the specific mention of what had trellises rather than the palm trees and crops is because it is the principal part; and also its destruction suffices as an indication of the destruction of the remainder. The clause ﴿and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ is conjoined to ﴿turning his palms over﴾, or is a circumstantial clause from his pronoun, meaning: while he was saying, wishing upon witnessing the destruction of his garden, that he had not associated (anyone) with Allah, so that his garden would have been spared from destruction; or this statement of his was in its true sense, not for what had escaped him of worldly purpose, but for the intention of repenting from shirk and regretting what had passed from him.

﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah﴾. (Fi'ah) is the subject of kana and (lahu) is its predicate, and (yansurunahu) is an attribute of (fi'ah), meaning a helping company. It is permissible for (yansurunahu) to be the predicate. Sibawayh preferred the first, and al-Mubarrad preferred the second, citing His words: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]. The meaning is: there was no group or company for him to take refuge with and be victorious through, nor did the men he boasted of before benefit him, and he was not one who defended himself by his own strength against Allah's destruction of his garden and His retribution against him.

﴿There, the guardianship is for Allah, the True﴾. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read (al-haqq) with a raised vowel as an attribute of (al-walayah). Ahl al-Madinah, Ahl Makkah, 'Asim and Hamzah read (al-haqqi) with a lowered vowel as an attribute of Allah, glory be to Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a verbal noun and for emphasis, as you say: "this is yours, truly." Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (al-wilayah) with a kasrah on the waw, and the rest read it with a fatha; they are two dialects with the same meaning. The meaning is: there, in that situation, the support belongs to Allah alone, and none other is able to provide it. It was also said that it is by inversion: the guardianship is for Allah, the True, there. ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾, meaning: He, glory be to Him, is best in reward for His friends in this world and the Hereafter. (﴿And best in outcome﴾), meaning: in consequence. Al-A'mash, 'Asim and Hamzah read (uqban) with a sukun on the qaf, and the rest read it with a damma; both have the same meaning, meaning: He is best in outcome for whoever hopes in Him and believes in Him. It is said: "This is the outcome of so-and-so's affair, and its 'uqba," meaning its end.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, concerning His words ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, that he said: "The jannah is the orchard. He had one orchard and one wall, and between them was a river, and for this reason they were two gardens; and for this reason he called it a garden because of the wall that surrounded it."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr al-Shaybani who said: "The River of Abu Qartas is the River of the Two Gardens." Ibn Abi Hatim said: it is a well-known river in al-Ramlah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and did not wrong anything from it﴾ that he said: "It did not diminish; every tree of the garden bore fruit."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that it means wealth.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah who said: "Ibn 'Abbas read (wa kana lahu thumurun) with a damma, and said: they are kinds of wealth."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning ﴿and he had fruit﴾ that he said: "gold and silver."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾ that he said: "ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Asma' bint 'Umays who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, taught me words to say at times of distress: Allah is my Lord, I do not associate anything with Him."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad transmitted in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from Yahya ibn Sulaym al-Ta'ifi from one he named, who said: "Musa asked his Lord for a need, and it was delayed for him, so he said: 'What Allah wills.' Then his need was before him, and he said: 'O Lord, I have been asking for my need for such-and-such a time, and now it has been given to me.' So Allah revealed to him: 'O Musa, do you not know that your saying "What Allah wills" is the most successful thing with which needs are sought?'"

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant in family, wealth or child, and he says: 'What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah,' except that Allah repels from him every calamity until his death comes to him." Then he recited: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah"﴾. Its isnad contains 'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas.

Abu al-Fath al-Azdi said: (p-862) "'Isa ibn 'Awn, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zurarah, from Anas: his hadith is not sound."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from another route from Anas something similar, as a mawquf report.

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab transmitted from him something similar, as a marfu' report.

Ahmad transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Prophet of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to me: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise beneath the Throne? I said: Yes. He said: Saying: there is no power and no strength except through Allah."

It is firmly established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to him: "Shall I direct you to a treasure of the treasures of Paradise? There is no power and no strength except through Allah." Hadiths and reports from the Salaf have come concerning the virtue of this phrase.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾ that he said: "like the scorched (juruz)."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿a reckoning from the heaven﴾ that he said: "a punishment. ﴿So it becomes a barren slippery earth﴾, meaning its produce has been reaped so that nothing remains in it. ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾, meaning gone, having sunk into the earth. ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to turn his palms over﴾ — he said: he clapped (his hands), ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, lamenting what had escaped him."

Then Allah, glorified is He, set forth another parable for the mighty ones of Quraysh, saying: ﴿And present to them the parable of the life of this world﴾. That is: mention to them what resembles the life of this world in its beauty, its freshness, and the speed of its passing away, so that they do not incline toward it. This parable has already been mentioned in Surat Yunus. Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this parable, saying: ﴿Like water which We send down from the sky﴾. It is also permissible that this be the second object of His saying "iḍrib" (present/strike), on the basis of taking it in the sense of "ṣayyir" (make/render): ﴿so the vegetation of the earth mingles with it﴾. That is: the vegetation of the earth mingled with the water until it became lush. It has also been said that the meaning is: the plants became intermingled with one another when the water descended upon them, since plants only intermingle and grow thick through rain, so the bā' in "bihi" (with it) is causal (sababiyyah). ﴿Then it becomes⁠ dry stalks (hashīman)﴾. Al-Hashīm is that which is broken. It is the vegetation that has been broken and crumbled because the water has been cut off from it. A "rajul hashīm" is a man of weak body. "Tahashshama 'alayhi fulān" means someone showed kindness to him (ta'aṭṭafa). "Ihtashama mā fī ḍar' al-nāqah" means he milked what was in the udder of the she-camel. "Hashsham al-tharīd" means he broke and crumbled the bread-and-broth dish. From this is the saying of Ibn al-Zab'arī:

"'Amr, the one who crumbled the tharīd for his people, while the men of Makkah were in famine and emaciated."

﴿The winds scatter it (tadhrūhu al-riyāḥ)﴾: they disperse it. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah said: "tadhrūhu" means "tansifuhu" (blows it away). Ibn Kaysan said: it carries it away and brings it back. The meanings are close.

Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif recited "tadhriyhi al-rīḥ" (with tadhriyhi). Al-Kisā'ī said: in the recitation of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is "tadhriyhi". It is said: "dharatহু al-rīḥ yadhrūhu" and "adhrat-hu tadhriyhi" (the wind scattered it).

Al-Farrā' related: "adhraytu al-rajul 'an faraslhi", i.e., I turned the man over from his horse.

﴿And Allah is over all things Omnipotent﴾: that is, over everything among things, He gives it life and causes it to perish by His power; He is not incapable of anything.

﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾. This is a rebuttal of the leaders who used to boast of wealth, riches, and children. Allah, glorified is He, informed them that these are among the things adorned in this world, not among the things that benefit in the Hereafter, as He said in another verse: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15], and He said: ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [al-Taghabun: 14]. For this reason, He followed this worldly adornment with His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds (al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt)﴾, that is, deeds of goodness, which are the acts of obedience performed by the poor among the Muslims. ﴿Better in the sight of your Lord for reward﴾: that is, better than this adornment of wealth and children in reward, and greater in return and benefit to their people. ﴿And better in hope (khayrun amalan)﴾: that is, better in hope. It means that these righteous deeds, for their doers, are better in hope than what the people of wealth and children hope for; because they attain through them in the Hereafter what those rich people were hoping for in this world. There is no good in the adornment of this world such that the Hereafter should be preferred over it; rather, this preference came in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The companions of the Garden will be better that Day in dwelling﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. The apparent meaning is that "al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt" is every deed of goodness. There is no basis for restricting them to prayer, as some have said, nor to a type of dhikr, as another has said, nor to what the poor emigrants used to do by considering the cause (sabab); because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. By this you know that the explanation of "al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt" in the ḥadīths with what will come does not preclude applying this term to other righteous deeds.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from ʿAlī, who said: "﴿Wealth and children﴾ is the tilth of this world, and righteous deeds are the tilth of the Hereafter, and Allah has combined them for some peoples."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: "﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾", he said: "Subḥān Allāh, al-Ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu Akbar."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Aḥmad, Abū Yaʿlā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Increase your store of the enduring good deeds." It was said: "What are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Takbīr, tahlīl, tasbīḥ, taḥmīd, and lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh."

al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Shāhīn, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū al-Dardāʾ, marfūʿan, with the wording: "Subḥān Allāh, al-Ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, Allāhu Akbar, and lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh; they are the enduring good deeds."

al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Ṣaghīr, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Abū Hurayrah, marfūʿan: "Take your shield." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, from which enemy that has come?" He said: "Rather, your shield from the Fire is: saying Subḥān Allāh, al-Ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu Akbar; for they will come on the Day of Resurrection going before, following after, and protecting, and they are the enduring good deeds."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report from the ḥadīth of Anas, marfūʿan, and he added takbīr and named them the enduring good deeds.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report marfūʿan from the ḥadīth of ʿĀʾishah, adding: "and lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā billāh."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report marfūʿan from the ḥadīth of ʿAlī.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated, through the route of al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās, marfūʿan, a similar report without the ḥawqalah.

al-Ṭabarānī narrated from Saʿd ibn Junādah, marfūʿan, a similar report.

al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh and Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, as his own statement, a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, as his own statement, a similar report.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah who said: "Everything that is obedience to Allah is among the enduring good deeds."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 47–53 (part 1 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "tusayyaru" (with a ta' with a damma and the ya' with a fatha, in the passive form), with "al-jibal" in the nominative as the deputy of the subject (nā'ib 'an al-fā'il).

Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read "tasiru" (with a ta' with a fatha and without the doubling), with "al-jibal" as the subject (fā'il).

The rest read "nusayyiru" (with the nun), with the subject being Allah, glory be to Him, and "al-jibal" in the accusative as the object. The first reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set moving﴾ [al-Takwir: 3], and the second reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the third reading, because it fits His saying "wa-hasharnahum" (and We gathered them). Some of the grammarians said: the estimate is: "And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord on the day We set the mountains in motion." It was also said: the governing element of the time-adverb is a deleted verb, and the estimate is: "And remember the day We set the mountains in motion." The meaning of setting the mountains in motion is removing them from their places and making them move as clouds move, as in His saying: ﴿And it passes by like the passing of clouds﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Then they return to the earth after Allah has made them as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust, becoming scattered particles of dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6].

The address in His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47] is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. The meaning of its being laid bare is its becoming manifest, with whatever covers it—mountains, trees and buildings—removed. It was also said: the meaning of its being laid bare is the bringing forth of what is within it of treasures and the dead, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 4], and He said: ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2]. So the meaning becomes: "And you will see the earth laid bare, with what is in its belly brought out." ﴿And We gather them﴾, i.e., the creatures. The meaning of gathering (hashr) is assembling, i.e., We assemble them to the place of standing from every place. ﴿And We leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We do not leave any of them. It is said: ghādarahu and aghdarahu, when he left him. 'Antarah said:

"I left him rolling in the dust, his joints (scattered), while the people were between wounded and slain."

i.e., I left him. From this comes "ghadr" (betrayal), because the betrayer abandons fidelity to the one betrayed. They said: the pool (ghadir) was named ghadir because the water went away and left it; and from this comes the ghada'ir (braids) of a woman, because she places them behind her.

﴿And they are presented before your Lord in rows﴾: the accusative of "saffan" is as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., arranged in rows, each nation and group being a row. It was also said: they are presented in one row, as in His saying: ﴿Then come in rows﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64], i.e., all together. It was also said: standing.

In the verse there is a comparison of their condition with the condition of an army being reviewed before the sultan. ﴿Certainly you have come to Us as We created you the first time﴾ — this is with a supposed saying, i.e., We said to them: "Certainly you have come to Us." The kaf in "kama khalaqnakum" is an adjectival qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, i.e., a coming like your coming when We created you the first time, or as two states: "as We created you the first time," i.e., barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, as is related in the hadith.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., We resurrected you and restored you as We created you, because His saying "Certainly you have come to Us" means: We resurrected you.

﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you a appointed time﴾. This is a turning away and a transition from one speech to another, for rebuke and reproach. It is an address to those who deny the resurrection, i.e., you claimed in the world that you would not be resurrected, and that We would never appoint for you a time to requite you for your deeds and fulfill what We promised you of resurrection and punishment.

The clause ﴿And the Book is placed﴾ is conjoined to "were presented," and by "the Book" is meant the records of deeds; He made it singular because the definite article in it is for the genus. The placing is either sensory, by placing each one's record in his hand—the fortunate one in his right hand, the wretched one in his left—or in the scale. Or it is intellectual, i.e., the deed of each one, good and bad, is made manifest through the reckoning taking place on that day.

﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾, i.e., afraid and frightened of what is in the Book placed there, because of what follows from it of disgrace in that assembly and of requital with the painful punishment. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ They call down woe upon themselves because they have fallen into destruction. The meaning of this call has already been established in al-Ma'idah. ﴿What sort of book is this, that it leaves neither small nor great [deed] but has enumerated it?﴾, i.e., what is the matter with it: it leaves no small disobedience and no great disobedience except that it comprises it, records it and registers it. ﴿And they will find what they did﴾ in the world of sins that bring punishment, or they will find the recompense of what they did ﴿present﴾, recorded and registered. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, i.e., He does not punish any of His servants without sin, nor does He diminish the reward of one who performs obedience from the recompense he deserves.

Then He, glory be to Him, returned to refuting the people of arrogance among (p-864) Quraysh, and mentioned the story of Adam and the arrogance of Iblis toward him, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saying to them: prostrate in the prostration of greeting and honour, as its verification has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ in obedience to the command of Allah and compliance with His request for prostration, ﴿except Iblis﴾, for he refused and was arrogant and did not prostrate. The clause ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the cause of his disobedience: that he was of the jinn and not of the angels, and therefore he disobeyed. The meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ is that he went out of the obedience of his Lord.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "fasaqat al-rutbah 'an qishrihā" (the date swelled and came out of its skin), because it came out of it.

Al-Nahhas said: it has been disputed concerning the meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ according to two views. The first: the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, that the meaning is: defiance came to him when he was commanded, so he disobeyed; thus the cause of the defiance was the command of his Lord, as you say: "I feed him for hunger." The other view is that of Qutrub: that the meaning, by deletion of the modifier, is: he defied by abandoning His command.

Then He, glory be to Him, expressed wonder at the condition of those who obeyed Iblis in disbelief and sins and opposed the command of Allah, saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies, apart from Me?﴾ It is as if He said: after what came from him of refusal and defiance, do you take him and take his offspring—i.e., his children, and it was said: his followers, figuratively—as allies, so that you obey them in place of My obedience and substitute them for Me, while they are, i.e., Iblis and his offspring, ﴿an enemy to you﴾, i.e., enemies. He used the singular because it is a noun of genus, or because it is likened to verbal nouns, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77], and His saying: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. The meaning: how do you do this deed and substitute for One who created you and blessed you with all the blessings you have, one from whom you have never had any benefit at all, but who is an enemy to you, watching for the occurrence of what harms you at every time? ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who place a thing in other than its place, who substitute the obedience of Satan for the obedience of their Lord. So evil is that exchange which they took in place of Allah, glory be to Him.

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun refers to the partners. The meaning: if they had been partners with Me in creating the heavens and the earth and in creating themselves, they would have witnessed the creation of that and shared in it with Me. But they did not witness that, and I did not make them witness it, so they are not partners with Me.

This is an argument from the absence of the necessarily-concomitant (al-mulzum al-musawi) to the absence of what is necessitated (al-lazim).

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists who sought to drive away the poor believers. The intent is that they were not partners with Me in the governance of the world, as proof that I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, and I did not take them as helpers; rather they are like the rest of creation. It was also said: the meaning is that these wrongdoers are ignorant of what the pen has run with from eternity, because they did not witness the creation of the world; so how could they judge that their state is good with Allah? The first of these views is preferable, because of the dislocation of the two pronouns that would follow in the other two views. This sentence is resumptive, explaining that they do not deserve the taking mentioned.

Abu Ja'far read "ma ashhadnahum" (We did not make them witness), and the rest read "ma ashhadtuhum" (I did not make them witness). This is supported by ﴿nor would I have taken the misleaders as helpers (aḍud)﴾. The word 'aḍud is used often in the sense of help, because the upper arm is the support of the hand; and from it is His saying: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35], i.e., We will help you and strengthen you through him. It is said: a'dadtu bi-fulan (I sought support in so-and-so) when you seek his help. The arm is mentioned by way of metaphor, and the misleaders are singled out for mention to increase the blame and reproach.

The meaning: I did not seek help from them in creating the heavens and the earth, nor did I consult them, and I was not taking the devils or the disbelievers as helpers. He used the singular "'aḍud" to match the rhyme of the verse-endings.

Abu Ja'far al-Jahdari read "wa-ma kunta" with a fatha on the ta', as the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., "And you were not, O Muhammad, taking them as helpers, nor was that proper for you." The rest read it with a damma on the ta'. For "'aḍud" there are eight dialectal forms, the most eloquent of which is a fatha on the 'ayn and a damma on the ḍad, and it is with this that the majority read. Al-Hasan read "'uḍudan" with a damma on both the 'ayn and the ḍad; 'Ikrimah read with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad; al-Ḍaḥḥak read with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the ḍad; 'Isa ibn 'Umar read with fatha on both. The dialect of Tamim is a fatha on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad.

Then He returned to frightening them with the conditions of the Resurrection, saying: ﴿And the day He says: "Call My partners whom you claimed"﴾. Hamzah, Yahya ibn Wathhab and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "naqulu" with the nun, and the rest read with the ya' (third person): i.e., remember the day when Allah, mighty and majestic, says to the disbelievers, as a rebuke and reproach to them: "Call My partners whom you claimed that they would benefit you and intercede for you." He, glory be to Him, attributed them to Himself, following what the polytheists believed; may Allah be exalted above that. ﴿So they call them﴾, i.e., they did what Allah had commanded them of calling upon the partners, ﴿but they do not respond to them﴾ at that time, i.e., there did not come from them even mere response to them, let alone that they would benefit them or repel anything from them.

﴿And We placed between them a barrier (mawbiq)﴾, i.e., We placed between these polytheists and those whom they had made partners with Allah a mawbiq. A group of exegetes mentioned that it is the name of a deep valley by which Allah, exalted is He, separated them; and according to this it is the name of a place.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: every barrier between two things is a mawbiq. al-Farra' said: the mawbiq is that which destroys.

The meaning: We made their association in the world a destruction for them in the Hereafter. It is said: waqiqa yawbaqu, so he is waqaq (destroyed); so al-Farra' mentioned it in the verbal nouns. Al-Kisa'i related: waqiqa yabiqu wubuqan, so he is wabiq; and by the destroyer, according to this, is meant the punishment of the Fire in which they share.

"And whoever buys the good repute of a name with his wealth, will guard his honour from every disgraceful destruction (mawbiq)."

But the meaning appropriate to the sense of the verse is the first meaning.

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and they will think that they are going to fall into it﴾. "The criminals" is placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate increased blame for them through this recorded description attached to them. The word "thann" (thinking) here means certainty. Al-Muwaqa'ah is close contact through falling into it. It was also said: the disbelievers see the Fire from a distant place, so they think this with a kind of supposition. ﴿And they will find no escape from it﴾, i.e., no place to turn to, or no turning away, because the Fire has encompassed them from every side.

Al-Wahidi said: al-masraf is the place to which one turns. Al-Qutaybi said: i.e., a place to turn to, or a refuge they seek. The meanings are close in all of these.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ that he said: there is no building on it and no tree. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related a similar statement from Mujahid.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Leaves out no small deed nor great one﴾, that he said: "The small (*saghirah*) is the smile, and the great (*kabirah*) is laughter."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Abi Hatim added from him that he said: "The small is smiling at the believers in mockery, and the great is guffawing at them in that way."

I say: *saghirah* and *kabirah* are indefinite nouns (*nakirah*) in a context of negation (*siyaq al-nafy*), so every sin characterized by smallness and every sin characterized by greatness falls under this. No sin remains that Allah has not counted. Whatever sin is ambiguous as to whether it is small or great, that classification is only relative to the servants, not relative to Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Among the angels there is a tribe called the Jinn, and Iblis was one of them. Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding His words ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ that he said: "He was the keeper of the gardens (*khazin al-jinan*), and so he was named *al-Jann*."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also reported from him that he said: "Iblis was among the most noble of the angels and the most honorable of them in lineage, and he was the keeper over the gardens."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "May God curse people who claim that Iblis was of the angels, while God says: ﴿He was of the jinn﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari reported from him that he said: "He was never of the angels for the blink of an eye. He is indeed the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from Mujahid.

Abu 'Ubayd, Hannad, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "It is a valley in Hell."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* reported from Anas regarding the verse that he said: "It is a valley in Hell of pus and blood."
