Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 47–53 (part 1 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "tusayyaru" (with a ta' with a damma and the ya' with a fatha, in the passive form), with "al-jibal" in the nominative as the deputy of the subject (nā'ib 'an al-fā'il).

Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read "tasiru" (with a ta' with a fatha and without the doubling), with "al-jibal" as the subject (fā'il).

The rest read "nusayyiru" (with the nun), with the subject being Allah, glory be to Him, and "al-jibal" in the accusative as the object. The first reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set moving﴾ [al-Takwir: 3], and the second reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the third reading, because it fits His saying "wa-hasharnahum" (and We gathered them). Some of the grammarians said: the estimate is: "And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord on the day We set the mountains in motion." It was also said: the governing element of the time-adverb is a deleted verb, and the estimate is: "And remember the day We set the mountains in motion." The meaning of setting the mountains in motion is removing them from their places and making them move as clouds move, as in His saying: ﴿And it passes by like the passing of clouds﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Then they return to the earth after Allah has made them as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust, becoming scattered particles of dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6].

The address in His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47] is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. The meaning of its being laid bare is its becoming manifest, with whatever covers it—mountains, trees and buildings—removed. It was also said: the meaning of its being laid bare is the bringing forth of what is within it of treasures and the dead, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 4], and He said: ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2]. So the meaning becomes: "And you will see the earth laid bare, with what is in its belly brought out." ﴿And We gather them﴾, i.e., the creatures. The meaning of gathering (hashr) is assembling, i.e., We assemble them to the place of standing from every place. ﴿And We leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We do not leave any of them. It is said: ghādarahu and aghdarahu, when he left him. 'Antarah said:

"I left him rolling in the dust, his joints (scattered), while the people were between wounded and slain."

i.e., I left him. From this comes "ghadr" (betrayal), because the betrayer abandons fidelity to the one betrayed. They said: the pool (ghadir) was named ghadir because the water went away and left it; and from this comes the ghada'ir (braids) of a woman, because she places them behind her.

﴿And they are presented before your Lord in rows﴾: the accusative of "saffan" is as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., arranged in rows, each nation and group being a row. It was also said: they are presented in one row, as in His saying: ﴿Then come in rows﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64], i.e., all together. It was also said: standing.

In the verse there is a comparison of their condition with the condition of an army being reviewed before the sultan. ﴿Certainly you have come to Us as We created you the first time﴾ — this is with a supposed saying, i.e., We said to them: "Certainly you have come to Us." The kaf in "kama khalaqnakum" is an adjectival qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, i.e., a coming like your coming when We created you the first time, or as two states: "as We created you the first time," i.e., barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, as is related in the hadith.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., We resurrected you and restored you as We created you, because His saying "Certainly you have come to Us" means: We resurrected you.

﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you a appointed time﴾. This is a turning away and a transition from one speech to another, for rebuke and reproach. It is an address to those who deny the resurrection, i.e., you claimed in the world that you would not be resurrected, and that We would never appoint for you a time to requite you for your deeds and fulfill what We promised you of resurrection and punishment.

The clause ﴿And the Book is placed﴾ is conjoined to "were presented," and by "the Book" is meant the records of deeds; He made it singular because the definite article in it is for the genus. The placing is either sensory, by placing each one's record in his hand—the fortunate one in his right hand, the wretched one in his left—or in the scale. Or it is intellectual, i.e., the deed of each one, good and bad, is made manifest through the reckoning taking place on that day.

﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾, i.e., afraid and frightened of what is in the Book placed there, because of what follows from it of disgrace in that assembly and of requital with the painful punishment. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ They call down woe upon themselves because they have fallen into destruction. The meaning of this call has already been established in al-Ma'idah. ﴿What sort of book is this, that it leaves neither small nor great [deed] but has enumerated it?﴾, i.e., what is the matter with it: it leaves no small disobedience and no great disobedience except that it comprises it, records it and registers it. ﴿And they will find what they did﴾ in the world of sins that bring punishment, or they will find the recompense of what they did ﴿present﴾, recorded and registered. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, i.e., He does not punish any of His servants without sin, nor does He diminish the reward of one who performs obedience from the recompense he deserves.

Then He, glory be to Him, returned to refuting the people of arrogance among (p-864) Quraysh, and mentioned the story of Adam and the arrogance of Iblis toward him, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saying to them: prostrate in the prostration of greeting and honour, as its verification has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ in obedience to the command of Allah and compliance with His request for prostration, ﴿except Iblis﴾, for he refused and was arrogant and did not prostrate. The clause ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the cause of his disobedience: that he was of the jinn and not of the angels, and therefore he disobeyed. The meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ is that he went out of the obedience of his Lord.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "fasaqat al-rutbah 'an qishrihā" (the date swelled and came out of its skin), because it came out of it.

Al-Nahhas said: it has been disputed concerning the meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ according to two views. The first: the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, that the meaning is: defiance came to him when he was commanded, so he disobeyed; thus the cause of the defiance was the command of his Lord, as you say: "I feed him for hunger." The other view is that of Qutrub: that the meaning, by deletion of the modifier, is: he defied by abandoning His command.

Then He, glory be to Him, expressed wonder at the condition of those who obeyed Iblis in disbelief and sins and opposed the command of Allah, saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies, apart from Me?﴾ It is as if He said: after what came from him of refusal and defiance, do you take him and take his offspring—i.e., his children, and it was said: his followers, figuratively—as allies, so that you obey them in place of My obedience and substitute them for Me, while they are, i.e., Iblis and his offspring, ﴿an enemy to you﴾, i.e., enemies. He used the singular because it is a noun of genus, or because it is likened to verbal nouns, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77], and His saying: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. The meaning: how do you do this deed and substitute for One who created you and blessed you with all the blessings you have, one from whom you have never had any benefit at all, but who is an enemy to you, watching for the occurrence of what harms you at every time? ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who place a thing in other than its place, who substitute the obedience of Satan for the obedience of their Lord. So evil is that exchange which they took in place of Allah, glory be to Him.

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun refers to the partners. The meaning: if they had been partners with Me in creating the heavens and the earth and in creating themselves, they would have witnessed the creation of that and shared in it with Me. But they did not witness that, and I did not make them witness it, so they are not partners with Me.

This is an argument from the absence of the necessarily-concomitant (al-mulzum al-musawi) to the absence of what is necessitated (al-lazim).

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists who sought to drive away the poor believers. The intent is that they were not partners with Me in the governance of the world, as proof that I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, and I did not take them as helpers; rather they are like the rest of creation. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the third reading, because it fits His saying "wa-hasharnahum" (and We gathered them). It was also said: the governing element of the time-adverb is a deleted verb, and the estimate is: "And remember the day We set the mountains in motion." The meaning of setting the mountains in motion is removing them from their places and making them move as clouds move, as in His saying: ﴿And it passes by like the passing of clouds﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Then they return to the earth after Allah has made them as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust, becoming scattered particles of dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6].

The address in His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47] is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. The meaning of its being laid bare is its becoming manifest, with whatever covers it—mountains, trees and buildings—removed. It was also said: the meaning of its being laid bare is the bringing forth of what is within it of treasures and the dead, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 4], and He said: ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2]. So the meaning becomes: "And you will see the earth laid bare, with what is in its belly brought out." ﴿And We gather them﴾, i.e., the creatures. The meaning of gathering (hashr) is assembling, i.e., We assemble them to the place of standing from every place. ﴿And We leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We do not leave any of them. It is said: ghādarahu and aghdarahu, when he left him. 'Antarah said:

"I left him rolling in the dust, his joints (scattered), while the people were between wounded and slain."

i.e., I left him. From this comes "ghadr" (betrayal), because the betrayer abandons fidelity to the one betrayed. They said: the pool (ghadir) was named ghadir because the water went away and left it; and from this comes the ghada'ir (braids) of a woman, because she places them behind her.

﴿And they are presented before your Lord in rows﴾: the accusative of "saffan" is as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., arranged in rows, each nation and group being a row. It was also said: they are presented in one row, as in His saying: ﴿Then come in rows﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64], i.e., all together. It was also said: standing.

In the verse there is a comparison of their condition with the condition of an army being reviewed before the sultan. ﴿Certainly you have come to Us as We created you the first time﴾ — this is with a supposed saying, i.e., We said to them: "Certainly you have come to Us." The kaf in "kama khalaqnakum" is an adjectival qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, i.e., a coming like your coming when We created you the first time, or as two states: "as We created you the first time," i.e., barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, as is related in the hadith.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., We resurrected you and restored you as We created you, because His saying "Certainly you have come to Us" means: We resurrected you.

﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you a appointed time﴾. This is a turning away and a transition from one speech to another, for rebuke and reproach. It is an address to those who deny the resurrection, i.e., you claimed in the world that you would not be resurrected, and that We would never appoint for you a time to requite you for your deeds and fulfill what We promised you of resurrection and punishment.

The clause ﴿And the Book is placed﴾ is conjoined to "were presented," and by "the Book" is meant the records of deeds; He made it singular because the definite article in it is for the genus. The placing is either sensory, by placing each one's record in his hand—the fortunate one in his right hand, the wretched one in his left—or in the scale. Or it is intellectual, i.e., the deed of each one, good and bad, is made manifest through the reckoning taking place on that day.

﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾, i.e., afraid and frightened of what is in the Book placed there, because of what follows from it of disgrace in that assembly and of requital with the painful punishment. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ They call down woe upon themselves because they have fallen into destruction. The meaning of this call has already been established in al-Ma'idah. ﴿What sort of book is this, that it leaves neither small nor great [deed] but has enumerated it?﴾, i.e., what is the matter with it: it leaves no small disobedience and no great disobedience except that it comprises it, records it and registers it. ﴿And they will find what they did﴾ in the world of sins that bring punishment, or they will find the recompense of what they did ﴿present﴾, recorded and registered. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, i.e., He does not punish any of His servants without sin, nor does He diminish the reward of one who performs obedience from the recompense he deserves.

Then He, glory be to Him, returned to refuting the people of arrogance among (p-864) Quraysh, and mentioned the story of Adam and the arrogance of Iblis toward him, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saying to them: prostrate in the prostration of greeting and honour, as its verification has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ in obedience to the command of Allah and compliance with His request for prostration, ﴿except Iblis﴾, for he refused and was arrogant and did not prostrate. The clause ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the cause of his disobedience: that he was of the jinn and not of the angels, and therefore he disobeyed. The meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ is that he went out of the obedience of his Lord.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "fasaqat al-rutbah 'an qishrihā" (the date swelled and came out of its skin), because it came out of it.

Al-Nahhas said: it has been disputed concerning the meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ according to two views. The first: the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, that the meaning is: defiance came to him when he was commanded, so he disobeyed; thus the cause of the defiance was the command of his Lord, as you say: "I feed him for hunger." The other view is that of Qutrub: that the meaning, by deletion of the modifier, is: he defied by abandoning His command.

Then He, glory be to Him, expressed wonder at the condition of those who obeyed Iblis in disbelief and sins and opposed the command of Allah, saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies, apart from Me?﴾ It is as if He said: after what came from him of refusal and defiance, do you take him and take his offspring—i.e., his children, and it was said: his followers, figuratively—as allies, so that you obey them in place of My obedience and substitute them for Me, while they are, i.e., Iblis and his offspring, ﴿an enemy to you﴾, i.e., enemies. He used the singular because it is a noun of genus, or because it is likened to verbal nouns, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77], and His saying: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. The meaning: how do you do this deed and substitute for One who created you and blessed you with all the blessings you have, one from whom you have never had any benefit at all, but who is an enemy to you, watching for the occurrence of what harms you at every time? ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who place a thing in other than its place, who substitute the obedience of Satan for the obedience of their Lord. So evil is that exchange which they took in place of Allah, glory be to Him.

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun refers to the partners. The meaning: if they had been partners with Me in creating the heavens and the earth and in creating themselves, they would have witnessed the creation of that and shared in it with Me. But they did not witness that, and I did not make them witness it, so they are not partners with Me.

This is an argument from the absence of the necessarily-concomitant (al-mulzum al-musawi) to the absence of what is necessitated (al-lazim).

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists who sought to drive away the poor believers. The intent is that they were not partners with Me in the governance of the world, as proof that I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, and I did not take them as helpers; rather they are like the rest of creation. It was also said: the meaning is that these wrongdoers are ignorant of what the pen has run with from eternity, because they did not witness the creation of the world; so how could they judge that their state is good with Allah? The first of these views is preferable, because of the dislocation of the two pronouns that would follow in the other two views. This sentence is resumptive, explaining that they do not deserve the taking mentioned.

Abu Ja'far read "ma ashhadnahum" (We did not make them witness), and the rest read "ma ashhadtuhum" (I did not make them witness). This is supported by ﴿nor would I have taken the misleaders as helpers (aḍud)﴾. The word 'aḍud is used often in the sense of help, because the upper arm is the support of the hand; and from it is His saying: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35], i.e., We will help you and strengthen you through him. It is said: a'dadtu bi-fulan (I sought support in so-and-so) when you seek his help. The arm is mentioned by way of metaphor, and the misleaders are singled out for mention to increase the blame and reproach.

The meaning: I did not seek help from them in creating the heavens and the earth, nor did I consult them, and I was not taking the devils or the disbelievers as helpers. He used the singular "'aḍud" to match the rhyme of the verse-endings.

Abu Ja'far al-Jahdari read "wa-ma kunta" with a fatha on the ta', as the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., "And you were not, O Muhammad, taking them as helpers, nor was that proper for you." The rest read it with a damma on the ta'. For "'aḍud" there are eight dialectal forms, the most eloquent of which is a fatha on the 'ayn and a damma on the ḍad, and it is with this that the majority read. Al-Hasan read "'uḍudan" with a damma on both the 'ayn and the ḍad; 'Ikrimah read with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad; al-Ḍaḥḥak read with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the ḍad; 'Isa ibn 'Umar read with fatha on both. The dialect of Tamim is a fatha on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad.

Then He returned to frightening them with the conditions of the Resurrection, saying: ﴿And the day He says: "Call My partners whom you claimed"﴾. Hamzah, Yahya ibn Wathhab and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "naqulu" with the nun, and the rest read with the ya' (third person): i.e., remember the day when Allah, mighty and majestic, says to the disbelievers, as a rebuke and reproach to them: "Call My partners whom you claimed that they would benefit you and intercede for you." He, glory be to Him, attributed them to Himself, following what the polytheists believed; may Allah be exalted above that. ﴿So they call them﴾, i.e., they did what Allah had commanded them of calling upon the partners, ﴿but they do not respond to them﴾ at that time, i.e., there did not come from them even mere response to them, let alone that they would benefit them or repel anything from them.

﴿And We placed between them a barrier (mawbiq)﴾, i.e., We placed between these polytheists and those whom they had made partners with Allah a mawbiq. A group of exegetes mentioned that it is the name of a deep valley by which Allah, exalted is He, separated them; and according to this it is the name of a place.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: every barrier between two things is a mawbiq. al-Farra' said: the mawbiq is that which destroys.

The meaning: We made their association in the world a destruction for them in the Hereafter. It is said: waqiqa yawbaqu, so he is waqaq (destroyed); so al-Farra' mentioned it in the verbal nouns. Al-Kisa'i related: waqiqa yabiqu wubuqan, so he is wabiq; and by the destroyer, according to this, is meant the punishment of the Fire in which they share.

The first is preferable, because among what they claimed was that they were partners of Allah were the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah; so the mawbiq is the place intervening between them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: mawbiq here means the appointed place of destruction, and it is established in the language that awbaqahu means "he destroyed him," and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And whoever buys the good repute of a name with his wealth, will guard his honour from every disgraceful destruction (mawbiq)."

But the meaning appropriate to the sense of the verse is the first meaning.

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and they will think that they are going to fall into it﴾. "The criminals" is placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate increased blame for them through this recorded description attached to them. The word "thann" (thinking) here means certainty. Al-Muwaqa'ah is close contact through falling into it. It was also said: the disbelievers see the Fire from a distant place, so they think this with a kind of supposition. ﴿And they will find no escape from it﴾, i.e., no place to turn to, or no turning away, because the Fire has encompassed them from every side.

Al-Wahidi said: al-masraf is the place to which one turns. Al-Qutaybi said: i.e., a place to turn to, or a refuge they seek. The meanings are close in all of these.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ that he said: there is no building on it and no tree. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related a similar statement from Mujahid.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Leaves out no small deed nor great one﴾, that he said: "The small (*saghirah*) is the smile, and the great (*kabirah*) is laughter."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Abi Hatim added from him that he said: "The small is smiling at the believers in mockery, and the great is guffawing at them in that way."

I say: *saghirah* and *kabirah* are indefinite nouns (*nakirah*) in a context of negation (*siyaq al-nafy*), so every sin characterized by smallness and every sin characterized by greatness falls under this. No sin remains that Allah has not counted. Whatever sin is ambiguous as to whether it is small or great, that classification is only relative to the servants, not relative to Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Among the angels there is a tribe called the Jinn, and Iblis was one of them. He used to whisper between the heavens and the earth. He disobeyed, so Allah became angry with him and transformed him into an accursed devil (*shaytan rajim*)."

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding His words ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ that he said: "He was the keeper of the gardens (*khazin al-jinan*), and so he was named *al-Jann*."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also reported from him that he said: "Iblis was among the most noble of the angels and the most honorable of them in lineage, and he was the keeper over the gardens."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "May God curse people who claim that Iblis was of the angels, while God says: ﴿He was of the jinn﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari reported from him that he said: "He was never of the angels for the blink of an eye. He is indeed the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi regarding His words ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "He says: I did not make the devils whom you took besides Me witness this." And regarding ﴿Nor was I one who would take the misguiders as helpers﴾ he said: "The devils as helpers. He said: Nor did I take them as helpers in anything for which they assisted Me."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿And We made between them a place of ruin (*mawbiq*)﴾ that he said: "It means a place of destruction (*muhlikan*)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from Mujahid.

Abu 'Ubayd, Hannad, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "It is a valley in Hell."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* reported from Anas regarding the verse that he said: "It is a valley in Hell of pus and blood."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn 'Amr that he said: "It is a deep valley in the Fire, by which Allah will separate, on the Day of Resurrection, between the people of guidance and the people of misguidance."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and they thought that they would fall into it﴾ that he said: "They knew (*'alimu*)."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 47–53 (part 1 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "tusayyaru" (with a ta' with a damma and the ya' with a fatha, in the passive form), with "al-jibal" in the nominative as the deputy of the subject (nā'ib 'an al-fā'il).

Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read "tasiru" (with a ta' with a fatha and without the doubling), with "al-jibal" as the subject (fā'il).

The rest read "nusayyiru" (with the nun), with the subject being Allah, glory be to Him, and "al-jibal" in the accusative as the object. The first reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set moving﴾ [al-Takwir: 3], and the second reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]. i.e., I left him. From this comes "ghadr" (betrayal), because the betrayer abandons fidelity to the one betrayed. They said: the pool (ghadir) was named ghadir because the water went away and left it; and from this comes the ghada'ir (braids) of a woman, because she places them behind her.

Abu Ja'far al-Jahdari read "wa-ma kunta" with a fatha on the ta', as the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., "And you were not, O Muhammad, taking them as helpers, nor was that proper for you." The rest read it with a damma on the ta'. For "'aḍud" there are eight dialectal forms, the most eloquent of which is a fatha on the 'ayn and a damma on the ḍad, and it is with this that the majority read. Al-Hasan read "'uḍudan" with a damma on both the 'ayn and the ḍad; 'Ikrimah read with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad; al-Ḍaḥḥak read with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the ḍad; 'Isa ibn 'Umar read with fatha on both. The dialect of Tamim is a fatha on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad.

Then He returned to frightening them with the conditions of the Resurrection, saying: ﴿And the day He says: "Call My partners whom you claimed"﴾. Hamzah, Yahya ibn Wathhab and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "naqulu" with the nun, and the rest read with the ya' (third person): i.e., remember the day when Allah, mighty and majestic, says to the disbelievers, as a rebuke and reproach to them: "Call My partners whom you claimed that they would benefit you and intercede for you." He, glory be to Him, attributed them to Himself, following what the polytheists believed; may Allah be exalted above that. ﴿So they call them﴾, i.e., they did what Allah had commanded them of calling upon the partners, ﴿but they do not respond to them﴾ at that time, i.e., there did not come from them even mere response to them, let alone that they would benefit them or repel anything from them.

﴿And We placed between them a barrier (mawbiq)﴾, i.e., We placed between these polytheists and those whom they had made partners with Allah a mawbiq. A group of exegetes mentioned that it is the name of a deep valley by which Allah, exalted is He, separated them; and according to this it is the name of a place.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: every barrier between two things is a mawbiq. al-Farra' said: the mawbiq is that which destroys.

The meaning: We made their association in the world a destruction for them in the Hereafter. It is said: waqiqa yawbaqu, so he is waqaq (destroyed); so al-Farra' mentioned it in the verbal nouns. Al-Kisa'i related: waqiqa yabiqu wubuqan, so he is wabiq; and by the destroyer, according to this, is meant the punishment of the Fire in which they share.

The first is preferable, because among what they claimed was that they were partners of Allah were the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah; so the mawbiq is the place intervening between them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: mawbiq here means the appointed place of destruction, and it is established in the language that awbaqahu means "he destroyed him," and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And whoever buys the good repute of a name with his wealth, will guard his honour from every disgraceful destruction (mawbiq)."

But the meaning appropriate to the sense of the verse is the first meaning.

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and they will think that they are going to fall into it﴾. "The criminals" is placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate increased blame for them through this recorded description attached to them. The word "thann" (thinking) here means certainty. Al-Muwaqa'ah is close contact through falling into it. It was also said: the disbelievers see the Fire from a distant place, so they think this with a kind of supposition. ﴿And they will find no escape from it﴾, i.e., no place to turn to, or no turning away, because the Fire has encompassed them from every side.

Al-Wahidi said: al-masraf is the place to which one turns. Al-Qutaybi said: i.e., a place to turn to, or a refuge they seek. The meanings are close in all of these.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ that he said: there is no building on it and no tree. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related a similar statement from Mujahid.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Leaves out no small deed nor great one﴾, that he said: "The small (*saghirah*) is the smile, and the great (*kabirah*) is laughter."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Abi Hatim added from him that he said: "The small is smiling at the believers in mockery, and the great is guffawing at them in that way."

I say: *saghirah* and *kabirah* are indefinite nouns (*nakirah*) in a context of negation (*siyaq al-nafy*), so every sin characterized by smallness and every sin characterized by greatness falls under this. No sin remains that Allah has not counted. Whatever sin is ambiguous as to whether it is small or great, that classification is only relative to the servants, not relative to Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Among the angels there is a tribe called the Jinn, and Iblis was one of them. He used to whisper between the heavens and the earth. He disobeyed, so Allah became angry with him and transformed him into an accursed devil (*shaytan rajim*)."

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding His words ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ that he said: "He was the keeper of the gardens (*khazin al-jinan*), and so he was named *al-Jann*."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also reported from him that he said: "Iblis was among the most noble of the angels and the most honorable of them in lineage, and he was the keeper over the gardens."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "May God curse people who claim that Iblis was of the angels, while God says: ﴿He was of the jinn﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari reported from him that he said: "He was never of the angels for the blink of an eye. He is indeed the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi regarding His words ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "He says: I did not make the devils whom you took besides Me witness this." And regarding ﴿Nor was I one who would take the misguiders as helpers﴾ he said: "The devils as helpers. He said: Nor did I take them as helpers in anything for which they assisted Me."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿And We made between them a place of ruin (*mawbiq*)﴾ that he said: "It means a place of destruction (*muhlikan*)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from Mujahid.

Abu 'Ubayd, Hannad, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "It is a valley in Hell."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* reported from Anas regarding the verse that he said: "It is a valley in Hell of pus and blood."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn 'Amr that he said: "It is a deep valley in the Fire, by which Allah will separate, on the Day of Resurrection, between the people of guidance and the people of misguidance."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and they thought that they would fall into it﴾ that he said: "They knew (*'alimu*)."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 47–53 (part 1 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "tusayyaru" (with a ta' with a damma and the ya' with a fatha, in the passive form), with "al-jibal" in the nominative as the deputy of the subject (nā'ib 'an al-fā'il).

Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read "tasiru" (with a ta' with a fatha and without the doubling), with "al-jibal" as the subject (fā'il).

The rest read "nusayyiru" (with the nun), with the subject being Allah, glory be to Him, and "al-jibal" in the accusative as the object. The first reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set moving﴾ [al-Takwir: 3], and the second reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the third reading, because it fits His saying "wa-hasharnahum" (and We gathered them). Some of the grammarians said: the estimate is: "And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord on the day We set the mountains in motion." It was also said: the governing element of the time-adverb is a deleted verb, and the estimate is: "And remember the day We set the mountains in motion." The meaning of setting the mountains in motion is removing them from their places and making them move as clouds move, as in His saying: ﴿And it passes by like the passing of clouds﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Then they return to the earth after Allah has made them as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust, becoming scattered particles of dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6].

The address in His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47] is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. The meaning of its being laid bare is its becoming manifest, with whatever covers it—mountains, trees and buildings—removed. It was also said: the meaning of its being laid bare is the bringing forth of what is within it of treasures and the dead, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 4], and He said: ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2]. So the meaning becomes: "And you will see the earth laid bare, with what is in its belly brought out." ﴿And We gather them﴾, i.e., the creatures. The meaning of gathering (hashr) is assembling, i.e., We assemble them to the place of standing from every place. ﴿And We leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We do not leave any of them. It is said: ghādarahu and aghdarahu, when he left him. 'Antarah said:

"I left him rolling in the dust, his joints (scattered), while the people were between wounded and slain."

i.e., I left him. From this comes "ghadr" (betrayal), because the betrayer abandons fidelity to the one betrayed. They said: the pool (ghadir) was named ghadir because the water went away and left it; and from this comes the ghada'ir (braids) of a woman, because she places them behind her.

﴿And they are presented before your Lord in rows﴾: the accusative of "saffan" is as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., arranged in rows, each nation and group being a row. It was also said: they are presented in one row, as in His saying: ﴿Then come in rows﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64], i.e., all together. It was also said: standing.

In the verse there is a comparison of their condition with the condition of an army being reviewed before the sultan. ﴿Certainly you have come to Us as We created you the first time﴾ — this is with a supposed saying, i.e., We said to them: "Certainly you have come to Us." The kaf in "kama khalaqnakum" is an adjectival qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, i.e., a coming like your coming when We created you the first time, or as two states: "as We created you the first time," i.e., barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, as is related in the hadith.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., We resurrected you and restored you as We created you, because His saying "Certainly you have come to Us" means: We resurrected you.

﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you a appointed time﴾. This is a turning away and a transition from one speech to another, for rebuke and reproach. It is an address to those who deny the resurrection, i.e., you claimed in the world that you would not be resurrected, and that We would never appoint for you a time to requite you for your deeds and fulfill what We promised you of resurrection and punishment.

The clause ﴿And the Book is placed﴾ is conjoined to "were presented," and by "the Book" is meant the records of deeds; He made it singular because the definite article in it is for the genus. The placing is either sensory, by placing each one's record in his hand—the fortunate one in his right hand, the wretched one in his left—or in the scale. Or it is intellectual, i.e., the deed of each one, good and bad, is made manifest through the reckoning taking place on that day.

﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾, i.e., afraid and frightened of what is in the Book placed there, because of what follows from it of disgrace in that assembly and of requital with the painful punishment. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ They call down woe upon themselves because they have fallen into destruction. The meaning of this call has already been established in al-Ma'idah. ﴿What sort of book is this, that it leaves neither small nor great [deed] but has enumerated it?﴾, i.e., what is the matter with it: it leaves no small disobedience and no great disobedience except that it comprises it, records it and registers it. ﴿And they will find what they did﴾ in the world of sins that bring punishment, or they will find the recompense of what they did ﴿present﴾, recorded and registered. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, i.e., He does not punish any of His servants without sin, nor does He diminish the reward of one who performs obedience from the recompense he deserves.

Then He, glory be to Him, returned to refuting the people of arrogance among (p-864) Quraysh, and mentioned the story of Adam and the arrogance of Iblis toward him, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saying to them: prostrate in the prostration of greeting and honour, as its verification has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ in obedience to the command of Allah and compliance with His request for prostration, ﴿except Iblis﴾, for he refused and was arrogant and did not prostrate. The clause ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the cause of his disobedience: that he was of the jinn and not of the angels, and therefore he disobeyed. The meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ is that he went out of the obedience of his Lord.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "fasaqat al-rutbah 'an qishrihā" (the date swelled and came out of its skin), because it came out of it.

Al-Nahhas said: it has been disputed concerning the meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ according to two views. The first: the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, that the meaning is: defiance came to him when he was commanded, so he disobeyed; thus the cause of the defiance was the command of his Lord, as you say: "I feed him for hunger." The other view is that of Qutrub: that the meaning, by deletion of the modifier, is: he defied by abandoning His command.

Then He, glory be to Him, expressed wonder at the condition of those who obeyed Iblis in disbelief and sins and opposed the command of Allah, saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies, apart from Me?﴾ It is as if He said: after what came from him of refusal and defiance, do you take him and take his offspring—i.e., his children, and it was said: his followers, figuratively—as allies, so that you obey them in place of My obedience and substitute them for Me, while they are, i.e., Iblis and his offspring, ﴿an enemy to you﴾, i.e., enemies. He used the singular because it is a noun of genus, or because it is likened to verbal nouns, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77], and His saying: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. The meaning: how do you do this deed and substitute for One who created you and blessed you with all the blessings you have, one from whom you have never had any benefit at all, but who is an enemy to you, watching for the occurrence of what harms you at every time? ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who place a thing in other than its place, who substitute the obedience of Satan for the obedience of their Lord. So evil is that exchange which they took in place of Allah, glory be to Him.

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun refers to the partners. The meaning: if they had been partners with Me in creating the heavens and the earth and in creating themselves, they would have witnessed the creation of that and shared in it with Me. But they did not witness that, and I did not make them witness it, so they are not partners with Me.

This is an argument from the absence of the necessarily-concomitant (al-mulzum al-musawi) to the absence of what is necessitated (al-lazim).

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists who sought to drive away the poor believers. The intent is that they were not partners with Me in the governance of the world, as proof that I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, and I did not take them as helpers; rather they are like the rest of creation. It was also said: the meaning is that these wrongdoers are ignorant of what the pen has run with from eternity, because they did not witness the creation of the world; so how could they judge that their state is good with Allah? The first of these views is preferable, because of the dislocation of the two pronouns that would follow in the other two views. This sentence is resumptive, explaining that they do not deserve the taking mentioned.

Abu Ja'far read "ma ashhadnahum" (We did not make them witness), and the rest read "ma ashhadtuhum" (I did not make them witness). This is supported by ﴿nor would I have taken the misleaders as helpers (aḍud)﴾. The word 'aḍud is used often in the sense of help, because the upper arm is the support of the hand; and from it is His saying: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35], i.e., We will help you and strengthen you through him. It is said: a'dadtu bi-fulan (I sought support in so-and-so) when you seek his help. The arm is mentioned by way of metaphor, and the misleaders are singled out for mention to increase the blame and reproach.

The meaning: I did not seek help from them in creating the heavens and the earth, nor did I consult them, and I was not taking the devils or the disbelievers as helpers. He used the singular "'aḍud" to match the rhyme of the verse-endings.

The meaning of its being laid bare is its becoming manifest, with whatever covers it—mountains, trees and buildings—removed. So the meaning becomes: "And you will see the earth laid bare, with what is in its belly brought out." ﴿And We gather them﴾, i.e., the creatures. The meaning of gathering (hashr) is assembling, i.e., We assemble them to the place of standing from every place. ﴿And We leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We do not leave any of them. It is said: ghādarahu and aghdarahu, when he left him. 'Antarah said:

"I left him rolling in the dust, his joints (scattered), while the people were between wounded and slain."

i.e., I left him. From this comes "ghadr" (betrayal), because the betrayer abandons fidelity to the one betrayed. They said: the pool (ghadir) was named ghadir because the water went away and left it; and from this comes the ghada'ir (braids) of a woman, because she places them behind her.

﴿And they are presented before your Lord in rows﴾: the accusative of "saffan" is as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., arranged in rows, each nation and group being a row. It was also said: they are presented in one row, as in His saying: ﴿Then come in rows﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64], i.e., all together. It was also said: standing.

In the verse there is a comparison of their condition with the condition of an army being reviewed before the sultan. ﴿Certainly you have come to Us as We created you the first time﴾ — this is with a supposed saying, i.e., We said to them: "Certainly you have come to Us." The kaf in "kama khalaqnakum" is an adjectival qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, i.e., a coming like your coming when We created you the first time, or as two states: "as We created you the first time," i.e., barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, as is related in the hadith.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., We resurrected you and restored you as We created you, because His saying "Certainly you have come to Us" means: We resurrected you.

﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you a appointed time﴾. This is a turning away and a transition from one speech to another, for rebuke and reproach. It is an address to those who deny the resurrection, i.e., you claimed in the world that you would not be resurrected, and that We would never appoint for you a time to requite you for your deeds and fulfill what We promised you of resurrection and punishment.

The clause ﴿And the Book is placed﴾ is conjoined to "were presented," and by "the Book" is meant the records of deeds; He made it singular because the definite article in it is for the genus. The placing is either sensory, by placing each one's record in his hand—the fortunate one in his right hand, the wretched one in his left—or in the scale. Or it is intellectual, i.e., the deed of each one, good and bad, is made manifest through the reckoning taking place on that day.

﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾, i.e., afraid and frightened of what is in the Book placed there, because of what follows from it of disgrace in that assembly and of requital with the painful punishment. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ They call down woe upon themselves because they have fallen into destruction. The meaning of this call has already been established in al-Ma'idah. ﴿What sort of book is this, that it leaves neither small nor great [deed] but has enumerated it?﴾, i.e., what is the matter with it: it leaves no small disobedience and no great disobedience except that it comprises it, records it and registers it. ﴿And they will find what they did﴾ in the world of sins that bring punishment, or they will find the recompense of what they did ﴿present﴾, recorded and registered. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾, i.e., He does not punish any of His servants without sin, nor does He diminish the reward of one who performs obedience from the recompense he deserves.

Then He, glory be to Him, returned to refuting the people of arrogance among (p-864) Quraysh, and mentioned the story of Adam and the arrogance of Iblis toward him, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saying to them: prostrate in the prostration of greeting and honour, as its verification has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ in obedience to the command of Allah and compliance with His request for prostration, ﴿except Iblis﴾, for he refused and was arrogant and did not prostrate. The clause ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the cause of his disobedience: that he was of the jinn and not of the angels, and therefore he disobeyed. The meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ is that he went out of the obedience of his Lord.

Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say: "fasaqat al-rutbah 'an qishrihā" (the date swelled and came out of its skin), because it came out of it.

Al-Nahhas said: it has been disputed concerning the meaning of ﴿so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ according to two views. The first: the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, that the meaning is: defiance came to him when he was commanded, so he disobeyed; thus the cause of the defiance was the command of his Lord, as you say: "I feed him for hunger." The other view is that of Qutrub: that the meaning, by deletion of the modifier, is: he defied by abandoning His command.

Then He, glory be to Him, expressed wonder at the condition of those who obeyed Iblis in disbelief and sins and opposed the command of Allah, saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies, apart from Me?﴾ It is as if He said: after what came from him of refusal and defiance, do you take him and take his offspring—i.e., his children, and it was said: his followers, figuratively—as allies, so that you obey them in place of My obedience and substitute them for Me, while they are, i.e., Iblis and his offspring, ﴿an enemy to you﴾, i.e., enemies. He used the singular because it is a noun of genus, or because it is likened to verbal nouns, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77], and His saying: ﴿They are the enemy﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4]. The meaning: how do you do this deed and substitute for One who created you and blessed you with all the blessings you have, one from whom you have never had any benefit at all, but who is an enemy to you, watching for the occurrence of what harms you at every time? ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who place a thing in other than its place, who substitute the obedience of Satan for the obedience of their Lord. So evil is that exchange which they took in place of Allah, glory be to Him.

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun refers to the partners. The meaning: if they had been partners with Me in creating the heavens and the earth and in creating themselves, they would have witnessed the creation of that and shared in it with Me. But they did not witness that, and I did not make them witness it, so they are not partners with Me.

This is an argument from the absence of the necessarily-concomitant (al-mulzum al-musawi) to the absence of what is necessitated (al-lazim).

It was also said: the pronoun refers to the polytheists who sought to drive away the poor believers. The intent is that they were not partners with Me in the governance of the world, as proof that I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, and I did not take them as helpers; rather they are like the rest of creation. It was also said: the meaning is that these wrongdoers are ignorant of what the pen has run with from eternity, because they did not witness the creation of the world; so how could they judge that their state is good with Allah? The first of these views is preferable, because of the dislocation of the two pronouns that would follow in the other two views. This sentence is resumptive, explaining that they do not deserve the taking mentioned.

Abu Ja'far read "ma ashhadnahum" (We did not make them witness), and the rest read "ma ashhadtuhum" (I did not make them witness). This is supported by ﴿nor would I have taken the misleaders as helpers (aḍud)﴾. The word 'aḍud is used often in the sense of help, because the upper arm is the support of the hand; and from it is His saying: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas: 35], i.e., We will help you and strengthen you through him. It is said: a'dadtu bi-fulan (I sought support in so-and-so) when you seek his help. The arm is mentioned by way of metaphor, and the misleaders are singled out for mention to increase the blame and reproach.

The meaning: I did not seek help from them in creating the heavens and the earth, nor did I consult them, and I was not taking the devils or the disbelievers as helpers. He used the singular "'aḍud" to match the rhyme of the verse-endings.

Abu Ja'far al-Jahdari read "wa-ma kunta" with a fatha on the ta', as the address to the Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., "And you were not, O Muhammad, taking them as helpers, nor was that proper for you." The rest read it with a damma on the ta'. For "'aḍud" there are eight dialectal forms, the most eloquent of which is a fatha on the 'ayn and a damma on the ḍad, and it is with this that the majority read. Al-Hasan read "'uḍudan" with a damma on both the 'ayn and the ḍad; 'Ikrimah read with a damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad; al-Ḍaḥḥak read with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the ḍad; 'Isa ibn 'Umar read with fatha on both. The dialect of Tamim is a fatha on the 'ayn and sukun on the ḍad.

Then He returned to frightening them with the conditions of the Resurrection, saying: ﴿And the day He says: "Call My partners whom you claimed"﴾. Hamzah, Yahya ibn Wathhab and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "naqulu" with the nun, and the rest read with the ya' (third person): i.e., remember the day when Allah, mighty and majestic, says to the disbelievers, as a rebuke and reproach to them: "Call My partners whom you claimed that they would benefit you and intercede for you." He, glory be to Him, attributed them to Himself, following what the polytheists believed; may Allah be exalted above that. ﴿So they call them﴾, i.e., they did what Allah had commanded them of calling upon the partners, ﴿but they do not respond to them﴾ at that time, i.e., there did not come from them even mere response to them, let alone that they would benefit them or repel anything from them.

﴿And We placed between them a barrier (mawbiq)﴾, i.e., We placed between these polytheists and those whom they had made partners with Allah a mawbiq. A group of exegetes mentioned that it is the name of a deep valley by which Allah, exalted is He, separated them; and according to this it is the name of a place.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: every barrier between two things is a mawbiq. al-Farra' said: the mawbiq is that which destroys.

The meaning: We made their association in the world a destruction for them in the Hereafter. It is said: waqiqa yawbaqu, so he is waqaq (destroyed); so al-Farra' mentioned it in the verbal nouns. Al-Kisa'i related: waqiqa yabiqu wubuqan, so he is wabiq; and by the destroyer, according to this, is meant the punishment of the Fire in which they share.

The first is preferable, because among what they claimed was that they were partners of Allah were the angels, 'Uzayr and the Messiah; so the mawbiq is the place intervening between them.

Abu 'Ubayda said: mawbiq here means the appointed place of destruction, and it is established in the language that awbaqahu means "he destroyed him," and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And whoever buys the good repute of a name with his wealth, will guard his honour from every disgraceful destruction (mawbiq)."

But the meaning appropriate to the sense of the verse is the first meaning.

﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and they will think that they are going to fall into it﴾. "The criminals" is placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate increased blame for them through this recorded description attached to them. The word "thann" (thinking) here means certainty. Al-Muwaqa'ah is close contact through falling into it. It was also said: the disbelievers see the Fire from a distant place, so they think this with a kind of supposition. ﴿And they will find no escape from it﴾, i.e., no place to turn to, or no turning away, because the Fire has encompassed them from every side.

Al-Wahidi said: al-masraf is the place to which one turns. Al-Qutaybi said: i.e., a place to turn to, or a refuge they seek. The meanings are close in all of these.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ that he said: there is no building on it and no tree. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related a similar statement from Mujahid.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Leaves out no small deed nor great one﴾, that he said: "The small (*saghirah*) is the smile, and the great (*kabirah*) is laughter."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Abi Hatim added from him that he said: "The small is smiling at the believers in mockery, and the great is guffawing at them in that way."

I say: *saghirah* and *kabirah* are indefinite nouns (*nakirah*) in a context of negation (*siyaq al-nafy*), so every sin characterized by smallness and every sin characterized by greatness falls under this. No sin remains that Allah has not counted. Whatever sin is ambiguous as to whether it is small or great, that classification is only relative to the servants, not relative to Allah, glorified is He.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Among the angels there is a tribe called the Jinn, and Iblis was one of them. He used to whisper between the heavens and the earth. He disobeyed, so Allah became angry with him and transformed him into an accursed devil (*shaytan rajim*)."

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding His words ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ that he said: "He was the keeper of the gardens (*khazin al-jinan*), and so he was named *al-Jann*."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also reported from him that he said: "Iblis was among the most noble of the angels and the most honorable of them in lineage, and he was the keeper over the gardens."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "May God curse people who claim that Iblis was of the angels, while God says: ﴿He was of the jinn﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari reported from him that he said: "He was never of the angels for the blink of an eye. He is indeed the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi regarding His words ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "He says: I did not make the devils whom you took besides Me witness this." And regarding ﴿Nor was I one who would take the misguiders as helpers﴾ he said: "The devils as helpers. He said: Nor did I take them as helpers in anything for which they assisted Me."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words ﴿And We made between them a place of ruin (*mawbiq*)﴾ that he said: "It means a place of destruction (*muhlikan*)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from Mujahid.

Abu 'Ubayd, Hannad, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "It is a valley in Hell."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th* reported from Anas regarding the verse that he said: "It is a valley in Hell of pus and blood."

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn 'Amr that he said: "It is a deep valley in the Fire, by which Allah will separate, on the Day of Resurrection, between the people of guidance and the people of misguidance."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and they thought that they would fall into it﴾ that he said: "They knew (*'alimu*)."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 47–53 (part 1 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "tusayyaru" (with a ta' with a damma and the ya' with a fatha, in the passive form), with "al-jibal" in the nominative as the deputy of the subject (nā'ib 'an al-fā'il).

Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read "tasiru" (with a ta' with a fatha and without the doubling), with "al-jibal" as the subject (fā'il).

The rest read "nusayyiru" (with the nun), with the subject being Allah, glory be to Him, and "al-jibal" in the accusative as the object. The first reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set moving﴾ [al-Takwir: 3], and the second reading is matched by His saying: ﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾ [al-Tur: 10]. Abu 'Ubayda preferred the third reading, because it fits His saying "wa-hasharnahum" (and We gathered them). Some of the grammarians said: the estimate is: "And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord on the day We set the mountains in motion." It was also said: the governing element of the time-adverb is a deleted verb, and the estimate is: "And remember the day We set the mountains in motion." The meaning of setting the mountains in motion is removing them from their places and making them move as clouds move, as in His saying: ﴿And it passes by like the passing of clouds﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Then they return to the earth after Allah has made them as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust, becoming scattered particles of dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6].

The address in His saying ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47] is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. The meaning of its being laid bare is its becoming manifest, with whatever covers it—mountains, trees and buildings—removed. It was also said: the meaning of its being laid bare is the bringing forth of what is within it of treasures and the dead, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 4], and He said: ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2]. The meaning of gathering (hashr) is assembling, i.e., We assemble them to the place of standing from every place. ﴿And We leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We do not leave any of them. i.e., I left him. From this comes "ghadr" (betrayal), because the betrayer abandons fidelity to the one betrayed. They said: the pool (ghadir) was named ghadir because the water went away and left it; and from this comes the ghada'ir (braids) of a woman, because she places them behind her.

﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you a appointed time﴾. This is a turning away and a transition from one speech to another, for rebuke and reproach. It is an address to those who deny the resurrection, i.e., you claimed in the world that you would not be resurrected, and that We would never appoint for you a time to requite you for your deeds and fulfill what We promised you of resurrection and punishment.

The clause ﴿And the Book is placed﴾ is conjoined to "were presented," and by "the Book" is meant the records of deeds; He made it singular because the definite article in it is for the genus. The placing is either sensory, by placing each one's record in his hand—the fortunate one in his right hand, the wretched one in his left—or in the scale. Or it is intellectual, i.e., the deed of each one, good and bad, is made manifest through the reckoning taking place on that day.

﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾, i.e., afraid and frightened of what is in the Book placed there, because of what follows from it of disgrace in that assembly and of requital with the painful punishment. ﴿And they will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ They call down woe upon themselves because they have fallen into destruction. Then He, glory be to Him, returned to refuting the people of arrogance among (p-864) Quraysh, and mentioned the story of Adam and the arrogance of Iblis toward him, saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, i.e., remember the time of Our saying to them: prostrate in the prostration of greeting and honour, as its verification has already passed. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ in obedience to the command of Allah and compliance with His request for prostration, ﴿except Iblis﴾, for he refused and was arrogant and did not prostrate. The first: the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, that the meaning is: defiance came to him when he was commanded, so he disobeyed; thus the cause of the defiance was the command of his Lord, as you say: "I feed him for hunger." The other view is that of Qutrub: that the meaning, by deletion of the modifier, is: he defied by abandoning His command.

Then He, glory be to Him, expressed wonder at the condition of those who obeyed Iblis in disbelief and sins and opposed the command of Allah, saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies, apart from Me?﴾ It is as if He said: after what came from him of refusal and defiance, do you take him and take his offspring—i.e., his children, and it was said: his followers, figuratively—as allies, so that you obey them in place of My obedience and substitute them for Me, while they are, i.e., Iblis and his offspring, ﴿an enemy to you﴾, i.e., enemies. The meaning: how do you do this deed and substitute for One who created you and blessed you with all the blessings you have, one from whom you have never had any benefit at all, but who is an enemy to you, watching for the occurrence of what harms you at every time? ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who place a thing in other than its place, who substitute the obedience of Satan for the obedience of their Lord. So evil is that exchange which they took in place of Allah, glory be to Him.

﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the pronoun refers to the partners. The meaning: if they had been partners with Me in creating the heavens and the earth and in creating themselves, they would have witnessed the creation of that and shared in it with Me. But they did not witness that, and I did not make them witness it, so they are not partners with Me.
