The estimated meaning is: did you see what befell me, or what happened to me, at that time and place?

That rock was at the meeting place of the two seas, which was the appointment. He mentioned the rock rather than the meeting place of the two seas because it includes an added specification of the place, since the meeting place might be a broad area that includes the place of the rock and other places. He attributed the forgetting to the fish rather than to the morning meal already mentioned, to clarify that this morning meal they sought was that very fish which they had taken as provision for themselves, and as the sign of finding what they sought.

Then he mentioned what functions as the cause of that forgetting, saying: ﴿And none but Satan made me forget it﴾, through the whispering that comes from him. The clause "that I should mention it" (*an adhkurahu*) is a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) from the pronoun in "made me forget it." In the codex (*mushaf*) of 'Abd Allah it reads: "And none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it."

﴿It took its way into the sea in a marvellous manner (*'ajaban*)﴾. The accusative of "marvellous" is because it is the second object, as passed with "tunnel." The adverbial phrase is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (*hal*). It is possible that this is from the words of Yusha', informing Moses that the fish took its way into the sea in a manner marvellous to people, and the wonder lies in a fish that had died and half of it had been eaten coming back to life, then leaping into the sea, while the trace of its passage remains in the water and the flow of the sea does not erase it. It is also possible that this is from the words of God, glory be to Him, to explain another aspect of the fish's matter, so the words between the two statements would be a parenthetical interjection.

﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking"﴾, meaning: Moses said to his young man, "That which you mentioned, the loss of the fish in that place, is what we were looking for, for the man we want is there." ﴿So they went back on their footsteps, retracing their way (*qasasan*)﴾, meaning: they returned by the road by which they had come, following their own tracks, so that they would not miss their way. The accusative of "retracing" is because it is a verbal noun of a deleted verb, or as a circumstantial state, meaning: following or tracing. In the language, *qasas* means following a track.

﴿So they found a servant of Ours﴾. He is al-Khidr according to the view of the majority of commentators, and the authentic hadiths indicate this. Whoever disagreed, and whose view is not considered, said: he is not al-Khidr but another scholar. It has been said that al-Khidr was so named because (p-868) whenever he prayed, the area around him turned green. It is also said his name was Balya son of Malkan. Then God, glory be to Him, described him, saying: ﴿Whom We had given mercy from Our presence﴾. It has been said the mercy is prophethood, and it was also said it is the blessing with which God favoured him. ﴿And taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾, which is what God taught him of the knowledge of the unseen, which He has reserved for Himself. In His words "from Our presence" there is magnification of the importance of that knowledge and exaltation of it. Al-Zajjaj said: In what Moses did, being one of the prophets, of seeking knowledge and travelling for it, is an indication that no one should abandon the pursuit of knowledge, even if he has reached its end, and that he should be humble before one who is more knowledgeable than himself.

Then God, glory be to Him, related to us what passed between Moses and al-Khidr after they met, saying: ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you, on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [that which is] right guidance (*rushdan*)?"﴾ In this question there is gentleness and great courtesy, for he asked his permission to be a follower of his, on condition that he teach him of what God had taught him of knowledge.

Guidance (*rushd*) is standing upon what is good and hitting upon what is correct. Its accusative is because it is the second object of "you teach me," meaning: knowledge with guidance by which I may be guided. It has been read as *rashadan* with two openings, and both are dialects, like *bukhl* and *bakhal* (both meaning stinginess).

In the verse there is evidence that the learner follows the scholar, even if their ranks differ. There is nothing in this that indicates al-Khidr is more excellent than Moses, for the excellent may take from the excellent, and the excellent may take from the less excellent if one of them has specialised in a knowledge that the other does not know.

Moses's knowledge was the knowledge of the legal rulings of the Sharia and of judging by their outward forms, while al-Khidr's knowledge was the knowledge of some of the unseen and the knowledge of inner realities.

﴿He said, "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me"﴾, meaning: al-Khidr said to Moses, "You cannot bear to be patient with what you see of my knowledge, because the outward matters that are your knowledge do not agree with that."

Then he affirmed this, pointing to the reason for not being able, saying: ﴿"And how can you have patience with that which you do not comprehend in knowledge?"﴾, meaning: how can you be patient with a knowledge whose outward aspect is objectionable while you do not know it? A person like you, being a bearer of Sharia, is not permitted to remain silent about an objectionable matter or to approve of it. "Knowledge" (*khubran*) is an accusative of specification (*tamyiz*), meaning: you have not encompassed it in your awareness. *Khubr* is knowledge of a thing, and one who is expert in affairs (*khabir*) is the one who knows their hidden aspects and what needs to be tested of them.

﴿He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient"﴾, meaning: Moses said to al-Khidr, "You will find me patient with you, committed to your obedience." ﴿And I will not disobey any command of yours﴾. The clause "and I will not disobey" is coordinated with "patient," so the restriction with "God willing" covers both patience and not disobeying. It was also said that the restriction by God's will applies only to patience, because it is a future matter whose outcome he does not know, while not disobeying is affirmed for the present. This is answered by saying that patience and not disobeying agree in that each is affirmed for the present, and in that each is something whose future state he does not know.

He said: ﴿"So if you follow me, do not ask me about anything (*shay'*)"﴾ of what you witness of my actions that contradict what the outward Sharia that God sent you with requires, ﴿until I myself make mention of it to you (*uhdith laka minhu dhikran*)﴾, meaning: until I myself am the one who begins to mention it to you, and explain its reason and what it leads to. These sentences introduced by "he said" (*qala*) are independent, because each one is an answer to an assumed question arising from what precedes it.

Al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad* and Ibn 'Asakir, through the chain of Muqatil son of Sulayman, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: Al-Khidr was a son of Adam by his loins, and his lifespan was extended until he would deny the Dajjal.

Al-Bukhari and others reported from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "He was named al-Khidr only because he sat on a white fleece, and behold, it was trembling beneath him, green." 

Ibn 'Asakir also reported it from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Mujahid: He was named al-Khidr only because whenever he prayed, the area around him turned green.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas﴾ he said: "Until I arrive."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿the junction of the two seas﴾. He said: "The sea of Persia and the sea of the Romans, and they are towards the east and the west."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the like of it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "(The junction of the two seas) is Ifriqiyya."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "It is Tangier."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿or I will journey for a long period (huqub)﴾. He said: "Seventy autumns (years)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said: "A long age (dahr)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: (they forgot their fish) ﴿nasiya hutahuma﴾. He said: "It was salted and split open along its belly."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, a tunnel (sarab)﴾. He said: "Its trace remained dry in the sea, as if it were in a rock."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿so they returned, retracing their footsteps (qasasan)﴾. He said: "Their going back by the way they had come."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿We had given him mercy from Us﴾. He said: "We had given him guidance and prophethood."

Know that numerous reports have been transmitted concerning the story of al-Khidr with Musa, mentioned in the Mighty Book. The most complete and perfect of them is what is related from Ibn Abbas, though they differ in some wording. All of them are transmitted through the chain of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him, and some of them are in both Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, some in one of them, and some outside both.

It has also been transmitted through the chain of al-Awfi from him, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded, and through the chain of Harun ibn Antarah from his father from him, in the works of Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir. We shall confine ourselves to the narration which is the most complete of the authenticated narrations in the Two Sahihs, for in it is what suffices without the others. It is as follows:

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "I said to Ibn Abbas: 'Nawf al-Bikali claims that Musa, the companion of al-Khidr, is not Musa of the Children of Israel.' Ibn Abbas said: 'The enemy of Allah lied. Ubayy ibn Ka'b narrated to us that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Musa stood up to address the Children of Israel, and he was asked: 'Which of the people is most knowledgeable?' He said: 'I am.' So Allah rebuked him because he did not attribute knowledge to Him. Allah revealed to him: 'Indeed, I have a servant at the junction of the two seas who is more knowledgeable than you.' Musa said: 'My Lord, how can I reach him?' He said: '(p-869) Take a fish with you in a basket, and wherever you lose the fish, he is there.' So he took a fish and put it in a basket. Then he set out, and his young companion Yusha' ibn Nun set out with him, until they came to the rock, placed their heads down and slept. The fish stirred in the basket, came out of it, and fell into the sea, taking its way into the sea as a tunnel. Allah withheld the flow of water from the fish, so that it became like an arch over it. When he awoke, his companion forgot to tell him about the fish. They journeyed the rest of their day and night until, the next day, Musa said to his young companion: ﴿Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours﴾. He said: Musa did not feel the fatigue until he had passed the place Allah had commanded him. His young companion said to him: ﴿Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish, and none but Satan made me forget to mention it; and it took its way into the sea in a marvellous manner﴾. He said: So the fish had its tunnel, and Musa and his companion had wonder. Musa said: ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾, so they returned, retracing their footsteps. Sufyan said: 'Some people claim that beside that rock is the spring of life, whose water does not touch anything dead without it coming to life.' He said: The fish had been partly eaten, and when water was sprinkled on it, it came to life. He said: So they returned, tracing back their trail until they reached the rock, and there was a man covered with a garment. Musa greeted him, and al-Khidr said: ﴿And how is there greeting in your land?﴾ He said: 'I am Musa.' He said: 'Musa of the Children of Israel?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'I have come to you so that you may teach me of what you have been taught, as guidance.' He said: ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me. O Musa, I have knowledge from Allah which He taught me that you do not know, and you have knowledge from Allah which Allah taught you that I do not know.﴾ Musa said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter.﴾ Al-Khidr said to him: ﴿If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.﴾ So they set out walking along the seashore. A ship passed by them and they spoke to its people that they should carry them. They recognised al-Khidr and carried him without a fare. When they boarded the ship, suddenly al-Khidr had pulled out a plank from the planks of the ship with an axe. Musa said to him: ﴿These people carried us without a fare, and you made a hole in their ship to drown its people; you have indeed done a grave thing﴾? He said: ﴿Did I not tell you that you will not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He said: ﴿Do not hold me to account for what I forgot, and do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.﴾"

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first (act) from Musa was forgetfulness."

He said: "A sparrow came and alighted on the edge of the ship, and pecked once into the sea. Al-Khidr said to him: 'My knowledge and your knowledge do not diminish the knowledge of Allah except as much as this sparrow has diminished from this sea.'"

Then they both came out of the ship, and while they were walking along the shore, al-Khidr saw a boy playing with the boys. Al-Khidr took his head in his hand, wrenched it off with his hand, and killed him. Musa said: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul without it having killed anyone? You have indeed done a dreadful thing.﴾ He said: ﴿Did I not tell you that you will not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He said: "This was more severe than the first." He said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me in your company; you have indeed received an excuse from me.﴾ So they went on until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they refused to host them. They found in it a wall about to collapse, and he set it upright. He said: "He leaned over." Al-Khidr said with his hand: "Like this," and set it upright. Musa said: ﴿A people to whom we came, and they did not feed us nor host us; had you wished, you could have taken a wage for it.﴾ He said: ﴿This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience.﴾

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We wished that Musa had been patient until Allah related to us their story."»

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ibn Abbas used to recite: (And there was behind them a king who seized every ship by force) ﴿wa kana amamahum malikun yakhudhu kulla safinatin ghasban﴾, and he used to recite: (As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, and his two parents were believers) ﴿wa amma al-ghulamu fa-kana kafiran wa kana abawahu mu'minin﴾. The remainder of Sa'id ibn Jubayr's narrations from Ibn Abbas, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, agree with this narration in meaning, although some of their wording differs, so there is no benefit in lengthening the discussion by mentioning them, and likewise the narrations of others than Sa'id from him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 71–82 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: (So they set out) i.e., Musa and al-Khidr, along the shore of the sea, seeking a boat. A boat passed by them, and they spoke to its people asking them to carry them, and they carried them. ﴿Until, when they had embarked in the boat, he made a hole in it.﴾ It was said: he pulled out a plank from its planks. It was said: two planks from the side facing the water. It was said: he tore a section of the boat's hull in order to damage it, so that the drowning would not quickly reach its people. (He said) Musa: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grievous thing.﴾ I.e., you have committed a great matter. It is said: amira al-amr (the matter became grave) when it grew great, and al-amr (the matter) is its noun form.

Abu 'Ubayda said: al-amr is a great calamity, and he recited:
"The rivals have met from me a terrible calamity, a dahya and an imr."
Al-Qutabi said: al-amr is "wonder." Al-Akhfash said: amira amruhu ya'mar when it became severe, and the noun is al-amr.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (li-yaghraqa ahluha) with a yā' (y) with fatḥa, and raf' of ahluha as the subject. The rest read with a tā' (t) with ḍamma and naṣb of ahluha as the object.

He (al-Khidr) said: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He reminded him of what he had said to him earlier: ﴿that you will not be able to have patience with me.﴾

Then Musa said to him (p-870): ﴿Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot.﴾ It is possible that "mā" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), i.e., "do not hold me accountable for my forgetting," or a relative pronoun, i.e., "do not hold me accountable for that which I forgot," and this is the saying of al-Khidr: ﴿So do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.﴾ So forgetting is either in its literal sense, on the assumption that Musa forgot that, or in the sense of leaving, on the assumption that he did not forget what he had been told, but left off acting upon it. ﴿And do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.﴾ Abu Zayd said: arhaqtuhu 'usran means: when you impose that upon him. The meaning is: deal with me with ease, not with hardship.

It was also read ('usuran) with two ḍammas.

﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him.﴾ I.e., al-Khidr. The word ghulām (boy) covers both the young man who has reached maturity and the small child. It was said: the boy was playing with the children, and al-Khidr tore off his head.

(He said) Musa: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul without it having killed anyone?﴾ Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Uways read zākiyatan with an alif after the zāy and a light yā', as an active participle. The rest read it with a doubled yā' without alif. Al-zākiyah means: one innocent of sins. Abu 'Amr said: al-zākiyah is the one who has not sinned, and al-zakiyyah is the one who sinned and then repented. Al-Kisa'i said: al-zākiyah and al-zakiyyah are two dialectal forms.

Al-Farra' said: al-zākiyah and al-zakiyyah are like al-qāsiyah and al-qasiyyah. The meaning of "without a soul" is: without killing a soul that is forbidden, so that this killing would be retribution. ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing.﴾ I.e., an abominable, reprehensible thing not known in the Sharia.

It was said: its meaning is that it is more reprehensible than the first matter, because killing cannot be remedied, unlike removing a plank from the boat, which can be remedied by returning it. It was also said: the nukr is less than the imr, because killing one soul is easier than drowning the people of the boat.

It was said: Musa found it hard to accept that he would kill a soul without a soul, and did not interpret for al-Khidr that he permits killing for other reasons.

(He said) al-Khidr: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He added the word "to you" here, because the cause of blame is greater and its motive stronger. It was said: the word "to you" was added for emphasis, as you say to one whom you rebuke: "To you I speak, and you I mean."

Musa said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this,﴾ i.e., after this time, or after this slain soul, ﴿then do not accompany me.﴾ I.e., do not make me a companion of yours. He forbade him from keeping his company despite his eagerness to learn, because his excuse was clear, and therefore he said: ﴿You have indeed reached from my side an excuse.﴾ He means: you have made yourself excused by opposing you three times. This is the speech of one who is deeply remorseful, whom the situation compelled to confess and to adopt the path of fairness.

Al-A'raj read (tuṣḥabanni) with a fatḥa on the tā' and the bā' and a doubled nūn. The majority read (tuṣāḥibnī). Ya'qub read (tuṣḥibnī) with ḍamma on the tā' and kasra on the ḥā', and Sahl transmitted it from Abu 'Amr.

Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is: do not leave me, I will accompany you.

The majority read (ladunnī) with a ḍamma on the dāl, except that Nafi' and 'Asim lightened the nūn, and the rest doubled it.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read (ludnī) with a ḍamma on the lām and a sukūn on the dāl. Ibn Mujahid said: it is an error.

Abu 'Ali said: this charge of error is perhaps from the side of the transmission; as for the analogy of Arabic, it is correct.

The majority read ('udhran) with a sukūn on the dhāl. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a ḍamma on the dhāl.

Al-Dani relates that Ubayy narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) with a kasra on the rā' and a yā' after it, attributing the excuse to himself.

﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food.﴾ It was said: it is Aylah. It was said: Antakiya. It was said: Barqa. It was said: a village of the villages of Adharbayjan. It was said: a village of the villages of Rome. ﴿But they refused to entertain them.⁠﴾ This clause is in the genitive position as a description of "a town." The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun for added emphasis, or because it is disliked to combine two pronouns in this word due to the difficulty involved, or for added condemnation of the people of the town by making them evident. ﴿They refused to entertain them⁠﴾ i.e., they refused to give them what was their due obligation of hospitality. Whoever takes this verse as evidence for the permissibility of asking and the lawfulness of begging has erred a clear error. Among this is the saying of some of the men of letters who ask people:
"If I am turned away, there is no shame in the turning away; before me Musa and al-Khidr were turned away."
The prohibition of asking for what cannot be averted is established in the Sunnah by many sound hadiths. ﴿And they found in it⁠﴾ i.e., in the town, ﴿a wall about to collapse.⁠﴾ Attributing the will (irada) to the wall is a metaphor.

Al-Zajjaj said: the wall does not have a real will, but the appearance of falling has manifested in it, just as the actions of those who will and intend appear, so it was described with will. From this is the saying of al-Ra'i:
"In a desert whose heads trembled, trembling like axes when they wish to cut."
The meaning of inqiḍāḍ is falling swiftly. It is said: the wall collapsed (inqaḍḍa) when it fell; and the bird swooped (inqaḍḍa) when it dropped from its flight and fell upon something. The meaning of ﴿he set it upright⁠﴾ is that he made it level, because he found it leaning and restored it as it was. It was said: he rebuilt it, and it was said: he propped it up with a pillar. It has already been mentioned in the sound hadith that he wiped it with his hand. Musa said: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it.⁠﴾ I.e., for its erection and repair, as an incitement by Musa to al-Khidr to take the wage.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: if you had wished, you would not have set it up until they gave us food, and that is the wage. Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Yazidi and al-Hasan read (latakhadhta); it is said: Fulan takhadha yattakhidhu takhdhan, like ittakhadha. The rest read (lattakhadhta).

Al-Khidr said: ﴿This is the parting between me and you,⁠﴾ with "parting" (firaq) in the construct with the adverbial noun in an extended sense, i.e., this speech and your objection regarding leaving the wage is what separates us.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "this is the parting between us," i.e., this is the separation of our connection, and "bayn" was repeated for emphasis. When al-Khidr said this to Musa, he began to explain the reason for which he did those actions that Musa objected to, saying: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience.⁠﴾ And ta'wil is the return of a thing to its outcome.

Then he proceeded to explain to him, saying: (As for the boat), meaning the one he tore, ﴿it belonged to poor people⁠﴾ — to the weak who cannot repel one who wants to oppress them — ﴿working on the sea,⁠﴾ and they had no property other than that boat, which they hired out to those who sail the sea, taking the fare. Al-Shafi'i used this verse as evidence that the faqir is in a worse condition than the miskin. ﴿So I wished to damage it⁠﴾ i.e., to make it defective by removing what I removed from it. ﴿And behind them was a king⁠﴾. The commentators said: it means in front of them, and "wara'" can mean "in front of"; the discussion of this has passed in His saying: ﴿And behind him is a severe punishment⁠﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. It was also said: he meant behind them, and their route on the return was past him. They had no knowledge that he ﴿seizes every boat by force⁠﴾, i.e., every boat that is sound, not defective. It has also been read with the addition of "sound" (ṣāliḥa), narrated from Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas.

A group read the sīn of (masakin) with a doubled sīn, and its meaning was disputed. It was said: they are the boat's sailors, because the massak is the one who holds the boat. The more apparent reading is the majority's with the light sīn.

(As for the boy), meaning the one he killed, ﴿his parents were believers⁠﴾ i.e., and he was not so. ﴿So we feared that he would overburden them⁠﴾ i.e., that the boy would overburden his parents. It is said: rahiqahu means "he overtook him," and arhaqahu means "he overwhelmed him."

The commentators said: its meaning is: we feared that his love would move them to follow him in his religion, which is disbelief. "Tughyānan" is the object of "yurhiqahumā," and "wa-kufran" is conjoined to it. It was said: the meaning is: we feared that he would overwhelm the two parents with tyranny against them and ingratitude for their blessing by disobeying them.

It was said: it is possible that "fa-khashīnā" is part of God's speech, and the meaning would be: We disliked it, like one who fears the bad outcome of a matter and so changes it; but this is very weak, for the speech is the speech of al-Khidr.

Some scholars have raised a difficulty about al-Khidr killing this boy for this reason. It was said: he was mature and had deserved that through his disbelief. It was said: he was committing highway robbery and so deserved killing for that. The meaning of "we feared that he would overwhelm them with tyranny and disbelief" would be that al-Khidr feared for the two parents that they would defend him and take his side, and so fall into sin, which might lead to disbelief and apostasy.

The upshot is that there is no difficulty in al-Khidr's killing him if he was mature and an unbeliever or a highway robber. This is regarding what the Islamic Sharia requires. It is possible that al-Khidr had a law from God, the Glorified, that permitted him to do that. As for if the boy was a child who had not reached maturity, it was said: al-Khidr knew, by God's informing him, that if he had reached maturity he would have been a disbeliever whose disbelief would cause his parents to be led astray and to disbelieve. Although the apparent Islamic Sharia rejects this, killing one who has no sin and upon whom the pen of obligation has not yet been applied, for fear that he would later do something after his maturity that would make his killing permissible, is not lawful in the Muhammadan Sharia, but it was lawful in another law, so there is no difficulty.

The majority have held that al-Khidr was a prophet.

﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him⁠﴾. The majority read (yubdilahumā) with a fatḥa on the bā' and a doubled dāl. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with a sukūn on the bā' and a light dāl. The meaning: we wished that God would give them, in place of this son, a son ﴿better than him in purity (zakāh)⁠﴾, i.e., in religion, righteousness and purity from sins, ﴿and nearer in kinship (ruḥm)⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (ruḥuman) with a ḍamma on the ḥā'. The rest read it with a sukūn. The meaning of ruḥm is mercy; it is said: raḥimahu Allāh raḥmatan ruḥmā, and the alif is for the feminine.

(As for the wall), meaning the one he repaired, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the town⁠﴾. The town is the village mentioned earlier, and in this is the permissibility of applying the name "town" to a village linguistically. ﴿Beneath it was a treasure belonging to them both.⁠﴾ It was said: it was great wealth, as the name "kanz" indicates, since it is collected property. Al-Zajjaj said: what is known in the language is that when "kanz" is used alone it means buried wealth; if it is not wealth, it is said "a treasure of knowledge" or "a treasure of understanding." It was also said: it was a golden tablet, and it was also said: written scrolls.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 71–82 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Their father had been righteous.﴾ His righteousness required that his two sons be looked after and that their wealth be preserved. It has been said that he is the one who buried him (the treasure). It has also been said that he was the seventh ancestor of the one who buried it, and it has been said the tenth. ﴿So your Lord intended﴾, that is, your Owner and the Manager of your affairs. He attributed the Lord to the pronoun of Musa (Moses) as an honour to him. ﴿That they reach their maturity﴾, that is, their full strength and the completion of their growth. ﴿And extract their treasure﴾ from that place under which is the wall. Had it collapsed, the treasure would have come out from under it. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾ to them both. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: they being shown mercy by Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾, that is, not by my own effort or opinion. This is an emphasis of what came before it, for by His saying ﴿So your Lord intended﴾ he (Khidr) made known that he had not done it on his own initiative.

﴿That is the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾, that is: that which has been mentioned of those clear matters that I have explained to you and whose aspects I have made plain, is the interpretation (ta'wīl) of what your patience could not contain and you could not refrain from remaining silent about. The meaning of ta'wīl here is the outcome (ma'āl) to which those matters led, namely the clarifying of what was unclear to Musa and the manifesting of its real aspect. The ta' is deleted from (tasti') for lightness (takhfīf).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Indeed you have done a grave thing﴾, that he said: "Munkaran (a dreadful thing)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid something similar. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding (imran): he said: "ʿAjaban (a marvel)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb regarding His words: ﴿Do not hold me to account for what I forgot﴾, that he said: "He did not forget, but it is among the ma'ārīḍ al-kalām (indirect or allusive speech)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: "Khidr was a servant whom eyes could not see, except for whomever Allah wished to show him. So none of the people saw him except Musa. Had the people seen him, they would have prevented him from breaching the ship and from killing the boy." I say: one should examine from where he derived this. If his basis is only his statement, "Had the people seen him etc.", then that does not necessitate what he mentioned. Firstly: it is permissible that he did that without the people of the ship and the people of the boy seeing him, not because he cannot be seen by eyes, but because he did it without their being aware of him. Secondly: it is possible that the people of the ship and the people of the boy knew him and knew that he would not do such things except by a command from Allah, as the prophets do, so they submitted to the command of Allah.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: (a pure soul), he said: "Muslim."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: "(It had) not reached the age of sins."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan something similar. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: (a dreadful thing), he said: "The munkar (dreadful) is more objectionable than the ʿajab (marvel)."

Ahmad narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: "Najdah al-Harurī (of the Kharijites) wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās asking him about killing children. He wrote back to him: 'If you are Khidr, knowing the disbeliever from the believer, then kill them.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah added through another route from him: "But you do not know. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade their killing, so separate from them."

Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The boy whom Khidr killed was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever. Had he lived, he would have burdened his two parents with rebellion and disbelief." (p-٨٧٢)

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿from my Lord as an excuse﴾ with a doubled letter (mathqalah)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: (to receive them as guests) with a doubled letter (mushaddadah)."

Ibn al-Anbari in al-Maṣāḥif and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he recited: ﴿They found in it a wall about to collapse﴾, and he (Khidr) demolished it, then sat down and built it.

I say: the narration of the two Sahihs that we have presented earlier, that he wiped it with his hand, is more preferable.

Al-Firyabi in his Mu'jam, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: (If you had wished, you would have taken for it a wage) with a lightened letter (mukhaffafah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May the mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Musa. Had he been patient, Allah would have related to us more of his story. But he said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me in your company﴾."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite: (And behind them was a king who seizes every sound ship by force)."

Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he recited it in this way. Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Zahiriyyah, who said: "ʿUthman wrote: 'And behind them was a king who seizes every ship by force.'"

Abu ʿUbayd, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to recite: (As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, and his two parents were believers).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿So your Lord feared that it would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Better than him in purity﴾, he said: "In religion." (And nearer in mercy), he said: "In affection." So they were given in exchange a female who bore a prophet.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, he said: "The treasure belonged to those before us and was forbidden to us. And spoils of war were forbidden to those before us and were made lawful for us. So let no man marvel and say: 'What is the matter with the treasure, that it was lawful for those before us and forbidden to us?' For Allah makes lawful from His command what He wills and forbids what He wills. These are the sunan (ordinances) and the fara'id (obligations): He makes lawful for one community and forbids for another."

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), "regarding His words: ﴿And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, he said: 'Gold and silver.'"

Al-Tabarani narrated from Abu al-Darda' regarding His words: ﴿And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, he said: "Treasures were made lawful for them and spoils of war were forbidden to them. And spoils of war were made lawful for us and treasures were forbidden to us."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Dharr, raising it (to the Prophet ﷺ), who said: "The treasure that Allah mentioned in His Book is a plate of pure gold, in which is written: 'I marvel at the one who is certain of destiny yet toils; I marvel at the one who mentions the Fire yet laughs; I marvel at the one who mentions death yet is heedless. There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.'" There are many narrations similar to this, but mentioning them yields no benefit.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, al-Humaydi in his Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Their father had been righteous﴾, he said: "They were protected because of their father's righteousness."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sets right through the righteousness of a righteous man his child, his child's child, and the people of his dwelling and the dwellings around him. They remain under Allah's protection for as long as he is among them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Indeed Allah sets right through the righteousness of a man his child and his child's child, and protects him in his dwelling and the dwellings around him, so they remain under Allah's veil and well-being."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of al-Hasan ibn ʿImarah from his father, who said: It was said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "We have not heard of the servant (fatā) of Musa being mentioned, though he was with him?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is said, among what is related of the story of the servant, that he drank from the water and was made immortal. Then the scholar (Khidr) took him, sealed him in a ship, and then sent it into the sea. It will keep carrying him until the Day of Resurrection, for it was not permissible for him to drink from it."

Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain is weak: al-Hasan is matrūk (abandoned in narration) and his father is unknown."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 71–82 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: (So they set out) i.e., Musa and al-Khidr, along the shore of the sea, seeking a boat. A boat passed by them, and they spoke to its people asking them to carry them, and they carried them. ﴿Until, when they had embarked in the boat, he made a hole in it.﴾ It was said: he pulled out a plank from its planks. It was said: two planks from the side facing the water. It was said: he tore a section of the boat's hull in order to damage it, so that the drowning would not quickly reach its people. (He said) Musa: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grievous thing.﴾ I.e., you have committed a great matter. It is said: amira al-amr (the matter became grave) when it grew great, and al-amr (the matter) is its noun form.

Abu 'Ubayda said: al-amr is a great calamity, and he recited:
"The rivals have met from me a terrible calamity, a dahya and an imr."
Al-Qutabi said: al-amr is "wonder." Al-Akhfash said: amira amruhu ya'mar when it became severe, and the noun is al-amr.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (li-yaghraqa ahluha) with a yā' (y) with fatḥa, and raf' of ahluha as the subject. The rest read with a tā' (t) with ḍamma and naṣb of ahluha as the object.

He (al-Khidr) said: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He reminded him of what he had said to him earlier: ﴿that you will not be able to have patience with me.﴾

Then Musa said to him (p-870): ﴿Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot.﴾ It is possible that "mā" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), i.e., "do not hold me accountable for my forgetting," or a relative pronoun, i.e., "do not hold me accountable for that which I forgot," and this is the saying of al-Khidr: ﴿So do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.﴾ So forgetting is either in its literal sense, on the assumption that Musa forgot that, or in the sense of leaving, on the assumption that he did not forget what he had been told, but left off acting upon it. ﴿And do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.﴾ Abu Zayd said: arhaqtuhu 'usran means: when you impose that upon him. The meaning is: deal with me with ease, not with hardship.

It was also read ('usuran) with two ḍammas.

﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him.﴾ I.e., al-Khidr. The word ghulām (boy) covers both the young man who has reached maturity and the small child. It was said: the boy was playing with the children, and al-Khidr tore off his head.

(He said) Musa: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul without it having killed anyone?﴾ Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Uways read zākiyatan with an alif after the zāy and a light yā', as an active participle. The rest read it with a doubled yā' without alif. Al-zākiyah means: one innocent of sins. Abu 'Amr said: al-zākiyah is the one who has not sinned, and al-zakiyyah is the one who sinned and then repented. Al-Kisa'i said: al-zākiyah and al-zakiyyah are two dialectal forms.

Al-Farra' said: al-zākiyah and al-zakiyyah are like al-qāsiyah and al-qasiyyah. The meaning of "without a soul" is: without killing a soul that is forbidden, so that this killing would be retribution. ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing.﴾ I.e., an abominable, reprehensible thing not known in the Sharia.

It was said: its meaning is that it is more reprehensible than the first matter, because killing cannot be remedied, unlike removing a plank from the boat, which can be remedied by returning it. It was also said: the nukr is less than the imr, because killing one soul is easier than drowning the people of the boat.

It was said: Musa found it hard to accept that he would kill a soul without a soul, and did not interpret for al-Khidr that he permits killing for other reasons.

(He said) al-Khidr: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He added the word "to you" here, because the cause of blame is greater and its motive stronger. It was said: the word "to you" was added for emphasis, as you say to one whom you rebuke: "To you I speak, and you I mean."

Musa said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this,﴾ i.e., after this time, or after this slain soul, ﴿then do not accompany me.﴾ I.e., do not make me a companion of yours. He forbade him from keeping his company despite his eagerness to learn, because his excuse was clear, and therefore he said: ﴿You have indeed reached from my side an excuse.﴾ He means: you have made yourself excused by opposing you three times. This is the speech of one who is deeply remorseful, whom the situation compelled to confess and to adopt the path of fairness.

Al-A'raj read (tuṣḥabanni) with a fatḥa on the tā' and the bā' and a doubled nūn. The majority read (tuṣāḥibnī). Ya'qub read (tuṣḥibnī) with ḍamma on the tā' and kasra on the ḥā', and Sahl transmitted it from Abu 'Amr.

Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is: do not leave me, I will accompany you.

The majority read (ladunnī) with a ḍamma on the dāl, except that Nafi' and 'Asim lightened the nūn, and the rest doubled it.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read (ludnī) with a ḍamma on the lām and a sukūn on the dāl. Ibn Mujahid said: it is an error.

Abu 'Ali said: this charge of error is perhaps from the side of the transmission; as for the analogy of Arabic, it is correct.

The majority read ('udhran) with a sukūn on the dhāl. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a ḍamma on the dhāl.

Al-Dani relates that Ubayy narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) with a kasra on the rā' and a yā' after it, attributing the excuse to himself.

﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food.﴾ It was said: it is Aylah. It was said: Antakiya. It was said: Barqa. It was said: a village of the villages of Adharbayjan. It was said: a village of the villages of Rome. ﴿But they refused to entertain them.⁠﴾ This clause is in the genitive position as a description of "a town." The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun for added emphasis, or because it is disliked to combine two pronouns in this word due to the difficulty involved, or for added condemnation of the people of the town by making them evident. ﴿They refused to entertain them⁠﴾ i.e., they refused to give them what was their due obligation of hospitality. Whoever takes this verse as evidence for the permissibility of asking and the lawfulness of begging has erred a clear error. Among this is the saying of some of the men of letters who ask people:
"If I am turned away, there is no shame in the turning away; before me Musa and al-Khidr were turned away."
The prohibition of asking for what cannot be averted is established in the Sunnah by many sound hadiths. ﴿And they found in it⁠﴾ i.e., in the town, ﴿a wall about to collapse.⁠﴾ Attributing the will (irada) to the wall is a metaphor.

Al-Zajjaj said: the wall does not have a real will, but the appearance of falling has manifested in it, just as the actions of those who will and intend appear, so it was described with will. From this is the saying of al-Ra'i:
"In a desert whose heads trembled, trembling like axes when they wish to cut."
The meaning of inqiḍāḍ is falling swiftly. It is said: the wall collapsed (inqaḍḍa) when it fell; and the bird swooped (inqaḍḍa) when it dropped from its flight and fell upon something. The meaning of ﴿he set it upright⁠﴾ is that he made it level, because he found it leaning and restored it as it was. It was said: he rebuilt it, and it was said: he propped it up with a pillar. It has already been mentioned in the sound hadith that he wiped it with his hand. Musa said: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it.⁠﴾ I.e., for its erection and repair, as an incitement by Musa to al-Khidr to take the wage.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: if you had wished, you would not have set it up until they gave us food, and that is the wage. Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Yazidi and al-Hasan read (latakhadhta); it is said: Fulan takhadha yattakhidhu takhdhan, like ittakhadha. The rest read (lattakhadhta).

Al-Khidr said: ﴿This is the parting between me and you,⁠﴾ with "parting" (firaq) in the construct with the adverbial noun in an extended sense, i.e., this speech and your objection regarding leaving the wage is what separates us.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "this is the parting between us," i.e., this is the separation of our connection, and "bayn" was repeated for emphasis. When al-Khidr said this to Musa, he began to explain the reason for which he did those actions that Musa objected to, saying: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience.⁠﴾ And ta'wil is the return of a thing to its outcome.

Then he proceeded to explain to him, saying: (As for the boat), meaning the one he tore, ﴿it belonged to poor people⁠﴾ — to the weak who cannot repel one who wants to oppress them — ﴿working on the sea,⁠﴾ and they had no property other than that boat, which they hired out to those who sail the sea, taking the fare. Al-Shafi'i used this verse as evidence that the faqir is in a worse condition than the miskin. ﴿So I wished to damage it⁠﴾ i.e., to make it defective by removing what I removed from it. ﴿And behind them was a king⁠﴾. The commentators said: it means in front of them, and "wara'" can mean "in front of"; the discussion of this has passed in His saying: ﴿And behind him is a severe punishment⁠﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. It was also said: he meant behind them, and their route on the return was past him. They had no knowledge that he ﴿seizes every boat by force⁠﴾, i.e., every boat that is sound, not defective. It has also been read with the addition of "sound" (ṣāliḥa), narrated from Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas.

A group read the sīn of (masakin) with a doubled sīn, and its meaning was disputed. It was said: they are the boat's sailors, because the massak is the one who holds the boat. The more apparent reading is the majority's with the light sīn.

(As for the boy), meaning the one he killed, ﴿his parents were believers⁠﴾ i.e., and he was not so. ﴿So we feared that he would overburden them⁠﴾ i.e., that the boy would overburden his parents. It is said: rahiqahu means "he overtook him," and arhaqahu means "he overwhelmed him."

The commentators said: its meaning is: we feared that his love would move them to follow him in his religion, which is disbelief. "Tughyānan" is the object of "yurhiqahumā," and "wa-kufran" is conjoined to it. It was said: the meaning is: we feared that he would overwhelm the two parents with tyranny against them and ingratitude for their blessing by disobeying them.

It was said: it is possible that "fa-khashīnā" is part of God's speech, and the meaning would be: We disliked it, like one who fears the bad outcome of a matter and so changes it; but this is very weak, for the speech is the speech of al-Khidr.

Some scholars have raised a difficulty about al-Khidr killing this boy for this reason. It was said: he was mature and had deserved that through his disbelief. It was said: he was committing highway robbery and so deserved killing for that. The meaning of "we feared that he would overwhelm them with tyranny and disbelief" would be that al-Khidr feared for the two parents that they would defend him and take his side, and so fall into sin, which might lead to disbelief and apostasy.

The upshot is that there is no difficulty in al-Khidr's killing him if he was mature and an unbeliever or a highway robber. This is regarding what the Islamic Sharia requires. It is possible that al-Khidr had a law from God, the Glorified, that permitted him to do that. As for if the boy was a child who had not reached maturity, it was said: al-Khidr knew, by God's informing him, that if he had reached maturity he would have been a disbeliever whose disbelief would cause his parents to be led astray and to disbelieve. Although the apparent Islamic Sharia rejects this, killing one who has no sin and upon whom the pen of obligation has not yet been applied, for fear that he would later do something after his maturity that would make his killing permissible, is not lawful in the Muhammadan Sharia, but it was lawful in another law, so there is no difficulty.

The majority have held that al-Khidr was a prophet.

﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him⁠﴾. The majority read (yubdilahumā) with a fatḥa on the bā' and a doubled dāl. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with a sukūn on the bā' and a light dāl. The meaning: we wished that God would give them, in place of this son, a son ﴿better than him in purity (zakāh)⁠﴾, i.e., in religion, righteousness and purity from sins, ﴿and nearer in kinship (ruḥm)⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (ruḥuman) with a ḍamma on the ḥā'. The rest read it with a sukūn. The meaning of ruḥm is mercy; it is said: raḥimahu Allāh raḥmatan ruḥmā, and the alif is for the feminine.

(As for the wall), meaning the one he repaired, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the town⁠﴾. The town is the village mentioned earlier, and in this is the permissibility of applying the name "town" to a village linguistically. ﴿Beneath it was a treasure belonging to them both.⁠﴾ It was said: it was great wealth, as the name "kanz" indicates, since it is collected property. Al-Zajjaj said: what is known in the language is that when "kanz" is used alone it means buried wealth; if it is not wealth, it is said "a treasure of knowledge" or "a treasure of understanding." It was also said: it was a golden tablet, and it was also said: written scrolls.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 71–82 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Their father had been righteous.﴾ His righteousness required that his two sons be looked after and that their wealth be preserved. It has been said that he is the one who buried him (the treasure). It has also been said that he was the seventh ancestor of the one who buried it, and it has been said the tenth. ﴿So your Lord intended﴾, that is, your Owner and the Manager of your affairs. He attributed the Lord to the pronoun of Musa (Moses) as an honour to him. ﴿That they reach their maturity﴾, that is, their full strength and the completion of their growth. ﴿And extract their treasure﴾ from that place under which is the wall. Had it collapsed, the treasure would have come out from under it. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾ to them both. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: they being shown mercy by Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾, that is, not by my own effort or opinion. This is an emphasis of what came before it, for by His saying ﴿So your Lord intended﴾ he (Khidr) made known that he had not done it on his own initiative.

﴿That is the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾, that is: that which has been mentioned of those clear matters that I have explained to you and whose aspects I have made plain, is the interpretation (ta'wīl) of what your patience could not contain and you could not refrain from remaining silent about. The meaning of ta'wīl here is the outcome (ma'āl) to which those matters led, namely the clarifying of what was unclear to Musa and the manifesting of its real aspect. The ta' is deleted from (tasti') for lightness (takhfīf).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Indeed you have done a grave thing﴾, that he said: "Munkaran (a dreadful thing)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid something similar. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding (imran): he said: "ʿAjaban (a marvel)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb regarding His words: ﴿Do not hold me to account for what I forgot﴾, that he said: "He did not forget, but it is among the ma'ārīḍ al-kalām (indirect or allusive speech)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: "Khidr was a servant whom eyes could not see, except for whomever Allah wished to show him. So none of the people saw him except Musa. Had the people seen him, they would have prevented him from breaching the ship and from killing the boy." I say: one should examine from where he derived this. If his basis is only his statement, "Had the people seen him etc.", then that does not necessitate what he mentioned. Firstly: it is permissible that he did that without the people of the ship and the people of the boy seeing him, not because he cannot be seen by eyes, but because he did it without their being aware of him. Secondly: it is possible that the people of the ship and the people of the boy knew him and knew that he would not do such things except by a command from Allah, as the prophets do, so they submitted to the command of Allah.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: (a pure soul), he said: "Muslim."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: "(It had) not reached the age of sins."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan something similar. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: (a dreadful thing), he said: "The munkar (dreadful) is more objectionable than the ʿajab (marvel)."

Ahmad narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, who said: "Najdah al-Harurī (of the Kharijites) wrote to Ibn ʿAbbās asking him about killing children. He wrote back to him: 'If you are Khidr, knowing the disbeliever from the believer, then kill them.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah added through another route from him: "But you do not know. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade their killing, so separate from them."

Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The boy whom Khidr killed was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever. Had he lived, he would have burdened his two parents with rebellion and disbelief." (p-٨٧٢)

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿from my Lord as an excuse﴾ with a doubled letter (mathqalah)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: (to receive them as guests) with a doubled letter (mushaddadah)."

Ibn al-Anbari in al-Maṣāḥif and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he recited: ﴿They found in it a wall about to collapse﴾, and he (Khidr) demolished it, then sat down and built it.

I say: the narration of the two Sahihs that we have presented earlier, that he wiped it with his hand, is more preferable.

Al-Firyabi in his Mu'jam, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubayy that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: (If you had wished, you would have taken for it a wage) with a lightened letter (mukhaffafah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May the mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Musa. Had he been patient, Allah would have related to us more of his story. But he said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me in your company﴾."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite: (And behind them was a king who seizes every sound ship by force)."

Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he recited it in this way. Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Zahiriyyah, who said: "ʿUthman wrote: 'And behind them was a king who seizes every ship by force.'"

Abu ʿUbayd, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to recite: (As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, and his two parents were believers).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It is in the codex of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿So your Lord feared that it would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Better than him in purity﴾, he said: "In religion." (And nearer in mercy), he said: "In affection." So they were given in exchange a female who bore a prophet.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, he said: "The treasure belonged to those before us and was forbidden to us. And spoils of war were forbidden to those before us and were made lawful for us. So let no man marvel and say: 'What is the matter with the treasure, that it was lawful for those before us and forbidden to us?' For Allah makes lawful from His command what He wills and forbids what He wills. These are the sunan (ordinances) and the fara'id (obligations): He makes lawful for one community and forbids for another."

Al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), "regarding His words: ﴿And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, he said: 'Gold and silver.'"

Al-Tabarani narrated from Abu al-Darda' regarding His words: ﴿And beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, he said: "Treasures were made lawful for them and spoils of war were forbidden to them. And spoils of war were made lawful for us and treasures were forbidden to us."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Dharr, raising it (to the Prophet ﷺ), who said: "The treasure that Allah mentioned in His Book is a plate of pure gold, in which is written: 'I marvel at the one who is certain of destiny yet toils; I marvel at the one who mentions the Fire yet laughs; I marvel at the one who mentions death yet is heedless. There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.'" There are many narrations similar to this, but mentioning them yields no benefit.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, al-Humaydi in his Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Their father had been righteous﴾, he said: "They were protected because of their father's righteousness."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sets right through the righteousness of a righteous man his child, his child's child, and the people of his dwelling and the dwellings around him. They remain under Allah's protection for as long as he is among them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Indeed Allah sets right through the righteousness of a man his child and his child's child, and protects him in his dwelling and the dwellings around him, so they remain under Allah's veil and well-being."

Ibn Jarir narrated through the route of al-Hasan ibn ʿImarah from his father, who said: It was said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "We have not heard of the servant (fatā) of Musa being mentioned, though he was with him?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is said, among what is related of the story of the servant, that he drank from the water and was made immortal. Then the scholar (Khidr) took him, sealed him in a ship, and then sent it into the sea. It will keep carrying him until the Day of Resurrection, for it was not permissible for him to drink from it."

Ibn Kathir said: "Its chain is weak: al-Hasan is matrūk (abandoned in narration) and his father is unknown."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 71–82 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: (So they set out) i.e., Musa and al-Khidr, along the shore of the sea, seeking a boat. A boat passed by them, and they spoke to its people asking them to carry them, and they carried them. ﴿Until, when they had embarked in the boat, he made a hole in it.﴾ It was said: he pulled out a plank from its planks. It was said: two planks from the side facing the water. It was said: he tore a section of the boat's hull in order to damage it, so that the drowning would not quickly reach its people. (He said) Musa: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grievous thing.﴾ I.e., you have committed a great matter. It is said: amira al-amr (the matter became grave) when it grew great, and al-amr (the matter) is its noun form.

Abu 'Ubayda said: al-amr is a great calamity, and he recited:
"The rivals have met from me a terrible calamity, a dahya and an imr."
Al-Qutabi said: al-amr is "wonder." Al-Akhfash said: amira amruhu ya'mar when it became severe, and the noun is al-amr.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (li-yaghraqa ahluha) with a yā' (y) with fatḥa, and raf' of ahluha as the subject. The rest read with a tā' (t) with ḍamma and naṣb of ahluha as the object.

He (al-Khidr) said: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He reminded him of what he had said to him earlier: ﴿that you will not be able to have patience with me.﴾

Then Musa said to him (p-870): ﴿Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot.﴾ It is possible that "mā" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), i.e., "do not hold me accountable for my forgetting," or a relative pronoun, i.e., "do not hold me accountable for that which I forgot," and this is the saying of al-Khidr: ﴿So do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.﴾ So forgetting is either in its literal sense, on the assumption that Musa forgot that, or in the sense of leaving, on the assumption that he did not forget what he had been told, but left off acting upon it. ﴿And do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.﴾ Abu Zayd said: arhaqtuhu 'usran means: when you impose that upon him. The meaning is: deal with me with ease, not with hardship.

It was also read ('usuran) with two ḍammas.

﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him.﴾ I.e., al-Khidr. The word ghulām (boy) covers both the young man who has reached maturity and the small child. It was said: the boy was playing with the children, and al-Khidr tore off his head.

(He said) Musa: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul without it having killed anyone?﴾ Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Uways read zākiyatan with an alif after the zāy and a light yā', as an active participle. The rest read it with a doubled yā' without alif. Al-zākiyah means: one innocent of sins. Abu 'Amr said: al-zākiyah is the one who has not sinned, and al-zakiyyah is the one who sinned and then repented. Al-Kisa'i said: al-zākiyah and al-zakiyyah are two dialectal forms.

Al-Farra' said: al-zākiyah and al-zakiyyah are like al-qāsiyah and al-qasiyyah. The meaning of "without a soul" is: without killing a soul that is forbidden, so that this killing would be retribution. ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing.﴾ I.e., an abominable, reprehensible thing not known in the Sharia.

It was said: its meaning is that it is more reprehensible than the first matter, because killing cannot be remedied, unlike removing a plank from the boat, which can be remedied by returning it. It was also said: the nukr is less than the imr, because killing one soul is easier than drowning the people of the boat.

It was said: Musa found it hard to accept that he would kill a soul without a soul, and did not interpret for al-Khidr that he permits killing for other reasons.

(He said) al-Khidr: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ He added the word "to you" here, because the cause of blame is greater and its motive stronger. It was said: the word "to you" was added for emphasis, as you say to one whom you rebuke: "To you I speak, and you I mean."

Musa said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this,﴾ i.e., after this time, or after this slain soul, ﴿then do not accompany me.﴾ I.e., do not make me a companion of yours. He forbade him from keeping his company despite his eagerness to learn, because his excuse was clear, and therefore he said: ﴿You have indeed reached from my side an excuse.﴾ He means: you have made yourself excused by opposing you three times. This is the speech of one who is deeply remorseful, whom the situation compelled to confess and to adopt the path of fairness.

Al-A'raj read (tuṣḥabanni) with a fatḥa on the tā' and the bā' and a doubled nūn. The majority read (tuṣāḥibnī). Ya'qub read (tuṣḥibnī) with ḍamma on the tā' and kasra on the ḥā', and Sahl transmitted it from Abu 'Amr.

Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is: do not leave me, I will accompany you.

The majority read (ladunnī) with a ḍamma on the dāl, except that Nafi' and 'Asim lightened the nūn, and the rest doubled it.

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read (ludnī) with a ḍamma on the lām and a sukūn on the dāl. Ibn Mujahid said: it is an error.

Abu 'Ali said: this charge of error is perhaps from the side of the transmission; as for the analogy of Arabic, it is correct.

The majority read ('udhran) with a sukūn on the dhāl. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with a ḍamma on the dhāl.

Al-Dani relates that Ubayy narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) with a kasra on the rā' and a yā' after it, attributing the excuse to himself.

﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food.﴾ It was said: it is Aylah. It was said: Antakiya. It was said: Barqa. It was said: a village of the villages of Adharbayjan. It was said: a village of the villages of Rome. ﴿But they refused to entertain them.⁠﴾ This clause is in the genitive position as a description of "a town." The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun for added emphasis, or because it is disliked to combine two pronouns in this word due to the difficulty involved, or for added condemnation of the people of the town by making them evident. ﴿They refused to entertain them⁠﴾ i.e., they refused to give them what was their due obligation of hospitality. Whoever takes this verse as evidence for the permissibility of asking and the lawfulness of begging has erred a clear error. Among this is the saying of some of the men of letters who ask people:
"If I am turned away, there is no shame in the turning away; before me Musa and al-Khidr were turned away."
The prohibition of asking for what cannot be averted is established in the Sunnah by many sound hadiths. ﴿And they found in it⁠﴾ i.e., in the town, ﴿a wall about to collapse.⁠﴾ Attributing the will (irada) to the wall is a metaphor.

Al-Zajjaj said: the wall does not have a real will, but the appearance of falling has manifested in it, just as the actions of those who will and intend appear, so it was described with will. From this is the saying of al-Ra'i:
"In a desert whose heads trembled, trembling like axes when they wish to cut."
The meaning of inqiḍāḍ is falling swiftly. It is said: the wall collapsed (inqaḍḍa) when it fell; and the bird swooped (inqaḍḍa) when it dropped from its flight and fell upon something. The meaning of ﴿he set it upright⁠﴾ is that he made it level, because he found it leaning and restored it as it was. It was said: he rebuilt it, and it was said: he propped it up with a pillar. It has already been mentioned in the sound hadith that he wiped it with his hand. Musa said: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it.⁠﴾ I.e., for its erection and repair, as an incitement by Musa to al-Khidr to take the wage.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: if you had wished, you would not have set it up until they gave us food, and that is the wage. Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Yazidi and al-Hasan read (latakhadhta); it is said: Fulan takhadha yattakhidhu takhdhan, like ittakhadha. The rest read (lattakhadhta).

Al-Khidr said: ﴿This is the parting between me and you,⁠﴾ with "parting" (firaq) in the construct with the adverbial noun in an extended sense, i.e., this speech and your objection regarding leaving the wage is what separates us.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "this is the parting between us," i.e., this is the separation of our connection, and "bayn" was repeated for emphasis. When al-Khidr said this to Musa, he began to explain the reason for which he did those actions that Musa objected to, saying: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience.⁠﴾ And ta'wil is the return of a thing to its outcome.

Then he proceeded to explain to him, saying: (As for the boat), meaning the one he tore, ﴿it belonged to poor people⁠﴾ — to the weak who cannot repel one who wants to oppress them — ﴿working on the sea,⁠﴾ and they had no property other than that boat, which they hired out to those who sail the sea, taking the fare. Al-Shafi'i used this verse as evidence that the faqir is in a worse condition than the miskin. ﴿So I wished to damage it⁠﴾ i.e., to make it defective by removing what I removed from it. ﴿And behind them was a king⁠﴾. The commentators said: it means in front of them, and "wara'" can mean "in front of"; the discussion of this has passed in His saying: ﴿And behind him is a severe punishment⁠﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. It was also said: he meant behind them, and their route on the return was past him. They had no knowledge that he ﴿seizes every boat by force⁠﴾, i.e., every boat that is sound, not defective. It has also been read with the addition of "sound" (ṣāliḥa), narrated from Ubayy and Ibn 'Abbas.

A group read the sīn of (masakin) with a doubled sīn, and its meaning was disputed. It was said: they are the boat's sailors, because the massak is the one who holds the boat. The more apparent reading is the majority's with the light sīn.

(As for the boy), meaning the one he killed, ﴿his parents were believers⁠﴾ i.e., and he was not so. ﴿So we feared that he would overburden them⁠﴾ i.e., that the boy would overburden his parents. It is said: rahiqahu means "he overtook him," and arhaqahu means "he overwhelmed him."

The commentators said: its meaning is: we feared that his love would move them to follow him in his religion, which is disbelief. "Tughyānan" is the object of "yurhiqahumā," and "wa-kufran" is conjoined to it. It was said: the meaning is: we feared that he would overwhelm the two parents with tyranny against them and ingratitude for their blessing by disobeying them.

It was said: it is possible that "fa-khashīnā" is part of God's speech, and the meaning would be: We disliked it, like one who fears the bad outcome of a matter and so changes it; but this is very weak, for the speech is the speech of al-Khidr.

Some scholars have raised a difficulty about al-Khidr killing this boy for this reason. It was said: he was mature and had deserved that through his disbelief. It was said: he was committing highway robbery and so deserved killing for that. The meaning of "we feared that he would overwhelm them with tyranny and disbelief" would be that al-Khidr feared for the two parents that they would defend him and take his side, and so fall into sin, which might lead to disbelief and apostasy.

The upshot is that there is no difficulty in al-Khidr's killing him if he was mature and an unbeliever or a highway robber. This is regarding what the Islamic Sharia requires. It is possible that al-Khidr had a law from God, the Glorified, that permitted him to do that. As for if the boy was a child who had not reached maturity, it was said: al-Khidr knew, by God's informing him, that if he had reached maturity he would have been a disbeliever whose disbelief would cause his parents to be led astray and to disbelieve. Although the apparent Islamic Sharia rejects this, killing one who has no sin and upon whom the pen of obligation has not yet been applied, for fear that he would later do something after his maturity that would make his killing permissible, is not lawful in the Muhammadan Sharia, but it was lawful in another law, so there is no difficulty.

The majority have held that al-Khidr was a prophet.

﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him⁠﴾. The majority read (yubdilahumā) with a fatḥa on the bā' and a doubled dāl. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with a sukūn on the bā' and a light dāl. The meaning: we wished that God would give them, in place of this son, a son ﴿better than him in purity (zakāh)⁠﴾, i.e., in religion, righteousness and purity from sins, ﴿and nearer in kinship (ruḥm)⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (ruḥuman) with a ḍamma on the ḥā'. The rest read it with a sukūn. The meaning of ruḥm is mercy; it is said: raḥimahu Allāh raḥmatan ruḥmā, and the alif is for the feminine.

(As for the wall), meaning the one he repaired, ﴿it belonged to two orphan boys in the town⁠﴾. The town is the village mentioned earlier, and in this is the permissibility of applying the name "town" to a village linguistically. ﴿Beneath it was a treasure belonging to them both.⁠﴾ It was said: it was great wealth, as the name "kanz" indicates, since it is collected property. Al-Zajjaj said: what is known in the language is that when "kanz" is used alone it means buried wealth; if it is not wealth, it is said "a treasure of knowledge" or "a treasure of understanding." It was also said: it was a golden tablet, and it was also said: written scrolls.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verses 71–82 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Their father had been righteous.﴾ His righteousness required that his two sons be looked after and that their wealth be preserved. It has been said that he is the one who buried him (the treasure). It has also been said that he was the seventh ancestor of the one who buried it, and it has been said the tenth. ﴿So your Lord intended﴾, that is, your Owner and the Manager of your affairs. He attributed the Lord to the pronoun of Musa (Moses) as an honour to him. ﴿That they reach their maturity﴾, that is, their full strength and the completion of their growth. ﴿And extract their treasure﴾ from that place under which is the wall. Had it collapsed, the treasure would have come out from under it. ﴿As a mercy from your Lord﴾ to them both. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: they being shown mercy by Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾, that is, not by my own effort or opinion. This is an emphasis of what came before it, for by His saying ﴿So your Lord intended﴾ he (Khidr) made known that he had not done it on his own initiative.

﴿That is the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾, that is: that which has been mentioned of those clear matters that I have explained to you and whose aspects I have made plain, is the interpretation (ta'wīl) of what your patience could not contain and you could not refrain from remaining silent about. The meaning of ta'wīl here is the outcome (ma'āl) to which those matters led, namely the clarifying of what was unclear to Musa and the manifesting of its real aspect. The ta' is deleted from (tasti') for lightness (takhfīf).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Indeed you have done a grave thing﴾, that he said: "Munkaran (a dreadful thing)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid something similar. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding (imran): he said: "ʿAjaban (a marvel)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb regarding His words: ﴿Do not hold me to account for what I forgot﴾, that he said: "He did not forget, but it is among the ma'ārīḍ al-kalām (indirect or allusive speech)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: "Khidr was a servant whom eyes could not see, except for whomever Allah wished to show him. So none of the people saw him except Musa. Had the people seen him, they would have prevented him from breaching the ship and from killing the boy."
