Al-Akhfash said: tabi'tu and atba'tu have the same meaning, like radiftu and ardaftu. From this is His saying: ﴿so a piercing flame pursued him﴾ [al-Saffat: 10]. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubaydah preferred the reading of the people of Kufa, and said: "Because it is from travelling."

He and al-Asma'i related that it is said: tabi'tuhu and atba'tuhu when one travels and does not catch up with him, and atba'ahu when one catches up with him.

Abu Ubaydah said: similar to this is ﴿so they overtook them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 60].

Al-Nahhas said: this is from the distinctions, and although al-Asma'i related it, it is not accepted except with knowledge or evidence. His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying ﴿so they overtook them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 60] does not mean in the hadith that they caught up with them. The hadith is only: when Musa and his companions came out of the sea, and Pharaoh and his companions entered the sea, the sea closed over them.

The truth in this is that taba', ittaba' and atba' are dialects with one meaning, which is travel.

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun﴾, meaning: the extremity of the earth from the direction of the west, because beyond this extremity is the encompassing ocean, and it is not possible to proceed in it. ﴿He found it setting in a spring of black mud﴾. Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (hami'atin) "hot" (hamiyah), meaning: hot.

The rest read (hami'atin) meaning: abounding in black mud (hama'ah), which is black clay. You say: hama'tu al-bi'r hama'an with the sukun, when you removed its mud, and hami'at al-bi'r hama'atahu with the vowel, when its mud increased. It is also possible that (hamiyah) is from hama'ah, so the hamzah was softened and turned into a ya'. The two readings may be combined, so it is said: it was hot and had mud.

It was said: perhaps when Dhu al-Qarnayn reached the shore of the encompassing ocean, he saw it that way from his viewpoint. It is not far-fetched to say: there is no barrier to Allah enabling him to cross the encompassing ocean until he reaches that spring in which the sun sets, and what prevents this, after Allah related of him that he reached the setting-place of the sun, and that He established him in the earth, and the sea is part of it? Mere improbability does not necessitate interpreting the Qur'an contrary to its apparent meaning.

﴿And he found near it a people﴾. The pronoun in (near it) refers either to the spring or to the sun.

It was said: they were a people whose clothing was the skins of wild beasts, and they were disbelievers. So Allah gave him the choice between punishing them and leaving them alone. He said: ﴿Either you punish, or you adopt among them goodness﴾, meaning: either you punish them by killing from the outset, or you adopt among them a matter of goodness, or a good matter, emphasizing by making the verbal noun an attribute of the matter. The intended meaning is calling them to the truth and teaching them the laws.

(He said) Dhu al-Qarnayn, choosing the call, which is the final part of the alternatives: ﴿As for him who does wrong﴾ to himself by persisting in polytheism and does not accept my call, (then we shall punish him) by killing in this world, ﴿then he will be returned to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter, (and He will punish him) therein (with a punishment unprecedented), meaning: a dreadful, terrible punishment.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah gave him the choice between the two matters.

Al-Nahhas said: Ali ibn Sulayman rejected this statement, because it has not been established that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet, so that he would be addressed with this. How would he say to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿then he will be returned to his Lord﴾, and how would he say (then we shall punish him), addressing Him with the plural "we"? He said: the estimate is: We said: O Muhammad. They said: O Dhu al-Qarnayn.

Al-Nahhas said: what he mentioned does not necessarily follow, since it is permissible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addressed him through a prophet of his time, and it may be that Dhu al-Qarnayn addressed those people, so what he mentioned does not follow.

It is possible that he was addressing the prophet to whom Allah spoke through him, or that he addressed his people whom he reached in that place.

Tha'lab said: the (an) in His saying ﴿either you punish, or you adopt﴾ is in the accusative position, and if it were in the nominative it would be correct, with the meaning of "as for him", like the saying of the poet:

"So travel, for either a need will be fulfilled for you two, or a good resting-place and a friend."

﴿As for him who believes﴾ in Allah and affirms my call, (and does) righteous deeds, of what faith requires, ﴿then for him is a reward, the best﴾. The people of Madinah, Abu Amr, Asim, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read (fa-lahu jaza'un) with the nominative, as a beginning: a reward, the good quality, with Allah; or the good deed, which is Paradise. This was said by al-Farra'.

The attribution of the reward to the best (al-husna), which is Paradise, is like the attribution of "the truth of certainty" and "the abode of the Hereafter". It is also possible that this reward is from Dhu al-Qarnayn, meaning: I will give it to him and bestow favour upon him. The rest of the Kufans read: ﴿fa-lahu jaza'an al-husna﴾ with the accusative for (jaza'an) and tanwin.

Al-Farra' said: its being in the accusative is as a specification (tamyiz).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: rewarded with it as a reward. Ibn Abbas and Masruq read (jaza'a) with the accusative without tanwin.

Abu Hatim said: it is with the tanwin deleted because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters. Al-Nahhas said: this, according to others, is an error, because it is not a place where tanwin is deleted due to the meeting of two unvowelled letters.

It was also read with (jaza'un) in the nominative with tanwin, as a beginning, with (al-husna) as an apposition to it, and the predicate is the prepositional phrase.

﴿And we shall speak to him of Our command, ease﴾, meaning: of what We command, a word of ease, not difficult or hard; or the verbal noun was used for him as an intensification.

﴿Then he followed a cause﴾, meaning: another way, other than the first way, which was the one by which he returned from the west, and travelled in it to the east.

﴿Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun﴾, that is, the place upon which the sun first rises over the inhabited earth, or the place of its rising, since there is no legal or rational barrier to his reaching it, as we have clarified previously. ﴿He found it rising over a people for whom We had made no screen against it﴾, that would shelter them, neither of houses nor of clothing. Rather they are barefoot and naked, and do not take shelter in anything of construction.

(p-٨٧٣)

It was said: because they were in a land where building could not be firmly established upon it.

﴿Thus [it was]; and We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾ That is: thus was the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn; he followed these means until he reached [his goal], and We knew, when We empowered him, what capacity he possessed for that kingship and for being independent in it. It was also said that the meaning is: We did not provide for them a covering like that covering which We provided for you from dwellings and garments. It was also said that the meaning is: thus he reached the rising place of the sun, just as he had reached its setting place. It was also said that the meaning is: thus does [the sun] rise upon a people like that tribe over whom it sets; so he judged among these people as he had judged among those, [punishing the wrongdoers and doing good to the believers]. The interpretation of "encompassing what was with him" in these aspects is according to what suits that, as we said in the first aspect.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: The Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, you only mention Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the prophets. You have heard their mention from us. So inform us about a prophet whom God did not mention in the Torah except in one place." He said: "And who is he?" They said: "Dhu al-Qarnayn." He said: "Nothing has reached me about him." So they left, rejoicing, having become proud in themselves, and they had not reached the door of the house when Gabriel descended with these verses: ﴿And they ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not. And I do not know whether Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet or not. And I do not know whether the prescribed punishments are expiations for their people or not."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: "Ali was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn: was he a prophet? He said: I heard your Prophet (ﷺ) say: He was a servant who advised God, so God advised him."

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, Ibn Abi Asim in al-Sunnah, and Ibn Mardawayh related through Abu al-Tufayl that Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali ibn Abi Talib about Dhu al-Qarnayn: was he a prophet or a king? He said: He was neither a prophet nor a king, but he was a righteous servant who loved God, so God loved him; he advised God, so God advised him. God sent him to his people, and they struck him on his horn, and he died. Then God revived him to fight them. Then God sent him to his people, and they struck him on his other horn, and he died. God revived him to fight them, and for this he was called Dhu al-Qarnayn. And among you there is one like him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Amr, who said: Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Akhras ibn Hakim, from his father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn and said: "He was a king who swept the earth with the means."

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah related from Khalid ibn Ma'dan al-Kula'i, as a marfu' report, the same. Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in Kitab al-Adad, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Umar ibn (p-875) al-Khattab that he heard a man calling out at Mina, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn!" So Umar said: "You have named [your children] with the names of the prophets; then what about the names of the angels?" There is in this chapter other than what we have mentioned, and what we have cited suffices.

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Uqbah ibn Amir al-Juhani a hadith containing that "a group of Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he informed them of what they had come for initially. Among what he told them was that he was a young man from the Romans, that he built Alexandria, that an angel ascended with him into the sky, and took him to the barrier." Its chain is weak, its text contains reprehensible content, and most of what is in it is from the reports of the Children of Israel.

Ibn Kathir mentioned the meaning of this in his tafsir and attributed it to Ibn Jarir and al-Umawi in his Maghazi. Then he said after that: "What is strange is that Abu Zur'ah al-Dimashqi, despite his high standing, related it in full in his book Dala'il al-Nubuwwah." End of quote.

al-Suyuti related it in full in al-Durr al-Manthur, and also related a long report from Wahb ibn Munabbih, attributing it to Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Shirazi in al-Alqab, and Abu al-Shaykh, and in it are very objectionable things. Likewise he related a long report from Muhammad al-Baqir, related by Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh. Perhaps these reports and similar ones are transmitted from the People of the Book, and we have been commanded neither to believe them nor to disbelieve them in what they transmit to us.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾, that he said: "Knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "You say that Dhu al-Qarnayn used to tie his horses to the Pleiades?" Ka'b said to him: "If I said that, then God said: ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through Uthman ibn Abi Hasir that Ibn Abbas mentioned to him that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan recited the verse in Surat al-Kahf as ﴿it set in a murky spring﴾ (ta'rubu fi 'aynin hamiyah). Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: we do not read it except as (hami'ah, 'muddy'). So Mu'awiyah asked Abd Allah ibn Amr: how do you read it? Abd Allah said: As you have recited it." Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: the Qur'an was revealed in my house. So he sent for Ka'b and said to him: Where do you find the sun setting in the Torah?" Ka'b said to him: "Ask the people of Arabic, for they know it better. As for me, I find in the Torah that it sets in water and mud," and he pointed with his hand to the west.

Ibn Abi Hasir said: "If I were with you two, I would support you with a statement that would increase you in insight regarding hami'ah."

Ibn Abbas said: "And what is it?" I said: "Among what we transmit is the saying of Tubba' about Dhu al-Qarnayn, regarding his zeal for knowledge and his following of it:"

> Dhu al-Qarnayn was a Muslim Umar, a king before whom kings are humbled and gathered,
> So he came to the east and the west seeking the means of kingship from a wise, guiding sage,
> And he saw the sun's setting at its going down in a spring of muddy clay and black slime.

Ibn Abbas said: "What is al-khalab?" I said: "Clay, in their speech." He said: "What is al-tha't?" I said: "Silt." He said: "What is al-kharmad?" I said: "Black." So Ibn Abbas called a boy and said: "Write down what this man is saying."

al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿in a murky spring﴾ (fi 'aynin hami'ah).

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, as a marfu' report, the same.

The Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 18, verses 83–95 (part 1 of 2):

.
When Allah, glory be to Him, had answered two of the questions of the Jews, and the discourse had reached the point where it reached, He began the third question and its answer. The ones asking here are the Jews.

Scholars differed greatly concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn. It was said: he is Alexander the son of Philip (al-Iskandar ibn Filqus), who ruled the whole world, the Greek, the founder of Alexandria.

Ibn Ishaq said: he is a man from the people of Egypt, named Marzaban ibn Marzabah, the Greek, from the descendants of Yunan ibn Yafith ibn Nuh.

It was also said: he is a king named Hurmus. It was said: a king named Hirdis. It was said: a young man from the Romans. It was said: he was a prophet. It was said: he was a righteous servant. It was said: his name was Abd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. It was said: Mus'ab ibn Abd Allah, from the descendants of Kahlan ibn Saba'.

Al-Qurtubi related, from al-Suhayli, that he said: "The apparent position from the science of reports is that there were two: one of them lived in the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and the other lived close to the time of Isa (peace be upon him)."

It was also said: he is Abu Karib al-Himyari. It was said: he is one of the angels. Al-Razi preferred the first view. He said: "Because the one whose kingdom reached such breadth and power as the revelation describes is none other than Alexander the Greek, as the books of history testify." He said: "So it is necessary to affirm with certainty that Dhu al-Qarnayn is Alexander." He said: "But there is a difficulty in this: he was a student of Aristotle the sage, and was upon his doctrine. So Allah's exalting him requires the judgment that Aristotle's doctrine is true and correct, and that is not something that can be done."

Al-Nisaburi said: "I say: not everything the philosophers held is false. Perhaps he took from them what was pure and left what was turbid. And Allah knows best."

Ibn Kathir preferred what al-Suhayli mentioned, that there were two, as we previously mentioned, and he explained that the first circumambulated the House with Ibrahim when he first built it, believed in him, followed him, and that his vizier was al-Khadir.

As for the second, he is Alexander of Macedon, the Greek, whose vizier was the famous philosopher Aristotle, and he lived about three hundred years before the Messiah.

The first one mentioned in the Qur'an was in the time of the Friend (Ibrahim). This is the meaning of what Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir, relating it on the authority of al-Azraqi and others. Then he said: "We have mentioned a good portion of his reports in the book al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, with what is sufficient in it."

Abu al-Su'ud related in his tafsir, from Ibn Kathir, that he said: "We have only made this clear, meaning that there were two, because many people believe that they are one, and that the one mentioned in the Mighty Qur'an is this later one. Thereby a great error and much corruption occur. How could it be otherwise? The first was a righteous, believing servant, and a just king, and his vizier was al-Khadir, and it has been said that he was a prophet. As for the second, he was a disbeliever, and his vizier was Aristotle the philosopher. The time between them was more than two thousand years. So where is this from that?" End of quote.

I say: perhaps he mentioned this in the book that he mentioned earlier, which he named al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, and he did not find it. What is derived from the books of history is that there were two, as al-Suhayli, al-Azraqi, Ibn Kathir and others mentioned, not as al-Razi mentioned, claiming that it is what the books of history testify to. The dispute has occurred over whether he was a prophet or not, and what is derived from that regarding the matter sought will come at the end of this discussion, God willing.

As for the reason he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn, al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari said: he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn because he reached the horn of the sun from its rising and the horn of the sun from its setting. It was said: he had two braids of hair, and braids are called qurun (horns). From this is the statement of the poet:

"So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of its horns (braids), drinking like one intoxicated with the cool water of al-Hashraj."

Al-Hashraj is a water from the waters of the Arabs. It was said: at the beginning of his kingdom he saw as if he were grasping the two horns of the sun, so he was named by that. It was said: he had two horns beneath his turban. It was said: he called to Allah, and his people struck him on one of his horns, then he called to Allah and they struck him on his other horn. It is said he was named so because he was of noble lineage on both sides, from a house of nobility from his father's and mother's side. It was said: because two generations of people passed away in his time while he was alive. It was said: because when he fought, he fought with both his hands and his stirrups together. It was said: because he was given knowledge of the outward and the inward. It was said: because he entered the light and the darkness. It was said: because he ruled Persia and Rome. It was said: because he ruled Rome and the Turks. It was said: because his crown had two horns.

His saying: ﴿Say: I shall recite to you from him a remembrance﴾, meaning: I shall recite to you, O askers, a report about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and that is by way of recited revelation.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to explain what He commanded His Messenger to say to them, that He would recite to them from him a remembrance. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, meaning: We empowered him by what We had prepared for him of the means. We gave him capability and power to act within it, made easy for him the travel in its places, and made its paths subservient to him, until he could take hold of it wherever he willed and however he willed. (So he followed a cause) of those causes.

The exegetes said: the meaning is a way that would lead him to the west of the sun.

Al-Zajjaj said: (so he followed a cause) of the causes he had been given. It was said: he followed from everything a knowledge by which he would be enabled to attain what he wanted. It was said: a means of reaching wherever he willed. ﴿Then he followed a cause﴾, meaning: another way, other than the first way, which was the one by which he returned from the west, and travelled in it to the east.

﴿Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun﴾, that is, the place upon which the sun first rises over the inhabited earth, or the place of its rising, since there is no legal or rational barrier to his reaching it, as we have clarified previously. ﴿He found it rising over a people for whom We had made no screen against it﴾, that would shelter them, neither of houses nor of clothing. Rather they are barefoot and naked, and do not take shelter in anything of construction.

(p-٨٧٣)

It was said: because they were in a land where building could not be firmly established upon it.

﴿Thus [it was]; and We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾ That is: thus was the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn; he followed these means until he reached [his goal], and We knew, when We empowered him, what capacity he possessed for that kingship and for being independent in it. It was also said that the meaning is: We did not provide for them a covering like that covering which We provided for you from dwellings and garments. It was also said that the meaning is: thus he reached the rising place of the sun, just as he had reached its setting place. It was also said that the meaning is: thus does [the sun] rise upon a people like that tribe over whom it sets; so he judged among these people as he had judged among those, [punishing the wrongdoers and doing good to the believers]. The interpretation of "encompassing what was with him" in these aspects is according to what suits that, as we said in the first aspect.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: The Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, you only mention Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the prophets. You have heard their mention from us. So inform us about a prophet whom God did not mention in the Torah except in one place." He said: "And who is he?" They said: "Dhu al-Qarnayn." He said: "Nothing has reached me about him." So they left, rejoicing, having become proud in themselves, and they had not reached the door of the house when Gabriel descended with these verses: ﴿And they ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not. And I do not know whether Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet or not. And I do not know whether the prescribed punishments are expiations for their people or not."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: "Ali was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn: was he a prophet? He said: I heard your Prophet (ﷺ) say: He was a servant who advised God, so God advised him."

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, Ibn Abi Asim in al-Sunnah, and Ibn Mardawayh related through Abu al-Tufayl that Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali ibn Abi Talib about Dhu al-Qarnayn: was he a prophet or a king? He said: He was neither a prophet nor a king, but he was a righteous servant who loved God, so God loved him; he advised God, so God advised him. God sent him to his people, and they struck him on his horn, and he died. Then God revived him to fight them. Then God sent him to his people, and they struck him on his other horn, and he died. God revived him to fight them, and for this he was called Dhu al-Qarnayn. And among you there is one like him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Amr, who said: Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Akhras ibn Hakim, from his father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn and said: "He was a king who swept the earth with the means."

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah related from Khalid ibn Ma'dan al-Kula'i, as a marfu' report, the same. Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in Kitab al-Adad, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Umar ibn (p-875) al-Khattab that he heard a man calling out at Mina, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn!" So Umar said: "You have named [your children] with the names of the prophets; then what about the names of the angels?" There is in this chapter other than what we have mentioned, and what we have cited suffices.

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Uqbah ibn Amir al-Juhani a hadith containing that "a group of Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he informed them of what they had come for initially. Among what he told them was that he was a young man from the Romans, that he built Alexandria, that an angel ascended with him into the sky, and took him to the barrier." Its chain is weak, its text contains reprehensible content, and most of what is in it is from the reports of the Children of Israel.

Ibn Kathir mentioned the meaning of this in his tafsir and attributed it to Ibn Jarir and al-Umawi in his Maghazi. Then he said after that: "What is strange is that Abu Zur'ah al-Dimashqi, despite his high standing, related it in full in his book Dala'il al-Nubuwwah." End of quote.

al-Suyuti related it in full in al-Durr al-Manthur, and also related a long report from Wahb ibn Munabbih, attributing it to Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Shirazi in al-Alqab, and Abu al-Shaykh, and in it are very objectionable things. Likewise he related a long report from Muhammad al-Baqir, related by Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh. Perhaps these reports and similar ones are transmitted from the People of the Book, and we have been commanded neither to believe them nor to disbelieve them in what they transmit to us.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾, that he said: "Knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "You say that Dhu al-Qarnayn used to tie his horses to the Pleiades?" Ka'b said to him: "If I said that, then God said: ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through Uthman ibn Abi Hasir that Ibn Abbas mentioned to him that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan recited the verse in Surat al-Kahf as ﴿it set in a murky spring﴾ (ta'rubu fi 'aynin hamiyah). Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: we do not read it except as (hami'ah, 'muddy'). So Mu'awiyah asked Abd Allah ibn Amr: how do you read it? Abd Allah said: As you have recited it." Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: the Qur'an was revealed in my house. So he sent for Ka'b and said to him: Where do you find the sun setting in the Torah?" Ka'b said to him: "Ask the people of Arabic, for they know it better. As for me, I find in the Torah that it sets in water and mud," and he pointed with his hand to the west.

Ibn Abi Hasir said: "If I were with you two, I would support you with a statement that would increase you in insight regarding hami'ah."

Ibn Abbas said: "And what is it?" I said: "Among what we transmit is the saying of Tubba' about Dhu al-Qarnayn, regarding his zeal for knowledge and his following of it:"

> Dhu al-Qarnayn was a Muslim Umar, a king before whom kings are humbled and gathered,
> So he came to the east and the west seeking the means of kingship from a wise, guiding sage,
> And he saw the sun's setting at its going down in a spring of muddy clay and black slime.

Ibn Abbas said: "What is al-khalab?" I said: "Clay, in their speech." He said: "What is al-tha't?" I said: "Silt." He said: "What is al-kharmad?" I said: "Black." So Ibn Abbas called a boy and said: "Write down what this man is saying."

al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿in a murky spring﴾ (fi 'aynin hami'ah).

al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, as a marfu' report, the same.

The Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 18, verses 83–95 (part 1 of 2):

.
When Allah, glory be to Him, had answered two of the questions of the Jews, and the discourse had reached the point where it reached, He began the third question and its answer. The ones asking here are the Jews.

Scholars differed greatly concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn. It was said: he is Alexander the son of Philip (al-Iskandar ibn Filqus), who ruled the whole world, the Greek, the founder of Alexandria.

Ibn Ishaq said: he is a man from the people of Egypt, named Marzaban ibn Marzabah, the Greek, from the descendants of Yunan ibn Yafith ibn Nuh.

It was also said: he is a king named Hurmus. It was said: a king named Hirdis. It was said: a young man from the Romans. It was said: he was a prophet. It was said: he was a righteous servant. It was said: his name was Abd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. It was said: Mus'ab ibn Abd Allah, from the descendants of Kahlan ibn Saba'.

Al-Qurtubi related, from al-Suhayli, that he said: "The apparent position from the science of reports is that there were two: one of them lived in the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and the other lived close to the time of Isa (peace be upon him)."

It was also said: he is Abu Karib al-Himyari. It was said: he is one of the angels. Al-Razi preferred the first view. He said: "Because the one whose kingdom reached such breadth and power as the revelation describes is none other than Alexander the Greek, as the books of history testify." He said: "So it is necessary to affirm with certainty that Dhu al-Qarnayn is Alexander." He said: "But there is a difficulty in this: he was a student of Aristotle the sage, and was upon his doctrine. So Allah's exalting him requires the judgment that Aristotle's doctrine is true and correct, and that is not something that can be done."

Al-Nisaburi said: "I say: not everything the philosophers held is false. Perhaps he took from them what was pure and left what was turbid. And Allah knows best."

Ibn Kathir preferred what al-Suhayli mentioned, that there were two, as we previously mentioned, and he explained that the first circumambulated the House with Ibrahim when he first built it, believed in him, followed him, and that his vizier was al-Khadir.

As for the second, he is Alexander of Macedon, the Greek, whose vizier was the famous philosopher Aristotle, and he lived about three hundred years before the Messiah.

The first one mentioned in the Qur'an was in the time of the Friend (Ibrahim). This is the meaning of what Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir, relating it on the authority of al-Azraqi and others. Then he said: "We have mentioned a good portion of his reports in the book al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, with what is sufficient in it."

Abu al-Su'ud related in his tafsir, from Ibn Kathir, that he said: "We have only made this clear, meaning that there were two, because many people believe that they are one, and that the one mentioned in the Mighty Qur'an is this later one. Thereby a great error and much corruption occur. How could it be otherwise? The first was a righteous, believing servant, and a just king, and his vizier was al-Khadir, and it has been said that he was a prophet. As for the second, he was a disbeliever, and his vizier was Aristotle the philosopher. The time between them was more than two thousand years. So where is this from that?" End of quote.

I say: perhaps he mentioned this in the book that he mentioned earlier, which he named al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, and he did not find it. What is derived from the books of history is that there were two, as al-Suhayli, al-Azraqi, Ibn Kathir and others mentioned, not as al-Razi mentioned, claiming that it is what the books of history testify to. The dispute has occurred over whether he was a prophet or not, and what is derived from that regarding the matter sought will come at the end of this discussion, God willing.

As for the reason he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn, al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari said: he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn because he reached the horn of the sun from its rising and the horn of the sun from its setting. It was said: he had two braids of hair, and braids are called qurun (horns). From this is the statement of the poet:

"So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of its horns (braids), drinking like one intoxicated with the cool water of al-Hashraj."

Al-Hashraj is a water from the waters of the Arabs. It was said: at the beginning of his kingdom he saw as if he were grasping the two horns of the sun, so he was named by that. It was said: he had two horns beneath his turban. It was said: he called to Allah, and his people struck him on one of his horns, then he called to Allah and they struck him on his other horn. It is said he was named so because he was of noble lineage on both sides, from a house of nobility from his father's and mother's side. It was said: because two generations of people passed away in his time while he was alive. It was said: because when he fought, he fought with both his hands and his stirrups together. It was said: because he was given knowledge of the outward and the inward. It was said: because he entered the light and the darkness. It was said: because he ruled Persia and Rome. It was said: because he ruled Rome and the Turks. It was said: because his crown had two horns.

His saying: ﴿Say: I shall recite to you from him a remembrance﴾, meaning: I shall recite to you, O askers, a report about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and that is by way of recited revelation.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to explain what He commanded His Messenger to say to them, that He would recite to them from him a remembrance. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, meaning: We empowered him by what We had prepared for him of the means. We gave him capability and power to act within it, made easy for him the travel in its places, and made its paths subservient to him, until he could take hold of it wherever he willed and however he willed. And among the completeness of his establishment in it, He made the night and the day equal for him in illumination. ﴿And We gave him of everything﴾ that relates to his aim (a cause), meaning: a way by which he reaches what he desires.

(So he followed a cause) of those causes.

The exegetes said: the meaning is a way that would lead him to the west of the sun.

Al-Zajjaj said: (so he followed a cause) of the causes he had been given. That is because he had been given a cause of everything, so he followed, from those causes he had been given, a cause for travel to the west. It was said: he followed from everything a knowledge by which he would be enabled to attain what he wanted. It was said: a means of reaching wherever he willed. It was said: of everything that people need. It was said: of everything that kings seek help with, such as conquering cities and subduing enemies. The root of sabab (cause) is a rope, and it was borrowed for everything by which one reaches something.

Ibn Amir, the people of Kufa, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read fa-atba'a with a cut hamzah (ātba'a). The people of Madinah, the people of Makkah and Abu Amr read it with a connected hamzah (fa-ttaba'a).

Al-Akhfash said: tabi'tu and atba'tu have the same meaning, like radiftu and ardaftu. From this is His saying: ﴿so a piercing flame pursued him﴾ [al-Saffat: 10]. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubaydah preferred the reading of the people of Kufa, and said: "Because it is from travelling."

He and al-Asma'i related that it is said: tabi'tuhu and atba'tuhu when one travels and does not catch up with him, and atba'ahu when one catches up with him.

Abu Ubaydah said: similar to this is ﴿so they overtook them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 60].

Al-Nahhas said: this is from the distinctions, and although al-Asma'i related it, it is not accepted except with knowledge or evidence. His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying ﴿so they overtook them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 60] does not mean in the hadith that they caught up with them. The hadith is only: when Musa and his companions came out of the sea, and Pharaoh and his companions entered the sea, the sea closed over them.

The truth in this is that taba', ittaba' and atba' are dialects with one meaning, which is travel.

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun﴾, meaning: the extremity of the earth from the direction of the west, because beyond this extremity is the encompassing ocean, and it is not possible to proceed in it. ﴿He found it setting in a spring of black mud﴾. Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (hami'atin) "hot" (hamiyah), meaning: hot.

The rest read (hami'atin) meaning: abounding in black mud (hama'ah), which is black clay. You say: hama'tu al-bi'r hama'an with the sukun, when you removed its mud, and hami'at al-bi'r hama'atahu with the vowel, when its mud increased. It is also possible that (hamiyah) is from hama'ah, so the hamzah was softened and turned into a ya'. The two readings may be combined, so it is said: it was hot and had mud.

It was said: perhaps when Dhu al-Qarnayn reached the shore of the encompassing ocean, he saw it that way from his viewpoint. It is not far-fetched to say: there is no barrier to Allah enabling him to cross the encompassing ocean until he reaches that spring in which the sun sets, and what prevents this, after Allah related of him that he reached the setting-place of the sun, and that He established him in the earth, and the sea is part of it? Mere improbability does not necessitate interpreting the Qur'an contrary to its apparent meaning.

﴿And he found near it a people﴾. The pronoun in (near it) refers either to the spring or to the sun.

It was said: they were a people whose clothing was the skins of wild beasts, and they were disbelievers. So Allah gave him the choice between punishing them and leaving them alone. He said: ﴿Either you punish, or you adopt among them goodness﴾, meaning: either you punish them by killing from the outset, or you adopt among them a matter of goodness, or a good matter, emphasizing by making the verbal noun an attribute of the matter. The intended meaning is calling them to the truth and teaching them the laws.

(He said) Dhu al-Qarnayn, choosing the call, which is the final part of the alternatives: ﴿As for him who does wrong﴾ to himself by persisting in polytheism and does not accept my call, (then we shall punish him) by killing in this world, ﴿then he will be returned to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter, (and He will punish him) therein (with a punishment unprecedented), meaning: a dreadful, terrible punishment.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah gave him the choice between the two matters.

Al-Nahhas said: Ali ibn Sulayman rejected this statement, because it has not been established that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet, so that he would be addressed with this. How would he say to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿then he will be returned to his Lord﴾, and how would he say (then we shall punish him), addressing Him with the plural "we"? He said: the estimate is: We said: O Muhammad. They said: O Dhu al-Qarnayn.

Al-Nahhas said: what he mentioned does not necessarily follow, since it is permissible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addressed him through a prophet of his time, and it may be that Dhu al-Qarnayn addressed those people, so what he mentioned does not follow.

It is possible that he was addressing the prophet to whom Allah spoke through him, or that he addressed his people whom he reached in that place.

Tha'lab said: the (an) in His saying ﴿either you punish, or you adopt﴾ is in the accusative position, and if it were in the nominative it would be correct, with the meaning of "as for him", like the saying of the poet:

"So travel, for either a need will be fulfilled for you two, or a good resting-place and a friend."

﴿As for him who believes﴾ in Allah and affirms my call, (and does) righteous deeds, of what faith requires, ﴿then for him is a reward, the best﴾. The people of Madinah, Abu Amr, Asim, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read (fa-lahu jaza'un) with the nominative, as a beginning: a reward, the good quality, with Allah; or the good deed, which is Paradise. This was said by al-Farra'.

The attribution of the reward to the best (al-husna), which is Paradise, is like the attribution of "the truth of certainty" and "the abode of the Hereafter". It is also possible that this reward is from Dhu al-Qarnayn, meaning: I will give it to him and bestow favour upon him. The rest of the Kufans read: ﴿fa-lahu jaza'an al-husna﴾ with the accusative for (jaza'an) and tanwin.

Al-Farra' said: its being in the accusative is as a specification (tamyiz).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: rewarded with it as a reward. Ibn Abbas and Masruq read (jaza'a) with the accusative without tanwin.

Abu Hatim said: it is with the tanwin deleted because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters. Al-Nahhas said: this, according to others, is an error, because it is not a place where tanwin is deleted due to the meeting of two unvowelled letters.

It was also read with (jaza'un) in the nominative with tanwin, as a beginning, with (al-husna) as an apposition to it, and the predicate is the prepositional phrase.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "You say that Dhu al-Qarnayn used to tie his horses to the Pleiades?" Ka'b said to him: "If I said that, then God said: ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through Uthman ibn Abi Hasir that Ibn Abbas mentioned to him that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan recited the verse in Surat al-Kahf as ﴿it set in a murky spring﴾ (ta'rubu fi 'aynin hamiyah). Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: we do not read it except as (hami'ah, 'muddy'). So Mu'awiyah asked Abd Allah ibn Amr: how do you read it? Abd Allah said: As you have recited it." Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: the Qur'an was revealed in my house. So he sent for Ka'b and said to him: Where do you find the sun setting in the Torah?" Ka'b said to him: "Ask the people of Arabic, for they know it better. As for me, I find in the Torah that it sets in water and mud," and he pointed with his hand to the west.

Ibn Abi Hasir said: "If I were with you two, I would support you with a statement that would increase you in insight regarding hami'ah."

Ibn Abbas said: "And what is it?" I said: "Among what we transmit is the saying of Tubba' about Dhu al-Qarnayn, regarding his zeal for knowledge and his following of it:"

> Dhu al-Qarnayn was a Muslim Umar, a king before whom kings are humbled and gathered,
> So he came to the east and the west seeking the means of kingship from a wise, guiding sage,
> And he saw the sun's setting at its going down in a spring of muddy clay and black slime.

Ibn Abbas said: "What is al-khalab?" I said: "Clay, in their speech." He said: "What is al-tha't?" I said: "Silt." He said: "What is al-kharmad?" I said: "Black." So Ibn Abbas called a boy and said: "Write down what this man is saying."

al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿in a murky spring﴾ (fi 'aynin hami'ah).

The Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 18, verses 83–95 (part 1 of 2):

.
When Allah, glory be to Him, had answered two of the questions of the Jews, and the discourse had reached the point where it reached, He began the third question and its answer. The ones asking here are the Jews.

Scholars differed greatly concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn. It was said: he is Alexander the son of Philip (al-Iskandar ibn Filqus), who ruled the whole world, the Greek, the founder of Alexandria.

Ibn Ishaq said: he is a man from the people of Egypt, named Marzaban ibn Marzabah, the Greek, from the descendants of Yunan ibn Yafith ibn Nuh.

It was also said: he is a king named Hurmus. It was said: a king named Hirdis. It was said: a young man from the Romans. It was said: he was a prophet. It was said: he was a righteous servant. It was said: his name was Abd Allah ibn al-Dahhak. It was said: Mus'ab ibn Abd Allah, from the descendants of Kahlan ibn Saba'.

Al-Qurtubi related, from al-Suhayli, that he said: "The apparent position from the science of reports is that there were two: one of them lived in the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and the other lived close to the time of Isa (peace be upon him)."

It was also said: he is Abu Karib al-Himyari. It was said: he is one of the angels. Al-Razi preferred the first view. He said: "Because the one whose kingdom reached such breadth and power as the revelation describes is none other than Alexander the Greek, as the books of history testify." He said: "So it is necessary to affirm with certainty that Dhu al-Qarnayn is Alexander." He said: "But there is a difficulty in this: he was a student of Aristotle the sage, and was upon his doctrine. So Allah's exalting him requires the judgment that Aristotle's doctrine is true and correct, and that is not something that can be done."

Al-Nisaburi said: "I say: not everything the philosophers held is false. Perhaps he took from them what was pure and left what was turbid. And Allah knows best."

Ibn Kathir preferred what al-Suhayli mentioned, that there were two, as we previously mentioned, and he explained that the first circumambulated the House with Ibrahim when he first built it, believed in him, followed him, and that his vizier was al-Khadir.

As for the second, he is Alexander of Macedon, the Greek, whose vizier was the famous philosopher Aristotle, and he lived about three hundred years before the Messiah.

The first one mentioned in the Qur'an was in the time of the Friend (Ibrahim). This is the meaning of what Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir, relating it on the authority of al-Azraqi and others. Then he said: "We have mentioned a good portion of his reports in the book al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, with what is sufficient in it."

Abu al-Su'ud related in his tafsir, from Ibn Kathir, that he said: "We have only made this clear, meaning that there were two, because many people believe that they are one, and that the one mentioned in the Mighty Qur'an is this later one. Thereby a great error and much corruption occur. How could it be otherwise? The first was a righteous, believing servant, and a just king, and his vizier was al-Khadir, and it has been said that he was a prophet. As for the second, he was a disbeliever, and his vizier was Aristotle the philosopher. The time between them was more than two thousand years. So where is this from that?" End of quote.

I say: perhaps he mentioned this in the book that he mentioned earlier, which he named al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah, and he did not find it. What is derived from the books of history is that there were two, as al-Suhayli, al-Azraqi, Ibn Kathir and others mentioned, not as al-Razi mentioned, claiming that it is what the books of history testify to. The dispute has occurred over whether he was a prophet or not, and what is derived from that regarding the matter sought will come at the end of this discussion, God willing.

As for the reason he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn, al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari said: he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn because he reached the horn of the sun from its rising and the horn of the sun from its setting. It was said: he had two braids of hair, and braids are called qurun (horns). From this is the statement of the poet:

"So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of its horns (braids), drinking like one intoxicated with the cool water of al-Hashraj."

Al-Hashraj is a water from the waters of the Arabs. It was said: at the beginning of his kingdom he saw as if he were grasping the two horns of the sun, so he was named by that. It was said: he had two horns beneath his turban. It was said: he called to Allah, and his people struck him on one of his horns, then he called to Allah and they struck him on his other horn. It is said he was named so because he was of noble lineage on both sides, from a house of nobility from his father's and mother's side. It was said: because two generations of people passed away in his time while he was alive. It was said: because when he fought, he fought with both his hands and his stirrups together. It was said: because he was given knowledge of the outward and the inward. It was said: because he entered the light and the darkness. It was said: because he ruled Persia and Rome. It was said: because he ruled Rome and the Turks. It was said: because his crown had two horns.

His saying: ﴿Say: I shall recite to you from him a remembrance﴾, meaning: I shall recite to you, O askers, a report about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and that is by way of recited revelation.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to explain what He commanded His Messenger to say to them, that He would recite to them from him a remembrance. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, meaning: We empowered him by what We had prepared for him of the means. We gave him capability and power to act within it, made easy for him the travel in its places, and made its paths subservient to him, until he could take hold of it wherever he willed and however he willed. And among the completeness of his establishment in it, He made the night and the day equal for him in illumination. ﴿And We gave him of everything﴾ that relates to his aim (a cause), meaning: a way by which he reaches what he desires.

(So he followed a cause) of those causes.

The exegetes said: the meaning is a way that would lead him to the west of the sun.

Al-Zajjaj said: (so he followed a cause) of the causes he had been given. That is because he had been given a cause of everything, so he followed, from those causes he had been given, a cause for travel to the west. It was said: he followed from everything a knowledge by which he would be enabled to attain what he wanted. It was said: a means of reaching wherever he willed. It was said: of everything that people need. It was said: of everything that kings seek help with, such as conquering cities and subduing enemies. The root of sabab (cause) is a rope, and it was borrowed for everything by which one reaches something.

Ibn Amir, the people of Kufa, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read fa-atba'a with a cut hamzah (ātba'a). The people of Madinah, the people of Makkah and Abu Amr read it with a connected hamzah (fa-ttaba'a).

Al-Akhfash said: tabi'tu and atba'tu have the same meaning, like radiftu and ardaftu. From this is His saying: ﴿so a piercing flame pursued him﴾ [al-Saffat: 10]. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubaydah preferred the reading of the people of Kufa, and said: "Because it is from travelling."

He and al-Asma'i related that it is said: tabi'tuhu and atba'tuhu when one travels and does not catch up with him, and atba'ahu when one catches up with him.

Abu Ubaydah said: similar to this is ﴿so they overtook them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 60].

Al-Nahhas said: this is from the distinctions, and although al-Asma'i related it, it is not accepted except with knowledge or evidence. His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying ﴿so they overtook them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 60] does not mean in the hadith that they caught up with them. The hadith is only: when Musa and his companions came out of the sea, and Pharaoh and his companions entered the sea, the sea closed over them.

The truth in this is that taba', ittaba' and atba' are dialects with one meaning, which is travel.

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun﴾, meaning: the extremity of the earth from the direction of the west, because beyond this extremity is the encompassing ocean, and it is not possible to proceed in it. ﴿He found it setting in a spring of black mud﴾. Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (hami'atin) "hot" (hamiyah), meaning: hot.

The rest read (hami'atin) meaning: abounding in black mud (hama'ah), which is black clay. You say: hama'tu al-bi'r hama'an with the sukun, when you removed its mud, and hami'at al-bi'r hama'atahu with the vowel, when its mud increased. It is also possible that (hamiyah) is from hama'ah, so the hamzah was softened and turned into a ya'. The two readings may be combined, so it is said: it was hot and had mud.

It was said: perhaps when Dhu al-Qarnayn reached the shore of the encompassing ocean, he saw it that way from his viewpoint. It is not far-fetched to say: there is no barrier to Allah enabling him to cross the encompassing ocean until he reaches that spring in which the sun sets, and what prevents this, after Allah related of him that he reached the setting-place of the sun, and that He established him in the earth, and the sea is part of it? Mere improbability does not necessitate interpreting the Qur'an contrary to its apparent meaning.

﴿And he found near it a people﴾. The pronoun in (near it) refers either to the spring or to the sun.

It was said: they were a people whose clothing was the skins of wild beasts, and they were disbelievers. So Allah gave him the choice between punishing them and leaving them alone. He said: ﴿Either you punish, or you adopt among them goodness﴾, meaning: either you punish them by killing from the outset, or you adopt among them a matter of goodness, or a good matter, emphasizing by making the verbal noun an attribute of the matter. The intended meaning is calling them to the truth and teaching them the laws.

(He said) Dhu al-Qarnayn, choosing the call, which is the final part of the alternatives: ﴿As for him who does wrong﴾ to himself by persisting in polytheism and does not accept my call, (then we shall punish him) by killing in this world, ﴿then he will be returned to his Lord﴾ in the Hereafter, (and He will punish him) therein (with a punishment unprecedented), meaning: a dreadful, terrible punishment.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah gave him the choice between the two matters.

Al-Nahhas said: Ali ibn Sulayman rejected this statement, because it has not been established that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet, so that he would be addressed with this. How would he say to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿then he will be returned to his Lord﴾, and how would he say (then we shall punish him), addressing Him with the plural "we"? He said: the estimate is: We said: O Muhammad. They said: O Dhu al-Qarnayn.

Al-Nahhas said: what he mentioned does not necessarily follow, since it is permissible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addressed him through a prophet of his time, and it may be that Dhu al-Qarnayn addressed those people, so what he mentioned does not follow.

It is possible that he was addressing the prophet to whom Allah spoke through him, or that he addressed his people whom he reached in that place.

Tha'lab said: the (an) in His saying ﴿either you punish, or you adopt﴾ is in the accusative position, and if it were in the nominative it would be correct, with the meaning of "as for him", like the saying of the poet:

"So travel, for either a need will be fulfilled for you two, or a good resting-place and a friend."

﴿As for him who believes﴾ in Allah and affirms my call, (and does) righteous deeds, of what faith requires, ﴿then for him is a reward, the best﴾. The people of Madinah, Abu Amr, Asim, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Amir read (fa-lahu jaza'un) with the nominative, as a beginning: a reward, the good quality, with Allah; or the good deed, which is Paradise. This was said by al-Farra'.

The attribution of the reward to the best (al-husna), which is Paradise, is like the attribution of "the truth of certainty" and "the abode of the Hereafter". It is also possible that this reward is from Dhu al-Qarnayn, meaning: I will give it to him and bestow favour upon him. The rest of the Kufans read: ﴿fa-lahu jaza'an al-husna﴾ with the accusative for (jaza'an) and tanwin.

Al-Farra' said: its being in the accusative is as a specification (tamyiz).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: rewarded with it as a reward. Ibn Abbas and Masruq read (jaza'a) with the accusative without tanwin.

Abu Hatim said: it is with the tanwin deleted because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters. Al-Nahhas said: this, according to others, is an error, because it is not a place where tanwin is deleted due to the meeting of two unvowelled letters.

It was also read with (jaza'un) in the nominative with tanwin, as a beginning, with (al-husna) as an apposition to it, and the predicate is the prepositional phrase.

﴿And we shall speak to him of Our command, ease﴾, meaning: of what We command, a word of ease, not difficult or hard; or the verbal noun was used for him as an intensification.

﴿Then he followed a cause﴾, meaning: another way, other than the first way, which was the one by which he returned from the west, and travelled in it to the east.

﴿Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun﴾, that is, the place upon which the sun first rises over the inhabited earth, or the place of its rising, since there is no legal or rational barrier to his reaching it, as we have clarified previously. ﴿He found it rising over a people for whom We had made no screen against it﴾, that would shelter them, neither of houses nor of clothing. Rather they are barefoot and naked, and do not take shelter in anything of construction.

(p-٨٧٣)

It was said: because they were in a land where building could not be firmly established upon it.

﴿Thus [it was]; and We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾ That is: thus was the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn; he followed these means until he reached [his goal], and We knew, when We empowered him, what capacity he possessed for that kingship and for being independent in it. It was also said that the meaning is: We did not provide for them a covering like that covering which We provided for you from dwellings and garments. It was also said that the meaning is: thus he reached the rising place of the sun, just as he had reached its setting place. It was also said that the meaning is: thus does [the sun] rise upon a people like that tribe over whom it sets; so he judged among these people as he had judged among those, [punishing the wrongdoers and doing good to the believers]. The interpretation of "encompassing what was with him" in these aspects is according to what suits that, as we said in the first aspect.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: The Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, you only mention Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the prophets. You have heard their mention from us. So inform us about a prophet whom God did not mention in the Torah except in one place." He said: "And who is he?" They said: "Dhu al-Qarnayn." He said: "Nothing has reached me about him." So they left, rejoicing, having become proud in themselves, and they had not reached the door of the house when Gabriel descended with these verses: ﴿And they ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn.﴾

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I do not know whether Tubba' was a prophet or not. And I do not know whether Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet or not. And I do not know whether the prescribed punishments are expiations for their people or not."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: "Ali was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn: was he a prophet? He said: I heard your Prophet (ﷺ) say: He was a servant who advised God, so God advised him."

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, Ibn Abi Asim in al-Sunnah, and Ibn Mardawayh related through Abu al-Tufayl that Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali ibn Abi Talib about Dhu al-Qarnayn: was he a prophet or a king? He said: He was neither a prophet nor a king, but he was a righteous servant who loved God, so God loved him; he advised God, so God advised him. God sent him to his people, and they struck him on his horn, and he died. Then God revived him to fight them. Then God sent him to his people, and they struck him on his other horn, and he died. God revived him to fight them, and for this he was called Dhu al-Qarnayn. And among you there is one like him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Amr, who said: Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Akhras ibn Hakim, from his father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn and said: "He was a king who swept the earth with the means."

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah related from Khalid ibn Ma'dan al-Kula'i, as a marfu' report, the same. Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in Kitab al-Adad, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Umar ibn (p-875) al-Khattab that he heard a man calling out at Mina, "O Dhu al-Qarnayn!" So Umar said: "You have named [your children] with the names of the prophets; then what about the names of the angels?" There is in this chapter other than what we have mentioned, and what we have cited suffices.

Ibn Abd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Uqbah ibn Amir al-Juhani a hadith containing that "a group of Jews asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he informed them of what they had come for initially. Among what he told them was that he was a young man from the Romans, that he built Alexandria, that an angel ascended with him into the sky, and took him to the barrier." Its chain is weak, its text contains reprehensible content, and most of what is in it is from the reports of the Children of Israel.

Ibn Kathir mentioned the meaning of this in his tafsir and attributed it to Ibn Jarir and al-Umawi in his Maghazi. Then he said after that: "What is strange is that Abu Zur'ah al-Dimashqi, despite his high standing, related it in full in his book Dala'il al-Nubuwwah." End of quote.

al-Suyuti related it in full in al-Durr al-Manthur, and also related a long report from Wahb ibn Munabbih, attributing it to Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Shirazi in al-Alqab, and Abu al-Shaykh, and in it are very objectionable things. Likewise he related a long report from Muhammad al-Baqir, related by Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh. Perhaps these reports and similar ones are transmitted from the People of the Book, and we have been commanded neither to believe them nor to disbelieve them in what they transmit to us.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾, that he said: "Knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "You say that Dhu al-Qarnayn used to tie his horses to the Pleiades?" Ka'b said to him: "If I said that, then God said: ﴿And We gave him from every thing a means﴾."

Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: we do not read it except as (hami'ah, 'muddy'). So Mu'awiyah asked Abd Allah ibn Amr: how do you read it? Abd Allah said: As you have recited it." Ibn Abbas said: "I said to Mu'awiyah: the Qur'an was revealed in my house. So he sent for Ka'b and said to him: Where do you find the sun setting in the Torah?" Ka'b said to him: "Ask the people of Arabic, for they know it better. As for me, I find in the Torah that it sets in water and mud," and he pointed with his hand to the west.

Ibn Abi Hasir said: "If I were with you two, I would support you with a statement that would increase you in insight regarding hami'ah."

Ibn Abbas said: "And what is it?" I said: "Among what we transmit is the saying of Tubba' about Dhu al-Qarnayn, regarding his zeal for knowledge and his following of it:"

> Dhu al-Qarnayn was a Muslim Umar, a king before whom kings are humbled and gathered,
> So he came to the east and the west seeking the means of kingship from a wise, guiding sage,
> And he saw the sun's setting at its going down in a spring of muddy clay and black slime.
