Then the Most High recounts the journey of Dhul-Qarnayn to another region, namely the northern quarter, after the means for it had been prepared. He said: ﴿Then he followed a way﴾, that is, a third path running across between the east and the west.

﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin, Yahya al-Yazidi and Abu Zayd, on the authority of al-Mufaddal, read (al-sadayn) with a fatha on the sin. The rest read it with a damma.

Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: if the barrier (sadd) is by the creation of Allah, the Most High, then it is with a damma on the sin, so that it has the meaning of a passive participle (maf'ul), that is, it is something that Allah made and created; and if it is the work of the servants, then it is with a fatha, so that it is a verbal noun (hadath).

Ibn al-A'rabi said: whatever stands in front of you and blocks what is behind it is a sadd and a sudd, like al-du'f and al-du'f, and al-faqr and al-fuqr. The two barriers (al-saddan) are two mountains on the side of Armenia and Adharbayjan. The accusative of (bayna) is because it is the object (maf'ul bihi), just as it is raised as the subject in His saying: ﴿Indeed your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

It was also said: the location of "between the two barriers" is the farthest extent of the land of the Turks on the side facing the east, not the two mountains of Armenia and Adharbayjan. Ibn Jarir related in his History that the ruler of Adharbayjan, at the time of its conquest, sent a man from the direction of al-Juzur, who observed it and described it as a lofty structure behind a deep, firm and impregnable trench. ﴿And he found beside them﴾, that is, behind them, figuratively for "beside them"; it was also said: in front of them, ﴿a people who scarcely understood any speech﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (yufqihuna) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the qaf, from aqfaha, meaning to make clear, that is, they do not make speech clear to others. The rest read it with a fatha on the ya' and the qaf, meaning they do not understand the speech of others. Both readings are sound, and their meaning is: they neither understand others nor make themselves understood, because they do not know any language other than their own.

(They said) — that is, these people who scarcely make themselves understood in speech. It was said: Dhul-Qarnayn's understanding of their speech was among the means that Allah had given him. It was also said: they said that to their interpreter, and he told Dhul-Qarnayn what they had said to him: ﴿O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are corrupters in the earth﴾. Ya'juj and Ma'juj are two non-Arabic names, as evidenced by their being diptotic (not taking tanwin), and this is the view of most scholars.

It was also said that they are derived from words: from "ajja al-zaleem" (the male ostrich ran in its gait) when it hastened, and "ta'ajjajat al-nar" (the fire blazed) when it flared up. The majority read them without hamza, while 'Asim read them with hamza.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The justification for their hamza, even though no root is known for it, is that the Arabs have hamzated letters for which no hamza has a known origin, such as their saying: kaba'a, ra'atha, and istasa'at al-rih (the wind became strong).

Abu 'Ali said: It is possible that both are Arabic. Whoever uses hamza, it is on the pattern yaf'ul, like yarbu', and whoever does not use hamza, it is possible that he lightened the hamza and changed it to an alif, like ra's.

As for Ma'juj, it is maf'ul from "ajja", and the two words are from one root in derivation. He said: their being unvoweled (not taking tanwin) is due to the assumption that they are Arabic, because of feminine gender and definiteness; as if it were the name of a tribe.

The lineage of them has been disputed. It was said they are of the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh; it was also said: Ya'juj are from the Turks, and Ma'juj are from the mountain and the Daylam.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Adam had a wet dream, his semen mixed with the dust, and they were created from that water.

Al-Qurtubi said: This is open to question, because the prophets do not have wet dreams; rather, they are of the descendants of Yafith, as Muqatil and others said. There has been disagreement about their description: some people describe them as small of body and short of stature, others describe them as large of body and tall of stature, and others say they have claws like the claws of beasts of prey, and that among them is a class who spread out one of their ears as a bed and cover themselves with the other. The scholars of the early generations and those after them have varied reports about their attributes and actions.

There has been disagreement about their corruption in the earth. It was said: it is their eating of the children of Adam. It was said: it is oppression, violence, killing and all other forms of corruption. It was said: they used to go out to the land of those people who complained of them to Dhul-Qarnayn in the spring season, leaving nothing green there without eating it.

﴿So shall we pay you a tribute?﴾ This question is out of courtesy toward Dhul-Qarnayn. (Kharajan) was also read.

al-Azhari said: al-kharaj applies to a tax, applies to the wealth of spoils (fay'), applies to the poll-tax (jizya), and applies to produce. Al-kharaj is also a term for what is levied from the obligations on property, and al-kharj is the verbal noun.

Qutrub said: al-kharj is the poll-tax and al-kharaj is on land. It was said: al-kharj is what each person pays out of his wealth, and al-kharaj is what the ruler collects. It was also said: the two have one meaning.

﴿On condition that you make between us and them a barrier﴾, that is, a rampart (radm), a barrier between us and them. (Sadda) was also read with a fatha on the sin.

al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the damma is the noun and the fatha is the verbal noun. al-Kisa'i said: the fatha and the damma are two dialects with one meaning, and the distinction between them reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala, Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn al-Anbari has already been mentioned shortly before.

Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see is a sadd with a damma, and what you do not see is a sadd with a fatha. We have already mentioned the explanation of those who read with fatha and with damma in "al-saddayn".

﴿He said: That in which my Lord has established me is better﴾, that is, Dhul-Qarnayn said to them: what Allah has spread out for me of power and dominion is better than your tribute. Then he asked them for help, saying: ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is, with men from among you who work with their hands, or help me with building tools, or with both of them together. al-Zajjaj said: with work that you do with me.

Ibn Kathir alone read (ma makkanani) with two nuns, and the rest read it with one nun.

﴿I will make between you and them a rampart﴾. This is the answer to the command. The radm is that in which some parts are placed upon others until they join.

al-Harawi said: it is said radamtu al-thulma, arduduha, with a kasra, radman, meaning I closed it. Radm is also a noun meaning a barrier. It was said: radm is more emphatic than sadd, since sadd is anything by which something is blocked, while radm is placing one thing upon another of stones or earth or the like until a strong barrier stands. From this comes radama thawbahu, when he patched it with thick, layered patches, one upon another. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

Have the poets left any of the stitched-together?

That is, of speech in which some parts ride upon others.

﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is, give me and hand me. (Zubar al-hadid) is the plural of zubra, which is a piece. al-Khalil said: a zubra of iron is a large piece. al-Farra' said: the meaning of "bring me blocks of iron" is bring them to me. When the ya' was dropped, an alif was added; accordingly, the accusative of (zubar) is by removing the preposition.

﴿Until, when he had leveled between the two cliffs﴾. The two cliffs (al-sadafan) are the two sides of the mountain.

al-Azhari said: The two sides of a mountain are called sadafan when they face each other, because they meet, that is, they converge. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Harawi said likewise.

A poet said:

Both cliffs are overwhelmed by its brightness, blazing like the lamp of darkness.

It may also be said that any tall, lofty building is a sadaf, as Abu 'Ubayda said.

Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read (al-sadafayn) with a fatha on the sad and the dal. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, al-Yazidi and Ibn Muhaysin read with a damma on the sad and the dal. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal. Ibn al-Majishun read with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal. Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading, because it is the most famous of the dialects.

The meaning of the verse: they gave him blocks of iron, and he began to build with them between the two mountains until he leveled them.

﴿He said: Blow﴾, that is, he said to the workers: blow upon these blocks with the bellows. ﴿Until, when he had made it fire﴾, that is, he made that which was blown upon — the blocks — fire, that is, like fire in its heat. Attributing the making to Dhul-Qarnayn is figurative, since he was the one who commanded the blowing.

It was said: he commanded that a layer of blocks and stones be placed, then he kindled wood and charcoal upon it with bellows until it became hot. Iron, when kindled over, becomes like fire. Then molten copper was brought and he poured it over that layer. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He said: Bring me, I will pour upon it molten copper﴾. The people of lexicography said: qitr is molten copper, and ifragh is pouring. Most commentators say likewise. A group said: qitr is molten iron. Another group, including Ibn al-Anbari, said: it is molten lead.

﴿So they were unable﴾. Its origin is istata'u; when two close letters, the ta' and the ta', came together, they were lightened by deletion. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said ma astati'u, ma as-ti'u, and ma astai'u.

The majority read it with lightening. Hamza alone read (fa-ma assta'u) with a shadda on the ta', as if he intended istata'u and assimilated the ta' into the ta'; this is a weak reading. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is not permissible.

al-A'mash read (fa-ma istata'u) in its original form. The meaning of (an yazharuhu) is that they climb over it, that is, Ya'juj and Ma'juj were not able to climb over that barrier because of its height and smoothness. ﴿Nor could they make a breach in it﴾. It is said: naqabtu al-hā'it, meaning I made an opening in it, so that one reaches what is behind it.

al-Zajjaj said: they could not climb over it because of its height and smoothness, and they could not dig through it from below because of its strength and hardness.

﴿He said: This is a mercy from my Lord﴾, that is, Dhul-Qarnayn said, pointing to the barrier: this barrier is a mercy from my Lord, that is, one of the traces of His mercy toward those who would have crossed the barrier and toward those behind them, whom harm would have reached had that barrier not existed. It was also said: the reference is to the enablement to build it. ﴿But when the promise of my Lord comes﴾, that is, the appointed time of my Lord for them to come out from it. It was also said: it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, and it is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿He will make it level﴾, that is, made even with the ground. From it is His saying: ﴿No! When the earth is leveled, leveled﴾ [al-Fajr: 21]. al-Tirmidhi said: that is, made level; it is said naqatun da'ma', when its hump has gone. al-Qutaybi said: that is, made crushed and pressed against the ground. al-Halimi said: broken into pieces. A poet said:

Is there anything other than a cave that crushed a cave and collapsed?

al-Azhari said: dakaktuhu, that is, I pounded it.

Whoever reads (dakka'an) with a madd — 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i — intends the comparison to the she-camel dakka', which has no hump; that is, like a dakka'; since the barrier is masculine, it is not described as dakka'.

The rest read (dakkan) with tanwin, as a verbal noun, with the meaning already mentioned. It may also be a verbal noun in the sense of a state, that is, crushed. ﴿And the promise of my Lord is always true﴾, that is, His promise of reward and punishment, or the known promise is a true established thing that will not fail. This is the last statement of Dhul-Qarnayn.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾, that he said: the two mountains of Armenia and Adharbayjan.

He also related from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿who scarcely understood any speech﴾, that he said: the Turks. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ya'juj and Ma'juj are a span and two spans, and the tallest of them is three spans, and they are of the descendants of Adam. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are of the descendants of Adam; if they were released they would corrupt the livelihoods of people, and no man of them dies without leaving behind a thousand or more of his offspring. And behind them are three nations: Ta'wil, Taris and Manasak."

al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Aws, from his father, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No man of them dies without leaving behind a thousand or more of his offspring."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 96–98 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are corrupters on the earth. They dig through the barrier every day, until when they nearly see the rays of the sun, the one in charge of them says: 'Return, and you will break through it tomorrow.' So they return to it stronger than before. Then, when their term is fulfilled and Allah wills to send them forth against the people, they dig until, when they nearly see the rays of the sun, the one in charge of them says: 'Return, and you will break through it tomorrow, if Allah wills,' and he makes an exception. So they return to it and it is in the same state as when they left it. They dig through it and come out against the people, and they drink up the water, and the people take refuge from them in their fortresses. They shoot their arrows toward the sky, and the arrows return stained with blood. They say: 'We have overcome those on the earth and have risen over those in the heaven, by force and by height.' Then Allah sends against them a worm (naghaf) in their necks, and they die." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, the beasts of the earth will grow fat and become sleek and will be filled with fat from their flesh."

It is established in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) woke up from his sleep with his face reddened, saying: 'There is no god but Allah. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this,' and he made a circle with his thumb and forefinger. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?' He said: 'Yes, when wickedness increases.'" Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So shall we assign for you a payment?﴾ that he said: a great reward.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying "a barrier" (radman) that he said: it is like the strongest partition.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also concerning His saying "blocks of iron" (zubar al-hadid) that he said: pieces of iron.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning "between the two cliffs" (bayn al-sadafayn) that he said: the two mountains. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: the summits of the two mountains.

These same (compilers) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying "molten copper" (qitran) [that he said: ...]. Al-Nahhas said: ...

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿So they were not able to scale it⁠﴾ that he said: to climb it. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij, who said: to ascend over it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying "He leveled it to dust" (ja'alahu dakka'): he said: "I do not know whether it refers to the two mountains or to what is between them."

Then the Most High recounts the journey of Dhul-Qarnayn to another region, namely the northern quarter, after the means for it had been prepared. He said: ﴿Then he followed a way﴾, that is, a third path running across between the east and the west.

It was said: it is oppression, violence, killing and all other forms of corruption. ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute?﴾ This question is out of courtesy toward Dhul-Qarnayn. (Kharajan) was also read.

﴿Until, when he had leveled between the two cliffs﴾. The two cliffs (al-sadafan) are the two sides of the mountain.

Both cliffs are overwhelmed by its brightness, blazing like the lamp of darkness.

The meaning of the verse: they gave him blocks of iron, and he began to build with them between the two mountains until he leveled them.

﴿He said: Blow﴾, that is, he said to the workers: blow upon these blocks with the bellows. ﴿Until, when he had made it fire﴾, that is, he made that which was blown upon — the blocks — fire, that is, like fire in its heat. Attributing the making to Dhul-Qarnayn is figurative, since he was the one who commanded the blowing.

Then molten copper was brought and he poured it over that layer. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He said: Bring me, I will pour upon it molten copper﴾. The people of lexicography said: qitr is molten copper, and ifragh is pouring. Most commentators say likewise. A group said: qitr is molten iron. Another group, including Ibn al-Anbari, said: it is molten lead.

The majority read it with lightening. Hamza alone read (fa-ma assta'u) with a shadda on the ta', as if he intended istata'u and assimilated the ta' into the ta'; this is a weak reading. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is not permissible.

al-A'mash read (fa-ma istata'u) in its original form. The meaning of (an yazharuhu) is that they climb over it, that is, Ya'juj and Ma'juj were not able to climb over that barrier because of its height and smoothness. ﴿Nor could they make a breach in it﴾. It is said: naqabtu al-hā'it, meaning I made an opening in it, so that one reaches what is behind it.

al-Zajjaj said: they could not climb over it because of its height and smoothness, and they could not dig through it from below because of its strength and hardness.

﴿He said: This is a mercy from my Lord﴾, that is, Dhul-Qarnayn said, pointing to the barrier: this barrier is a mercy from my Lord, that is, one of the traces of His mercy toward those who would have crossed the barrier and toward those behind them, whom harm would have reached had that barrier not existed. It was also said: the reference is to the enablement to build it. ﴿But when the promise of my Lord comes﴾, that is, the appointed time of my Lord for them to come out from it. It was also said: it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, and it is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿He will make it level﴾, that is, made even with the ground. From it is His saying: ﴿No! When the earth is leveled, leveled﴾ [al-Fajr: 21]. al-Tirmidhi said: that is, made level; it is said naqatun da'ma', when its hump has gone. al-Qutaybi said: that is, made crushed and pressed against the ground. al-Halimi said: broken into pieces. A poet said:

Is there anything other than a cave that crushed a cave and collapsed?

al-Azhari said: dakaktuhu, that is, I pounded it.

Whoever reads (dakka'an) with a madd — 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i — intends the comparison to the she-camel dakka', which has no hump; that is, like a dakka'; since the barrier is masculine, it is not described as dakka'.

The rest read (dakkan) with tanwin, as a verbal noun, with the meaning already mentioned. It may also be a verbal noun in the sense of a state, that is, crushed. ﴿And the promise of my Lord is always true﴾, that is, His promise of reward and punishment, or the known promise is a true established thing that will not fail. This is the last statement of Dhul-Qarnayn.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾, that he said: the two mountains of Armenia and Adharbayjan.

He also related from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿who scarcely understood any speech﴾, that he said: the Turks. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ya'juj and Ma'juj are a span and two spans, and the tallest of them is three spans, and they are of the descendants of Adam. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are of the descendants of Adam; if they were released they would corrupt the livelihoods of people, and no man of them dies without leaving behind a thousand or more of his offspring. And behind them are three nations: Ta'wil, Taris and Manasak."

al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Aws, from his father, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No man of them dies without leaving behind a thousand or more of his offspring."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 96–98 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are corrupters on the earth. They dig through the barrier every day, until when they nearly see the rays of the sun, the one in charge of them says: 'Return, and you will break through it tomorrow.' So they return to it stronger than before. Then, when their term is fulfilled and Allah wills to send them forth against the people, they dig until, when they nearly see the rays of the sun, the one in charge of them says: 'Return, and you will break through it tomorrow, if Allah wills,' and he makes an exception. So they return to it and it is in the same state as when they left it. They dig through it and come out against the people, and they drink up the water, and the people take refuge from them in their fortresses. They shoot their arrows toward the sky, and the arrows return stained with blood. They say: 'We have overcome those on the earth and have risen over those in the heaven, by force and by height.' Then Allah sends against them a worm (naghaf) in their necks, and they die." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, the beasts of the earth will grow fat and become sleek and will be filled with fat from their flesh."

It is established in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) woke up from his sleep with his face reddened, saying: 'There is no god but Allah. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this,' and he made a circle with his thumb and forefinger. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?' He said: 'Yes, when wickedness increases.'" Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So shall we assign for you a payment?﴾ that he said: a great reward.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying "a barrier" (radman) that he said: it is like the strongest partition.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also concerning His saying "blocks of iron" (zubar al-hadid) that he said: pieces of iron.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning "between the two cliffs" (bayn al-sadafayn) that he said: the two mountains. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: the summits of the two mountains.

These same (compilers) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying "molten copper" (qitran) [that he said: ...]. Al-Nahhas said: ...

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿So they were not able to scale it⁠﴾ that he said: to climb it. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij, who said: to ascend over it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying "He leveled it to dust" (ja'alahu dakka'): he said: "I do not know whether it refers to the two mountains or to what is between them."

Then the Most High recounts the journey of Dhul-Qarnayn to another region, namely the northern quarter, after the means for it had been prepared. He said: ﴿Then he followed a way﴾, that is, a third path running across between the east and the west.

﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin, Yahya al-Yazidi and Abu Zayd, on the authority of al-Mufaddal, read (al-sadayn) with a fatha on the sin. The rest read it with a damma.

Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: if the barrier (sadd) is by the creation of Allah, the Most High, then it is with a damma on the sin, so that it has the meaning of a passive participle (maf'ul), that is, it is something that Allah made and created; and if it is the work of the servants, then it is with a fatha, so that it is a verbal noun (hadath).

Ibn al-A'rabi said: whatever stands in front of you and blocks what is behind it is a sadd and a sudd, like al-du'f and al-du'f, and al-faqr and al-fuqr. The two barriers (al-saddan) are two mountains on the side of Armenia and Adharbayjan. The accusative of (bayna) is because it is the object (maf'ul bihi), just as it is raised as the subject in His saying: ﴿Indeed your bond has been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94].

It was also said: the location of "between the two barriers" is the farthest extent of the land of the Turks on the side facing the east, not the two mountains of Armenia and Adharbayjan. Ibn Jarir related in his History that the ruler of Adharbayjan, at the time of its conquest, sent a man from the direction of al-Juzur, who observed it and described it as a lofty structure behind a deep, firm and impregnable trench. ﴿And he found beside them﴾, that is, behind them, figuratively for "beside them"; it was also said: in front of them, ﴿a people who scarcely understood any speech﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (yufqihuna) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the qaf, from aqfaha, meaning to make clear, that is, they do not make speech clear to others. The rest read it with a fatha on the ya' and the qaf, meaning they do not understand the speech of others. Both readings are sound, and their meaning is: they neither understand others nor make themselves understood, because they do not know any language other than their own.

(They said) — that is, these people who scarcely make themselves understood in speech. It was said: Dhul-Qarnayn's understanding of their speech was among the means that Allah had given him. It was also said: they said that to their interpreter, and he told Dhul-Qarnayn what they had said to him: ﴿O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are corrupters in the earth﴾. Ya'juj and Ma'juj are two non-Arabic names, as evidenced by their being diptotic (not taking tanwin), and this is the view of most scholars.

It was also said that they are derived from words: from "ajja al-zaleem" (the male ostrich ran in its gait) when it hastened, and "ta'ajjajat al-nar" (the fire blazed) when it flared up. The majority read them without hamza, while 'Asim read them with hamza.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The justification for their hamza, even though no root is known for it, is that the Arabs have hamzated letters for which no hamza has a known origin, such as their saying: kaba'a, ra'atha, and istasa'at al-rih (the wind became strong).

Abu 'Ali said: It is possible that both are Arabic. Whoever uses hamza, it is on the pattern yaf'ul, like yarbu', and whoever does not use hamza, it is possible that he lightened the hamza and changed it to an alif, like ra's.

As for Ma'juj, it is maf'ul from "ajja", and the two words are from one root in derivation. He said: their being unvoweled (not taking tanwin) is due to the assumption that they are Arabic, because of feminine gender and definiteness; as if it were the name of a tribe.

The lineage of them has been disputed. It was said they are of the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh; it was also said: Ya'juj are from the Turks, and Ma'juj are from the mountain and the Daylam.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Adam had a wet dream, his semen mixed with the dust, and they were created from that water.

Al-Qurtubi said: This is open to question, because the prophets do not have wet dreams; rather, they are of the descendants of Yafith, as Muqatil and others said. There has been disagreement about their description: some people describe them as small of body and short of stature, others describe them as large of body and tall of stature, and others say they have claws like the claws of beasts of prey, and that among them is a class who spread out one of their ears as a bed and cover themselves with the other. The scholars of the early generations and those after them have varied reports about their attributes and actions.

There has been disagreement about their corruption in the earth. It was said: it is their eating of the children of Adam. It was said: it is oppression, violence, killing and all other forms of corruption. It was said: they used to go out to the land of those people who complained of them to Dhul-Qarnayn in the spring season, leaving nothing green there without eating it.

﴿So shall we pay you a tribute?﴾ This question is out of courtesy toward Dhul-Qarnayn. (Kharajan) was also read.

al-Azhari said: al-kharaj applies to a tax, applies to the wealth of spoils (fay'), applies to the poll-tax (jizya), and applies to produce. Al-kharaj is also a term for what is levied from the obligations on property, and al-kharj is the verbal noun.

Qutrub said: al-kharj is the poll-tax and al-kharaj is on land. It was said: al-kharj is what each person pays out of his wealth, and al-kharaj is what the ruler collects. It was also said: the two have one meaning.

﴿On condition that you make between us and them a barrier﴾, that is, a rampart (radm), a barrier between us and them. (Sadda) was also read with a fatha on the sin.

al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the damma is the noun and the fatha is the verbal noun. al-Kisa'i said: the fatha and the damma are two dialects with one meaning, and the distinction between them reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala, Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn al-Anbari has already been mentioned shortly before.

Ibn Abi Ishaq said: what your eyes see is a sadd with a damma, and what you do not see is a sadd with a fatha. We have already mentioned the explanation of those who read with fatha and with damma in "al-saddayn".

﴿He said: That in which my Lord has established me is better﴾, that is, Dhul-Qarnayn said to them: what Allah has spread out for me of power and dominion is better than your tribute. Then he asked them for help, saying: ﴿So help me with strength﴾, that is, with men from among you who work with their hands, or help me with building tools, or with both of them together. al-Zajjaj said: with work that you do with me.

Ibn Kathir alone read (ma makkanani) with two nuns, and the rest read it with one nun.

﴿I will make between you and them a rampart﴾. This is the answer to the command. The radm is that in which some parts are placed upon others until they join.

al-Harawi said: it is said radamtu al-thulma, arduduha, with a kasra, radman, meaning I closed it. Radm is also a noun meaning a barrier. It was said: radm is more emphatic than sadd, since sadd is anything by which something is blocked, while radm is placing one thing upon another of stones or earth or the like until a strong barrier stands. From this comes radama thawbahu, when he patched it with thick, layered patches, one upon another. From this is the saying of 'Antara:

Have the poets left any of the stitched-together?

That is, of speech in which some parts ride upon others.

﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, that is, give me and hand me. (Zubar al-hadid) is the plural of zubra, which is a piece. al-Khalil said: a zubra of iron is a large piece. al-Farra' said: the meaning of "bring me blocks of iron" is bring them to me. When the ya' was dropped, an alif was added; accordingly, the accusative of (zubar) is by removing the preposition.

﴿Until, when he had leveled between the two cliffs﴾. The two cliffs (al-sadafan) are the two sides of the mountain.

al-Azhari said: The two sides of a mountain are called sadafan when they face each other, because they meet, that is, they converge. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Harawi said likewise.

A poet said:

Both cliffs are overwhelmed by its brightness, blazing like the lamp of darkness.

It may also be said that any tall, lofty building is a sadaf, as Abu 'Ubayda said.

Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read (al-sadafayn) with a fatha on the sad and the dal. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, al-Yazidi and Ibn Muhaysin read with a damma on the sad and the dal. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read with a damma on the sad and a sukun on the dal. Ibn al-Majishun read with a fatha on the sad and a damma on the dal. Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading, because it is the most famous of the dialects.

The meaning of the verse: they gave him blocks of iron, and he began to build with them between the two mountains until he leveled them.

﴿He said: Blow﴾, that is, he said to the workers: blow upon these blocks with the bellows. ﴿Until, when he had made it fire﴾, that is, he made that which was blown upon — the blocks — fire, that is, like fire in its heat. Attributing the making to Dhul-Qarnayn is figurative, since he was the one who commanded the blowing.

It was said: he commanded that a layer of blocks and stones be placed, then he kindled wood and charcoal upon it with bellows until it became hot. Iron, when kindled over, becomes like fire. Then molten copper was brought and he poured it over that layer. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He said: Bring me, I will pour upon it molten copper﴾. The people of lexicography said: qitr is molten copper, and ifragh is pouring. Most commentators say likewise. A group said: qitr is molten iron. Another group, including Ibn al-Anbari, said: it is molten lead.

﴿So they were unable﴾. Its origin is istata'u; when two close letters, the ta' and the ta', came together, they were lightened by deletion. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is said ma astati'u, ma as-ti'u, and ma astai'u.

The majority read it with lightening. Hamza alone read (fa-ma assta'u) with a shadda on the ta', as if he intended istata'u and assimilated the ta' into the ta'; this is a weak reading. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is not permissible.

al-A'mash read (fa-ma istata'u) in its original form. The meaning of (an yazharuhu) is that they climb over it, that is, Ya'juj and Ma'juj were not able to climb over that barrier because of its height and smoothness. ﴿Nor could they make a breach in it﴾. It is said: naqabtu al-hā'it, meaning I made an opening in it, so that one reaches what is behind it.

al-Zajjaj said: they could not climb over it because of its height and smoothness, and they could not dig through it from below because of its strength and hardness.

﴿He said: This is a mercy from my Lord﴾, that is, Dhul-Qarnayn said, pointing to the barrier: this barrier is a mercy from my Lord, that is, one of the traces of His mercy toward those who would have crossed the barrier and toward those behind them, whom harm would have reached had that barrier not existed. It was also said: the reference is to the enablement to build it. ﴿But when the promise of my Lord comes﴾, that is, the appointed time of my Lord for them to come out from it. It was also said: it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, and it is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿He will make it level﴾, that is, made even with the ground. From it is His saying: ﴿No! When the earth is leveled, leveled﴾ [al-Fajr: 21]. al-Tirmidhi said: that is, made level; it is said naqatun da'ma', when its hump has gone. al-Qutaybi said: that is, made crushed and pressed against the ground. al-Halimi said: broken into pieces. A poet said:

Is there anything other than a cave that crushed a cave and collapsed?

al-Azhari said: dakaktuhu, that is, I pounded it.

Whoever reads (dakka'an) with a madd — 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i — intends the comparison to the she-camel dakka', which has no hump; that is, like a dakka'; since the barrier is masculine, it is not described as dakka'.

The rest read (dakkan) with tanwin, as a verbal noun, with the meaning already mentioned. It may also be a verbal noun in the sense of a state, that is, crushed. ﴿And the promise of my Lord is always true﴾, that is, His promise of reward and punishment, or the known promise is a true established thing that will not fail. This is the last statement of Dhul-Qarnayn.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾, that he said: the two mountains of Armenia and Adharbayjan.

He also related from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿who scarcely understood any speech﴾, that he said: the Turks. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ya'juj and Ma'juj are a span and two spans, and the tallest of them is three spans, and they are of the descendants of Adam. 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are of the descendants of Adam; if they were released they would corrupt the livelihoods of people, and no man of them dies without leaving behind a thousand or more of his offspring. And behind them are three nations: Ta'wil, Taris and Manasak."

al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of 'Amr ibn Aws, from his father, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No man of them dies without leaving behind a thousand or more of his offspring."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 18, verse 96–98 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Ya'juj and Ma'juj are corrupters on the earth. They dig through the barrier every day, until when they nearly see the rays of the sun, the one in charge of them says: 'Return, and you will break through it tomorrow.' So they return to it stronger than before. Then, when their term is fulfilled and Allah wills to send them forth against the people, they dig until, when they nearly see the rays of the sun, the one in charge of them says: 'Return, and you will break through it tomorrow, if Allah wills,' and he makes an exception. So they return to it and it is in the same state as when they left it. They dig through it and come out against the people, and they drink up the water, and the people take refuge from them in their fortresses. They shoot their arrows toward the sky, and the arrows return stained with blood. They say: 'We have overcome those on the earth and have risen over those in the heaven, by force and by height.' Then Allah sends against them a worm (naghaf) in their necks, and they die." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, the beasts of the earth will grow fat and become sleek and will be filled with fat from their flesh."

It is established in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) woke up from his sleep with his face reddened, saying: 'There is no god but Allah. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this,' and he made a circle with his thumb and forefinger. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?' He said: 'Yes, when wickedness increases.'" Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated something similar from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿So shall we assign for you a payment?﴾ that he said: a great reward.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying "a barrier" (radman) that he said: it is like the strongest partition.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also concerning His saying "blocks of iron" (zubar al-hadid) that he said: pieces of iron.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning "between the two cliffs" (bayn al-sadafayn) that he said: the two mountains. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: the summits of the two mountains.

These same (compilers) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying "molten copper" (qitran) [that he said: ...]. Al-Nahhas said: ...

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿So they were not able to scale it⁠﴾ that he said: to climb it. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij, who said: to ascend over it.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying "He leveled it to dust" (ja'alahu dakka'): he said: "I do not know whether it refers to the two mountains or to what is between them."

﴿And We will leave some of them that day surging against one another.﴾ This is part of Allah's speech, the Exalted, after the end of Dhu al-Qarnayn's account. The pronoun in "some of them" (ba'dihim) refers to Gog and Magog (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj). That is, We will leave some of Gog and Magog on the day the promise comes, or on the day Gog and Magog emerge, surging against some others among them. It is said: "the people surged" (māja al-nās) when some of them enter into others, bewildered, like the surge of water. The meaning is that they will be agitated and will mix with one another. It has also been said that the pronoun in "some of them" refers to all creation, and the day is the Day of Resurrection, meaning: We will make some of creation, from among the jinn and mankind, surge against others. It has also been said that the meaning is: We will leave Gog and Magog on the day (p-878) when the barrier is complete and its construction is perfected, some of them surging against others. The explanation of "And the Trumpet will be blown" has already been given in al-An'am. It has been said that this is the second blast, based on His saying afterwards: ﴿Then We will gather them in a gathering﴾, since the particle "fa" (then) indicates this. The first blast is not mentioned because the purpose here is to mention the conditions of the Resurrection.

The meaning: We will gather the creatures after their bodies have dissolved and turned to dust, in a complete gathering, in the most perfect description, the most wondrous form, and the most marvellous manner.

﴿And We will present Hell that day to the disbelievers, a presentation﴾. The meaning of "presentation" here is exposure, i.e., We will expose Hell to them so that they witness it on the day of Our gathering them. In this there is a great warning to the disbelievers, because of the terror and dread that will befall them when they see it.

Then He described the aforementioned disbelievers with His saying: ﴿Those whose eyes were under a covering from My remembrance﴾. That is, their eyes in the world were under a covering, which is that which covers a thing and conceals it from all sides. "From My remembrance" means from the cause of My remembrance, which is the signs that one who reflects and takes heed sees, so that he remembers Allah with monotheism and glorification. Thus the effect is attributed to the cause. Or it means from the Great Qur'an, and from contemplating its meanings and reflecting on its benefits.

Then, when He, the Exalted, described them as blind to the cosmic signs or the revealed signs, or both, He wished to describe them as deaf to hearing the truth, so He said: ﴿and they were unable to hear﴾. That is, they are unable to listen to what contains the truth from the speech of Allah and the speech of His Messenger. This is more eloquent than if He had said "and they were deaf," because the deaf may be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these have no ability at all. In the mention of the covering of the eyes and the inability to hear there is an image of their blindness to sight-based witnessing and their turning away from the evidences of hearing.

﴿Do those who disbelieve think﴾. Here "ḥusbān" means "ẓann" (supposition). The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the "fa" is for coordination with an implied preceding element, like its parallels.

The meaning: Did they suppose that they would benefit from what they worshipped, while turning away from reflecting on the signs of Allah and rebelling against accepting the truth? The meaning of ﴿that they take My servants as protectors besides Me﴾ is that they take them as protectors instead of Allah, namely the angels, the Messiah, and the devils, as objects of worship. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Do they suppose that this will benefit them?" It has been read as "afaḥsab" with the sīn sukūn, and its meaning is: "Is it sufficient for them and does it reckon for them, that they take them as protectors?" This is taken as a subject and predicate. "From My remembrance" means from the cause of My remembrance, which is the signs that one who reflects and takes heed sees, so that he remembers Allah with monotheism and glorification. Then, when He, the Exalted, described them as blind to the cosmic signs or the revealed signs, or both, He wished to describe them as deaf to hearing the truth, so He said: ﴿and they were unable to hear﴾. ﴿Do those who disbelieve think﴾. Here "ḥusbān" means "ẓann" (supposition). The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the "fa" is for coordination with an implied preceding element, like its parallels.

The meaning: Did they suppose that they would benefit from what they worshipped, while turning away from reflecting on the signs of Allah and rebelling against accepting the truth? The meaning of ﴿that they take My servants as protectors besides Me﴾ is that they take them as protectors instead of Allah, namely the angels, the Messiah, and the devils, as objects of worship. It has been read as "afaḥsab" with the sīn sukūn, and its meaning is: "Is it sufficient for them and does it reckon for them, that they take them as protectors?" This is taken as a subject and predicate. It means that this is not sufficient for them nor beneficial for them with Allah as they supposed. ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a nuzul (lodging)﴾. That is, We have made it ready for them as a nuzul in which they enjoy themselves upon their arrival.

Al-Zajjaj said: the nuzul is the dwelling and the abode. It has also been said that it is what is prepared for a guest, so it is sarcasm toward them, like His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 21]. The meaning is that Hell is prepared for them with Us as a guest is prepared for a visitor.

The meaning of "the loss of effort" is its nullification and its wasting. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative position, as a dispraise.

The answer will be: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord﴾. It is also permissible that it be in the genitive position, as an adjective of "those most losing" or as a substitute for it, and the answer then is also "Those" and what follows. The first of these possibilities is the most preferable.

The first blast is not mentioned because the purpose here is to mention the conditions of the Resurrection.

The meaning: We will gather the creatures after their bodies have dissolved and turned to dust, in a complete gathering, in the most perfect description, the most wondrous form, and the most marvellous manner.

﴿And We will present Hell that day to the disbelievers, a presentation﴾. The meaning of "presentation" here is exposure, i.e., We will expose Hell to them so that they witness it on the day of Our gathering them. In this there is a great warning to the disbelievers, because of the terror and dread that will befall them when they see it.

Then He described the aforementioned disbelievers with His saying: ﴿Those whose eyes were under a covering from My remembrance﴾. That is, their eyes in the world were under a covering, which is that which covers a thing and conceals it from all sides. "From My remembrance" means from the cause of My remembrance, which is the signs that one who reflects and takes heed sees, so that he remembers Allah with monotheism and glorification. Thus the effect is attributed to the cause. Or it means from the Great Qur'an, and from contemplating its meanings and reflecting on its benefits.

Then, when He, the Exalted, described them as blind to the cosmic signs or the revealed signs, or both, He wished to describe them as deaf to hearing the truth, so He said: ﴿and they were unable to hear﴾. That is, they are unable to listen to what contains the truth from the speech of Allah and the speech of His Messenger. This is more eloquent than if He had said "and they were deaf," because the deaf may be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these have no ability at all. In the mention of the covering of the eyes and the inability to hear there is an image of their blindness to sight-based witnessing and their turning away from the evidences of hearing.

﴿Do those who disbelieve think﴾. Here "ḥusbān" means "ẓann" (supposition). The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the "fa" is for coordination with an implied preceding element, like its parallels.

The meaning: Did they suppose that they would benefit from what they worshipped, while turning away from reflecting on the signs of Allah and rebelling against accepting the truth? The meaning of ﴿that they take My servants as protectors besides Me﴾ is that they take them as protectors instead of Allah, namely the angels, the Messiah, and the devils, as objects of worship. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Do they suppose that this will benefit them?" It has been read as "afaḥsab" with the sīn sukūn, and its meaning is: "Is it sufficient for them and does it reckon for them, that they take them as protectors?" This is taken as a subject and predicate. It means that this is not sufficient for them nor beneficial for them with Allah as they supposed. ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a nuzul (lodging)﴾. That is, We have made it ready for them as a nuzul in which they enjoy themselves upon their arrival.

Al-Zajjaj said: the nuzul is the dwelling and the abode. It has also been said that it is what is prepared for a guest, so it is sarcasm toward them, like His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 21]. The meaning is that Hell is prepared for them with Us as a guest is prepared for a visitor.

﴿Say: Shall We inform you of those most losing in their deeds?﴾ "A'māl" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). The plural indicates the intention of kinds of them.

The place of the relative clause, which is ﴿those whose effort was lost in the life of this world﴾, is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it was said: "Who are they?" and it was answered: "They are those whose effort was lost." The meaning of "the loss of effort" is its nullification and its wasting. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative position, as a dispraise.

The answer will be: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord﴾. It is also permissible that it be in the genitive position, as an adjective of "those most losing" or as a substitute for it, and the answer then is also "Those" and what follows. The first of these possibilities is the most preferable.

The clause ﴿while they think that they are doing good work﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "ḍalla" (was lost), meaning: and their state is that they suppose they are doing good in that, benefiting from its effects.

The clause ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, presented to complete the loss and explain its cause. This is according to the first, preferred view, not the other views, since those are the answer as we have stated. The meaning of their disbelief in the signs of their Lord is their disbelief in the evidences of His Oneness, from the cosmic and the revealed signs. The meaning of their disbelief in His meeting is their disbelief in the Resurrection and what follows it of the matters of the Hereafter. Then He ordered upon this His saying: ﴿So their deeds are nullified﴾, i.e., the deeds they did which they supposed to be good, and this is loss and error. Then He judged against them with His saying: ﴿So We will not assign for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾, meaning they will have no value with Us and We will not regard them. It has also been said: no scale will be set up for them by which their deeds are weighed, because that happens only for the people of good and evil deeds among the monotheists, and these have no good deeds.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: the Arabs say, "Fulān has no weight with us," meaning no value, because of his baseness, and a man is described as having no weight because of his lightness, his quick rashness, and his lack of steadiness.

The meaning according to this is that they will not be considered, and they will have no value or rank with Allah. Mujahid read "yuqīmu" with the yā' (third person), meaning "Allah will not establish," and the rest read it with the nūn.

Then the Exalted explained the outcome of these people and what their affair will come to, and said: ﴿That﴾, i.e., what We have mentioned of the kinds of threat, is their recompense. The reason for this is that they combined with disbelief the taking of the signs of Allah and His messengers in mockery. So the "bā'" in ﴿because they disbelieved﴾ is causal. The meaning of their being a mockery is that they are ridiculed.

The early scholars differed in identifying these most losing in deeds. It was said: the Jews and the Christians. It was said: the disbelievers of Makkah. It was said: the Khawarij (Ḥarūriyya, the early Kharijite dissenters). It was said: the monks, the people of the cloisters. The more preferable approach is to apply the verse generally to everyone who is characterized by those described attributes.

Then, after this threat to these disbelievers, the Exalted mentioned the promise to the believers, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, i.e., they combined both, so that they were the opposite of the description of those before them. Al-Mubarrad said: "Firdaws," as far as I have heard from Arabic speech, is a dense growth of trees, most of which are grapevines.

The meaning: the fruits of the Garden of Firdaws were for them as a prepared lodging, emphasizing their honour. "Abiding therein" (khālidīna fīhā) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. Likewise the clause ﴿they will not desire any change from it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Ali that he read "afaḥsbu alladhīna kafarū" (with the sīn sukūn). Abu 'Ubayda said: with the sīn jazm and the bā' with ḍamma.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ikrima that he read it in the same way.

It is said: "the people surged" (māja al-nās) when some of them enter into others, bewildered, like the surge of water. The meaning is that they will be agitated and will mix with one another. It has also been said that the pronoun in "some of them" refers to all creation, and the day is the Day of Resurrection, meaning: We will make some of creation, from among the jinn and mankind, surge against others. It has also been said that the meaning is: We will leave Gog and Magog on the day (p-878) when the barrier is complete and its construction is perfected, some of them surging against others. The explanation of "And the Trumpet will be blown" has already been given in al-An'am. It has been said that this is the second blast, based on His saying afterwards: ﴿Then We will gather them in a gathering﴾, since the particle "fa" (then) indicates this. The first blast is not mentioned because the purpose here is to mention the conditions of the Resurrection.

The meaning: We will gather the creatures after their bodies have dissolved and turned to dust, in a complete gathering, in the most perfect description, the most wondrous form, and the most marvellous manner.

﴿And We will present Hell that day to the disbelievers, a presentation﴾. The meaning of "presentation" here is exposure, i.e., We will expose Hell to them so that they witness it on the day of Our gathering them. In this there is a great warning to the disbelievers, because of the terror and dread that will befall them when they see it.

Then He described the aforementioned disbelievers with His saying: ﴿Those whose eyes were under a covering from My remembrance﴾. That is, their eyes in the world were under a covering, which is that which covers a thing and conceals it from all sides. "From My remembrance" means from the cause of My remembrance, which is the signs that one who reflects and takes heed sees, so that he remembers Allah with monotheism and glorification. Thus the effect is attributed to the cause. Or it means from the Great Qur'an, and from contemplating its meanings and reflecting on its benefits.

Then, when He, the Exalted, described them as blind to the cosmic signs or the revealed signs, or both, He wished to describe them as deaf to hearing the truth, so He said: ﴿and they were unable to hear﴾. That is, they are unable to listen to what contains the truth from the speech of Allah and the speech of His Messenger. This is more eloquent than if He had said "and they were deaf," because the deaf may be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these have no ability at all. In the mention of the covering of the eyes and the inability to hear there is an image of their blindness to sight-based witnessing and their turning away from the evidences of hearing.

﴿Do those who disbelieve think﴾. Here "ḥusbān" means "ẓann" (supposition). The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the "fa" is for coordination with an implied preceding element, like its parallels.

The meaning: Did they suppose that they would benefit from what they worshipped, while turning away from reflecting on the signs of Allah and rebelling against accepting the truth? The meaning of ﴿that they take My servants as protectors besides Me﴾ is that they take them as protectors instead of Allah, namely the angels, the Messiah, and the devils, as objects of worship. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Do they suppose that this will benefit them?" It has been read as "afaḥsab" with the sīn sukūn, and its meaning is: "Is it sufficient for them and does it reckon for them, that they take them as protectors?" This is taken as a subject and predicate. It means that this is not sufficient for them nor beneficial for them with Allah as they supposed. ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a nuzul (lodging)﴾. That is, We have made it ready for them as a nuzul in which they enjoy themselves upon their arrival.

Al-Zajjaj said: the nuzul is the dwelling and the abode. It has also been said that it is what is prepared for a guest, so it is sarcasm toward them, like His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 21]. The meaning is that Hell is prepared for them with Us as a guest is prepared for a visitor.

﴿Say: Shall We inform you of those most losing in their deeds?﴾ "A'māl" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). The plural indicates the intention of kinds of them.

The place of the relative clause, which is ﴿those whose effort was lost in the life of this world﴾, is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it was said: "Who are they?" and it was answered: "They are those whose effort was lost." The meaning of "the loss of effort" is its nullification and its wasting. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative position, as a dispraise.

The answer will be: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord﴾. It is also permissible that it be in the genitive position, as an adjective of "those most losing" or as a substitute for it, and the answer then is also "Those" and what follows. The first of these possibilities is the most preferable.

The clause ﴿while they think that they are doing good work﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "ḍalla" (was lost), meaning: and their state is that they suppose they are doing good in that, benefiting from its effects.

The clause ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, presented to complete the loss and explain its cause. This is according to the first, preferred view, not the other views, since those are the answer as we have stated. The meaning of their disbelief in the signs of their Lord is their disbelief in the evidences of His Oneness, from the cosmic and the revealed signs. The meaning of their disbelief in His meeting is their disbelief in the Resurrection and what follows it of the matters of the Hereafter. Then He ordered upon this His saying: ﴿So their deeds are nullified﴾, i.e., the deeds they did which they supposed to be good, and this is loss and error. Then He judged against them with His saying: ﴿So We will not assign for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾, meaning they will have no value with Us and We will not regard them. It has also been said: no scale will be set up for them by which their deeds are weighed, because that happens only for the people of good and evil deeds among the monotheists, and these have no good deeds.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: the Arabs say, "Fulān has no weight with us," meaning no value, because of his baseness, and a man is described as having no weight because of his lightness, his quick rashness, and his lack of steadiness.

The meaning according to this is that they will not be considered, and they will have no value or rank with Allah. Mujahid read "yuqīmu" with the yā' (third person), meaning "Allah will not establish," and the rest read it with the nūn.

Then the Exalted explained the outcome of these people and what their affair will come to, and said: ﴿That﴾, i.e., what We have mentioned of the kinds of threat, is their recompense. The reason for this is that they combined with disbelief the taking of the signs of Allah and His messengers in mockery. So the "bā'" in ﴿because they disbelieved﴾ is causal. The meaning of their being a mockery is that they are ridiculed.

It was said: the Khawarij (Ḥarūriyya, the early Kharijite dissenters). It was said: the monks, the people of the cloisters. The more preferable approach is to apply the verse generally to everyone who is characterized by those described attributes.

Likewise the clause ﴿they will not desire any change from it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the chain of Harun ibn 'Antara, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We will leave some of them﴾, the verse. He said: the jinn and mankind will surge, some of them against others.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿they were unable to hear﴾. He said: they were unable to understand hearing.

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Ali that he read "afaḥsbu alladhīna kafarū" (with the sīn sukūn). Abu 'Ubayda said: with the sīn jazm and the bā' with ḍamma.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'Ikrima that he read it in the same way.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through the chain of Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, who said: I asked my father about ﴿Say: Shall We inform you of those most losing in their deeds?﴾ "Are they the Ḥarūriyya?" Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: it is the vineyard in the Nabataean language. Ibn Abi Shayba, Hannad, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith that Ibn 'Abbas asked Ka'b about Firdaws, and he said: "It is the gardens of grapevines in the Syriac language."

And Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿They will not desire any change from it﴾, that he said: "a place of transfer."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 18, verses 109–110:**

When Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the various kinds of proofs, He drew attention to the perfection of the Qur'an, so He said: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: Ink (midad) is so called because it supplies (yumidd) the writer, and its root meaning is increase and the coming of one thing after another. The oil with which a lamp is lit is also called midad. The word "sea" here refers to the genus (jins).

The meaning is: If the words of Allah's knowledge and wisdom were written, and it were supposed that the entire genus of the sea were ink for them, the sea would be exhausted before the words were exhausted. And even if We brought the like of the sea as ink, it would also be exhausted. It has also been said, in explaining the meaning: If the sea were ink for the pen, and the pen were writing, ﴿the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted﴾. His words ﴿and even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ are a statement from Him, glory be to Him, not included under His words "Say: If...", and it contains added emphasis and affirmation. The "wa" (and) joins what follows to an implied clause indicated by what precedes it, meaning: the sea would be exhausted before His words were exhausted, even if it did not come with the like of it as a supplement, and even if We brought the like of it as a supplement. Madad means increase.

It has also been said that by "words" (kalimat) He means the eternal speech, which has no end or limit. Although it is one, it is permissible to express it with the plural form because of the many benefits it contains, and the Arabs have used the plural form to express the singular. Al-A'sha said:

*"And a face clear of color, pure, adorned, with the neck, there are lubbat (chest-hollows) for it and wrists."*

Here he used lubbat (plural) to mean lubbah (singular, the hollow of the chest).

Al-Jubba'i said: His words ﴿before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾ indicate that His words are exhaustible in general, and whatever is established as non-existent cannot be eternal.

It was answered that the intended meaning is the expressions that indicate the objects related to that eternal attribute. It was also said in reply: The exhaustion of one thing before the exhaustion of another does not indicate the exhaustion of the other thing, nor its non-exhaustion. Therefore the verse conveys only the abundance of Allah's words, beyond what human minds can grasp. As for whether they are finite or infinite, there is no proof of that in the verse.

The truth is that Allah's words follow His known objects, and those are infinite; therefore His words are infinite.

Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read ﴿even if We brought the like of it as midad﴾, and it is so in the Codex of Ubayy. The rest read madadan. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿before it is exhausted﴾ with the yā' (third person masculine, yanfada), and the rest read it with the tā' (second/third feminine, tanfada).

(p-880) Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to adopt the way of humility, so He said: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you﴾. That is: my condition is restricted to humanity and does not go beyond it to angelhood. Whoever is like this does not claim to encompass the words of Allah. However, he is distinguished from them by the revelation that comes to him from Allah, glory be to Him, so He said: ﴿It is revealed to me﴾. This attribute alone is sufficient to distinguish him from all other kinds of humans. Then He explained that what is revealed to him is His words: ﴿that your God is one God﴾, having no partner in His divinity. In this there is guidance toward monotheism (tawhid). Then He commanded them to righteous action and monotheism, so He said: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾. Raja' (hope) is the expectation of the attainment of good in the future. The meaning is: whoever has this hope, which is the condition of the believers, ﴿let him do righteous deeds﴾, which is what the Shari'ah has indicated to be an act of good for which its doer is rewarded, ﴿and let him not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ from among His creation, whether he be righteous or wicked, animate or inanimate. Al-Mawardi said: All the people of interpretation (ta'wil) said in explaining this verse that the meaning is: he should not show off with his deed to anyone.

I say: The entry of the manifest shirk, which the polytheists used to commit, under this verse is primary over the entry of the hidden shirk, which is showing off (riya'). There is no obstacle to the entry of this hidden shirk under it. The only obstacle is to its being the intended meaning of this verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿for the words of my Lord﴾: he said: "the knowledge of my Lord." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning the verse, he said: it means: the water of the sea would be exhausted before the speech of Allah and His wisdom would be exhausted. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-iman transmitted from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾, the verse, he said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists who worshipped another god alongside Allah, and it is not about the believers.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn Abbas who said: "A man said: O Prophet of Allah, I stand in positions seeking the face of Allah, and I love that my station be seen. He did not answer him with anything until this verse was revealed: ﴿and let him not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾."

Ibn Mandah, Abu Nu'aym in al-Sahabah, and Ibn Asakir transmitted through the chain of al-Suddi al-Saghir, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Jundub ibn Zuhayr, when he prayed, fasted or gave charity and was mentioned with goodness, was pleased by it, so he increased in that for the people's talk, and Allah did not intend it. So this verse was revealed concerning that: ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, I free a slave and I love that it be seen, and I give charity and I love that it be seen. So the verse was revealed: ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾, the verse." This report is mursal (its chain lacks a companion).

Hannad also transmitted it in al-Zuhd from him as well.

Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-iman transmitted from Abu Sa'id ibn Abi Fadalah al-Ansari, who was among the Companions: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: When Allah gathers the first and the last for a Day about which there is no doubt, a caller will call out: Whoever associated anyone with Allah in a deed he did for Allah, let him seek its reward from other than Allah, for Allah is the most independent of partners from partnership."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Hurayrah that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, a man fights in the way of Allah while seeking a gain of worldly goods?" He said: "He has no reward." The people found that great, so the man came back and said: "He has no reward." (The narration is as stated.)

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Ikhlas, Ibn Jarir in his Tahdhib, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Shaddad ibn Aws who said: "In the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we used to count showing off (riya') as the minor shirk."

Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted, also from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Whoever prays to be seen has committed shirk, whoever fasts to be seen has committed shirk, and whoever gives charity to be seen has committed shirk." Then he recited: ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾, the verse.

Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym transmitted, also from Shaddad, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: Allah says: I am the best partner for whoever associates someone with Me. Whoever associates anything with Me, then his deed, both little and much, belongs to his partner whom he associated with Me. I am free of him."

Ahmad, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir in his Tahdhib, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of what I fear for you more than the al-Masikh (the Dajjal)? It is the hidden shirk: that a man stands praying for the position of a man."

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Shaddad ibn Aws: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: I fear for my Ummah shirk and hidden desire. I said: Will your Ummah commit shirk after you? He said: Yes. Indeed, they will not worship the sun, the moon, a stone, or an idol, but they will show off to the people with their deeds. I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the hidden desire? He said: One of them wakes up fasting, then a desire from his desires presents itself to him, so he abandons his fast and indulges in his desire."

Ahmad, Muslim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), from his Lord that He said: "I am the best of partners. Whoever does a deed in which he associates other than Me, I am free of it, and it belongs to the one he associated." And in another wording: "Whoever associates anyone with Me, it belongs entirely to him."

There are many hadiths on this subject warning against showing off, and that it is the minor shirk, and that Allah does not accept it. The author of al-Durr al-Manthur has compiled them in this place, so let one refer to it. However, they do not indicate that it is the intended meaning of the verse. Rather, manifest shirk enters under it primarily. And even if the cause of revelation was showing off, as what we have mentioned indicates, the consideration is by the generality of the wording, not by the specific cause, as is established in the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

There has also been transmitted, specifically concerning the virtues of this verse, what al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hakim, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If nothing had been revealed to my Ummah except the ending of Surat al-Kahf, it would have sufficed them."

Ibn Rahawayh, al-Bazzar, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, al-Shirazi in al-Alqab, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites in a night: ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾, the verse, will have a light from Aden Abyan to Mecca, filled by the angels." Ibn Kathir said after transmitting it: "Very strange indeed."

(p-881) Ibn al-Duraysi transmitted from Abu al-Darda', who said: Whoever memorizes the ending of al-Kahf will have a light on the Day of Resurrection from his neck to his foot.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan that he recited this verse: ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾, and said: It is the last verse revealed of the Qur'an.

Ibn Kathir said: This report is problematic, for this verse is the ending of Surat al-Kahf, and al-Kahf in its entirety is Meccan. Perhaps Mu'awiyah meant that nothing came after it that abrogates it or changes its ruling; rather, it is established and definitive (muhkam). So this was confused for some of the narrators, and he transmitted it by meaning according to what he understood.
